OF

DON ANDRÉS BELLO

[PDF 2]

Santiago, September 5, 1872.

Whereas the National Congress has discussed and approved the following

B I L L O F L AW

A rt . 1.º In recompense for the services rendered to the country by Mr. Don Andrés Bello as writer, professor and codifier, Congress decrees the sum of fifteen thousand pesos, to be entered in thirds in the corresponding budgets, so that a complete edition of his unpublished and published works may be made.

A rt . 2.º The University shall appoint one or two commissioners to come to an understanding with those of the family of the illustrious author, in order to proceed to the edition of the said works, making the contracts with the printers, obtaining against receipts the funds that may be decreed, expending them and answering for their expenditure.

A rt . 3.º The edition shall be of no fewer than two thousand copies, and of these five hundred shall be delivered to the State, which may not sell them for less than two pesos a volume. The remainder of the edition shall belong to the respective heirs.

A rt . 4.º The text of this law shall be printed on the reverse of the first page of each volume.

And whereas, the Council of State having been heard, I have approved and sanctioned it; therefore let it be promulgated and carried into effect as a law of the republic.

Federico Errázuriz.

Abdón Cifuentes.

V olume I

PHILOSOPHY OF THE UNDERSTANDING

SANTIAGO DE CHILE

PRINTED BY PEDRO G. RAMÍREZ

1881

[PDF 4]

There is in this century a fact that saddens the soul by its far-reaching and disastrous consequences. This fact, universally observed and resisted by generous minds, is the growth of indifference in matters of philosophy and of religion.

In Europe, England, Germany and France, three great centers of human activity, are so especially of philosophical activity; Italy can present names as illustrious as Rosmini, D’Azeglio, Gioberti and Galluppi; and Spain is honored by Balmes and Donoso Cortés. Nevertheless, the school of Thomas Reid, Adam Smith and Dugald Stewart has fallen into skepticism, and the positivist school now flourishes in Great Britain. In Germany, the great philosophical movement owed to Kant has ended in the Hegelian school, divided between materialism and skepticism. In France, in spite of the efforts of the spiritualist school of Jouffroy, Victor Cousin and Damiron, skepticism, materialism and the positivist school are making great progress. Yet able metaphysicians have revived the glorious traditions of the great Catholic school, [PDF 5] which has known how to preserve the titles of truth concerning God, the human soul and the universe. And the Institut de France has crowned works such as those of Nourrisson, intended to make known the importance of the philosophy of the Fathers of the Church and that of the Middle Ages, so unjustly judged by ignorance or bad faith: there is, then, in Europe, against the deleterious influence of positivism and skepticism, a wholesome current of sound principles and of true philosophy.

Among us a youth wholly unacquainted with philosophical studies and influenced by the evil doctrines of the Old World turns materialist on a whim, or declares itself positivist because that doctrine is more in harmony with the skeptical state of its mind and with that fever for comfort and material progress which afflicts modern societies. These baneful doctrines advance without reaction or counterweight, through the little love there is for eternal truth and the almost complete want of judgment and of criterion to distinguish the true from the false.

From the foregoing observations the importance of the publication of the “Philosophy of the Understanding” will be readily understood: the work of a man who for more than a quarter of a century exercised among us the magistracy of letters; the second work that Chilean literature has produced which can justly bear the title of Philosophy. The influence that the “Philosophy of the Understanding” is bound to exert, not only through the authority of Mr. Bello but also through its own intrinsic merit, moves us to offer, as a guide to the reader, a few brief observations, since we cannot undertake the detailed analysis of a work in which the most fundamental questions of Philosophy are treated, and in which he has condensed [PDF 6] abundant doctrine, the labor of many years and the profound thought of an indisputable talent.

Mr. Bello proposed to write a text-book that should serve for the course in the subject at the National Institute; but the study which he made of the various philosophical subjects carried him too far, and he wrote a masterly work, by the importance of the questions it proposes and the profundity with which it treats them.

He divides Philosophy into Philosophy of the Understanding, which comprises Mental Psychology and Logic, and Moral Philosophy, which is composed of Moral Psychology and Ethics. Only the first has he left written: the Philosophy of the Understanding, that is, Mental Psychology and Logic.

Mr. Bello shows himself well acquainted with the modern philosophers, with whom he often discusses the great philosophical questions. And although the influence which the English philosophers and Kant have exercised upon his mind is evident, nevertheless the independence of his thought leads him in many cases to dissent from their opinions and to give solutions so new that they strike even himself: “When I feel myself obliged,” he says, “to separate from the opinion of so many eminent philosophers, I cannot but distrust myself, however powerful the reasons that militate in my favor may appear to me. I must say, nevertheless, that the more I meditate on the subject, the more I am persuaded that the writers to whom I allude have adopted without sufficient examination the doctrines of the schools.”

The most important part of the Philosophy of the Understanding is Mental Psychology. In effect, rarely has a more powerful and penetrating glance been directed to the phenomena of consciousness; rarely has a more profound and delicate analysis been made [PDF 7] of sensation and of the perception of relations; and rarely, finally, have an intelligence more richly nourished and more free from prejudice, so good a will and so pure a love of the truth, been applied to the arduous metaphysical questions.

Nevertheless,   we     believe        that      the        Philosophy   of   the Understanding ought not to be read without some corrective. Mr. Bello has paid, like the greater part of philosophers, his tribute to the weakness of human reason. The restricted sense in which he has taken Philosophy, since, according to him, it is “the knowledge of the human mind and the right direction of its acts,” has obliged him to confine Metaphysics within the narrow limits of Mental Psychology and Logic, to no small detriment of the method, of the clearness, and even of the importance of so noble an object.

The incomplete method and the sensationalist definitions adopted by Mr. Bello ought to have led him to sensationalism and even to materialism; but his powerful mind succeeds at times in freeing itself from the iron circle in which he has methodically enclosed it, and takes the daring flight to the lofty region of final causes with such energy, showing such life, vigor and grandeur, that we know not what to admire more, the strength of the mind or the audacity of wishing to confine it within limits so narrow.

In consequence of the deficient method and of the sensationalist or skeptical definitions and principles, he fails to recognize the idea of the infinite, gives a false notion of eternity, of cause, of substance, and distorts several other metaphysical notions and principles. We wish to dwell only upon the two notions which seem to us the most momentous, the notion of cause and that of substance. The notion of cause, according to him, is that of constant succession, and that of substance is that of [PDF 8] permanence. These two notions, which give rise to the two most fruitful principles of our knowledge, having been falsified, he has fallen into errors of considerable gravity.

Cause is a force, a principle which reveals itself by its effects. Between the effect and the cause there is a relation of generation. A phenomenon which begins reveals to us a generating or producing principle. On occasion of a new fact reason rises beyond the fact to perceive the force, the energy, which produces what is attested by experience. “The idea of cause,” says Rattier, “is not reduced to that of succession. When it is said that fire is the cause of the fluid state of wax, it is not understood merely that the phenomenon of fluidity follows upon the phenomenon of the approach of the fire, but that there is in the fire a property, a force, a power to which we refer the production of the phenomenon of fluidity.”

Our soul manifests itself to us at every instant as the source, as the type of every idea of cause. It gives us the true idea of causality in the varied productions of the intelligence: when by its own energy and fecundity it unfolds itself and in a certain manner reproduces itself in each of its innumerable thoughts; when, these being manifested by speech, it pours forth in torrents the light in science, or the charm, the beauty and the life in the transports of poetry; when it attracts and draws after it the multitudes electrified by manly and sublime eloquence; and when it occupies the whole earth with the marvelous productions of art, scattering everywhere pleasure and well-being. We perceive the idea of cause in the phenomena of voluntary activity, in the effusions of love, in the efforts of virtue, in the struggle of the soul agitated by a strong passion; in those efforts [PDF 9] constantly renewed we see a multiplied production, a true causality. Reason, after having perceived in a primitive fact of consciousness the relation of causality, raises it spontaneously to the character of an absolute law of the intelligence and of things.

This, which seems to us so evident, has been misunderstood by Mr. Bello. He maintains that the notion of cause is that of constant succession; that when we seek a cause, we do not seek a being which contains in a virtual and eminent manner the new phenomenon, but an antecedent phenomenon with which the second is necessarily connected. He does not see, then, in the admirable order of the world that prodigious concatenation of causes and effects, but, like Leibniz, a certain pre-established harmony by means of the necessary connections of phenomena among themselves. But as the necessity of these connections cannot be found in contingent things, they suppose a prior cause which has willed and ordained them, whose connection with the effects which it produces is of absolute necessity. Hence it is that we are obliged to admit that Infinite Intelligence which orders all that is created.

Now, if the principle of causality is no other than that of constant succession, founded on the necessary connection of every new phenomenon with a preceding one, a grave difficulty presents itself: how is it to be reconciled with free causes, chiefly with that first volition which in the production of the universe has been sovereignly spontaneous and free? Mr. Bello cuts the knot and says: “This volition is an effect without a cause that determined it in every respect; an exception to the principle of causality [PDF 10] And this exception once admitted, it is evident that the principle of causality, in the sense in which it is generally taken, is not necessary with an absolute necessity, and that if it is subject to one exception, it may be equally so to others. In short, it is not a universal principle. . . . . .

“The principle of causality is the work of God, it is one of the laws established by God. . . . . .

“The empirical principle and the principle of causality are two laws destined to act in a different manner in brute and inert beings, and in intelligent and free beings; necessary each in its own sphere but not necessary with an absolute necessity.”

We regret not to follow the philosopher in the interesting and sagacious discussion of this principle, in that intelligent and noble struggle in which, grasping certain unshaken truths, he strives to stay himself on the slippery slope which leads him to the abyss.

In effect, Mr. Bello, as if giddy at the sight of the chasm, has recourse to the first cause to save the principle of causality, and his soul, profoundly religious, after setting forth with all possible force and novelty the arguments for the existence of God, takes pleasure in showing His principal attributes and in presenting Him as pouring out with profusion life and happiness upon the infinite scale of created beings.

“God,” he says, “is the adorable name of the first cause, necessary with an absolute necessity, immense, eternal, sovereignly free, creative, infinite in intelligence, in power, in all His attributes. . . . . . Supreme Intelligence is not only the principle of order but the type of the perfection of order; and since justice, veracity and beneficence constitute the very essence of the [PDF 11] moral order, whose laws the Creator has stamped upon the conscience and upon the heart of man, it is necessary that the Principle of order be absolutely just, veracious and beneficent.

“Contemplating the emanations of the supreme source of being, we recognize at once that the Supreme Being takes pleasure in pouring out life and happiness.

“He pours out life profusely in the air, on the earth, in the waters; but, however incalculable be the number of living creatures that everywhere present themselves to the sight, what is that compared with the thousands of millions that people the microscopic world? And even that is nothing. The same profusion of life exists without doubt in all the planets which form the world of which our sun is the center; and in all the worlds of the stupendous number of suns that people space.

“The beneficent providence with which He attends to the well-being and happiness of so many living creatures is shown at once in the correlation of the necessities of life with the means which He has given to all for satisfying them. And He has not united animal pleasure and happiness to this satisfaction alone, but to desire as a principle of activity, which for living creatures is of itself a pleasure, and to hope, which is the anticipation, the perfume, so to say, of happiness.

“And what shall we say of the intense, of the exquisite pleasures of the intelligence, of the imagination, of the moral affections?”

Thus far Mr. Bello.

This is a page worthy of Malebranche or of Fénelon. Nevertheless, without the principle of causality it is only a concatenation of sonorous phrases, void of meaning. In truth, if reason demands a first cause of being, [PDF 12] a supremely intelligent orderer, a principle of order, and an author of life and of happiness, it is only by virtue of the metaphysical value, of the absolute necessity of the principle by which it clearly perceives that there can be no effect without a cause. Its absolute universality once denied, a single exception once admitted, it is no longer possible to ascend to the First Cause. Being, order, motion, life and intelligence may be effects without a cause; there is no intrinsic repugnance in admitting it. Moreover, absolute necessity once denied, the principle does not exist, because to demonstrate its truth it is necessary, as Mr. Bello has done, to fall into a vicious circle, proving the truth of the principle by the will of God, and the existence of God by the truth of the principle.

The error concerning the notion of substance is of no less moment.

Some modern philosophers reject the opinion of the ancients, who considered substance as something to which qualities are added, and maintain that these are only diverse aspects under which being is perceived. These two opinions differ little, and both agree in considering substance as a being, a permanent subject in which are verified the changes which these phenomena present to us.

The notion of substance, which includes that of entity, that of the relation of the permanent to the variable, and that of the subject of the variations not inherent in another, engenders in our mind the absolute principle of immediate evidence: the modes of being suppose being, or, what is the same thing, there can be no modes without a modified substance.

Mr. Bello does not say expressly what it is that [PDF 13] he understands by substance; but from his conclusions concerning the substantiality of the self and of matter it is inferred that he does not admit the true notion of it.

Mr. Cousin, distinguishing in the self the modes of the substance, maintains that we perceive immediately the modes and not the substance itself. Mr. Bello combats him and says that this is a philosophical error caused by the influence which abstract names exert upon our mind, and concludes that we perceive intuitively the substantial self. And further on he says: “Properly we perceive no other substance than that of the individual self, and this serves us as a type to represent to ourselves that which by an instinctive and irresistible analogy we attribute to other intelligent and sentient beings.”

And as to the substance of bodies, we can affirm nothing else than “that there exist outside of us causes of sensation.” “But this power which causes sensation exists in something real. Shall we imagine this real identity in what we call matter? Or shall we place it in the Great Spirit, creator and preserver?” Upon this we can affirm nothing, and its investigation is of very little importance.

“The theory of Berkeley,” he says, “may be admitted as a possible supposition in the eyes of Philosophy. There is in reality no repugnance between the anti-material theory and the principle of substantiality, which makes it necessary to conceive in every action an agent, in every accidental quality a substance, in every influence a real being that influences. The causes of sensations have variable characters; they present themselves to us under different modifications. These modifications exist without doubt in them. If material causes are nothing more than mere influences of [PDF 14] the divine energy, the modes of material causes are modes of acting of the divine energy and exist therefore originally in the divine substance, under the forms of general laws.”

“Substantiality being taken away from matter, the physical universe is a great void peopled with vain appearances in nothing different from a dream; but if it be admitted that this long dream is in all its parts consistent with itself and that all sentient beings dream it at the same time, it matters little that it be so called.”

According to this, the sun, the moon and that prodigious number of immense masses which revolve in the celestial spaces, are nothing more than groups of divine influences; and all the beings that people this so fruitful earth, our country, our families and our friends, are so many other groups of the same influences; and divine influences in collision, the contentions of men and their great armies in bloody war: the inconsolable husband who weeps the death of his beautiful and chaste companion, weeps an illusion: the tender mother who presses to her bosom the beloved child, embraces an illusion. And God, who has given us a constant and invincible propensity to believe in the existence of bodies, is the universal deceiver of these feeble minds.

Our reason deceives us, which tells us that the qualities, causes of our sensations, must be attached to a substance which serves them as a subject; that this substance must keep congruity with those qualities, because the modes of the entity must be of the same nature as itself, that is, that there cannot exist in one and the same being modifications which destroy one another or which are repugnant to its essence.

[PDF 15]

Now then, if the constant and invincible propensity given by God to believe in the existence of bodies, and our reason, which makes us perceive substance by means of qualities, deceive us, the inevitable consequence is skepticism. Mr. Bello ought to have admitted it; but this time also his faith, his religious spirit, have saved him in spite of an inconsistency.

“But,” he says, “although the theory of Berkeley might in strictness be admitted as a possible supposition in the eyes of Philosophy, it is incontestable that it is opposed to some of the most essential dogmas of Catholicism and of almost all the Christian Churches.”

The futility of this argument is easily understood against a theory of which Hume, who denied with Berkeley the existence of bodies, could say: “I dine, I play a game of back-gammon, I converse, and am merry with my friends; and when after two or three hours’ amusement, I would return to these speculations, they appear so cold, and strained, and ridiculous, that I cannot find in my heart to enter into them any farther. Here then I find myself absolutely and necessarily determined to live, and talk, and act like other people in the common affairs of life.”

Mr. Bello’s errors concerning the substantiality of matter arise: 1st, from maintaining that consciousness, perceiving the unity and permanence of our soul, intuits the substantial self, and that this is the only substance perceived; 2nd, that the qualities of bodies, causes of our sensations, may be modes of the divine substance; and 3rd, that the propensity to admit the substantiality of bodies and the judgment of reason which makes us perceive the individual substance as the subject to which [PDF 16] these qualities adhere, are not legitimate grounds of judging.

Mr. Bello’s Logic is only an incomplete treatise on method. In this part the author, knowing the importance of principles for giving solidity to any method whatever, has admitted as necessary with an absolute necessity the principle of contradiction, that of sufficient reason, that of causality and that of substance. This would amount to a retractation of what he has maintained in the Psychology; but as he attributes the same character to the principle of induction or the empirical principle, it is evident that he does not give its true metaphysical value to absolute necessity.

In expounding his doctrine on judgment, the proposition, reasoning, and the Aristotelian syllogism, he frequently dissents from the doctrine of the Schoolmen, and almost always with little foundation. Nevertheless, we believe that this part of Mr. Bello’s Philosophy will be read with profit; and that it has great interest by the much study which it reveals, by the sagacity of its observations, and by the varied knowledge which the author has set down in it.

Finally, it seems to us that the Philosophy of the Understanding ought to figure among the principal works of the illustrious writer, and that, in spite of the defects we have noted, by its importance, and in its kind, it is the first that has been published in Chile and even in all America.

Would that the reading of this work might elevate so many young intelligences of our country subject to the cui bono, and stimulate them to the cultivation of the noblest of the human sciences.

THE EDITOR.

October 1881.

[PDF 17]

## INTRODUCTION

I

Notion and division of Philosophy.—Mental Psychology and Logic, or Philosophy of the Understanding.—Moral Psychology and Ethics, or Moral Philosophy.—II The human mind is the true object of Philosophy: its proper notion.—III Faculty and act: they are phenomena of consciousness.—Unity and identity of the soul in the variety of its acts.—General division of the mental faculties: those of the understanding and those of the will.

## PHILOSOPHY

The object of Philosophy is the knowledge of the human mind and the right direction of its acts.

Our mind is known to us only through the affections it undergoes and the acts it performs. Of its inmost nature we know nothing.

These affections and acts are of two kinds. By the one sort it knows, investigates truth, and assures itself that it possesses it. By the other it wills, desires happiness, and strives to attain and retain it.

## PHILOS.   1

[p. 2]

Every affection, every act, supposes a special power or faculty: if we feel, we can feel; if we judge, we have the faculty of judging. The soul has, accordingly, powers or faculties of two classes: by the one we know; by the other we desire. The aggregate of the former is called mind, understanding, intelligence: the aggregate of the latter, will.

Philosophy, in so far as its object is to know the faculties and operations of the understanding, is called Mental or Intellectual Psychology, and in so far as it gives rules for the right direction of these faculties and operations, is named Logic. In so far as its object is to know the faculties and acts of the will, it is called Moral Psychology; and finally, in so far as it gives rules for the right direction of our voluntary acts, we give it the name of Ethics.

Mental Psychology and Logic compose the Philosophy of the Understanding; Moral Psychology and Ethics, Moral Philosophy. (a)

(a) Metaphysics, or the science of first truths, which is in part Ontology (the science of

being, or of the most general qualities of whatever exists), comprising Pneumatology (which treats of spirits) and Theodicy (which inquires by means of reason into the existence and attributes of the Divinity), will not form special sections in this book. The matters I have just enumerated are closely connected with Mental Psychology and Logic, because the analysis of our intellectual acts gives us the foundation and the first expression of all those notions, and because the theory of judgment and of reasoning leads us naturally to the knowledge of the principles or first truths which serve as a guide to the understanding in the investigation of all other truths. I have therefore scattered Metaphysics through Mental Psychology and Logic, and have given in the form of an Appendix what seemed to me less intimately bound up with the science of the human understanding.

[p. 3]

## MENTAL PSYCHOLOGY

II

The human mind is a being that has consciousness of its acts, and that can to a certain extent determine them at its pleasure. What it is that distinguishes it from other beings of the same nature, that is, endowed with consciousness and will, is a question insoluble for us. Everything of which we have consciousness exists in the mind, or, properly speaking, is the mind itself, acting or suffering in a certain particular manner at a given instant. Of what does not actually pass in the mind, we have not, nor can we have, consciousness.

When, according to the common manner of speaking, we feel pain in some part of our body, that pain of which we have consciousness exists in the mind, and is the mind itself experiencing a particular modification and perceiving it in itself immediately and directly. It is true that this spiritual modification is accompanied by certain phenomena confined to the body and especially to the nervous system; phenomena which may consist in certain mechanical, physical, chemical, electrical changes, or of whatever kind one pleases. But these phenomena we do not perceive immediately, we have no consciousness of them, nor do we come to know them until much later, and even then imperfectly, by means of investigations and observations which we carry out with sight, touch and the other senses, whose agency we employ in studying material things in the only way possible to us, which, as we shall presently see, is indirect and symbolic.

We use the words mind and soul as synonyms. We designate [p. 4] with them our I, our own mind, and the human mind in general, to which we attribute by analogy the nature and qualities of our own.

III

Faculty and act are correlative words, which explain one another.

Every action or passion of the soul, every action which it exerts upon itself or upon another being, and every affection produced in it by an action of itself or of another being, is an act of the soul. Nor let it seem strange that we call that an act in the soul which is often the effect of an action of its own or of another’s; for in the modifications of our mind that seem most passive there is always something active which distinguishes them from the absolute inertia of matter.

We are not always conscious of each of the acts of the soul, because many of them are so fleeting and rapid that it is not possible for us to notice them. But at least it is consciousness that originally gives us the knowledge of all the different kinds of acts of which our soul is susceptible, and it is not rational to admit the reality of any kind of spiritual acts of which we have never had consciousness.

Faculty is nothing else than the possibility of performing an act; and we have accordingly as many different intellectual faculties as there are various kinds of acts of which the human mind is capable. The nature of a faculty lies wholly in the nature of the act, because the possibility of the act is all that constitutes the faculty.

We must not conceive the spiritual faculties as different particular organs of the soul; for in each of them and in each of its acts the whole soul is present, the I. The soul that feels is the very soul that remembers, that judges, that reasons, that desires, that fears, that loves, that hates, and, however [p. 5] attentively it contemplates itself, it is not possible for it to refer its various modifications to different portions or localities of itself. Consciousness testifies to us in the clearest manner the simplicity or indivisibility of the soul and its constant identity with itself in all its acts.

To classify rightly the different spiritual faculties it would be necessary first to know them; but for the present we can only presuppose the most obvious and most generally known division; we refer to the understanding the faculties which we use to examine objects and investigate truth, that is, what really passes in our soul or outside of it; and we attribute to the will certain acts by means of which we direct ourselves toward the objects that serve for our well-being or pleasure, or withdraw from the objects that cause us uneasiness or pain.

Entering, then, upon the examination of the faculties of the understanding, we shall begin with that which we most continually exercise and which intervenes in the exercise of all the others.

[PDF 22]

On perception.

I. General idea of perception.—Elements of which it consists.—Knowledge of external objects.—Sensation.—Material being.—Qualities of matter: they appear in the soul only as sensations.—The verb estar always denotes every quality or state of a body.—Sensation is an act exclusively proper to the soul. —Actual and renewed sensations.—The organic impression: it must not be confounded with sensation.—Reference of the soul to an extraneous cause. —The impression is the proximate cause of sensation.—Perception is a judgment: it is intuitive or sensitive.—II. Notion of consciousness.—Intuitive perception, or perception of consciousness.—Characters of intuitive judgment. —Sensitive perception: its primary element is the organic impression.— Sensation follows, then intuition and the reference or judgment.—The action of the external object.—Internal and external sensitive perception.— Consciousness is not the inner sense.—Grounds of the foregoing division.— Intuition is one of the inseparable elements of perception.—Vulgar prejudice which attributes to the organs the faculty of feeling.—Objective reality which the soul gives to sensations.—Philosophy can do nothing about the knowledge of matter in itself.—Observation on the essential unity of the mind.—Memory.—Recollection.—Fancy.—Ideas.—Knowledge.

I

Perception is, in general, an act in which the soul acquires the knowledge of a certain quality or particular state of an object, by virtue of a certain action which the object actually exerts upon it. We do not attempt to define perception, but only to point it out, or to show the circumstances in which this faculty is realized.

[p. 7]

We have to note in perception the subject that perceives, that is, the soul; the particular object perceived, which may be the percipient soul itself, or something distinct from it; the particular action which the object exerts upon the soul, and which corresponds to a particular quality or state of the object; and, finally, the actuality of that action, that is, its existence at the very moment of the perception.

Between the actions of objects upon the soul and the qualities of objects there is the same correlation as between the acts and the faculties of the soul or of any agent whatever. Just as every act supposes in the agent the faculty or power of developing it, so each of the various particular actions of an object upon the soul supposes in it a particular quality, which is truly nothing else than the power or faculty of developing that action. Objects make themselves known to us by their qualities, or in other terms, by the different actions that correspond to those qualities and in which those qualities are developed.

Everything that is capable of producing sensation is called material being or matter. Let it be noted also that of a material being which is known to us by a single sense (as the pink, so long as it is known to us only by its smell) we could have only an entirely obscure and elementary knowledge. But when other sensations come afterwards to join the first, all referring themselves to the same being, there results from this union a complex object, which is the better known to us the greater the number of elementary sensations of which it has been the cause. This aggregate of sensations by means of which we know a complex object forms a complex idea.

Let us take, for example, the perception of the smell of a pink. The soul, the I, is the subject that perceives. The smell of the pink is the object perceived. The smell of the pink exerts upon the nose a particular action which is transmitted by the nerves to the brain and by means of the brain affects the soul in a particular manner, in an indefinable manner, but one which we distinguish from all the other affections of which the soul is susceptible. This affection, contemplated by consciousness, constitutes the perception [p. 8] of an action and of a particular quality, to which the name of smell has been given. The action in which that quality is actually developed coexists with the perception; and what remains or revives afterwards of this perception in the soul, when the action of the smell has ceased for a longer or shorter time, is no longer actual perception, but renewed perception, recollection, idea.

But the soul, consciousness, the I, does not directly perceive the smell of the pink; what it directly perceives is a particular modification of itself, which for it has no relation to any being distinct from itself. In what manner this modification of its own is converted into a cognition, into a perception of a certain quality of an object distinct from it; in what manner the absolute passes into the relative, the subjective into the objective, we shall endeavor to explain farther on. For the present we shall observe that when a certain particular modification is actually produced in the soul by the action of a material being, to which we in consequence attribute a quality, we give to that modification of the soul the name of sensation.

To take another example: the soul perceives that particular affection which we call fatigue. The soul is the subject that perceives the fatigue, that is, that state in which our body or some one of our members finds itself in consequence, for example, of prolonged or violent exercise: that particular state is the object perceived, because it produces, by means of the nerves and the brain, a particular affection in the soul; an affection which is also sensation, and which, contemplated by consciousness, constitutes a perception of that corporeal state which we call fatigue. So long as that spiritual affection coexists with the corporeal state that produces it, we have an actual perception; when the latter ends, what remains or revives afterwards of the said affection in the soul is a renewed perception, a recollection, an idea.

Sensation, as is seen in these two examples, is the modification produced in the soul by a material agent. But there is a difference between these two cases. The smell of the pink acts upon the soul through the intermediary of the organism; whereas [p. 9] in the perception of fatigue it is the organism itself which by a state of its own produces the modification of the soul; in the first case, the material agent to which we attribute a quality acts mediately upon the soul; in the second, the material agent, the organism to which we attribute a state, acts upon the soul immediately. But in neither the one case nor the other is the quality or state an object directly perceived by consciousness; what consciousness directly perceives is the sensation; which is thus converted into a perception or knowledge of a certain material quality or state.

Both the sensation produced by the organism and the sensation produced by an extraneous material being symbolize qualities: we indicate one and the same quality by saying a withered rose and by saying that rose is withered. But there is a difference: the first expression simply symbolizes the quality; the second says something more; it denotes that the quality in question is one of those which succeed one another in the object and present it under various forms. Each of these forms is what is called a state; such are, for example, in the living body hunger, thirst, pain, etc., and in inanimate bodies the being cold or hot to the touch. The Castilian verb estar is applied with perfect propriety to this indication, which generally does not suit the verb ser: such has been the origin of the word estado [state].

It is evident that in the two preceding examples, together with the indirect perception of a material quality or state, that is, of the smell or of the fatigue, there is the immediate and direct perception of an act which, although produced by the organism or by an external body acting upon it, belongs neither to the external body nor to the organism, but to the soul: this act is the sensation. The soul perceives the sensation in itself in the same manner as it perceives in itself its judgments, desires, volitions and various other modifications of its own which are not sensations, since they are not due to the actual excitation of an external body or of our own organism.

Sensations, as has been said, may be actual or renewed, and we cannot fail to recognize that between the one kind and the [p. 10] other there is generally a great resemblance, together with a great difference in force and vividness, which is commonly much greater in the former.

The modification which takes place by any means in the nervous system, the brain included, and which we regard as the proximate cause of the sensation, because we know no intermediate agency between it and the sensation, is usually called organic impression. Impression is a word that admits of two meanings in our language, one active and the other passive: thus, when we stamp a seal on wax, we may understand by impression either the impulse of the seal or the stamp which the wax receives. But in the language I have proposed to adopt, it has seemed to me convenient to avoid this ambiguity of meaning: what I call organic impression is analogous only to the stamp; it signifies the modification effected in the organ by any cause, known or unknown, not the action of this cause upon it.

It is necessary not to confound, as is commonly done, the sensation with the organic impression which produces it. We ought to regard them as two things entirely distinct and separate. The first belongs essentially to the soul, the second to matter. The soul perceives in its own being intuitively, that is, immediately and directly, the sensation, and refers it to the organic impression as to its proximate cause, representing or symbolizing this cause by means of the sensation and conceiving as many differences and varieties in the organ as it perceives in the sensation. What alterations take place in the organs when we feel weariness, sleepiness, hunger, thirst, or any other of those states which we cannot conceive except in living bodies, are things which we do not know by the testimony of consciousness, but by observations and deductions in which sight, touch, smell, or any other of the perceptive faculties that we call external senses intervenes, by whose agency we know the material qualities which we attribute to any kind of corporeal thing, living or destitute of life, such as color, sound, smell, softness or hardness, motion, weight, etc.

[p. 11]

When the soul refers the sensation to a remote cause, that is, to an external body which acts upon the organism, it does not perceive the qualities or states of the remote cause either, except in so far as it perceives differences in the sensation. It distinguishes neither smell from sound, nor the smell of the pink from that of the rose, nor the color of gold from the color of silver, nor the sound of the violin from the sound of the flute, except in so far as it distinguishes from one another the sensations which, by means of the organism which these qualities impress, take place in it.

The proximate cause of every sensation is an organic impression, whether or not we know the material agency from which this proceeds, and which constitutes the remote cause of the sensation.

The very reference which we make of the sensation to its proximate or remote cause is not an immediate perception of consciousness, is not a mere intuitive perception; it is a judgment subsequently formed; and this judgment is what, added to the sensation and to the intuition of the sensation, truly constitutes the perception of an organic state or of any material quality whatever.

From what has been said it follows that we have two general classes of perceptions: the intuitive, by means of which we know what actually passes in our own soul, and the sensitive or representative, in which, by the agency of sensation, we represent to ourselves the qualities and states of extraneous material substances or the qualities or states of the organism.

And from what has been said it is inferred that in every sensitive or representative perception an intuition or intuitive perception necessarily intervenes.

II

We know, then, what passes in our soul by means of the soul itself, which sees, contemplates itself, se ipsa intuitur [it beholds itself]; or, to use another expression, which has consciousness of what passes in it, conscia sibi est [it is conscious to itself]. Thus, [p. 12] consciousness may signify either the faculty or the act: a double sense which is shared by several other words that refer to the soul, such as perception, memory, imagination, thought. (a)

In the perceptions of consciousness, however simple they may appear to us, two elements are distinguished without difficulty. First, the soul acts upon itself: a modification of its own produces in it a new modification, which consists in this, that the soul sees, contemplates the original modification. This kind of contemplation is properly an intuition. But this new modification, this intuition, is not the whole perception of consciousness. The soul refers the modification perceived, the modification-object, to its own being, to the I, regarding the I as the subject of it, and as one and the same thing with it; and from these elements, intuition and reference of the intuition, the perception of consciousness is formed, the intuitive perception.

Whenever the soul conceives and affirms a relation, we say that it forms a judgment: the reference is a judgment: the soul, in intuitive perception, conceives and affirms the relation of identity of the object with the subject, of the I that experiences a modification with the I that has intuition of it. A judgment enters, then, as a necessary element into every intuitive perception.

In intuitive perception consciousness presents itself to us under two aspects: passive, in so far as it contemplates the modification-object and in a certain manner reflects it; active, in so far as it conceives and affirms a relation of identity between the being that experiences the modification-object and the being in whom resides the consciousness that reflects it.

III

Let us pass to the sensitive perceptions; let us analyze them; let us separate in these phenomena what constitutes them essentially,

(a) In the English language a distinction is made: conscience is the faculty, con‐

sciousness is the act. [p. 13] what belongs properly to the soul, from the corporeal actions which precede or accompany them.

Every sensitive perception supposes a peculiar modification of some organ, an organic impression; and many perceptions of this class suppose, besides the organ impressed, an external corporeal cause which produces the impression.

Thus, when we feel pain, there is ordinarily some part of our body to which we refer it, without its being necessary for that purpose that an external agent should present itself to us at the same time, acting on that part, and, by impressing it, give birth in our mind to the sensation of pain, which we refer to this impression as to its proximate cause; a sensation which, intuited by our mind, constitutes the perception of the pain, and represents to us by the varieties of the sensation the various modes and degrees of the pain. It is not necessary, then, in this kind of perceptions to refer them to a remote cause, whether because none presents itself to us, or because we leave out of account one which does in fact present itself.

In the perceptions of which we speak there is, then, primarily and essentially an organic impression, which is a material element; in the second place, a particular sensation which corresponds by a law of nature to the organic impression; in the third place, an intuition of the sensation, and in the fourth, a reference of the sensation to the organ impressed. This reference is a judgment in which the soul conceives and affirms a relation of causality between the organic impression and the sensation.

Of the four phenomena enumerated, the first, as we have said, belongs to our body; the other three take place in the soul; and as in one of them the soul intuits a sensation, it is evident that in this kind of sensitive perceptions an intuitive perception always enters as a necessary element. Sensation, too, is necessary in them, and for that reason I qualify them as sensitive perceptions; whereas in intuitive perceptions generally considered sensation is an accidental object, because not only the sensation [p. 14] but any other modification of the soul, e.g., a desire, can be an object of consciousness.

But in sensitive perception it happens many times that the organic impression is manifestly produced by some corporeal agent which actually acts upon the organ. We should not see, for example, if visible objects did not impress the organ of sight, that is, the eyes, the retina, the nerves that run from the retina to the brain, and the brain itself. We know only in a most imperfect manner the nature of the impressions which this organic apparatus receives from objects, and which, carried to the cerebral extremity, produce consecutively in the soul various sensations. We do not know at all how it happens that the modifications of the organic apparatus excite the sensations. The fact, nevertheless, is indubitable: a ligature, a strong compression, a paralysis in any of the parts which compose this apparatus, would disturb the corresponding perceptions and might perhaps deprive us of them forever.

Consequently, in sensitive perceptions of this second kind there is one phenomenon more than in the former, the action of a corporeal agent which produces the organic impression and is the remote cause of the sensation: the five essential phenomena which take place in these sensitive perceptions are, then, first, a corporeal agency upon an organ; second, an organic impression; third, a particular sensation which corresponds to the organic impression; fourth, consciousness of the sensation; and fifth, reference of the sensation to its remote cause. The first two phenomena belong to our body; the other three to the mind which animates it. In this second kind of perceptions sensation is no less a necessary element than in the first, and we have therefore two classes of sensitive perceptions: the one which refer the sensation to its proximate cause, and the other which refer it to its remote cause. The first we shall call internal sensitive perceptions, because their objects are not only confined to our own body, but symbolize qualities or states of the organism, which cannot [p. 15] exist or be conceived except in some animated body, such as hunger, sleepiness, weariness, and all the pleasures or pains which we refer to the organs. And we shall give the name of external sensitive perceptions to the second, because they refer themselves to their remote cause, which is ordinarily a corporeal agent distinct from our own body. It happens indeed that the remote cause is sometimes found in one part of our body which impresses another part of it; e.g., a hand on the head. But in this case our hand exerts upon the head the same kind of action as any extraneous body, and we should not see in this action a mode of being proper to a living body, but a mode of being of those which belong indifferently to living bodies and to those which are not so: as color, tactility, extension, motion, etc.

Sensitive perceptions, internal as well as external, present an infinite variety: each kind of sensation corresponds to a special perceptive faculty which is called sense. Thus in external sensitive perceptions we have the five senses called external: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, which are distinguished from one another by the respective organs impressed, namely, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the tongue and palate, and the outer surface of our body; and we may add to these five external senses some other, as we shall see hereafter. Internal sensitive perceptions likewise present an innumerable variety of kinds; but it would be difficult to make in them a classification of internal senses sufficiently distinct and complete; and even for those which we can distinguish we lack adequate names, and can only designate them by compound denominations, such as sense of hunger, sense of sleep, sense of voluntary motion, etc.

To sum up: perceptions are all divided into intuitive or of consciousness, characterized by the relation of identity between the percipient subject and the object perceived, which is the soul itself; and sensitive or representative perceptions, in which the object perceived is a material quality or state [p. 16] represented by a sensation, and the reference to this object consists in a relation of causality in which the quality or state is the cause and the sensation the effect. Sensitive perceptions are divided in their turn into internal and external: in the former the object is an organic impression, and the modification perceived is consequently one of those which, as has been said before, cannot exist or be perceived except in the very body which we animate: in the latter, on the contrary, the modification perceived is a quality or state of which living bodies and those which are not so are equally susceptible.

External sensitive perceptions always accede to internal sensitive perceptions, because they always suppose an organ impressed; but it is not always when we perceive organic impressions that we perceive a corporeal agent which excites them.

There is no perception in which consciousness does not intervene, nor sensitive perception in which there is not a sensation that symbolizes a corporeal quality or state.

It is proper to observe that the direct perceptions of consciousness, in which the percipient subject and the object perceived are identified, do not form a particular sense, as seems to be implied by the denomination of inner sense which is generally given to consciousness, because sense and sensation are correlative words, and in intuitive perceptions there is no representation or symbolization of any object by means of sensation, inasmuch as the object is the soul itself directly perceived by the soul. Any sensation whatever, like any other of the modifications of our mind, may be directly perceived by consciousness, and so it happens, as we have said, in all sensitive perceptions; but so long as we do not convert this sensation into a symbol of a corporeal quality or state, the perception is merely intuitive. The denomination, then, of inner sense given to consciousness is opposed to the basis of the classification which it has seemed to us convenient to adopt.

To set in its full light our division of the perceptions, [p. 17] we shall observe that one and the same sensation may be the object of an intuitive perception, and the symbol of a corporeal quality or state, as happens in every sensitive perception, internal or external. In general, when at the same time that we experience a sensation the remote cause from which it results manifests itself, we refer the sensation to the remote cause, and the sensitive perception is external. But nothing prevents our referring that same sensation to the organ impressed. In this manner an identical sensation may serve as the symbol of two sensitive perceptions, one external and the other internal, according to the signification we give it.

For example: there is a spontaneous buzzing of the ears which is very like the buzzing of certain insects. When we judge it spontaneous, we refer it to the organ. If we saw the insect flying at a little distance, the reference would at once change, we should perceive in the buzzing an action, a quality of the insect, and the sensitive perception would pass from internal to external.

But even when a manifest agent produces the impression in the organ, who forbids us, leaving out of account the external agency, to regard the sensation as a sign of the organic effect? The sensitive perception will then be internal or external, as we choose. The sensation which a red body produces in the soul may signify either the red color or the impression produced by this color in the organic apparatus that serves the sense of sight: all will depend on the reference.

In any case, and in every kind of sensitive perceptions, it is necessary that before regarding the sensation as the symbol of a thing distinct from the soul, we regard it as an actual modification of the soul and have an intuitive perception of it. Without this intuitive perception we can have no perception of any kind. It is true that the various elements of perception seem to us to form an indivisible whole, and we cannot perceive the least interval between them; but their essential difference is not on that account less manifest.

We shall observe also that to feel, in the signification of experiencing sensations, is proper and peculiar to the soul. The senses have, then, their seat in the soul, they are the soul itself

## PHILOS.   2

[p. 18]

applied to corporeal objects, and we must reject the vulgar prejudice which confounds them with the organs by means of which they are exercised. It is the soul properly that sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches. It, and not the body, is that which feels fatigue, sleepiness, hunger, etc. The organs are mere instruments of perception. To say that the eyes see is to speak metaphorically; it is, as Reid observes, like saying that a telescope sees. The hand touches as one inanimate body touches another; to touch, in the sense of perceiving by touch, is proper and peculiar to the soul.

The signification which the soul gives to sensations, making them representative of what is not itself; the conversion of the subjective into the objective, is one of the principal keys of the theory of the understanding. If in internal sensitive perceptions sensibility and consciousness itself seem to us diffused over all the organs; if we believe that we feel and live in them, whereas the seat of the perceptions and of all the modifications of which the soul has consciousness can be no other than the soul itself, the I; in external sensitive perceptions the soul clothes bodies with the rich and variegated livery of its sensations, and does not know and distinguish them except in so far as it knows and distinguishes the sensations of which it composes their forms, colors and other qualities. Thus what we believe we perceive in a direct manner in our organs and in inanimate bodies is nothing more than our own soul, diversely modified. The perceptions of consciousness are the only direct, intuitive ones; those of the internal and external senses are symbolic and representative.

When we say that we know sensible things by means of our own sensations, serving ourselves of these as of signs or symbols which stand in the soul in the place of those things, these words must be understood literally. The olive is a symbol of peace; but we know peace by means independent of the symbol. It is not so in sensitive perception. We do not know the various modifications of our organs and the various corporeal qualities except in so far as we know the various sensations proximately or remotely produced by them.

We might indeed, by means of external sensitive perceptions, study and know to a certain extent the structure [p. 19] of our organs and the physical, chemical, or other alterations which they undergo, when the soul experiences certain affections which it refers to them as to their proximate cause; for example, when it feels pain in one of them. This is the study to which the physiologist and the physician particularly devote themselves, and which is carried on by means of external sensitive perceptions. But what do we attain with the aid of these? Only the knowledge of qualities which we know only by the sensations that symbolize them. The same applies obviously to external sensitive perceptions. If we wish to inquire, for example, what alterations take place in the sonorous body when it impresses the auditory apparatus which produces the sensation of sound, we find that it experiences more or less rapid vibrations which we know only by means of sight and touch, and which are not accessible to consciousness except by means of visual and tactile sensations that symbolize their remote cause.

This is the definitive result of all study of matter. What matter and material qualities are in themselves, and not merely as causes of sensations, we do not know, nor is this knowledge accessible to the mental faculties with which we are endowed.

The modifications which the soul reveals to itself are commonly regarded as qualities which successively and continually superpose themselves upon a substance or support which is as it were the ground of the soul. But we must be on our guard against the fascinations exercised over us by the metaphorical words of which we of necessity avail ourselves to help us to conceive this mysterious evolution of spiritual phenomena. The soul is wholly and entirely, according to what we have said before, in each one of its acts, and it is necessary to reconcile with the apparent differences which consciousness shows us in the soul the identity and the indivisible unity of which we have constantly an indispensable intuition.

The soul has the faculty of renewing perceptions. This faculty is called Memory. When perceptions are renewed in the same order in which we have experienced them, memory has more properly this name, and its acts are called [p. 20] recollections. When this order is altered and we combine renewed perceptions which originally have not been together in the soul, memory is called Imagination, Fancy. If I represent to myself the rose on the bush that produces it and on whose branches I have seen it, I exercise memory properly so called: if I represent to myself a myrtle that bears roses, or a flower that I have not seen, in which I combine the form of the lily with the color of the rose, I exercise imagination. But imaginations, fancies, no less than the representations of memory proper, are always composed of renewed perceptions.

Perceptions renewed by simple memory or by imagination are called ideas. Idea signifies image; renewed perceptions have been called images of actual perceptions by reason of the resemblance which they truly bear to them.

Ideas which are accompanied by the sure judgment of the reality of objects are called cognitions.

[PDF 37]

On intuitive perceptions and on consciousness.

I. General notion of intuitive perception.—Examination of the objection of Thomas Brown.—The soul is susceptible of experiencing innumerable affections at one and the same time.—Objection which regards consciousness as memory.—II. By intuition the soul perceives itself identical.—Unity and continuity of the soul.—III. Notion of the substantial I.—Doctrine of Mr. Cousin.

I

That the soul has the faculty of perceiving what passes in it is a thing so obvious that it seems impossible it should ever have been put in doubt. Without this faculty, how could Psychology, the science of the soul, ever have existed? And not this science alone, but no other, nor language itself, could have existed. It is of absolute necessity to perceive our thoughts in order to express them. (a)

There has not been wanting, however, here and there a philosopher who has peremptorily denied the existence of intuitive perceptions and of consciousness; and none has assailed so vigorously the almost universal opinion which recognizes it, as the profound and sagacious Thomas Brown, successor of Dugald Stewart in one of the chairs of philosophy in the University of Edinburgh.

(a) Consciousness in its general psychological acceptation is not to be confound‐

ed with moral consciousness (conscience), which judges of the rectitude or depravity of our voluntary acts.

[p. 22]

Spiritual phenomena are not, according to him, objects of consciousness, but consciousness itself; and to regard it as a distinct faculty is to duplicate it without necessity. But are not the experiencing of a sensation, for example, and the perceiving that we experience it, evidently different things? Might not the soul rejoice or grieve, hope or fear, without contemplating itself in these various modifications? Even if that were impossible to it, the two acts ought to appear to us inseparable, not identical.

If the soul feels, and at the same time perceives that it feels, says Brown, it is necessary to admit that it may be found at one and the same time in two different states, that of sensation and that of consciousness; which, according to him, is a manifest absurdity.

But the truth is that the human soul may experience, not only two, but innumerable affections and modifications at one and the same time. This multitude of contemporaneous spiritual states is a frequent fact, or, to speak more properly, a continual one. Probably only one of them will fix the attention vividly at a given instant; but the others will not on that account cease to exist at that same instant. A few most familiar observations will suffice to demonstrate it.

If, an object being present to the soul, it were necessary that it should disappear from it to give place to another object, how should we perceive their resemblance, their difference, or any relation whatever between them? How would the understanding have engendered the ideas of order, symmetry, harmony, rhythm? Every comparison supposes two or more simultaneous perceptions, whether the objects actually strike the soul, or memory makes them revive. (b)

Absorbed in a profound meditation we walk over

(b) Brown himself, a few lines after having laid down that to suppose the soul in two

different and simultaneous states is an absurdity, acknowledges that in the comparison of two diverse sensations, as that of the odor of a rose and that of the sound of a flute, the soul considers the two at one and the same time, and moreover refers them to itself as subject. See the XIth of his Lectures on the Philosophy of the Human Mind. [p. 23] a field which we have often traversed and in which all the objects are perfectly familiar to us. So slight will be the notice, so feeble the sensations which the soul then receives of them, that perhaps we shall not be able afterwards to recall them by renewing them, and yet it is incontestable that we perceive them without distracting ourselves for a moment from the matter on which thought is exercised and which seems to absorb it. The mere direction of our steps supposes, on the one hand, the perceptions of a thousand small accidents of the ground, and on the other an infinity of volitions, which produce in our body the movements necessary to avoid stumbling or falling. And all these perceptions and volitions arise, and coexist, and succeed one another, without disturbing or suspending the dominant thought. Let us suppose that in place of the crag or the trunk which we have seen many times and to which we now pay no heed, a strange shape, a corpse, were to present itself to our eyes. The new object would disperse, would deaden all the other ideas present; it would take possession of the soul. And why does the strange move us in this manner, and the familiar not? Doubtless because in the midst of our meditation we perceive the one and the other, and distinguish between the familiar and the strange. Unless we say that strange things, by a kind of inconceivable magic, cut the thread of our thoughts before being perceived, before the soul receives the first notice of them.

Why, when we wish to think attentively upon something, do we complain of the noises that disturb the attention, scatter it, distract it? The distraction which they cause supposes that their perceptions coexist, if only for an instant, with the thought that occupies us and on which we desire to fix ourselves.

If it were true that the soul could not be in two different states at one time, we should have the readiest and the most efficacious of all anodynes in our own thought. Afflicted with a pain, it would suffice to think of something else in order to cease to feel it. Or rather, if that doctrine were true, the object that interested us most, or that produced in our organs the strongest impressions, would not [p. 24] have power to dislodge from the mind the feeblest and most frivolous idea that might at the moment occupy it, nor would it find access to the soul, save by waiting, watching, so to speak, for an interstice between two successive modifications in order to slip in and wound it.

The general prepossession of the impossibility of two simultaneous spiritual states proceeds from supposing that we can attend to one thing only, and that the state or modification to which we attend reduces all the others to a complete nullity. Both suppositions are erroneous. Comparison is a multiplied attention; and the ideas attended to dominate, but do not extinguish the others; unless in that abnormal state which we call ecstasy, rapture, a state in which certain recollections and fancies take possession of the whole soul, and render it insensible even to the most powerful organic impressions.

An elegant contemporary writer pretends that the faculty called consciousness or inner sense is nothing else than memory. We know, according to him, not what passes but what has passed in the soul; we do not perceive it actually, but recollect it. But what is the recollection which the soul makes of a state or modification of its being, but this same state or modification renewed with more or less vividness? and if the soul can perceive its renewed modifications, why not its original modifications, while they exist? Will it be said that, in recollecting, we do not renew but perceive directly the former modification? This would be to acknowledge a retrospective consciousness far more difficult to conceive than the intuitive consciousness which is exercised upon present modifications.

In reality, that the soul has the power of knowing what passes in it, is a thing on which all are substantially agreed. Whether this knowledge consists in an intuition coexisting with its object, or in a retrospective intuition; whether it constitutes a necessary complement, an essential part of all spiritual phenomena, or, although associated with all of them, ought to be referred to a distinct faculty, sui generis, is what the difference reduces itself to. The gravest error of those who reject consciousness [p. 25] as an intuitive, distinct faculty, lies in believing all the acts and modifications of the soul to be necessarily successive, so that at each instant one only occupies it exclusively.

There are vivid, attentive perceptions, and weak, fugitive ones. Of the latter there is an incalculable number at every moment.

Consciousness perceives itself. I am conscious of a sensation is not, as Brown pretends, a tautological proposition signifying the same as this other: I have a sensation. The second supposes only the consciousness of the sensation; the first requires something more, the consciousness of the consciousness.

But this second consciousness, it will be said, must in its turn produce a third, from which a fourth will successively arise, and so on indefinitely. It is to be believed, however, that in this successive reproduction the force of the intuition rapidly weakens until it vanishes altogether.

Intuition is not a sensation, nor consciousness a sense. To admit the slightest analogy between consciousness and the senses would be to justify those who have sought to ridicule it by comparing it to the eye that strives to look at itself, or to the madman who leans out of the window to see himself pass along the street. Thus the title of inner sense commonly given to it is, as has been said before, a mere metaphor.

The existence of intuition is evident; its nature, inscrutable; like the nature of sensation and of all the other elementary modifications of the soul.

II

The simplest form of perception is that in which the soul perceives itself: subject and object at once.

In intuitive perceptions the soul not only perceives its own modifications, but perceives them as its own. It perceives, then, a relation of identity between the soul that is affected in a certain manner, and the soul that perceives itself to be so affected; between [p. 26] the soul, for example, that feels or desires, and the soul that perceives that feeling or desire.

This relation of identity is a simple idea. It seems at first sight that a relation can never be a simple conception, because in perceiving it between two objects we perceive at the least three things, the objects compared and the relation between them. But the perceptions of the objects which are compared are not parts of the relation, but its necessary antecedent. When the soul perceives itself identical, it certainly perceives two terms which are identified: but the perceptions of these two terms are the matter on which the relation turns, not elements of it.

The soul perceives itself identical, not only by perceiving a given affection as its own, but by perceiving itself as the subject of the whole series of its affections which it recollects. In this relation of identity spread over the whole vast chain of its recollections, it perceives the continuity of its being.

The soul perceives itself in its intuitions, not only as identical and continuous, but as one; it is not possible for it to refer a certain affection to one part of its being, and a certain affection to another part. We are not able to regard the soul as a substance divided into several departments, to each of which a certain kind of affections corresponds; and even when diverse modifications or affections coexist at one time in the soul, it is impossible for us to place them in distinct parts of one and the same substance. The soul is not for our consciousness an aggregate of distinct parts, but a single, simple, indivisible whole.

Thus consciousness is that which gives the primitive type of the relations of identity, continuity and unity; a type which we afterwards employ as a sign, to represent to ourselves all that we call identical, continuous and one.

[p. 27]

## III

In earliest infancy we learn to employ with perfect propriety the word I, which belongs to all languages, and whose right use manifestly involves the idea of a being identical, continuous, one, perceived by consciousness; identity, continuity, unity, which the child, guided by an irresistible analogy, afterwards attributes to the thou, to every man, to every living creature.

The soul, regarding itself as identical, continuous and one under all its simultaneous and successive modifications, places all these modifications in itself, as in something that serves them for seat and support; otherwise it could not consider them as its own. From which it is inferred that it perceives this something intuitively, and that the intuitive perception of its modifications, far from giving us a posteriori the notion of the substantial I, involves it, as a necessary element of itself.

But it is said: the relation which we conceive between a modification of the I and the I as substance or subject, has something that distinguishes it from all other relative notions. We do not conceive resemblance except by comparing two things which we know separately; we do not judge that a portrait is like its original except because we know the original and the portrait separately; we do not judge that two and two are four, except because we know separately the aggregate 2 + 2 and the aggregate 4; nor does it seem to us that fire produces heat except because we see the fire and on approaching it feel heat. But it is not so in the relation of identity which we perceive between a modification of the soul and the soul itself. The one being given, we not only suppose the other, but cannot do otherwise than suppose it; and this without our having had any previous notion of the I as substance or subject, because we can have no other than this very conception in which we regard the soul as the basis or seat of the modification. In all other respects the substantial I remains wrapped in a profound obscurity.

“In the judgment in which the I is revealed to us,” says Mr. Cousin [p. 28] “there are two things, the modification and the substance; and the first gives us immediately the second: a prodigious logic, for ordinarily in order to perceive a relation we need two terms, whereas, in the present case, the term which we see gives us that which we do not see and the relation which unites them.”

This doctrine presents, in my judgment, insoluble difficulties. The modifications are nothing else than the substance itself modified. To perceive the one and not to perceive the other is absolutely impossible.

The error of those who have believed that we perceive the modifications and not the substance, proceeds from the prestige which abstract names exercise over us; a prestige from which so many erroneous conceptions arose in the philosophical schools of the ancients, and of which, even after the triumph of the Nominalists, not a few vestiges are preserved. We speak of the modifications and of the substance as of real things superposed upon another real thing; in the way that garments which cover a body are put upon it; an absurd conception, though glossed over with specious language.

The soul forms with all its modifications a single, indivisible, identical object; without thereby ceasing to perceive differences among its various modifications, because there is no incompatibility between the different and the identical.

The identity, the continuity, the unity of the I are not perceived in the modifications, they are perceived in the soul itself. The modifications are not identical, continuous, one; identity, continuity, unity belong to the soul; they cannot be separated from the soul, save by the aid of those fantastic images which are associated with abstract names and to which we involuntarily give a reality which they have not.

But what! it will perhaps be said: do we not perceive the modifications of matter without perceiving in any way the substance in which they reside? We answer that we never perceive directly the modifications of matter; we perceive them only representatively by means of the sensations which it produces in the soul.

“Nothing is clearer, it is said, than the objects of consciousness; [p. 29] and the idea of substance is most obscure. How, then, shall it be acquired by consciousness? We know nothing of substance: its nature is entirely hidden from us. If any one knows substance, let him describe it; if it is not given to him to describe it, let him confess that it cannot be the object of an immediate perception.”

Thus reasons the illustrious head of the eclectic school. But do we, by chance, know the nature of any thing whatever, even of those which consciousness contemplates? It is not given to us to describe sensation, and yet we shall not on that account say that sensation is not an immediate object of intuitive perception.

We perceive, then, intuitively our own soul, although it is neither possible for us to describe it, nor do we know its nature save so far as the phenomena which consciousness attests extend.

[PDF 46]

On external sensitive perceptions.

I. Elements comprised in external action.—The organic impression is little known.—Sensation exists exclusively in the soul.—Reference, or objective judgment, is the capital question in Philosophy.—Difference in external perceptions: some are plesioscopic and others aposcopic.—Cognitions that come from touch and sight.—Influence of the connection of sensations on judgment or objective reference.—II. Primary perceptions and suggested perceptions.—III. Law of objective reference in plesioscopic perceptions.— Correspondence of visual sensations with tactile qualities by means of the experience of suggested judgments.—Relation of the picture on the retina to the work of the painter.—Excellence of tactile geometry.—Its gradual exercise by means of the analogical procedure.—Relation of what precedes to the phenomenon of vision.—Plesioscopic perceptions: taste and smell are referred to them.—Excellence of the sense of touch.—Its relation to the other senses.—Tactile affections determine every representation of the external world.

We have seen that the phenomenon of sensitive external perception (which for brevity we shall hereafter call external perception) is preceded by two physical phenomena: the action of a material substance upon the organ, and the organic impression. We have likewise seen that external perception is essentially composed of three phenomena which pass in our mind: the sensation which arises in it in consequence of the organic impression; the intuitive perception of the sensation, and the reference which we make of the sensation to a material being that is acting at the moment upon the organ; a reference in which we symbolize with the sensation a quality of this being.
