We must, [p. 31] then, recognize five distinct and successive elements in the phenomenon of sensitive external perception: the first two belong to matter, the other three to the mind.

External action may at times be negative. The absence or diminution of a stimulus which acts almost continuously, as light, or whose varying intensity is capable of producing sensations now agreeable, now painful, as happens in the unknown cause that produces the sensation of heat, becomes the object of distinct and vivid perceptions. We perceive, then, positively, darkness, cold, silence. In all languages there are signs that represent this kind of negative causes; and what is more, some of them, darkness, for instance, and cold, have long been considered as material substances. God divided the light from the darkness, says the author of Genesis, accommodating himself to the vulgar understanding.

Of the nature of organic impressions we know nothing thoroughly. Is there in the nerves a fluid to which each action of a corporeal substance imparts a particular movement? Or do they consist of fibres which the impressions cause to vibrate in one way or another? Or do the actions that affect them diversely modify their chemical constitution? These questions belong rather to physiology than to the science of the understanding; and even if we could resolve them satisfactorily, the difficulty would not on that account cease to stand entire, which consists in explaining how sensation arises in the soul in consequence of the modification, whatever it may be, that takes place in the nerves and in the brain.

All that we know is that corporeal causes impress the nerves and the brain in various ways, and that to each variety of impression in this organic apparatus there corresponds a peculiar sensation in the soul.

Sensations, perceptions, as we have already said, exist exclusively in the soul. If the eyes saw and the nose smelled, there would be nothing more in common between my perceptions of colors and my perceptions of odors, than between the perceptions of Peter and the perceptions of John. We are irresistibly moved to believe that it is one and the same substance which in us [p. 32] sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches; that which feels pleasure or pain, aversion or desire; that which compares and judges; that which perceives itself; and this substance is the soul.

The total effect which a body produces in us, and by means of which we arrive at the knowledge of its qualities, that is, of the various actions which it exerts upon us, embraces, then, two kinds of phenomena absolutely distinct; the one consist in the mechanical, chemical, electrical, or any other kind of changes which the action of the perceived object produces, mediately or immediately, in the organ; the others comprise the modifications of which we are conscious, and by means of which we distinguish from one another the objects that affect us. Not by the movements, or by the addition or subtraction of molecules, that take place in the nerves and in the brain, but by the affections of which we are conscious, by the sensations, do we distinguish fire from snow, white from black, hard from soft.

The substance in which these affections are produced and which exercises the acts of consciousness that advises us of them, is the soul.

Nothing in common between the world of consciousness and the world of the senses. The first is wholly within the subject: perfect unity, absolute indivisibility, are the characters it presents to us. The second, which is known to us only by the sensations that symbolize it, and by perceptions that transform, so to say, the subject into object, has for attributes multiplicity, extension.

Reference is that which converts the subjective into the objective; it is the bridge over the abyss that lies between consciousness and the external universe: an important element, which has attracted attention from the earliest age of Philosophy, and a battle-field among the different schools. We shall explore its origin, its development, and the laws to which it is subject. For the present we can take only a few steps in this investigation; but we shall return to it from time to time, as our observations furnish us with means for carrying it forward.

Comparing the various external perceptions with one another, we shall find [p. 33] in them a notable difference as regards the situation of the objects or remote causes to which we refer the sensations. The perceptions of touch, for example, give us notice of the hardness or softness, smoothness or roughness of bodies that immediately touch the surface of our own; whereas by means of sight we perceive colors, magnitudes and forms of bodies that are at times at an immense distance from our eyes. We shall distinguish these two families of external perceptions by calling the first plesioscopic, because they make known to us qualities of objects that act immediately upon the organs; and the second aposcopic, for the contrary reason. The perceptions of touch and of taste are plesioscopic; those of sight, hearing and smell, aposcopic.

Everyone knows that in the perceptions of both families the sensations are produced by corporeal causes acting immediately upon the organs. If we see a distant body, it is because the light that comes to us from its surface impresses our eyes. If we hear a bell ringing perhaps a league away, it is because the vibrations it communicates to the air immediately affect our ears.(a) If we smell a rose that is two or three yards from us, it is because the effluvia that the rose is giving off come to strike our nostrils immediately. In what, then, does it consist that by means of the affections of sight, hearing and smell we do not seem to perceive the qualities of the bodies that immediately impress our organs, but of bodies situated at times at a considerable distance from us? Why do we not speak of the fragrance of the effluvia, but of the fragrance of flowers; nor of the sound of the air which a bell sets vibrating, but of the sound of the bell; nor of the colors

(a) The Spanish word oído has two meanings which we must not confound. It

signifies a sense, a faculty of the soul, and it denotes also the organic apparatus of membranes and nerves placed in the interior part of each ear, and prolonged to the brain. It is this second that the word has here, and the only one to which we always give the plural. [p. 34] of the light that strikes the eyes, but of the colors of the bodies that send it to us?

The reason is obvious. Touch and sight are the most important of the five senses. We owe to them incomparably more knowledge, and of more importance for the satisfaction of our needs, than to the others. The knowledge, for example, of the placing of bodies in space, a knowledge without which it is evident that we could not dispose of bodies, nor make them serve our well-being or pleasure, we owe to touch and to sight. Hence, no doubt, it came about that we referred to these two senses the information that comes to us from the others. Observing that a certain affection of smell constantly accompanied certain affections of sight and of touch, by means of which we perceived a certain color, figure and magnitude, it was natural to us to associate the former with the latter and to refer them all to one and the same cause. We attributed, then, to the body endowed with that color, figure and magnitude one quality more, that of affecting the sense of smell in a particular manner. In the same way, seeing and touching a body which, when struck by another, constantly produced a particular affection of hearing, we identified the cause of this affection with the cause of the visual and tactile affections that nature associated with it. We attributed, then, to a certain body endowed with certain qualities of which touch and sight informed us, another quality more, that of producing under certain circumstances that affection of hearing.

Our understanding obeys this law. If a sensation is produced by a series of remote causes, A, B, of which A acts upon B, and B upon the organ, and if B is not of a nature to affect sight or touch, but A is, the sensation produced by B will seem to us to proceed from A; that is, we shall represent to ourselves in it a quality of A, or, in other terms which signify absolutely the same, we shall perceive in it a quality of A. The odoriferous effluvia are neither visible nor tangible, but the rose that exhales them is so. The vibrations of the air cannot be seen or touched, but the bodies that produce them are within reach of sight and of touch. We shall refer, therefore, the sensations excited in the soul by the odoriferous effluvia [p. 35] and by the aerial vibrations, not to the effluvia and the air, but to the visible and tangible bodies that give off the effluvia and set the air vibrating.

We see, then, that in the aposcopic perceptions of hearing and of smell there enters a judgment, by means of which we refer the auditory or olfactory sensation, not to the agent that immediately impresses the organ, but to an agent distant from the organ; an agent that produces, in whatever way it may be, visual and tactile sensations, between which and the auditory or olfactory sensations we have observed constant connections.

It seems at first sight that sensation and judgment, or objective reference, are one single thing, elementary and indivisible. But this depends on the intimate connection which the two elements have come to have with each other. There is no reason whatever why the sensation should represent to us of itself a quality of the body that we call odorous or sonorous, and not of the effluvia or of the air, which are in reality the agents that, impressing the organs at close quarters, excite the sensations of sounds and odors. If the first representation takes place, and not the second, it is by reason of the constant union we have observed between the auditory or olfactory sensations and the visual and tactile sensations; a union from which we have inferred that the cause from which the latter proceed is the cause from which the others proceed also. Sight and touch, senses which by their importance ought to claim our attention from the first, gave us the first ideas of bodies or external causes. We referred, consequently, the auditory and olfactory sensations to the objects of sight and of touch, which were for us the only external objects; and we represented to ourselves by means of them, or believed we perceived, which is the same thing, particular qualities of these objects. The sensation in the aposcopic perceptions of hearing and of smell is a sign: by the value which experience taught us to give to this sign, sounds and odors became for us characters of objects that we saw and touched; and this objective reference became so familiar to us, and was so intimately united with the sensation, that the two came to seem to us one and the same thing.

[p. 36]

II

But besides the objective reference that is proper to each sense, there are commonly in the aposcopic perceptions certain accessory judgments which truly are not part of them and which nevertheless seem to us at first sight to belong to them.

Let us confine ourselves to hearing and smell. After we had learned by observation to refer the auditory or olfactory sensations to distant bodies, which by virtue of this reference we call sonorous or odorous, it happened often that the auditory or olfactory sensations were accompanied by certain judgments, more or less vague, of the distance and situation of the sonorous or odorous bodies that produced them, and that were not at the time within reach either of sight or of touch. We inferred, for example, from the greater or less intensity of the auditory sensation, the distance of the sonorous body, and we learned also to distinguish by means of certain modifications of the auditory sensation, though in an inexact and obscure manner, whether the sonorous body was before or behind, to the right or to the left, in a word, its situation with respect to ourselves. The same, though in a still more vague and indistinct manner, took place in the olfactory perceptions. Taught to estimate distances and situations by touch and sight, we found afterwards constant relations between certain particular modes of the auditory or olfactory sensations and certain distances and situations; from which it resulted that even deprived of the assistance of sight and of touch, we were able, by means of certain modifications of the sound or of the odor, to estimate to a certain point the distances and situations of the sonorous or odorous bodies. In this way the sensations of hearing and those of smell became signs of visual and tactile accidents which neither hearing nor smell can perceive of themselves.

We must, then, distinguish in the aposcopic sensations of hearing and of smell two kinds of judgments: some constitute the essential objective reference, and by means of them we represent to ourselves in the bodies that we know by touch and sight, qualities [p. 37] strictly auditory and olfactory, that is, sounds or odors, of which sight and touch could never have given us the least idea; and by means of the others we represent to ourselves distances and situations properly visual or tactile, inaccessible of themselves to the auditory or olfactory perceptions. In this way the auditory and olfactory perceptions became significative and indicative of perceptions of sight and touch, which we had not at the moment, but which we should have if the objects were within reach of these two senses. To judgments of this second kind we may give the name of suggested perceptions, because although they are not in reality actual perceptions, they accompany them and are intimately bound up with them; and the judgments of the first kind we shall distinguish by the title of primary perceptions, because these are the ones that are produced properly and peculiarly by the exercise of the respective aposcopic senses. Distances, and the situations of bodies in space, are accidents to the knowledge of which touch and sight led us.(b)

If, then, we estimate by means of hearing the situation and distance of bodies which we neither touch nor see, it is by virtue of connections previously observed; it is because certain modes of the auditory sensation indicate, suggest, the ideas of the situation and distance of the body that sounds. In the same way, if on hearing a sound whose cause we neither touch nor see, we recognize in it now the tolling of a bell, now the explosion of a firearm, now the din of bodies that roll, that collide, that burst, the articulate voice of man, the song of a bird, the murmur of water, the whistling of the wind; it is not because hearing perceives of itself the physical constitution, the visible or palpable accidents of the body that sounds, but because the modifications of the sound indicate, suggest, the ideas of that constitution or those accidents, by virtue of the connections we have observed between the latter and the former. The sense of smell does as much in its turn, though

(b) Originally touch alone, as we shall see hereafter. [p. 38] in a more vague and obscure manner. For this suggestion, in which from the affections of one sense we infer, we divine, so to speak, qualities and agencies that can be perceived only by other senses, is what constitutes the accessory references, the suggested perceptions; and it is not to be doubted that in the aposcopic perceptions of hearing and of smell, both the essential and primary judgments and the suggested ones are due to a kind of induction or instinctive reasoning founded on observations; in a word, to experience.

III

From what we have said hitherto it seems to be gathered that sight and touch are the fundamental senses to which we refer the perceptions of hearing and of smell, and we might express the same thing by saying that the visible and palpable qualities are the foundation, the subject upon which we superpose the auditory or olfactory qualities. Let us take one step more. Let us examine the knowledge which the intelligence owes to sight.

The perception of color is produced by a most tenuous fluid that lies between the objects and the eyes, and that impresses the eyes diversely according to the modifications it receives from the objects. Nevertheless, we do not refer the visual sensations to this fluid, that is, to the light. We represent to ourselves by means of them qualities, not of the light, but of the distant bodies that modify it; and the reason of this objective reference is obvious. The various modifications of the light which correspond to the various qualities of the tactile surfaces that send it to the eyes are not perceived by the soul; nor are the various organic impressions that correspond to these modifications of the light. What we directly perceive are the sensations which these impressions excite in their turn in the soul, and of which consciousness is the witness. Between the varieties of the visual sensations and the varieties of the organic impressions there are constant connections: there are likewise between the varieties of the organic impressions and the various modifications [p. 39] of the luminous fluid that impresses the organism: there are, finally, between the modifications of the luminous fluid and the varieties of the tactile surfaces that send it to us. In this fourfold chain, when we exercise the sense of sight, we know only the two extreme links: the visual sensations, contemplated by consciousness, and the tactile surfaces, known by means that do not depend on sight. We refer, consequently, the sensations to the tactile surfaces; and we seem to see in the visual sensations qualities of the tactile surfaces; particular qualities of which touch could never have informed us, and the knowledge of which we owe to this objective reference, which is essential and primary to sight, and which in reality constitutes this knowledge itself. To these qualities the name of colors was given.

We may, then, express in a more general manner that law of the understanding which we deduced from the perceptions of hearing and of smell. If a sensation is produced by a series of remote causes, A, B, of which A acts upon B, and B upon the organ, and if B is not perceptible to touch, but A is, the sensation produced by B will seem to us to proceed from A; that is, we shall perceive by means of it a quality of A.

The aposcopic perception of colors is peculiar to sight, and the bodies to which we attribute them are for that reason called visible. But if by means of this sense we knew only that such or such a body of a certain color exists outside of us, and received only notices of the tactile qualities of this body as vague and obscure as those of hearing and of smell, its utility would be reduced to very little. What gives sight an immense importance is the multitude, the clearness and the determinateness of its judgments or suggested perceptions.

Let us figure to ourselves the organ of sight as a surface that is in contact with a small picture of the external universe, formed by the extremities of the rays of light that come to us from the objects. We know that the eye is an instrument destined to produce on the retina this small picture, and that it produces it in effect with sufficient regularity and precision. Let us call [p. 40] visual situations, distances, magnitudes and figures those of the objects in this picture on the retina; tactile situations, distances, magnitudes and figures those which we should discover if, deprived of sight, we should grope our way toward the objects and feel their surface. It is clear that the different details of the ocular picture would produce differences correlative to them in the visual sensations; and as those details have constant relations with the tactile situations, distances, magnitudes and figures of the visible objects, there cannot but be also constant relations between these tactile qualities and the visual sensations; whence it follows that, instructed in this connection by experience, we were able to gather from the visual sensations the tactile qualities, and so to perceive the latter in the former by means of suggested judgments, which seem to us primary perceptions by reason of the rapidity with which they are produced, and which have the advantage of being as minute as they are precise and rapid. We owe in this way to sight many suggested perceptions of qualities which in reality belong not to the domain of this sense but to that of touch, and of which touch itself could inform us only slowly and with difficulty, or perhaps not at all. How much time should we not spend in studying by groping the details of the façade of a vast edifice, of which sight informs us minutely in a few moments? And in what manner should we come to know without it the situation, distance and dimensions of those bodies which it is not possible for us to approach?

The ocular picture is with respect to the external universe what the canvas on which the painter has undertaken to copy it is with respect to the latter; and between these two copies there is in reality a great resemblance. In the canvas which the painter sets before us we do not see the true details of the objects he represents, that is, their tactile situations, distances, magnitudes and figures; and we may convince ourselves of this by observing in how various ways the painter represents to us one and the same object according to the situation and distance from which he seeks to portray it. The face that is supposed to be seen from the front is in reality very different from that which is supposed to be seen from above or from below, [p. 41] from the right side or from the left, or from any other direction; and yet he who looks at the canvas believes he sees in all these faces one and the same, because the visual details, which are the work of the painter, suggest to him who looks at the canvas the corresponding tactile details. The same is applicable to the picture on the retina.

But we should be grossly deceived if we thought that the ocular picture serves in vision as the painted canvas does, because the painted canvas we see, and the ocular picture we do not see, and nearly the whole of mankind do not so much as know that it exists.

The picture on the retina presents to the sense of sight a phantasmagoria that lacks a fixed situation and determinate dimensions, but among whose colors and shadows there are offered to us relative situations, distances and sizes, and consequently various figures and perspectives; details, in short, similar to what we see in the painter’s work, and from which we deduce the tactile universe, in the same manner as we deduce it from the painted picture. We translate, so to speak, the visual geometry of the phantasmagoria produced by the picture on the retina into a tactile geometry, which is of the greatest importance to us for availing ourselves of objects and making them serve our needs. The visual geometry acts only momentarily, and in performing its office vanishes, leaving not the least vestige of itself: the tactile geometry is what enriches the memory with all the knowledge we acquire of the tactile objects that form the vast domain of matter.

This kind of translation is entirely instinctive in several species of animals, that is, it is executed by a natural faculty which they have not acquired by observing; for we see them, from their birth, move about with address and hit upon the objects they need. In children the contrary happens. They pass some weeks before attempting to use their hands to grasp objects; they try touch by groping; and it is much later that they are capable of estimating by sight, with any tolerable success, the tactile accidents of objects with which they are not familiar. We see also that this knowledge which sight [p. 42] gives us of tactile accidents reaches only as far as an estimate or computation can go which, founded on observable connections, suffers from all the inexactitudes and errors that may find room either in the incompleteness of the observations, or in the natural indeterminateness of the data, or in the inattention of the observer, or in the difficulty of the computation itself. Like what happens in other reasonings, we compute the tactile accidents from the visual affections, sometimes well, sometimes ill. Everything proves, then, that men have learned little by little to see, that is, to refer colors to distant bodies, and to judge by sight of tactile situations, distances, sizes and forms. We begin the apprenticeship from the moment the light first strikes our eyes, and exercising it ceaselessly while we are awake, we have come to perform this computation with a marvelous rapidity, to the point of its seeming to us that the judgments suggested by the visual sensations form part of the primary perceptions of sight; with which we have so intimately amalgamated them that they appear to us one and the same thing with them, and it becomes difficult for the understanding to separate the one from the other. For this reason we have given to these judgments the name of suggested perceptions.

To many it will perhaps seem improbable that the understanding should be capable of these reasonings and computations at that tender age to which we refer the apprenticeship of sight. But they are all reducible to mere analogies; and we cannot doubt that this kind of reasoning is familiar to man from the first dawn of intelligence. A child does not reason by laying down premises and drawing consequences from them, with the precision of dialectic; the greater part of men reach old age without ever having reasoned in this manner. The analogical procedure is exercised in infancy without the least effort on the child’s part. At the age of four years we see him form correctly the plurals of nouns, the diminutives, and the regular terminations of our verbs, which are so rich in inflections. We see him moreover employ the tenses with a marvelous propriety, and make in the practice of the language subtle distinctions, which the grammarians do not always succeed in defining and in which [p. 43] foreigners frequently stumble after some years of practice. All this children learn by themselves, without design and without labor; and many times when they commit grammatical faults, it is because the language they form for themselves is more faithful to the rules of analogy than that which common usage has authorized. What difficulty is there, then, in conceiving that this analogical procedure should begin, from the moment the child opens his eyes, to exercise and develop itself upon the connections which nature has established between the modes of the visual sensations and the accidents of tactile objects, connections which are of so much interest to him?

It cannot be doubted that all vision proceeds from the impression which the rays of light make upon the retina; and if we do not refer the visual sensation to them, it is by virtue of the general law by which we always refer sensations to distant corporeal causes, when these, and not those which immediately impress our organs, are within reach of touch. Instructed by the instinctive analogies which experience develops, it happens that at the moment the instantaneous picture formed by the extremities of the rays of light strikes the nerves, we remove it, so to speak, from ourselves, we enlarge it and wrap the world of tactile existences in it; but there is not an instant, not even the smallest, in which we see it under its true dimensions and in the place which it really occupies. The reason is evident. It is the indispensable medium of vision and cannot consequently be seen. What we call seeing is to refer the visual sensations to the external objects from which the light comes to our eyes.

It is scarcely necessary to observe that, once instructed by touch in the art of referring the visual sensations to tactile objects, we were able to refer them to objects that of themselves are impalpable, such as mist, smoke, clouds, etc. The impossibility in which we find ourselves of correcting these reports of sight by comparing them with those of touch has produced illusions at times; such as that of the tactile reality which the vulgar attribute to the firmament.

The marvelous ministry of sight, as significative and [p. 44] divinatory of touch, is a subject which elsewhere we shall endeavor to explain and illustrate in a more complete and satisfactory manner.

IV

Let us pass to the plesioscopic perceptions. Those of taste accompany those of touch so inseparably that we cannot but attribute flavors to the tactile substances that impress the palate and the tongue, organs, at one and the same time, of the perceptions of both senses.

Smell gives us sometimes plesioscopic perceptions. In a chemical laboratory, for example, we attribute certain odors to certain invisible and impalpable substances that act immediately upon the organ. Moreover, the agency of aeriform substances in olfaction being known, we may refer to it in all cases the affections of smell. And who prevents us from doing as much in hearing, with respect to the medium that transmits sound, and in vision, with respect to light? He who knows the procedure of nature in the material action from which the affections of the aposcopic senses arise may say with all truth that he has plesioscopic perceptions of the substances which, acting immediately upon the organs, affect them.

The agency of gases, of odoriferous effluvia, of sonorous aerial vibrations and of luminous rays is perceived neither by touch nor by sight; but it is deduced by reasonings, founded on observations and experiments, which resolve themselves into tactile perceptions, or into perceptions of sight, as representative and divinatory of touch. Besides, we figure these substances to ourselves as aggregates of molecules or corpuscles that have tactile qualities, and that differ from the bodies we can grasp and touch only by their extreme tenuity. Hence it follows that touch is the extended sense par excellence: that all the others do no more than superpose qualities and characters of certain particular kinds upon tactile objects, or suggest, by virtue of preceding associations, the reports [p. 45] which touch would give us if we applied it to them; and that the external universe is for us a system of things, magnitudes, forms, distances and situations, truly or imaginarily palpable.

Touch, then, if I may be permitted the expression, has been the master of the aposcopic senses; but sight has been the first disciple of touch. Taught by it, it has repeated the lessons of this sense to the others; and by means of the suggested perceptions of situation, distance, size and figure, it has served us to supply in a multitude of cases the perceptions of touch, dispensing us from consulting it; which is wherein the immense utility of sight consists.

We owe in the last result to the experience of touch the primary and suggested judgments that enter into the perceptions of the other senses. But who has given to touch its objective reference? Whence does it proceed that, experiencing a tactile sensation, I see in it not a spontaneous modification of my being, but a modification produced by a cause that is not I, and that is outside of me? Is this reference due to an instinct innate in us, or is it the work of reasoning? For the present let it suffice us to have shown that the tactile affections are the cause, the subject, the substance upon which we superpose all the others in order to represent to ourselves the external universe.

[PDF 62]

Internal sensitive perceptions.

Perceptions of the internal senses: they represent the organic impression as proximate cause.—They differ from external sensitive perceptions.— Elements they comprise.—In both there is the organic impression, but the objective reference is different.—Threefold relation of visual sensation.— Kinds of internal sensitive perceptions: sense of effort.—Reference to Brown. —They are different from external sensitive perceptions.—Various causes of internal perceptions.—Perception of heat: its different aspects.—Relation of touch and sight to internal perceptions.—All objective reference resolves itself into a tactile perception.—Appendix 1.º: result of the preceding analysis. —1.º Importance of the sense of touch in sensitive perceptions.—2.º Intervention of judgment in every kind of perception.—The I as subject and object at once.—Activity of the soul: Laromiguière’s opinion.—3.º Faculties exercised in perception.—Appendix 2.º: to feel and to perceive.—The sensationalist     school.—Feeling.—The      sensible.—Sensibility.—Sense.—Inner sense.

I

Our body is not known to us only by touch and by the other external senses. The perceptions, whether of well-being or pleasure, or of discomfort, uneasiness or pain, which we attribute to various parts of the machine we animate, or to the whole of it, represent to us bodily modifications very different from those we perceive in inanimate bodies. The perception of a pain in the stomach or the head, of a smarting in this part, of a throbbing in that, of a stabbing in another; the perceptions [p. 47] of the internal efforts with which we produce voluntary exertions; those of the states of mobility or inertia, of vigor or debility, which accompany joy, sadness, anger, fear—all these perceptions, and others whose catalogue would be long and difficult, form a great number of distinct kinds that belong to none of the external senses. They represent to us modifications proper to the animated body; and the organs of these perceptions are the very parts to which we refer, more or less distinctly, the sensitive affections of which consciousness is witness; so that in them the organ and the object are identified. If the perceptions of the external senses represent remote causes, causes which by acting upon our organs impress them, the perceptions of the internal senses represent to us proximate causes, organic impressions. In neither the one nor the other is there an intuition of objects, but only of signs to which we give an objective value; spiritual signs, sensations, which represent bodily qualities or states, with which they have not and cannot have the least resemblance.

Between external sensitive perceptions and internal sensitive perceptions there is a line of separation which in no case permits them to be confounded. The former have for their object qualities that are found in every species of bodies, organized or not; the latter have for their object qualities or states that can be perceived only in organized bodies, and by the very soul that gives them animation and life. Thus the color of the skin is perceived by the same sense as that of any organic substance whatever; sleep and hunger are perceived by internal senses.

The perceptions of the internal senses are resolved, like those of the external, into sensation, perception, intuition and objective reference. The perception of hunger, for example, is resolved into the sensation produced in the soul in consequence of a certain material modification of the alimentary organs, into the consciousness or intuitive perception of this sensation, and into the judgment which refers the sensation to those organs, and represents to us in it a particular state of the same.

[p. 48]

The organic state by means of which the sensation is immediately produced, and the sensation by means of which the soul receives notice of the organic state, are two entirely distinct things, the former being a corporeal phenomenon which we represent to ourselves by means of the sensation, and which we know only through it, and the latter a spiritual phenomenon which the soul perceives intuitively in itself.

Since every sensation can be referred to its organ and thus produce an internal sensitive perception, it is clear that the sensations by which we represent to ourselves the qualities of external bodies may serve at the same time to represent to us the organic impressions from which they immediately emanate. The sensation, for example, by which I represent to myself the color of snow may serve at the same time to represent to me the organic affection produced in the eyes by the luminous rays which the snow reflects. The intellectual sign of the color of the snow, and the intellectual sign of the impression produced by the snow upon the organ of sight, are one and the same; but the objective reference is different. The object of the first is the snow under a certain color; the object of the second is the organ of sight under a certain impression. One and the same sensation signifies in our understanding two things, its proximate cause and its remote cause.

Although every external perception is at the same time internal, it is rare that the objective reference which characterizes the latter excites attention vividly. Only when the organic impression passes beyond ordinary limits by the force of the impression or by the delicacy of the organ, as when the light of a candle which in other circumstances would not offend us affects diseased eyes painfully, is the perception plainly double: at the same time that we see the candle, we feel pain and refer it to the organ.

We have seen that we may regard the visual sensation as the sign of a more or less remote cause, that is to say, as the sign of a quality of the luminous fluid which immediately affects the eyes, as the sign of a quality of the body which sends it to us. Consequently, every visual sensation is for us a triple sign, which represents to [p. 49] us now qualities of the distant bodies which we see, now modifications of the organ; giving us in the first case an external aposcopic perception, in the second an external plesioscopic perception, and in the third an internal perception. In all three the sensation is one and the same: but the reference is different. In all aposcopic perceptions the sensation is at once a state of the soul, in which the I recognizes itself, and a sign to which we can give three different significations.

The first family of internal perceptions comprises those which are at the same time external. If we make use of the sensation as of a symbol to represent to ourselves a quality of the body which mediately or immediately affects the organ, the perception is external; if with the sensation we symbolize the organic impression, the perception is internal.

In this first family of internal sensitive perceptions the soul has knowledge of a remote cause by means of an external sensitive perception; in other internal perceptions the soul has knowledge of a remote cause by means of an intuitive perception. Here is an example: we see, recollect or imagine a pitiable object which moves us profoundly: this emotion consists in organic affections, which perhaps go so far as to oppress the chest painfully and to make us shed tears: we have then internal sensitive perceptions of these organic states, and there is manifested to us at the same time a remote cause, namely, the mental contemplation of that object, perceived by consciousness.

The internal perceptions that belong to this second family are very numerous and various. We shall consider first a kind which seems to me very worthy of attention by reason of the multitude and importance of the cognitions which, as we shall see farther on, it helps to supply us with. I speak of the perceptions of the sense of effort.

We call effort the purely organic modification which takes place in some part of our body in consequence of the soul’s willing to execute a movement with it. The effort

## PHILOS.   4

[p. 50]

is proper to the body, as volition is to the soul, and consists, as is well known, in a muscular contraction: volition acts in an unknown manner upon the brain, and this action is transmitted by the nerves to the muscle or muscles that must contract in order that the movement may take place; a contraction which produces a sensation in the soul, as so many other organic modifications produce one, and which consequently awakens in the soul an internal sensitive perception. Probably there is no effort of any of the muscles that serve for voluntary movements which does not excite a corresponding sensation, by means of which we distinguish it from the efforts of the other muscles, and from other modifications of the efforts of that same muscle.(a) Not that we can in this way, by a kind of instinctive anatomy, distinguish and count our muscles, and recognize each of those that concur in the movements in which several are exercised at once, and each of the modifications of which each effort is susceptible; for unless we study by means of touch and sight the interior structure of man, we shall know nothing of it, save that we have limbs and that we move them when and as we please, without having the least idea of the complicated play of machinery which we set in motion by merely willing it. What I say is that we perceive and distinguish from one another the material modes of being which we call efforts, inasmuch as we perceive and distinguish from one another the sensations produced by them. The effort that moves an eyelid produces in the soul a different sensation from the effort that moves the lips and the tongue. The series of efforts necessary to pass the hand over a spherical surface produces a series of sensations very different from that which would be produced by the series of efforts necessary to pass the hand over a prismatic or conical surface. By means of consciousness we perceive this variety of sensations; and when touch and sight have

(a) I adopt here the ideas and in part the language of Professor Brown. [p. 51] given us knowledge of our own corporeal form and made us observe the connections between each affection of the sense of effort and each visible or tangible movement of a part of our body, it was not difficult for us to refer the sensations of this kind to their proximate causes, I mean, to the organs of the respective voluntary movements: though in a more or less vague manner, according as those organs are more or less within reach of sight and touch.

“Obscure as the feelings of muscular exertion may seem in certain cases, there are others,” says Brown, “in which they are not without considerable energy. Without referring to the morbid state of the organs which renders them painfully sensible, what is the feeling of fatigue but a perception of the sense of effort, of which our muscles are as truly the organs as our eyes are of sight, and our ears of hearing? When a limb has been long exercised, the repetition of the contraction of its muscles is accompanied, not with a slight and obscure sensation, but with one which, passing through various stages of uneasiness, arrives at last at severe pain. Even without previous fatigue, every considerable effort produces a lively sensation. Of the pleasure which attends moderate exercise, every one must have been conscious in himself, even in his years of maturity, when he seldom has recourse to it for the pleasure alone; and must remember the delightful feeling of joy that accompanied voluntary movement in the first years. It is by the pleasure of exertion, and the pain of inexertion, that we are roused from that indolence, into which, with great injury to ourselves and to society, we otherwise might sink.”

It is clear that the faculty we have of perceiving the efforts which the will produces in our body is a sense, a faculty of the same class as sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch; that is to say, a faculty that perceives corporeal qualities or modes of being by means of the sensations which certain organs of our body cause to arise in the soul. In this sense, as in the others, we must distinguish the sensation that corresponds to the organic modification, and the judgment which [p. 52] refers it to an arm, a foot, the head, the tongue, the eyelids, in short, to the particular organ which we move. This is a judgment, analogous to that which in the perceptions of smell, for example, refers the affections of this sense to the nose. But in the perceptions of smell the understanding goes farther. By means of olfactory affections we represent to ourselves not only organic affections, but material remote causes; whereas by the sense of effort, to which we owe the perception of voluntary movement, we perceive properly nothing material but the organic impressions.

It is true that muscular contractions are produced by determinations of the will, and that, since we perceive these, we perceive truly remote causes of the sensations of effort. But the perception of these causes is not representative but intuitive; it is not effected by means of a sensation to which we give the value of a sign, as happens in the external senses, but immediately by the soul, which contemplates itself. The remote cause of the sensitive affections which produce external perceptions is a corporeal substance; that of the affections of the internal sense of effort is the soul itself. We perceive the first by the external senses, and the second by consciousness.

Something similar happens with many other internal sensitive perceptions.

One object moves us to laughter; another moves us to tenderness until we shed tears; another makes us shudder with horror. The phenomenon is complex. The soul sees, recollects, imagines an object capable of affecting it agreeably or painfully; and there is then produced an intuitive perception, which is accompanied in our body by certain particular organic impressions, for example, the oppression of the chest and throat, weeping, shuddering, laughter, nausea: at times the impression is less lively, and is reduced to a slight excitation, agreeable or painful. But whatever be the effects caused by the mental contemplation, all of them are elements of internal sensitive perceptions, which the soul, enlightened by experience, refers to different parts of the organism.

[p. 53]

These complex phenomena are commonly called emotions, feelings, affects, passions, such as joy, sadness, anger, fear, fondness, aversion, pity, horror, admiration, shame and various others.

It is hardly necessary to observe that by the words pleasure, grief, pain we understand in ordinary language the organic impression. But the true seat of all these affections is the soul, which perceives intuitively the remote cause, and by means of the internal sensitive perception, the proximate cause.

There is another family of internal sensitive perceptions, whose remote cause, that is, the present stimulus from which the organic modifications emanate, is entirely unknown to us. Hunger follows fasting, fatigue violent exercise, sleep the use of narcotic drinks, etc.; but in these cases we do not perceive an agency of our I, as in the preceding family, nor do we refer the sensation to any corporeal substance that is actually impressing the organs.

There are, then, three families of internal sensitive perceptions.

In the first, the remote cause of the sensation is a corporeal agency, perceived mediately and immediately by some one of the external senses.

In the second, the remote cause of the sensation is a mental agency which affects the organs and is perceived by consciousness: this agency belongs sometimes to the understanding, as happens when a mental contemplation, an idea or collection of ideas, affects us more or less vividly; and at other times it is a determination of the will which produces a muscular contraction called effort.

And in the third, the remote cause which actually awakens the organic impression is wholly unknown to us.

II

The word heat signifies sometimes a quality of external bodies, of which we have an external sensitive perception, as when by immediate contact we perceive that a [p. 54] solid or liquid substance, or the atmosphere that surrounds us, is hot; sometimes an organic modification, of which we have an internal sensitive perception, as when in fever or after violent exercise we feel heat. When we attribute heat to a body that is in contact with our own, the external perception is plesioscopic. If we attribute it to a body somewhat distant from us, e.g., to the fire of the hearth, we should perceive aposcopically a quality of the fire; for then the organic modification would be produced by the caloric, or by the agent, whatever it may be, which, set in motion by the substances that are at an elevated temperature, acts immediately upon our organs; and nevertheless, we should not refer the sensation to the caloric, but to the distant substance that impels or emits it.

Consequently, the perception of heat is sometimes external and sometimes merely internal; and in the first case it is sometimes plesioscopic and sometimes aposcopic.

The perception of heat is commonly reduced to touch, because it frequently accompanies the perceptions of that sense; but this is not always so, as we have just seen; and even when it is so, the quality represented by the sensation of heat is not properly tangible, any more than flavors are, although the affections of taste are inseparably united with those of touch. The perceptions of heat belong truly to a particular sense, whose organs are even more extensive than those of touch, since they embrace not only the whole surface of our body, but also our internal parts.

As the different degrees of heat or of cold form a continuous series, the corresponding sensations also form a series, and we may reduce them all to one and the same sense, whether external or internal.

[p. 55]

## III

I believe that in order to explain the perceptions it is necessary for us to suppose particular instincts by virtue of which we refer the sensations to their organs. First, because touch and sight may have made known to us from very early the connection between many kinds of sensations and the respective organs. Was it not extremely easy, e.g., to observe the part which the eyes, the ears, the nose and the palate had respectively in the spiritual modifications produced by colors, sounds, odors and flavors? Could we fail to refer to the chest and throat the affections which, when we suffer intense affliction and anguish, disturb the breathing, produce palpitations and sighs, and choke the voice? Secondly, because having learned to know in a great number of cases, by the concurrence of internal perceptions with external, the situation of the organs, it was not difficult for us to acquire more or less exact knowledge of the same kind in many others, by means of proportions and analogies which became little by little habitual to us; in the same way that, by comparing the reports of the hands with the intimations of the eyes, we learned to form a judgment of the situation and distance of bodies by sight alone, and having acquired this faculty, we extended it by means of proportions and analogies to all distances and situations, even beyond those limits within which touch could serve as master to sight. In confirmation of which we shall observe that, just as by means of visual perceptions we form vague and frequently erroneous judgments concerning distances and situations that pass beyond the compass in which we are accustomed to confront them with the knowledge derived from touch, so nothing is more rough-and-ready, or more exposed to illusions and errors, than the reference of sensations to determinate regions of the body, when the organic modifications are not in some way within reach of the external senses.

It seems to me, then, probable that to touch and to sight, and in the last [p. 56] result to touch alone, is due the reference of all sensations to their organs. But this supposes that we knew, at least superficially, our own body, and that we distinguished it from foreign bodies.

By touch, and by the other external senses with the aid of touch, we knew the form, dimensions, color and other qualities of our body, which are common to it with inanimate matter. By touch, and by sight as representative of touch, we know the continuity of its parts, and its independence of the bodies that surround it. Moreover, by confronting with one another the reports of touch, it became manifest to us that if in touching foreign bodies we experienced simple sensations, in touching our own body we experienced double and reciprocal sensations. Having thus come to distinguish from all other bodies the one which we animate, and to trace mentally its limits, we are able to refer all sensations to their organs in a more or less precise manner, according as these were more or less within reach of observation.

But even if it had been necessary that particular instincts should intervene in the formation of this judgment, it would be none the less certain that internal perceptions, like external ones, are composed, leaving consciousness out of account for the present, of two distinct parts, sensation and objective reference. And whatever hypothesis we may adopt on the generation of references, it will always be constant that they lead us in all cases to touch, since we always place in tangible objects, or in objects which we imagine to be such, the proximate or remote material causes of all sensitive operations. The judgment which refers each sensation to a more or less determinate tangible organ is made so easily and rapidly that the soul seems to us to be present in the organ and almost to be identified with it. And since a multitude of internal perceptions is produced in us at every step, we imagine that all the parts of our corporeal machine enjoy continuously and simultaneously the presence of the I, and that the existence of which we have intuition penetrates and vivifies them all.

[p. 57]

This schooling of the senses by touch presupposes in tactile perceptions an objective reference which cannot be resolved into any other, and which is the basis of all the others. In the first exercise of this sense it is evident that we could not represent external objects to ourselves as remote causes which, acting upon the organs, affected the soul, because in order that we should form such judgments it was necessary that we should know our structure beforehand, and this knowledge has been, as we have seen, a slow and progressive work of touch. Clearing away, then, from our tactile perceptions every idea of organic structure, we can only represent the objects perceived by this sense as causes distinct from and independent of the I. But here there presents itself to us anew that important and difficult question: how has this primitive judgment, origin and foundation of all objective references, arisen in us? Do we owe it to an instinct? Do we owe it to other means of perception than those we have hitherto considered? Do we owe it to reasoning?

## APPENDIX I

## RESULT OF THE PRECEDING ANALYSIS

The analysis of the perceptions which has furnished the subject of the preceding chapters will doubtless have seemed excessively prolix; but without it the results which I am about to enumerate would be vague and obscure, and would never have a right to be accepted with that confidence which in matters of pure observation can be inspired only by a minute examination of the facts.

The first of these results is one that has already been stated repeatedly: the supreme importance of touch in sensitive perceptions. All sensible symbols are superposed upon a matter, really or imaginarily tangible. The most tenuous material agents, the most delicate, the most inaccessible to touch, are represented to us as aggregates of molecules which by their extreme smallness cannot be grasped or touched, [p. 58] but which have magnitude and figure, like the bodies which we touch and grasp, and which, sufficiently condensed, could, like these, be touched and grasped.

Another important result of the preceding observations is the essential intervention of judgment in all our intuitive and sensitive perceptions. We perceive none of the qualities of a corporeal object, none of the affections of our organs, save by means of objective references, that is to say, by means of judgments. Without the judgment which refers the sensation to a cause distinct from the I, the soul could perceive the sensation intuitively, and nothing more.

And if in the exercise of the senses there is a reference to the proximate or remote cause of the sensation, in the acts of consciousness there is a reference to our own soul, to our I, considered at one and the same time as object and as subject. Clear away this judgment which makes us see certain acts or modes as acts or modes of our I, and what will the reports of consciousness come to be? A vain and insignificant phantasmagoria. That which gives them substance and signification, that which makes them true perceptions, is the judgment.

In every judgment we conceive a relation. In every judgment the soul draws from the juxtaposition of two elements a third entity, distinct from each of them and from their mere aggregate. The soul is, then, fecund, is active, in judgment, and consequently in every kind of perception.

Some philosophers have made the activity of the soul consist in this, that, being affected by the organs, it exerts in its turn a kind of reaction upon them.(a) But the activity which is proper to the understanding lies, so to speak, deeper. It consists properly in drawing from two spiritual modes a third spiritual mode, which is distinguished from each of the other two and from the aggregate of both.

Lastly, the analysis of perceptions has made us recognize in them the exercise of three intellectual faculties

(a) See Laromiguière, Leçons de Philosophie, Part 1, lesson 4. [p. 59] of different kinds; the faculty of intuiting, that is, the faculty which the I, the soul, has of contemplating itself; the faculty of feeling, that is, of experiencing sensations, and the faculty of judging. The first two are strictly elementary: I do not believe that they can be resolved into others. In judgment, on the contrary, there are two distinct acts, the mere conception of a relation, and the assent of the soul, which recognizes the reality of the relation; and it is in this second act that judgment most essentially consists. Therefore the faculty of judging is resolved into two distinct elementary faculties. But in the study of relations, or relative qualities, what is of most importance is the conception, which is what differentiates them and what characterizes their various kinds. To this, then, we shall chiefly attend, and shall regard the assent, when it accompanies them, only as their sanction and realization.

## APPENDIX II

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE VULGAR OR TROPICAL USE OF CERTAIN

## WORDS

There is an essential difference between feeling and perceiving. To feel is to experience sensations; a term which I believe ought to be limited to those affections of the soul that are the immediate consequence of organic impressions. Sensation is an element of perception, and not of every perception, but of sensitive perception alone. It may give, like any other state or mode of the soul, an object, but not an element, to the perceptions of consciousness.

Thus, then, we take the words feel and sensation in a signification much less extensive than that of the sensationalist school, for which sensation is perception, is judgment, is reasoning, is desire, volition, etc.; which sees, in short, in all the affections, in all the operations of the soul, nothing more than transformed sensation; a system which reduces itself in reality to varying the signification of the word, applying it to all [p. 60] the states and to all the acts of the soul of which we are conscious.

But the common usage of our language also commonly gives to the verb to feel a signification different from that in which I have believed that psychologically we ought to fix it. We apply it often, in the ordinary way of speaking, to certain slight perceptions of hearing and of touch, as when one says that he feels steps, or that he has felt an earthquake. We also commonly designate by it internal sensitive perceptions and those complex modes which we have denominated feelings, emotions, passions. In these significations one feels hunger, thirst, sleep, weariness; one feels the death of a beloved person; one feels sympathy with the sufferings of others; one feels horror, aversion, sadness, joy: phrases all of them psychologically inexact. This multitude of significations of the verb to feel was without doubt what led to the imagining that all the acts of the soul were nothing more than transformed sensation.

The word sensible is still more various in its vulgar acceptations. Applied to remote corporeal causes it signifies what can produce organic impressions strong enough to give rise to sensations. So it is when we say that a body gives sensible heat, or that the heat of a small portion of air is not so. So we call the skin sensible, and the hair and nails insensible. We also commonly designate with this word the faculty of experiencing sensations, as when we say that animals are sensible, and that plants do not appear to be so. Finally, we express with it the susceptibility to delicate and lively emotions, and in this signification we bestow the epithet sensible on certain persons and deny it to others.

The word sensibility likewise admits of a variety of significations, corresponding to the second, third or fourth of those I have just indicated. In the second of them we concede sensibility to the skin, in the third to animals, in the fourth to persons who are keenly impassioned by causes which in other individuals would scarcely produce slight emotions.

I am very far from pretending that the vulgar acceptations which I have pointed out should be banished from language. I should wish only [p. 61] that their psychological inexactness be noted, and that we confine ourselves to regarding them as mere tropes.

The word sense ought to signify the mere susceptibility which the soul has of being affected by organic modifications. Sense in this psychological acceptation would denote, then, merely some one of the kinds of sensibility in which the soul is affected at once by a certain kind of organic modifications, leaving out of account the objective reference. But it is not so. A different signification is universally given to the word sense, denoting by it a perceptive faculty, by means of which we refer to certain proximate or remote causes the sensations that arise from organic modifications. Such is the signification involved in the phrases sense of sight, sense of hearing, sense of effort, etc. But it is necessary to note the different value of these phrases: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch carry with them the idea of sense; which does not happen in effort, hunger, thirst, fatigue, etc., which signify only the organic impressions, objects of the perceptive faculty.

By an extension of this same tropical usage consciousness is called inner sense. But in admitting such a signification we must not forget the essential difference that separates the acts of consciousness from the acts that belong to the external and internal senses.

Consciousness intuits, contemplates immediately and directly its object; the senses symbolize, by means of the sensations which we intuit, remote causes, frequently unknown.

[PDF 78]

On relative perceptions.

Perception of a relation.—Terms of the relation and relative terms.— Homologous and antilogous relations.—Absolute qualities and relative qualities.—The absolute and the relative are variable characters.—Every relation is inherent in the objects compared.—Activity in the conception of relations. —Conception and perception of a relation.—The conception of a relation takes place only among the modes of the soul.—Relation of the soul to its own being.—It is not possible to conceive any relation between corporeal qualities and the modes of the soul.—Conception of the relation of other relations.—There are, then, primary and secondary relations.—Simple and compound qualities.—Which are the elementary relations.

When two perceptions or two ideas are brought together in the understanding, it often happens that from their coexistence there arises spontaneously a third spiritual affection, which differs from each of them and from the mere aggregate of both.

Suppose that the perceptions of a lily and of snow coexist in the understanding. From the mental juxtaposition, so to speak, of the two colors in the understanding, which is what is called comparison, there arises the perception of the resemblance between the two colors; and it is not possible for anyone to confound this third perception with the perception of the color of the lily, or with the perception of the color of the snow, or with the perception of the mere aggregate of both colors. We perceive then a special relation, the relation of resemblance between the colors of the two objects.

In the same manner, when the perception of fire and that of the heat which is produced in my hand [p. 63] when I bring it near to it coexist in the understanding, there arises the perception of a special relation which we call that of cause and effect, or of causality, which it is not possible to conceive either in the fire, or in the heat produced in the hand, considered separately.

In a like manner arise the perceptions of many other kinds of relations, such as that of the contiguity of the house I inhabit and the neighboring house, that of the succession of the thunder to the lightning, etc.

The objects between which we perceive it are called the terms of the relation, and those which we attribute to them by virtue of a relation, such as similar, cause, effect, prior or posterior, contiguous or distant, etc., are called relative terms.

But it is to be remarked that if these relative terms are often one and the same with respect to the objects compared, as happens in the relations of resemblance and contiguity (for if B is similar or contiguous to C, C is by the same fact similar or contiguous to B), it happens many other times that the contrary is the case, and the attribute we give to one of the objects compared is of a signification not only different but contrary to that of the attribute we give to the other, as happens in the relation of cause and effect; for if we conceive that fire is the cause of heat, we conceive by the same fact that heat is the effect of fire; and if we conceive that autumn is prior to winter, we conceive by the same fact that winter is posterior to autumn. From this point of view we may call homologous relations those in which we apply to the terms attributes of the same signification, such as resemblance and contiguity, and antilogous relations those in which the attributes are of contrary signification, such as that of causality and that of succession.

Qualities, and consequently perceptions and ideas, and the words we employ to signify them, are generally divided into absolute and relative, those being called relative which involve relations, and absolute the others. Relative quality and relation are one and the same thing.

The perception of an absolute quality supposes that we refer a modification of the soul to the soul, if the perception is intuitive; from which it seems to follow that even the qualities that [p. 64] we call absolute are in strictness relative. In order, then, to distinguish absolute qualities from relative, we must leave out of account those invariable and necessary relations which enter as constitutive elements into all possible qualities. And the same must be said of all the qualities which by their special nature involve others.

Moreover, if I judge that a jasmine is white, it is because I mentally compare it with another flower or other flowers to which we give the same title, and because we find resemblance between the one and the other. But this relation lies wholly in the attribute we give to the new flower, and I cannot but conceive and affirm it by the very fact of perceiving its whiteness.

It is another thing when we recognize in a person the quality of son or father, or in any thing whatever the quality of cause or effect, because these words do not include in themselves the term to which the quality they express refers. Every relation supposes two terms, one to which the relative quality is attributed, and another to which this quality refers. If we say, for example, that Abel was a son, we necessarily suppose that he was so of some one, and we do not complete the idea of the relation except by adding of Adam: without this the word son would not comprehend the relation in its entirety; and this is what characterizes the words which are truly relative.

The word descendant is of itself truly relative, like son or father, and obliges us to think of an ascendant or ascendants from whom descends the person or persons to whom that title is attributed; but as soon as this person or persons enter into the attribute to complete the relation, the word ceases to be relative. So it is with the word Heraclidae, which signifies descendants of Hercules.

Nevertheless, when relations are designated in general, leaving out of account the terms between which we conceive them, we are wont to express them by means of abstract substantives, such as resemblance, difference, contiguity, cause, effect, etc.; which, consequently, always retain their nature of relative words, whether or not the respective terms accompany them, as when we say: resemblance is a [p. 65] indefinable relation; attraction is the cause of the fall of heavy bodies; every phenomenon supposes a cause; sensation is the effect of an action of the organism upon the soul.

The absolute and the relative are, then, variable characters, which depend not only on our manner of conceiving things, but on the signs with which we represent them in language.

Relation belongs to neither of the objects compared, considered in themselves, nor does it consist in the aggregation of the qualities which are compared. It belongs to the objects compared in such wise that it is not possible to conceive it, in whole or in part, unless the soul sees them, so to speak, side by side. We could not, for example, conceive, wholly or partially, the resemblance between the color of the lily and that of the snow, unless we perceived or recollected both colors at one time; nor the succession between the lightning and the thunder, unless the memory of the lightning and the perception or the memory of the thunder existed at the same time in the soul. Experiencing simultaneously in these cases the perceptions, actual or renewed, of the two things compared, we perceive between them the particular relations which we signify by saying that they are similar, or that one is before and the other after.

By comparison is ordinarily understood a certain voluntary endeavor by which we attend to two or more objects at one time in order to perceive their relations. Here we shall leave out of account this intervention of the will. It often happens that relations are conceived, are engendered in our mind, and are perceived by it, in consequence of the fortuitous simultaneity of two or more mental affections, without the least design or effort on our part, and many times against our will.

In the perception of a relation the soul is essentially active: it draws from the perceptions compared what does not exist separately in any of them, and for that reason I have said that the soul in this act conceives, engenders. But to conceive and to perceive are not always exactly the same thing, because perception supposes the internal affirmation of the relation which is conceived. There are purely imaginary relations and relations which we believe true and real.

## PHILOS.      5

[p. 66]

We conceive relations now between corporeal qualities, or remote causes of sensations; now between organic impressions, or proximate causes of sensations; now between the various modes or acts of the soul, in respect of one another or of the soul. We can, for example, conceive that two colors, or two pains, or two desires resemble each other, or that one desire is more intense than another, or that a desire succeeds a sensation, or that the soul is as it were the substance or support of the various modifications which it experiences, or with which it is identified.

It is clear that the relations between the proximate or remote causes which affect sensibility cannot be conceived directly, but only representatively. If the color of one body seems to us similar to the color of another body, it is because the visual sensations excited by both seem to us to resemble each other. If two or more tangible objects seem to us to be presented in a certain successive order, it is because the tactile sensations with which we perceive them are excited in us according to this order. How does a sick man judge that the pain he feels to-day is more intense than the pain he felt yesterday? Because he compares an affection which actually exists in the soul with another affection which existed in it, and which memory represents to him, and because he conceives between the two that particular relation which we signify by saying that one thing is more and another is less. In general, we conceive no relation except between the modes of the soul. There is only one particular relation which seems an exception to this assertion. When the soul perceives in itself any modification whatever and refers it to itself, it does not perceive a relation between two modes of its own, but its own being or substance modified in two particular ways.

Of the relations, then, which exist between corporeal qualities and between organic affections we have, and can have, no direct knowledge, because we do not perceive corporeal qualities or organic affections as they are in themselves, but only so far as our sensations represent them. All that our understanding can do is to represent to itself material relations by means of those which it directly perceives in comparing one sensation with another.

[p. 67]

As all relations have been originally conceived by consciousness, the perceptions of consciousness are consequently of two species: absolute or relative.

We can conceive relations of relations. The judgment I form in comparing the color of the violet with that of the lilac seems to me similar to the judgment I form in comparing the smell of the carnation with the smell of the clove: the relation between those colors seems to me similar to the relation between these smells; I conceive, in short, and cannot but conceive, resemblance between two resemblances. We can in the same manner conceive resemblance between two relations of succession, or succession between two relations of resemblance. Relations are, then, of different orders: some primary, which we conceive between absolute qualities; and others secondary, which we conceive by comparing one relation with another.

Qualities, absolute as well as relative, are simple or complex. If the perception is simple, the corresponding quality will appear so to us also, and consequently will be so for us, because in our understanding the being of qualities cannot be other than what perceptions show us, or represent to us, or symbolize to us in them. The smell of the rose, for example, is a simple absolute quality. The successive order between a volition and the movement of a limb is a relative quality of the same kind. On the contrary, the quality which is known to us by two or more different perceptions is complex. The taste of the wine which the two paternal ancestors of Sancho Panza tasted, and in which, along with the taste of wine, they found a taste of iron and of Cordovan leather, was nevertheless for these two tasters a simple absolute quality, because they did not perceive in the wine three different tastes, but one only, in which by means of subsequent relative perceptions they found resemblances to other tastes. But the coloring of a surface painted in various hues, each of which is the object of a different perception, is a complex absolute quality. A complex quality, but relative, is also the extraposition between two tangible and contiguous points, A, B; because we conceive that A is outside of B and [p. 68] B is outside of A, perceiving that we make a certain effort to touch them successively with one and the same point of the surface of our body. The perception of the extraposition between A and B resolves itself, then, into three different perceptions: that of the successive order between the touching of A and the effort, that of this effort itself, and that of the successive order between the effort and the touching of B; that is, into one absolute perception, which is the second of those I have just enumerated, and two relative perceptions, which are the first and the third.

When we try to explain something to ourselves or to make it known to others, we contemplate, or cause to be contemplated, its various parts, and resolve it mentally into the elements of which it is composed. But the understanding does not then act upon the objects themselves, but upon the perceptions it has of them. Simple qualities, the qualities to whose knowledge we have arrived by simple perceptions, are not, then, susceptible of definition or explanation, nor can we indicate them except by indicating the respective perceptions. We cannot represent to ourselves the white or black color except as the cause of that particular sensation of sight which has made it known to us; nor could we make it known to another, except by placing him in a situation to experience what we have experienced, or to recollect what he himself has experienced. In the same way, the elementary relations, e.g., that of the resemblance of two homogeneous colors, or that of the succession of these two sounds, a, e, although we recognize and distinguish them perfectly, are inexplicable and indefinable. Who does not distinguish the relation which we express by saying that one color is like another, from that which we express by saying that one sound was heard after another? And yet it is impossible to define or explain what it is that constitutes the resemblance or the succession of things.(a)

(a) The explanation which is generally given of what resemblance is appears to

me erroneous. The same I say of the attempts which have been made to explain succession. But these two questions must be left for a later place.

[p. 69]

Of relations, as we have said, some are primary or of the first order, others secondary or of a further order, that is, relations of relations. We have seen likewise that some are perceived intuitively by consciousness; and others represented by those which we intuitively perceive between sensations. Finally, we have divided them into simple and complex. There remains another difference, which we have already treated of, but which it seems to me convenient to inculcate. There are homologous relations, by virtue of which we give to the objects compared the same denomination; and antilogous relations, by virtue of which we give to the objects compared denominations of contrary signification. The relation of resemblance, for example, is homologous: if A has resemblance to B, B has it necessarily to A; and we say indifferently of either of the two that it is similar to the other, or we say of both that they are similar to each other. But the relation of causality is antilogous. If A is the cause of B, B is necessarily the effect of A; denominations of signification not only different, but contrary.
