The elementary relations into which the others resolve themselves, if not always, at least more frequently, are those of resemblance or difference, that in which we conceive that two things are equal or that one thing is more and another less, that of coexistence and succession, that of identity or distinction, and that of quality or substance. The complex relations (which consist in different combinations of the elementary) are of innumerable and most diverse species.

[PDF 86]

On resemblance and difference.

Division of the chapter.—Importance of the relation of resemblance.— Section 1.—I. Relation may be primary and secondary.—Perception of resemblance and difference.—Primary resemblance.—Complete resemblance. —Greater resemblance.—Threefold relation of difference analogous to that of resemblance.—Every relation of resemblance is a comparative judgment. —Resemblance and difference are equivalent to the distance or nearness of objects.—II. Partial point of view of objects.—Resemblance, like difference, is usually expressed by generic names.—III. Resemblance and difference resolve the assemblage of objects into classes.—Section 2.—IV. Resemblance is not the perception of what there is in common in objects.—This is proved in simple qualities.—Complex resemblances resolve themselves into those of simple qualities.—Section 3.—V. Importance of the relation of resemblance in the formation of language.—Qualities of objects: what they are in themselves.—The quality of an object is not to be confounded with the attribute or predicate.

This chapter is divided into three sections. In the first I propose to analyze the various relations to which we give the title of resemblances or differences; in the second I shall examine the explanation which is generally given of resemblance; in the third we shall see the influence which this relation has had upon the structure of language.

Among the elementary relations there is none of more importance. The understanding owes to it the coordination, the inventory, so to speak, of all that it learns and knows; without it neither language nor any other system of signs would be possible. The relation of resemblance is that which serves as guide to the philosopher in translating the apparent variety of phenomena into the real uniformity [p. 71] which the laws of nature formulate. What chiefly gives light and beauty to style is the vividness of the resemblances with which it colors ideas. Everything turns upon resemblances, in thought and in the signs of thought.

A relation so important is an essential object of study. It is of the utmost necessity to understand it well, in order to penetrate into the theory of intellectual phenomena. I shall be permitted, then, to dwell upon it for some time.

## FIRST SECTION

I

When we conceive that two objects resemble each other, the relation may be primary or secondary.

It often happens that two perceptions which present themselves simultaneously to the understanding, whether actual or only recollected, give rise to a third, more or less vivid, of the resemblance which the objects of the first two seem to us to have to each other; and provided that this third perception is not accompanied by the judgment whether the resemblance perceived is great or small, strong or weak (for which it is evident that we must compare this resemblance with others, and conceive between them a relation of a different species, which is that of more and less), the resemblance perceived is a primary relation.

But we cannot have many of these primary perceptions of resemblance (whether we experience them actually or only recollect them) without the relative perception of more and less arising, so that there are some resemblances comparatively vivid, and others weak. Then it is clear that we perceive relations of relations.

We arrive in this way at conceiving resemblance as a quality susceptible of infinite degrees, from that in which one object seems to us an exact repetition of the other, to that in which the resemblance seems to us to vanish altogether: to the [p. 72] highest degrees of resemblance we give the name of resemblances, and to the lowest degrees of resemblance we give the name of differences. In this sense resemblances and differences are nothing but different degrees of primary resemblance, and consequently are relations of relations.

It is rare that, in comparing two objects, we find no resemblance between them. Two horses, for example, of which we say that they are different, have nevertheless a very great resemblance to each other; a resemblance which we suppose and recognize when we give to the one and the other the common denomination horse. In what, then, does it consist that we find them different? In this, that their resemblance seems to us inferior to that which horses commonly have to one another. Were it superior, though not yet complete, we should call them similar. Hence resemblances and differences are often higher or lower degrees of resemblance between them; secondary relations; relations of relations. When we say, then, that two horses resemble each other, we do not mean merely that we perceive resemblance between them, but that this resemblance is one of the most vivid that is wont to exist between objects of the same class. And when we say that two horses differ, neither do we mean that there is no resemblance whatever between them; on the contrary, it is necessary that they have some, in order that we may consider them as belonging to one and the same class of beings, and that we may in consequence give them a common name. What we mean is that their resemblance seems to us to be among the least vivid that are wont to present themselves to us between the objects of a class.

It seems that in this intellectual scale of degrees of resemblance there ought to be a fixed point at which resemblances cease and differences begin, so that when the relation reached a certain particular degree of strength it would constantly take the first denomination, and when it did not reach it, the second. So it would be if in the judgment we form of the more or less of resemblance we referred to the whole amplitude of the scale, from its maximum term, in which one object is a faithful repetition of another, to the minimum term or zero, in which the [p. 73] resemblance is an evanescent quantity. But it is not so. In these judgments we refer to partial scales, I mean to more or less considerable parts of the total scale. All these partial scales coincide at the apex or maximum term; but the position of the minimum term is exceedingly variable; and consequently so is also the position of that middle term which serves as a limit between the resemblances to which we give the name of such and the resemblances which we are wont to call differences.

From this it follows that according as the class in which we consider two objects varies, the judgment we form of their resemblance necessarily varies. A tiger and a lamb, if we extend our view over the universality of animate things, will appear to us similar; if we confine it to the mammalian quadrupeds, we shall probably form a different judgment. If in the first case we call them similar and in the second not, it is because in the first the resemblance seems to us vivid, referred to a vast scale of resemblances, and in the second it seems to us weak, referred to a scale of much smaller amplitude.

We express also a secondary relation when, under the title of resemblance, we understand complete resemblance, that degree of resemblance in which one object would appear to us an exact repetition of the other, or, if you will, that degree in which two mental representations of one and the same invariable object resemble each other. In effect, when we judge that one object completely resembles another, we implicitly compare this resemblance with lesser ones. Without this implicit comparison we should perceive resemblance, but not complete resemblance.

We give, then, to the word resemblance three different senses: that of primary resemblance, into which the relation of more and less does not enter at all; that of complete resemblance; and that of resemblance greater than the mean resemblance of the class.

The word difference also signifies three different relations: non-resemblance, which is primary difference; a degree of resemblance lower than that of complete resemblance; and a degree of resemblance lower than the mean resemblance of the class in which the objects are considered.

[p. 74]

It would seem that there ought not to be any case in which we perceive a primary difference. What things can we compare that have not, in some respect, a resemblance to each other? The white and the black resemble each other as colors; all material substances, as capable of impressing the sensitive organs; all things that exist, or to which we attribute a fictitious existence, in this very reason of existing.

But a long time must have passed before the intelligence rose to these lofty generalizations, which suppose the perception of resemblances exceedingly faint or of little importance for ordinary life; and in this long period many of the differences that afterwards became relations of relations were primary relations.

The maxima, means and minima I have indicated are not to be understood so literally, as if the estimation of resemblances and differences were susceptible of mathematical exactness. When we say that two objects are similar or different, in the sense that their resemblance is greater or less than the mean of that collection of objects to which we extend our mental view, we perform two comparisons, each of which produces a different relative perception. The comparison of one object with the other gives us the perception of the resemblance that exists between them; and the comparison of this resemblance with those which are wont to exist between any objects whatever of the collection, makes us conceive it as great or small; which is the concept that we most ordinarily declare by the words resemblance or difference.

In this second comparison no mean is distinctly presented to the understanding; but the confused recollection of the resemblances perceived in the class produces nearly the same effect: just as, when we judge that a man is of great stature, we do not compare him precisely with a mean human stature: it is the confused memory of the human statures we are accustomed to see that suggests this judgment.

The double comparison mentioned is necessary to explain the various title of resemblance or difference which we give to a relation [p. 75] that is invariable, namely the resemblance between two objects which remain in one and the same being and in the same qualities, and which, considered in one class, appear to us to resemble each other, while in others we pronounce them different. From this double comparison it also arises that it is said, not only vulgarly but in philosophical language, that two objects, two men, for example, or two trees, have no resemblance whatever: an expression in which the minimum resemblance of the class is always left out of account.

Perceiving greater or less resemblance in things, we see them as it were approach or recede from one another. Between the color of the rose and that of snow we find, so to speak, a greater distance than between the color of snow and that of the lily; and between two sensations that belong to different senses, the distance seems to us greater still. Nearness and distance present themselves naturally to the soul as symbols of the greater or less resemblance between things, or of what we ordinarily call resemblance or difference. Nothing is more common in language than to represent these relations by metaphors drawn from the reciprocal situation of bodies in space.a

One and the same relation is called, as we have seen, resemblance or difference, according to the various aspects in which we regard it. This is exactly what happens with the relation of nearness or distance. In the great scene which the universe presents to the imagination, the moon is near to the earth and the earth to the sun, and on the contrary we regard these globes as

a Leaving aside the Greek language, where resemblances and differences were

often indicated by words which in their origin had signified, or which still signified, nearness and distance, in Latin similis comes from simul [together], a root also of simulare and simulacrum. From these Latin origins the Castilians took semejar [to resemble], as the French sembler [to seem] and resembler [to resemble]. From sembler, going back to the primitive meaning, asembler was formed, to join. Diferir [to differ] is to carry to different parts, as asemejarse [to resemble] is to join together. So great is the analogy which the common run of men believe they perceive between resemblance and nearness, difference and distance. [p. 76] enormously distant from one another, when we think of the distances which we are accustomed to measure and calculate for the uses of common life. If we narrow the ideal perspective, limiting it to our globe, we shall judge that Peru is far from Spain; and if we circumscribe it to a province, a distance of a few leagues will seem to us considerable. Reducing the perspective more and more, we may find a relation of distance between two quarters of the same city, between two apartments of the same house, or between two pieces of furniture in the same apartment.

Perhaps it will be imagined that the giving to two invariable objects the title now of similar, now of different, consists in our regarding them, so to speak, from different sides, and in the comparison falling upon different qualities. Two objects of the same color present themselves to us under different tangible forms; attending to the colors, we perceive resemblance, and attending to the forms, difference. But how do we perceive that the objects resemble each other under the first aspect? If, attending to color, we call two objects before us similar, it is because we judge that this resemblance is greater than that which ordinarily exists in the colors of objects of the same class: if from the same point of view we formed a contrary judgment, we should call them different. And how do we perceive that the two objects differ in tangible form? By comparing the degree of resemblance which we primarily perceive between their forms with the degrees of resemblance that are wont to present themselves to us between the forms of objects of the same class, and perceiving that these latter degrees are ordinarily higher: if from the same point of view we formed a contrary judgment, the forms of the two objects would seem to us to resemble each other. When we find, then, resemblance between two objects attending to color, and difference attending to tangible form, we make two different judgments, in each of which we perceive a secondary relation, comparing the degree of resemblance with a mean.

What we have said hitherto applies especially to the case in which the relation is wont to be expressed by saying, for example, that the objects compared are similar or different; we [p. 77] then avail ourselves of nouns or phrases which explicitly signify the relation of resemblance or difference.

II

But it often happens that the sign we employ to indicate this relation is a generic noun or phrase; e.g., man, eagle, fruit-bearing tree, full-crowned tree, animal covered with scales, etc. To say that an object is an eagle is to say that it has with the objects called eagles as much resemblance as these birds constantly have among themselves; that is, that it has with eagles a resemblance which is at least equal to the minimum of the class.

The beings comprised under a common denomination, under a generic noun or phrase, have each its peculiar qualities; a certain color, form, size; a certain degree of solidity, hardness, roughness, elasticity; a certain smell, taste, sound, etc. Each of these qualities is susceptible of many variations within one and the same class of beings; sometimes in one and the same individual. Thus not only does each quality vary much in different trees, but one and the same tree presents it to us in a long series of successive states, from that of the seed and the germ to that of adult age, in which the individual has developed a bulky form, composed of roots, trunk, branches, flowers and fruits, or rather, until it withers and dies. Each quality is consequently a variable type; variable from one individual to another; susceptible, perhaps, of successive variations in one and the same individual. The type of the tree is composed of all these particular types in which the tree takes various forms, various dimensions, various colors, various qualities, within a certain limit; that is, always preserving in each of them the minimum resemblance of the class.

When I say, then, that an object is an oak, I mean that, comparing it with the complex type of the objects I call oaks, I find that each of the qualities is comprised within the range of variations which, in [p. 78] the oaks, I have observed; I find, in short, that the new object has with oaks as much resemblance as the oaks I have observed constantly have among themselves. Resemblance in these cases is a secondary relation: I compare an object with a certain class of objects; and I not only find resemblance between the former and the latter, but, referring this resemblance to a certain scale, I find it equal, at the least, to the minimum of the class; and this is what we give to understand by saying that the object is an oak.

It will happen many times that we hesitate in this judgment. He who sees an eel for the first time does not probably call it a fish, but a serpent. In the variable type of the form of the fish which memory presents to him, the particular form of the eel has no place as yet. But finding afterwards that in all other respects the new object enters into the complex type of fishes, while in many of them it does not enter into the complex type of serpents, he changes his judgment, and calls it fish; adding from that time to the type of the form of fishes a new modification. Thus, by means of the observations we make in the whole course of our life, we go on determining with more and more precision the limits of each class, that is, the range of the modifications of which each of the qualities of the beings we comprehend in it is susceptible.

If after the comparison it seems to us that the type of the class is not applicable to the object, we say that it is not, for example, an oak, a fish, a metal. The negation then expresses difference; and difference is a degree of resemblance inferior to that of the minimum of the class.

III

Under another aspect the relation of resemblance may still present itself to us.

When we compare an object with a class of objects, we may find a certain resemblance between the former and the latter from the point of view of a particular quality, e.g. form; without [p. 79] our being therefore bound to give it the name of the class, because for this there would be required the conformity of the object with some one of the variable types of the class, from the point of view of all the qualities which the objects comprised in it present. We then have recourse to the words which explicitly signify the relation of resemblance, combining them with the name of the class. We say, for example, that the eel is like a serpent. The resemblance then refers, implicitly, to a particular quality, form; but the resemblance of form does not by itself authorize us to give the eel the name of serpent, except in a metaphorical sense. And if the phrase is negative, if we say, e.g., that a certain fruit is not like a pear, we shall mean that it has not with pears (especially from the point of view of the particular quality to which we attend, form and color, for example) the minimum degree of resemblance which pears constantly have among themselves.

## SECOND SECTION

IV

The idea commonly given of the relation of resemblance seems to me erroneous. According to it, to perceive resemblance between two objects is to perceive what they have in common. It is supposed that the two spiritual affections, simple or complex, which form the ideas of the two objects, A, B, are each divisible into two parts, of which the part P or Q is produced exclusively by A or B, and the part M is produced uniformly by both; M P being the total affection produced by A, and M Q the total affection produced by B. The greater, then, the common part M in relation to the peculiar part P or Q, the more similar will the objects appear to us: if they have no common part, the difference between them will be complete; and if they have no peculiar part, the resemblance will be complete.

But from this it would necessarily follow that between two things [p. 80] that are simple, which we know by means of elementary affections, we could find no other resemblance than the most perfect and complete; for if such things and the affections produced by them which make them known to us were each divided into two parts, one common and the other peculiar, they would cease to be simple. And who will deny that we can perceive resemblance between two objects of which we have simple perceptions, two colors, for example, without the resemblance between them being so perfect that the one is repeated in the other? The color of the poplar leaf resembles the color of the willow leaf: both are green; and yet we do not fail to perceive difference between the one and the other; so that, finding them at once similar and different, we cannot nevertheless resolve them into two parts, of which one is common and the other peculiar.

Let there be two colors, A, F, and let us suppose that A passes into F through a series of intermediate tints, B, C, D, E. Although the painter, mixing the colors A, F in various proportions, can produce the intermediate tints B, C, D, E, the sensations that represent them will not for that reason cease to be most simple; and no one surely will imagine that because an intermediate color C is made to result by mixing a certain quantity of A and a certain quantity of F, there is presented to consciousness, in the perception of that intermediate color, a complex sensation, composed of the sensation A and the sensation F. The sensation of the violet color, as consciousness perceives it, is no less simple than that of the colors blue or red, by mixing which we can produce the former. If we perceive, then, that in that series of colors there is resemblance between A and B, it is neither because the sensations produced by these two colors are exact repetitions of each other, for we suppose that there is a certain difference between them, nor because the said colors consist of a common element and a peculiar one, separately perceptible, since it is impossible for us to resolve the sensation produced by each color into different sensations.

I see the greatest evidence in the three following propositions: 1st. The sensation which represents to us any of the various shades or gradations of a color, from the degree of its greatest purity to that in which it is confounded with another, is [p. 81] as simple as the sensation which represents to us any of the extreme shades. 2nd. In a quality which the understanding knows by means of any simple spiritual affection, we cannot perceive different qualities. 3rd. The relations of resemblance that we perceive between simple qualities which do not completely resemble each other do not alter the simplicity of the spiritual affections by means of which we knew those qualities before comparing them. The human understanding lacks the faculty of decomposing its simple affections.

Let us pass to complex resemblances. Let us suppose two objects, each of which is known by affections of the soul of various kinds, and consists, therefore, of different qualities, which we shall call in the one of them A, B, C, D, and in the other a, b, c, d; so that A and a are qualities of the same kind, B and b qualities of another kind different from the preceding, and likewise C and c, D and d. The complete resemblance of the said objects resolves itself into the simple resemblances between A and a, between B and b, between C and c, between D and d. In this way the resemblance of two trees may be composed of a great number of partial resemblances: the trunk of both, for example, is cylindrical, the branches spreading, the form pyramidal, the leaves ovate, the color of these dark green, that of the bark brown, etc. Many of these partial resemblances are also complex: the pyramidal form, for example, consists of base, apex, sides, angles of the sides with each other and with the base; and the decomposition being carried to its last term, the trees may resemble each other at once in all or in the greater part of the elements which our sensations represent to us in them. The vividness of the complex resemblance is proportioned to the number, importance and vividness of the elementary resemblances.

Now, at the same time that we find great resemblance, or rather, a great number of resemblances, between two complex objects, it often happens that we perceive nothing that is rigorously common to the two. Two objects resemble each other in form and color, and nevertheless the form of the one is very far from being the exact repetition of the form of the other, and

## PHILOS.   6

[p. 82]

their respective colors approach each other, without our ceasing on that account to distinguish them. If we compare these two objects part by part, and carry the parallel to the last perceptible elements, perhaps we shall not find that nature has cast two of these in one and the same mold.

The resemblance of simple objects is simple, and consequently indefinable. The resemblance of complex objects is complex and resolves itself into simple relations of resemblance, which we can make use of to define or explain the complex resemblance.

Those who consider similar objects as composed of two portions, one common to all of them, and the other not, appear to me to suppose in the universe nothing but complete resemblances and differences, ignoring the successive gradations and the intermediate tints of which a simple quality is susceptible without ever ceasing to be such, and by means of which it goes on receding, so to speak, progressively from itself.

## THIRD SECTION

V

The perception of resemblance is what has given occasion to the general denominations with which we designate objects, and by means of which they have been distributed into mental collections, which we call classes, genera and species. This alone shows the great part which resemblance must have played in the formation of language. It being impossible to give a proper name to each of the objects we know, recourse was instinctively had to the expedient of imposing on them general denominations, or common nouns or appellatives, which is all one, according to the resemblances we went on observing in them. By virtue of the simplest and most obvious resemblances, some were called white, others green, red, yellow, blue; these sweet, those bitter; some rough, some smooth, [p. 83] etc.; and by virtue of more complex or more recondite resemblances, we gave them the names of bodies, spirits, animals, plants, stones, minerals, men, dogs, horses, tigers, soldiers, shepherds, merchants, old men, youths, children, etc. The resemblance of relations gave occasion to the establishment of other classes with other names, such as similar, different, prior, posterior, cause, effect, great, small, high, low, etc. By means of these common names there were distributed into classes all the objects of which we could have knowledge, and even all those which fancy could represent to us; and one and the same object received various names and belonged consequently to various classes, according to the resemblances it presented, now with some, now with other objects. The object, for example, which I have before my eyes belongs to the classes entity, body, vegetable, tree, green, leafy, tall, full-crowned; and is characterized in language by these and various other names.

Tal and cual [such, such as] are synonyms of similar; and quality originally signified the same as similar.a To ask what qualities an object has is the same as to ask what resemblances it has with the objects we already know.

I do not mean that qualities, considered as causes

a The usage of languages, by showing the true signification of words, leads us

sometimes to the origin of ideas. Let us observe the usage of these two words, tal and cual [such, such as].

Speaking of a Levite it is said in the book of Judges (Scio’s translation): “He took a knife, and dividing the corpse of his wife into twelve pieces, sent them to all the borders of Israel; and when they saw this, every one exclaimed, saying: ‘Never was such a thing seen in Israel.’” Who does not perceive that such here means the same as similar? We might vary the exclamation by saying: “Behold an event such as was never seen in Israel;” such as would signify the same as such, and consequently the same as similar. In the primitive language there was a single form for the two turns, and in the second it would have been said: “Behold an event such that it was never seen in Israel.” The identity of meaning of the words which grammarians denominate demonstrative with those which are called relative, is an indubitable philological fact, and no less important in the theory of the understanding than in that of languages. [p. 84] and objects of our perceptions, cease to be something absolute in themselves, and apart from all comparison of some objects with others. The smell and the color of a rose, that which makes it act in a particular way upon the sense of smell and sight, would not cease to exist in it, even if all corporeal nature were reduced to it alone. If on this supposition our soul could experience sensations and refer them to the rose, it is clear that they would represent to us the modes of being of the rose stripped of all relation with other objects. But let us restore the universe, and let us frame speech. Do we wish to indicate the affections of the soul which the perception of an object produces? We cannot do so, except by means of common names, which correspond to classes founded upon the relation of resemblance. To indicate the modes of acting of an object upon the soul, or what we call its modes of being, its qualities, is, by the nature of language, to indicate other known objects, which act in a similar manner upon the soul. In this way resemblances came to represent qualities, the modes of being. Cualidad in Castilian always has this second meaning; but there are not wanting languages in which this same word is taken, according to the different cases, now in the first, now in the second acceptation.a

Employing, then, common names, we indicate the resemblances of the object to which we apply them with other objects which are already known; and by means of these resemblances we make known the qualities of the former. But let it not be believed on this account that all common names and all the resemblances of which an object is susceptible correspond to as many distinct qualities. When I say that a flower is white and fragrant, I express two distinct qualities, of which the first is represented by a visual sensation, and the second by an olfactory sensation. Likewise, when I say that an object is hard and rough, I express two distinct qualities; for although hardness and

a In Greek, for example, hopoiótes is equivalent to the two Castilian words seme‐

janza and cualidad [resemblance and quality]. [p. 85] roughness are both represented by series of tactile sensations, mingled, as we shall see hereafter, with sensations of effort, these series are very different in their composition and signification. But when I say that a certain body has color, and that it is of a red color, and that it is of a scarlet color, although I express different resemblances, since the resemblance which all colors have among themselves is one thing, and that which makes me call some of them red another, and that which moves me to give to some of these the name of scarlet another, I do not suppose, notwithstanding, in all these expressions, applied to a certain body at a given instant, more than one identical quality represented by one identical sensation. That which in that particular body I call simply color, is the same as that which in that body I call red, and the same as I call scarlet. The whole difference is that the first resemblance makes that quality known somewhat vaguely and the other two in a manner sufficiently circumscribed, particularly the third.

Let us call qualities of objects those which we perceive, and attributes or predicates the signs by which we represent them in language: it is easy to see that there is not between the former and the latter the correlation or parallelism which many philosophers have imagined. A complex denomination, such as that of scarlet-red or sky-blue, may signify an elementary perception, and consequently a quality in which it is not possible to perceive distinct parts. To imagine, then, that two colors, the deep blue and the sky blue, resemble each other because each of them has two parts, one common, signified by the word blue, and another peculiar, signified by the word deep or sky, is to confound the understanding with language, qualities with attributes; and that confusion is what has given occasion to the false concept which has generally been formed of the relation of resemblance.

We shall return to this want of correspondence between qualities and attributes when we treat of generalization.

[PDF 102]

On the relation of equality and of more and less.

This relation is combined with that of resemblance: it is elementary and indefinable.—The relation of more and less presupposes that of resemblance. —Classifications of the sciences, without the relation of more and less.— Formation of language.—The substantive and the adjective.—In the more and less a relation of relation is sometimes comprised.—Tanto and cuanto express the relation of equality.—Ideas of quantity and number.—Every quantitative determination expresses a relation of equality.—Representation of every quantity by means of signs.—Numerical denomination is a sign-idea.—Elementary character of the numerical conception.—The idea of extension is also quantitative.—Measures of extension: they are numerical relations and consequently of equality.—Acceptation of the word measure.— Number as an aggregation of individuals.—Discrete quantities and continuous quantities.—The quantity of matter is discrete.—Corpuscular or atomistic hypothesis.—The quantities of extension and of weight are continuous. —Weight is an ideal measure, different from that which the atomistic system supposes.—The measure of continuous quantity is not adapted to duration; it has for its measure only a rational quantity.—Confused quantity, or quantity of intensity and vividness.—Measure of heat.—The degrees of heat.— Conclusion.—Appendix on the idea of the infinite.—The intuition of the infinite.—The idea of a finite thing does not suppose that of the infinite.—The infinite, as a sign-idea, is the only knowledge we can attain.

In comparing qualities, we conceive not only resemblances between them, but relations of another kind by virtue of which A appears to us, for example, more white than B, and B less white than A, or perhaps A and B appear to us equally white. We have already seen that a relation of this kind is frequently combined with that of resemblance, forming a [p. 87] relation of relation: we shall now consider it in itself. It may, then, present itself to us under three different forms, of which the second is the inverse of the first, and the third is the common limit of the other two. Under any of them the relation of equality or of more and less is elementary and indefinable.

It might be thought that if A appears to us greater than B, it is because we see in A the quantity B and another besides, which we call C; from which it seems to follow that the relation of more and less is in all cases complex, one of its elements being the relation of equality. But the resolution of the relation A>B into (B+C)>B does not advance us a step, because in this second expression the relation expressed by the sign > subsists without any decomposition. Apart from this reason, which I believe conclusive, there are many cases in which the resolution of A into B+C is impossible, or at least obscure. A length may appear to us greater than another, though we do not perceive the equality of the second with a certain determinate part of the first; and when we judge that one color is deeper than another, it is impossible to resolve the first into two portions, one of which equals the second.

The relation of more and less presupposes that of resemblance; in other terms, the relation of equality or inequality cannot be conceived except by comparing qualities of one and the same kind: resemblance, on the contrary, exists in very many things in which we can neither conceive nor imagine the more and less. We find, for example, a multitude of degrees in whiteness, in fragrance, in the vividness of ideas, in the acuteness of pains; but we cannot perceive more or less in the straight, the parallel, the circular, the triangular, the square, the prismatic, the cubic; at least, taking these words in their mathematical signification. In general, we cannot perceive the more or less in those qualities which reduce themselves to the mere existence of certain conditions in the objects compared. Consequently, whenever the minimum resemblance of the objects consists in the mere existence of determinate conditions (which is what commonly happens in the botanical and zoological classifications [p. 88] ), the name of that class, applied to an object, represents in it a quality in which we cannot conceive more or less. An object is not properly more man, nor more tree, nor more stone than another. And the same thing may be verified, in certain respects, in all classes, by whatever names they may be designated. It could not, for example, be said that space is more or less extended than matter, because in this comparison we should leave out of account the development of extension, which is what in it can be greater or less, and should attend only to the existence of a condition, that is, to the presence or absence in the objects compared of extraposition of points.

The names which signify classes founded upon the mere existence of a condition are ordinarily used as substantives. But as soon as, varying their signification, they admit of more or less, they take on the character of adjectives. Man, for example, is a being endowed with the aggregate of qualities which are characteristic of the human species; to possess or not to possess this aggregate of qualities is an invariable condition. But we may also understand by man the male endowed with courage and resolution in an eminent degree, and then it is clear that we have no longer to do with invariable conditions but with qualities susceptible of more and less, and for that reason we may use the name as an adjective, saying, for example, Peter is more of a man than John.

There are also adjectives which signify invariable conditions. One thing is not more or less finite than another, nor more or less infinite, nor more or less extended, understanding by extended that in which we can conceive extraposition of parts, nor more or less material, understanding by matter all that which can impress the senses, etc.

When we say, without confining ourselves expressly to a particular quality, that one body is greater than another, extension or volume is understood. When we speak of more or fewer men, trees or stones, we refer to number. When we speak of a great man or of a great writer, the quality to which we confine ourselves is moral force, the eloquence [p. 89] , the wit, according to the case. Quantity always refers to a quality, whether we express it, or whether either the usage of the language or the circumstances in which one speaks suggest it to the understanding without its being necessary to express it.

As, by attending to the resemblance or difference of qualities, we have distributed things into classes, so, by attending to the more or less of qualities, and comparing them in this respect with one another, we have subdivided these classes.

The relation of more and less is often combined with itself, forming relations of relations. If A appears to us much greater than B, we perceive not only the superiority of A over B, but this very superiority appears to us great with respect to that which is wont to exist between objects of one and the same class.

We are not always accustomed to express the second term of the relation of more and less. When we say, for example, that one ship is of greater capacity than another, we express the second term; but when we say that a tower is high, that a house is large, that a pain is intense, that a perception is vivid, we leave it unspoken, because in this case it is understood, without need of further expression, that the parallel is made with the average height of towers, with the average size of houses, or with the average degree of the intensity of pains, or of the vividness of perceptions.

Tanto and cuanto signify the same as equal; and from cuanto was derived cuantidad or cantidad (quantity), which in its origin signified equality.(a) What is it, in effect, to state the quantity of a

(a) The use of these words clearly shows their primitive signification. When we

say, tiene tanta hermosura como gracia [she has as much beauty as grace], the sense is the same as when we say, tiene igual hermosura que gracia [she has beauty equal to grace]; the construction alone varies, in which language is often capricious. In these verses of Lope de Vega: “Cuanto contento encierra / Cantar su herida el sano, / I en la patria su cárcel el cautivo; / Tanto en cantar mi libertad recibo” [As much contentment as the healed man finds in singing of his wound, and the captive in singing of his prison in his native land, so much do I receive in singing of my liberty] the synonymous signs tanto and cuanto, applied to the two terms of the comparison, express the equality between them. [p. 90] thing? To state its measure, that is, to state another known thing to which the first is equal.

But as the more or less of a quality is in the quality itself, before all comparison or measure (for the foundation of the relations we perceive in things must necessarily exist in them), that more or less of qualities, in so far as subject to comparison or measure, was properly called quantity.

Number is that quantity which we consider in similar things from the point of view of their aggregation. That in which there is no aggregation is called one, as one horse, one tree. When there is an aggregate or collection, we determine it by the words two, three, etc. The idea of number involves that of resemblance, because the understanding aggregates, to form number, only things which are or appear to it to be similar, or which belong, by reason of their resemblance, to a certain class, as three horses, four animals, six trees.

Comparing one number with another, we perceive that they are equal, or that one is greater and the other less. This quantity of aggregations is distinguished from all others by a peculiar character: its successive increments are perfectly distinct, and as easy to discern as to represent in memory and in language. Nothing is less exposed to confusion (whether we make it the object of our own thoughts, or transmit it by means of language to the understandings of others) than the ideas signified by the words two, four, twenty, a hundred, etc.

Since to determine a quantity is to find or designate another quantity of the same kind, but familiar or known, to which the first is equal, we determine a numerical quantity by means of the equality between it and another known numerical quantity. This second is the measure of the quantity which is compared with it, and which it represents and makes known.

It was a matter of indifference to choose as the measure of numerical quantities any kind whatever of numerical quantity, provided that it [p. 91] were familiar to us, and we could easily find the equality between the more or less of the measuring quantity and the more or less of the numbers which we might wish to measure with it. Any aggregate whatever which lent itself indefinitely to these two conditions might serve us as a measure of the numerical quantities of all other aggregates.

Nature gave us in the fingers of our hands the first aggregate that served us as a measure. This aggregate lends itself readily to the computation, counting or measurement of numerical quantities, for we carry it with us everywhere; and as it is so familiar to us, its varieties of more and less represent to the understanding with the greatest clearness the numerical quantities or, to adopt the common and abbreviated mode of expressing this idea, the numbers which we measure with it.

The numerical signs of the Romans are in great part mimetic hieroglyphs of the varieties of more and less of this measuring quantity. The signs I, II, III, IIII (for in ancient times the sign IV was not used) represent so many fingers of one hand; the sign V represents the five fingers of the extended hand; the signs VI, VII, VIII, VIIII (in ancient times the sign IX was not used) represent the one hand, and besides one, two, three, or four fingers of the other; and the sign X, which is composed of two V’s joined at their vertices, represents all the fingers of both hands extended.

But this measuring aggregate did not lend itself with facility to the further increments of numerical quantity. To extend its application, it became necessary to multiply the hands, representing upon a surface as many hands or fingers as were required for equality of measure. As the simple sign of greatest value was that of the number ten, proceeding by tens we became familiarized with the decuple progression, adopted in the greater part of languages for the indication of numerical quantities.

Following the procedure we have just indicated, those numerical quantities could be readily represented which did not require a great number of signs. They went as far as XXXXVIIII, [p. 92] hieroglyph of nine hands and four fingers, or forty-nine units.

Language next presented to us a more complete and infinitely more convenient instrument. We gave names to numbers, and, linking these names one with another in memory, we composed the series 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc., capable of being continued indefinitely, as far as we pleased, by adding new simple and compound names, parallel to the signs of the Arabic numeration. If, then, an aggregate of grains presents itself and I wish to determine its number, I do no more than apply the series of names which I carry with me in memory to the series of grains which I have before me, pronouncing, on seeing the first, one, on touching or seeing the second, two, on touching or seeing the third, three, and so on successively until none is left. Each of these names indicates to me the place which it occupies in the series; and the name which corresponds to the last grain suggests to me all the steps by which I have arrived, or can arrive, at it, and thus gives me the power of representing clearly to myself and to others the total number of grains.

The artificial procedure by which we form these names, continuing the series as far as we wish, supplies us, then, with an infinite variety of measures, which lend themselves to all imaginable things, which can be carried everywhere in memory, and which, applying themselves with the utmost facility to the numbers of all the aggregates we perceive or have occasion to indicate to others, have besides the advantage of being expressed with a clearness and precision which language attains in no other kind of relations.

In truth, the numbers which we can represent distinctly in the understanding are few. In what does the mental representation of two hundred thousand differ from the mental representation of two hundred and fifty thousand? But it is not necessary to go so far. In what does the mental representation of twenty differ from the mental representation of twenty-one? Their names sketch for us confused images of the procedure by which we might arrive at them, if [p. 93] we should attempt it; images in which we merely catch a rough glimpse of aggregates more or less great, but indeterminate, and so much the more indistinct and obscure the farther we advance in the procedure and the more rapidly they are formed. There remains to us, then, by this means in the understanding no other distinctive mark of a particular number somewhat high, than the very name with which we pronounce it and which we have the faculty of decomposing, though we almost never resort to it. We avail ourselves in this case, as in many others, of sign-ideas, which take the place of true ideas, and which awaken only vague and indefinable shadows, capricious offspring of the imagination. In what, then, consists the clearness and precision of numerical denominations? Solely in the facility of decomposing them, employing for that purpose different multiples of the unit. We readily conceive the number nine as composed of the aggregates four and five, or of the aggregates three and six. We readily conceive the number ten, which is called a ten, as composed, for example, of the aggregates six and four. We then conceive the number one hundred, called a hundred, as composed of ten tens; the aggregate one thousand, called a thousand, as composed of ten hundreds; the aggregate 7643, as composed of seven thousands, six hundreds, four tens and three units, etc. It is true that after a few steps in this decomposition, the decomposition itself would no longer leave true ideas or mental representations; it would become potential instead of actual; but it would always furnish us with precise denominations of the difference and of any other elementary relations between any two numbers whatever, and would enable us to carry out upon their names, as sign-ideas of the numbers, prolonged and exact reasonings, to which writing, that is, Arithmetic, has given the utmost facility and security.

Extension, linear, superficial or solid, is another of the qualities with which we most frequently associate the idea of quantity, which in this particular sense is more properly called magnitude, size, bulk. We determine the quantity of extension of a thing or, to express ourselves [p. 94] more briefly, we determine the extension of a thing, by comparing it with another extension of the same kind which serves it as a measure. For measures were preferred the extensions best known of all, and such as could be found at hand, whenever it was a question of applying them physically to the others. Such were, for example, the length of the human foot for measures of length; the surface of the square foot for measures of surface, and the volume of the cubic foot for measures of volume. But as the length of the foot of the adult man is extremely various, it became necessary to fix it, by substituting a board of wood or metal of determinate length, which has preserved in many countries the name of foot. We have various measures of length, such as inch, span, foot, yard, mile, league, etc.; the same holds in the other kinds of extension. But even if we had many more, how could we determine by them, by means of the relation of equality, modes so infinitely various as those of the quantity of extension? Number supplies this want. The length of the foot once known, for example, we were able to take as known the length of as many feet as were necessary to equal, placed continuously and successively, the length in question. Other measures, greater and smaller, which had a determinate relation to the foot, were adopted at the same time, such as the yard (three feet), the inch (the twelfth part of the foot). For the convenience of language, names were likewise given to the multiples of these measures, and in place of a certain number of hundreds or thousands of feet, they said a stadium, a mile, a league. Forming in the same manner aggregates of tenths, hundredths and thousandths of the foot, or of any other familiar length, we can now measure and represent a quantity of this kind with whatever precision we please.

The word measure has signified two things: the entire quantity with which we equal another, and in this sense, which is that in which we have used it hitherto, the measure of the length of this table is 7 feet, 8 inches and 43 hundredths of an inch; or the unit of measure, that is, the quantity which, taken a certain [p. 95] number of times, is equal to another quantity, and in this sense the foregoing expression of the length of the table involves three different measures, the foot, the inch, and the hundredth of an inch. To avoid doubts, we shall say in the first sense measure, and in the second unit of measure or simply unit.

In number properly so called, which is the aggregation of similar individuals, for example, men, trees, houses, there is a natural unit, which is the individual: namely, the man, the tree, the house. An individual is properly that which cannot be divided into other things of its kind. A table, for example, may be divided into a thousand pieces, but none of these will any longer be a table. On the contrary, in a portion of water, there being for us no individuals, there is likewise no natural unit. For if we take that portion and divide it into any number of parts, and each of these into others smaller, until we stop at the smallest perceptible particles, in each subdivision the water will remain similar to itself, and always water.

Quantities are discrete which consist of individual units, naturally distinct. Continuous quantities, on the contrary, are those in which there is no distinction of individuals, and which we can consequently divide and subdivide as we please, adopting for unit of measure any quantity of the same kind that seems to us convenient, and even varying the unit at our pleasure. Such are the quantities of extension and of weight.

But certain quantities are continuous for us because it is not possible for our senses to reach the natural unit. Thus, in the corpuscular or atomistic hypothesis, according to which all bodies are aggregates of atoms, or of particles ultimately indivisible, the quantity of matter would be for us a discrete quantity, if our senses were able to perceive the natural unit, the atom, and to count the number of atoms of which each material substance is composed. In default of this natural unit we avail ourselves of an arbitrary unit, taking, for example, a cubic foot of water for the [p. 96] measure of the quantity of matter of any portion whatever of this liquid.

If the quantity of matter is, in the atomistic hypothesis, a rigorously discrete quantity, and continuous only for us, by reason of the inadequacy of our perceptive faculties, other quantities, on the contrary, are absolutely without a natural unit, and are rigorously continuous. Such is the quantity of extension. Let us divide, for example, and subdivide the volume of a body as many times as we please: let us pursue this operation with the understanding, where the senses leave it; each subdivision will give us volumes more or less small; but always volumes, that is, quantities of extension, ulteriorly divisible. For how is it possible to conceive volume without conceiving figure? And how is it possible to conceive figure without conceiving a whole, which results from parts differently situated? And how is it possible to conceive a part of these, if we do not represent it to ourselves under a certain volume?

The quantity of weight is another rigorously continuous quantity. For let us suppose a quantity of matter as small as the imagination can conceive it: let us descend to the millionths of a grain of wheat. Each of these must have a certain quantity of weight, which is ulteriorly divisible into two halves, three thirds, four fourths, etc.

It is to be observed, however, that the equality of quantities of weight, by virtue of which we measure one by another, is not a matter of perception but of reasoning. We perceive the weight, or the force with which a body tends to descend to the earth, by means of the effort which is necessary to sustain it. In order, therefore, that we might perceive the equality of two quantities of weight, it would be necessary that we could perceive the equality of two respective efforts; a perception of which we are not capable, at least with the degree of exactness which is indispensable for the uses of life. If we judge, then, with certainty that one weight is equal to another, it is because we infer it from the equilibrium of the two in the balance, or from some other analogous observation.

There are quantities which we cannot measure by means of others [p. 97] of the same kind. If we have ground for believing that they are proportional to others which can be compared with one another, the equalities and proportions which we observe in these represent to us the equalities and proportions of those. We say in this case that one kind of quantity is measured by another.

Thus it is believed to happen with quantities of matter. If this expression signifies the number of atoms or elementary molecules, absolutely indivisible, of which bodies are composed, it results that in one and the same kind of bodies and under the same conditions, the quantity of matter bears proportion to the volume, and consequently to the weight. But, in comparing different bodies, weight cannot be considered as the measure of the quantity of matter, except on the supposition that all the elementary molecules, all the material atoms, have exactly equal weight; a supposition of which, even admitting the atomistic theory, I do not believe we have sufficient proof.

This is so if by quantity of matter is understood the number of elementary molecules. And if we do not understand this expression so, what other sense can we give it? Either it is necessary to regard quantity of matter and quantity of weight as synonymous expressions (in which case to say that the first is measured by the second would not be to affirm a fact, but to make a definition), or it must be confessed that our valuation of the quantity of matter rests upon two suppositions, which have not been proved up to the present, nor can perhaps be proved: that of the corpuscular or atomistic theory, and that of the exact equality of weight of the elementary molecules among themselves.(a)

## PHILOS.                               7

(a) It is not impossible that the material molecules are infinitely divisible, so that

the division never reaches in them a term at which they can no longer be resolved by the forces of nature into physically separable parts. Nor is there any repugnance in supposing, the atomistic theory granted, that the elementary molecules have not all the same weight, or that there are some destitute of all weight.

[p. 98]

We can measure continuous quantity, either by applying to it successively an identical unit, as when we measure the length of a room by the length of the yard; or by applying to it simultaneously many units which are equal or which have a determinate ratio to one another, as when we measure the weight of a body placed in one of the scales of the balance, by equilibrating it with two, three, four or more bodies placed in the other scale, whose weights are either all equal or have some known ratio to one another. There is only one continuous quantity which we cannot measure in either of these ways, and that is the quantity of duration. Let us measure, for example, the duration A by the duration of a certain number of rotations of the earth: it is clear that in such a case we do not apply to the duration A identical units successively, but distinct units, and units among which it is impossible for us to perceive whether the quantities of duration are equal or have a determinate ratio to one another. Being unable to compare the rotations with one another so as to perceive whether their quantities of duration are equal, or in what ratio these stand to one another, we compare them with another series of phenomena, for example, with the oscillations of a pendulum. Two rotations being accomplished during equal numbers of oscillations of the pendulum, we judge that the durations of the former are equal to one another, and we shall be so much the more warranted in forming this judgment, the greater the number of comparisons that give us the same result of equality, whether by observing successively many rotations, or by making many pendulums oscillate simultaneously.

By comparing in this manner two or more series of phenomena, natural or artificial, we assure ourselves of the isochronism of the units of each phenomenon: a relation which is not perceived immediately, but is deduced from others by reasoning.

There is another kind of quantity which we call confused, because in it the aggregation of parts is in no way perceived, as it is perceived in discrete and continuous quantities. This kind of quantity is ordinarily called intensity or vividness; and it is the only one which we can conceive in a multitude of [p. 99] qualities and affections, for example, pleasure, pain, attention.

That of heat is a quantity of the same kind. When I perceive that heat increases, I do not discern the new quantities which are added to the previous quantity; and if, comparing two bodies, A and B, I find that A is hotter than B, I cannot on that account perceive in the heat of A two distinct portions, between one of which and the heat of B there is a relation of equality.

The confusion of the parts makes it impossible, in order to measure these quantities, to apply to them, successively or simultaneously, an identical quantity of their kind; an impossibility which constitutes confused quantities essentially.

It is true that we may sometimes find such a connection between a confused quantity and a discrete or continuous quantity, that as the first increases the second increases at the same time; but so long as it is not proved that the increments of both are proportional, which from the very nature of confused quantities is impossible, the second quantity cannot properly be regarded as a measure of the first. Experience shows that, within certain limits, as the heat of a body increases, the liquids with which it is put in contact are notably dilated. This observation led to the invention of the thermometer, an instrument which places before the eye the various quantities of dilatation of a liquid contained in it, indicating thus the increment and decrement of the heat which produces them. But there is no reason whatever for believing that the quantities of dilatation of a liquid correspond to proportional quantities of heat. In reality we do not know what precise meaning should be given to the expression quantity of heat. We are ignorant of the nature of the agent which, acting upon matter, dilates it, evaporates it, consumes it, fuses it, reduces it to ashes, and which, acting upon the living body, produces the organic impression from which results the sensation of heat in the soul. We can measure neither the quantity of the agent, nor the forces which it displays in the production of those effects. Giving to this unknown agent the name of caloric, and applying to bodies the thermometer [p. 100] , we shall be able to say, at most, that two quantities of caloric are equal, or that one is greater than another; but in this second case the thermometer is incapable of showing us the ratio in which they stand.

We represent to ourselves the various modes of confused quantity as successive steps which the quantity takes, now in one direction, now in the contrary, according as it increases or decreases. For this reason we call these modes degrees, which means steps.

At the beginning all quantities were for us confused. Perceiving obscurely their equalities and inequalities, we accustomed ourselves little by little to compare them with determinate units, which we learned to multiply and divide. Thus we arrived at the idea of the aggregation of homogeneous parts from which measurable quantities result. But all these were at first discrete for us. Time appeared to us simply a succession of days, distance a succession of steps. Continuous quantity was the last of which we were able to form an idea. The indeterminateness of the unit, and infinite divisibility, are the distinguishing marks of continuous quantity, the second of which could not be comprehended until late; and to the greater part of men this epoch of the understanding never comes.

## APPENDIX

In the idea of every continuous quantity the idea of the infinite is involved; and although this is not the fitting place to examine this second idea, I think it necessary to anticipate here some observations upon it. To say that we have an intuition of the absolute and abstract infinite, that is, separated from the things which we represent to ourselves as infinite, is to hazard a proposition belied by our own consciousness; let each one consult his own, and say whether he finds in his understanding an idea which represents the infinite as finite things are represented, which have been subject to the reach of the senses or of consciousness. [p. 101] things are represented, which have been subject to the reach of the senses or of consciousness.

It is said that we cannot conceive a finite thing without the infinite, by that very fact, presenting itself to the understanding, and an idea of infinitude being formed in it. But in this argument two distinct things are confounded. It is not the same thing to have an idea of a finite thing, as to conceive it as a finite thing. The latter certainly supposes that the understanding has formed some idea of the infinite, from which it distinguishes the idea of the object to which it applies the contrary qualification: the former does not suppose it. In order that a child may represent distinctly to itself two apples or three pears, it is not necessary that the idea of an infinite number of apples or of pears should occur to it, and much less that of the abstract infinite, that is, separated from all number, from all extension, from all that is susceptible of more and less.

We have two kinds of ideas: the one proper, which are nothing else than remembered perceptions, absolute or relative; the other improper, imperfect, supplementary; intellectual signs which take the place of ideas properly so called, with respect to the things which the perceptive faculties of the understanding cannot reach. The idea of the infinite belongs to this second kind. We have, without doubt, an intellectual sign to represent it to ourselves, a sign which is not strictly an idea, but which takes the place of one and serves us equally well.

When we say that the series 1 + ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + 1/16 + 1/32 + etc. is equal to 2, the infinite number of terms of which the first member of this equation is composed is sufficiently signified by the possibility of continuing the progression as far as we please without any limit. A progression continuable ad libitum [at pleasure], and the negation of a term which limits it, are the elements of the sign-idea which represents the infinity of the number of terms; and there is no danger of this idea leading us into error, so long as we do not suppose a final term in the aforesaid progression. In this manner we can conceive the infinite in any matter whatever: its sign-idea is that of a progression, of an aggregation, carried to a certain point, and therefore truly finite, but susceptible of being continued at our [p. 102] pleasure, without end; a susceptibility represented, if it is permissible to say so, by the et cetera of the mathematical formula. This intellectual sign is that which serves us for all our thoughts and speculations upon the infinite; and with it we must needs content ourselves, however it may grieve us, because in our understanding there is room for no other.

[PDF 119]

On succession and coexistence.

The perception of before and after is relative, and yet elementary like that of coexistence.—Succession, as a series of determinations of a cause, gives the first idea of duration.—Objection of Thomas Reid.—Quantitative determination of duration.—The idea of duration, as a continuous quantity, is only a further progress of the same idea.—Duration expresses the constancy of a being according to another duration taken as a unit of measure.—Reference to the preceding chapter.—The idea of duration may be resolved into the idea of time.—Idea of eternity; it is relative to that of time.—Every conception of time, the vastest, has no objective existence; it is a sign-idea.— Computation of time.—Appendix on the opinion of the sensationalist school, with that of Mr. Cousin.—The idealist school.

The conception of A’s being before B, or of B’s being after A, which is to express one idea in different ways, arises from the two perceptions of A and B, one of which at least must be recollected; for if they were actual, we could conceive no succession between A and B, but coexistence; and it is distinguished no less from the perception of A and the perception of B, than from the simple aggregate of both. Consequently, the perception of before and after, or of what we call succession, is a relative perception.

From the fact of experiencing successive affections it does not necessarily follow that we must perceive succession. How, then, does it come about that the two perceptions of A and B produce a judgment of a certain kind, by virtue of which we say that A is [p. 104] succeeded by B, or that B is preceded by A? I believe it is impossible to give a reason for it, and that we must regard it as one of the primordial phenomena of the understanding. There is no man of so slight a capacity that he does not distinguish the succession of things from their resemblance and from all the other relations he is able to conceive between them; and yet it seems to me impossible to explain it.

We shall place it, then, among the elementary relations.

Priority and posteriority are truly one and the same form of succession, but considered, if one may so say, from opposite sides. Succession and coexistence are two forms of one and the same kind of relation, and constitute, so to speak, the boundary between priority and posteriority. The terms of succession are antilogous, and those of coexistence homologous. Both seem to me equally elementary and indefinable.

By the succession of our perceptions we perceive, intuitively or representatively, the succession of acts with which any cause operates upon our mind, producing intuitions, if the cause is our own mind, or sensations, if the cause is a corporeal object. This cause then seems to us to succeed itself. If it gives us a long series of perceptions, there will arise from these a long series of judgments, in each of which the object we are considering will seem to us to succeed itself. Thus we form the first idea of duration. To say that a thing seems to us to succeed itself in a series, more or less long, of acts, between which we suppose not the smallest interval, is to say that it seems to us to endure more or less.

It will be objected, on the authority of Thomas Reid, that if a series of acts has duration, it is because each act in itself has it; for otherwise duration would consist of parts that had no duration; which would be as absurd as to say that the extended is composed of unextended parts. To say, then, that duration is a series of acts would be the same as to say that duration is a series of durations. There would remain, [p. 105] then, to be explained wherein consists the duration of each of the acts that compose the series.

But this difficulty only proves that our first ideas of the duration of things could not have been so perfect as those which we afterwards form by reasoning. All duration consists necessarily of successive acts, each of which, however brief and fugitive we may suppose it, must endure more or less; but it is evident that there exists a limit at which we can no longer perceive anything but elementary successive acts. Otherwise the perception of duration would consist of an infinite number of perceptions, which is absurd.

Duration, then, with respect to the understanding that perceives it, is a series of indivisible acts which we call instants. Consequently, we perceive duration as a quantity consisting of individual units, that is, as a discrete quantity. And since our first ideas of any objects whatever can be nothing else than our perceptions committed to memory, it is evident that the first idea of duration must have represented it to us under this type of discrete quantity. This idea will doubtless be imperfect, compared with that which we form later, or rather, with that which the metaphysician and the mathematician form by reasoning, and to which the greater number of men never attain. But, imperfect as it may be, we have in it all that is necessary for comparing durations, perceiving their more and their less, measuring them, and, in a word, for the exercise of all the intellectual functions which have duration for their object.

Not only does this seem to me to be the way in which we at first conceive duration, but I believe that we cannot in any other way apprehend originally any species of continuous quantity, because the idea of continuous quantity, as we have already observed, involves the idea of infinite divisibility, and because we can form this second idea only by imagining divisions and subdivisions without limits. To each subdivision we apply the idea of a discrete quantity, and the indefinite progress of the subdivisions is what forms the type of continuous quantity. Adding, then, in the progress of the [p. 106] intelligence, to the vulgar and primitive concept of duration the concept of its infinite divisibility, so that each succession of the series resolves itself imaginarily into other series of successions, without any limit, we arrive at length at an idea of duration as perfect as it is possible for the human understanding to form.

We compare one duration with another, and judge of their respective quantity, by means of the simultaneity or coexistence of our perceptions. Let there be, for example, two objects, I, Z, of which I excites in us the successive perceptions a, b, c, and Z the successive perceptions m, n, o, p, q. If we suppose that a coexists with o, b with p, and c with q, the duration of Z will appear to us composed of two portions, one of them equal to the whole duration of I, and therefore the duration of Z will appear to us greater than the duration of I. Nor is it necessary, in order to judge of the respective duration of two objects, that the coexistence of the perceptions produced by them should actually take place; for if an object gives us perceptions between which more or less intervals have elapsed, the experience we have of the constant duration of a being, although revealed only at longer or shorter intervals, enables us to supply by the imagination the actual perceptions which in those intervals we have failed to have, and to affirm deductively the coexistence of the object with all those which in the same intervals produced perceptions in us, or which would have produced them, had we been within their reach. In this manner a particular duration may be adopted as a unit of measure for all the others. But, as all duration is of itself transitory and fugitive, it is necessary to adopt as a unit of measure a phenomenon which is continually reproduced and with durations which we have reason to suppose equal. Such is the alternation of light and darkness which we call day, or the period of the different phases of the moon, which for many peoples constitutes the month, or that of the different seasons which forms the year. These units of measure are natural and obvious, and are in use among the most barbarous nations. For measuring durations less than the day, as hours, minutes and [p. 107] seconds, we compare them with certain series of artificial phenomena, continually produced by means of machines constructed for this sole purpose, and all the more necessary the more intellectual culture and industry advance. As to the isochronism of the successive units which measure duration, we refer to the preceding chapter.

It is to be noted that when we perceive that many things coexist, the duration of each of them is identified in our mind with the durations of all the others, or in other words, we conceive that all of them have a common duration; for as we apply to them an identical measure of years, months, days, hours, etc., we represent the quantity measured, which is different in each of them, by the measuring quantity, which is one and the same for all. And since the universe presents to us an immense aggregate of beings which coexist, it is in a certain way natural to us to consider duration as something common to all of them, and belonging exclusively to none. Duration in this sense is called, more properly, time; duration does not truly exist except in the things that endure; time seems to us to have an independent and separate existence, to which the existence of all the objects we perceive is referred.

It follows from this that time is a creature of the imagination; because duration does not exist except in the things that endure, as extension or whiteness does not exist except in things extended or white.

Nature, by establishing a continuous succession of days and years, and a constant ratio between the duration of the day and that of the year, has formed a graduated scale of time, which men have perfected by forming of a quantity of years the century, dividing the year into months, each of which is composed of a determinate number of days; subdividing the day into hours, the hour into minutes, and the minute into seconds. As we can add days to days, years to years, and centuries to centuries, imaginarily, it results that this scale is infinite, and that it is not given us to perceive or imagine any duration which does not coexist with a segment of it, which consequently measures it. The [p. 108] duration of the first Punic War, for example, is measured by saying that it lasted so many years, months and days. Moreover, by fixing on this scale one or more points at determinate distances from the present moment, and referring to them the beginning and the end of any duration whatever, we determine the individual segment of the scale with which the duration in question coincided. Let one of these points be, for example, the beginning of the vulgar era, the interval between which and the present moment, though incessantly increasing, is known to all. By saying that the first Punic War began on such a year, month and day before Christ, and ended on such a year, month and day before the same epoch, we determine on the scale of time the individual segment with which the duration of that war coexisted.
