When it is asked how long a thing lasted, we wish to know the length, so to speak, of the coexistent segment of the scale; and when it is asked at what time a thing happened, we wish to know the interval between its existence and a fixed point, whose distance from the present moment is supposed to be known. Whence it is seen that besides understanding by the word time an indefinite duration, corresponding to a series of centuries, years and days in which no beginning or end is fixed, it is also taken in the sense of a particular segment of this infinite scale; whether the length of this segment alone is expressed, as when it is said that a person lived so many years, or his situation on the scale is determined by means of a fixed point in it generally known, as when it is said that a person lived from such a year of the vulgar era to such a year of the same.

The infinity of time is called eternity. The least perceptible parts of time are called moments or instants. Each instant is called present with respect to that act of our mind with which it coexists. Time is an indefinite and continuous series of present moments.

Time is like an indefinite straight line along which the present moment moves in a constant direction and with a uniform velocity, dividing it into two parts, past time and future time. The duration of all events [p. 109] and of all phenomena, spiritual or material, past or future, forms so many segments of this line, and all the instants perceived or perceptible form so many points in it. But our understanding does not stop here. It imagines fractions of time much smaller than the perceptible, and divides and subdivides them to infinity. It imagines minds for whom the millionth part of a second, or the millionth of this millionth, is as easily perceptible as the entire unit is to us. It comes many times to represent by figures, in the duration of the phenomena it observes, fractions of duration which by their extreme swiftness are altogether imperceptible to us. Supposing, for example, a uniform motion along a straight line a million leagues in length, if we have means of ascertaining that a body traverses this length in a second of time, a very simple arithmetical operation will show us that each league is traversed in a millionth of a second.

But let it be borne in mind that these imaginations, these ideas, of quantities too high or too minute, do not form true ideas, true imaginations, true mental representations, adequate to their object, but merely sign-ideas, ideas of numbers or of names, which perform in the understanding the office of the others.

The past is the only part of time of which we can have knowledge: the future is an unknown land into which we take a step at every instant. The events of which we have been witnesses, and, from another and more comprehensive point of view, the notable facts which history records, leave in the course of time so many landmarks to which all other existences are referred. Each of these landmarks is an epoch. The destruction of Troy, the founding of Rome, the birth of the Saviour, are so many epochs, and each of them gives a beginning to an era, that is, to a series of years, which begin to be counted from the respective epoch. Nor is it necessary that this or that landmark should have coincided with the year to which we refer it, provided that the interval between that year and the present moment be determined in any manner. Thus, although the year of the birth of Christ [p. 110] has not coincided with the first of our vulgar era, as in fact it did not coincide, no inconvenience for computations follows from this, provided that the relation between the initial year of the era and the year of the birth of the Saviour be determined; for the essential thing is to assign for each era a fixed point of comparison known to all, whatever the historical name that may be given it. Others understand by era, epoch, and by epoch, era. The transition between these two ideas is so slippery that without noticing it we frequently slide from the one to the other.

## APPENDIX

M. Cousin accuses Locke of confounding two distinct ideas, succession and duration. I distinguish these ideas, though in a manner which assuredly does not square with the doctrine of the illustrious French philosopher. According to my way of conceiving, the perception of the first is not a simple conception of the idea of the second, that is, a certain mode of the soul, upon which, according to the laws of the understanding, there follows in it the idea of the second, which is supposed to be wholly distinct. Duration is a series of successions. Succession is, so to speak, the integrant element of duration. A thing endures because it continually succeeds itself, without any interval.

The sensationalist school erred without doubt, if, as is imputed to it, it believed it found in sensation alone, or in intuition alone, passive modifications of the soul, all that was needed to form the idea of duration and of time. It was not necessary that, perceiving first the lightning and then the thunder, first a judgment and then a desire, we should conceive that the one was before and the other after. We might have been so constituted that from each of these two pairs of perceptions there should not arise in the soul a concept, a perception, in which we should see them succeed one another. This concept is the work of the soul exercising its activity upon the sensations and the intuitions, necessary [p. 111] no doubt in order that the soul may form it, but necessary as conditions, not as elements.

The idealist school, on the other hand, although it had reason for regarding the idea of duration and of time as a peculiar product of the activity of the soul, had none for separating the idea of succession from the idea of duration and of time, of which it is the element. This idea is not a mere condition, which being fulfilled the idea of duration and of time rises in the soul as if by enchantment. The condition must figure farther back: it is in the perceptions from whose comparison results the conceiving that one object is before and another after; a relative concept, like that of resemblance or of quantity, and which, like all those of its class, arises in the soul by virtue of the juxtaposition, so to say, of two perceptions, of two affections of the soul; but without these serving as its elements.

“It is an evident paralogism,” says Mr. Cousin, “to explain duration by succession, since succession cannot be explained except by duration. In effect, where would the elements of succession succeed one another, if not in some duration? Where would there be succession, that is, distance between ideas, if not in the space of ideas and of minds, that is, in time?”—According to our way of conceiving, it is most certain that successions exist in duration, but not as the furniture that adorns it exists in a building, and without which it might exist, but as the stones of which it is composed exist in that same building, or as the integrant parts of any whole exist in it. What is there in this that is sophistical or repugnant to the testimony of our consciousness? Duration is explained, then, by succession, and succession is inexplicable, like resemblance, like the more and less, like all the elementary relations.

“If succession is not merely the measure of time, but time itself; if the succession of ideas is not merely the condition of the conception of time, but this conception itself, it follows that when the succession of our ideas is more or less rapid, time is more or less short, not in appearance but in reality: in deep sleep, in lethargy, we do not think; [p. 112] therefore then neither do we endure; therefore then nothing endures, an extravagant result, but a necessary consequence of the confusion of the idea of succession with the idea of time.”—It is not to the purpose to estimate the force of this argument against the theory of Locke. Referring it to the ideas which I have set forth, we shall observe in the first place, that the measure of the quantity of duration is not precisely the number of ideas which succeed one another in the understanding, but the quantity of some duration which is familiar to us, because every quantity is regularly measured by another quantity of its kind. We shall observe in the second place, that the number of the ideas which successively pass through the understanding would be the worst of the measures we could choose for determining the quantity of duration. Perhaps that measure was the first of all; but if so, experience was not long in making known to us the inexactness of its inductions, and in recommending to us for that end the phenomena which the universe unfolded to our view in a uniform and constant order. We shall observe, finally, that although the intellectual concept of succession is the work of the soul, it does not on that account cease to have in the phenomena compared an absolute foundation, which is independent of the soul.

“If from the moment we conceive succession, we consider it as taking place in time, the idea of time must chronologically precede the idea of succession; we cannot conceive succession without presupposing the idea of time.”—But can we conceive time except as an aggregate of successions? It is absolutely impossible for us to conceive it otherwise. Here, then, is a vicious circle: time presupposes succession, and succession time. The only means of solving the difficulty is to admit an original concept of simple, primigenial succession; a concept inexplicable, though most clear, represented in language by the words before and after. By adding successions to successions, we form time; and it is not at all strange that, this epoch of reason being reached, we cannot conceive succession except in time, nor time except as a continuous aggregate of successions. In vain should we wish to withdraw ourselves from the elementary and primitive concept of [p. 113] all ideas of duration and of time, succession: in the theory of Cousin it is as necessary as in ours; for in it, as in ours, time is a series of successions, and to conceive time it is necessary to conceive succession. In any case we have to admit an elementary relation of before and after; and the question comes down to knowing whether the understanding begins with it or with a complex concept which necessarily involves it.

As to the infinity of time, is it not certain that we conceive it as a mere possibility of relations without end? Let us conceive the first instant of created things; the imagination represents to itself eras and eras prior to that first instant, in an unlimited progression: eras in which other things or the same might have endured, if the Creative Omnipotence had so willed.

I

Between two natural phenomena there is often such a connection that, when one of them takes place, the other takes place consecutively. If a grain of salt is put into water, the salt dissolves; if a spark falls upon a heap of powder, the powder catches fire and [p. 115] explodes; if wax is brought near the fire, it melts. We are accustomed to express this connection by saying that one of the two phenomena produces the other: we say, for example, that the contact of the spark or of some other burning body produces the explosion of the powder. We are accustomed also in such cases to attribute a certain action to one thing upon another, and so we say that water dissolves salt, or that wax is melted by fire. But the terms which we most commonly employ to signify the constant succession of two phenomena are cause and effect, which we apply to the two facts, antecedent and consequent. When we say that the contact of fire is the cause of the explosion of the powder, or that the dissolution of the salt is the effect of its immersion in the water, we neither understand nor give to understand anything else than that the one of the two facts constantly follows the other; that so it has happened hitherto, and that so it will happen always.

Causality, then, or the relation which we conceive between the cause and the effect, is nothing else than the constant succession of two determinate phenomena.

It may perhaps be said that in the relation of causality there is something more than constant successions, because by means of it we conceive one substance as endowed with a certain power or activity over another. But the idea of power resolves itself into the idea of causality, as I have just explained it. When we say that fire has the power or virtue of melting wax, we mean nothing else than that, when wax is placed near the fire, it melts; that so it has happened and will happen always; that these two things, fire near the wax and melted wax, have such a connection with each other that, the first being given, the second is given consecutively.

Power, then, is nothing else than the very relation of causality considered as a quality of the substance whose presence intervenes in the second phenomenon and, in given circumstances, brings it about, whether or not the succession actually takes place. This same relation, considered as a quality of the substance in which the effect is produced, is called susceptibility or capacity. Water has the power [p. 116] or virtue, which is all one, of dissolving salt, and salt is capable or susceptible of dissolving in water.

The idea of constant succession plainly involves not only the idea of the resemblance of the antecedents and the idea of the resemblance of the consequents, but the idea of generality, which extends the connection of these facts to all times and places.

The connection which the understanding forms between causes and effects results from a tendency or instinct, which appears common to man and to many other species of animals, by virtue of which we take it for granted that, in equality of circumstances, it constantly happens that certain facts are followed by certain others. Our thoughts and our actions turn upon the principle that this order which we have observed in nature is permanent. When we conceive, then, a succession of two facts as constant, not only does memory present it to us in all the cases of the same kind that we recollect, but we infer it in all the cases of the same kind that we do not recollect, or that have never been and never will be within our reach. From which it follows that in the idea of the constant succession of two facts memory and reasoning intervene at once.

To observe these connections, to determine exactly their circumstances, is the great business of experience in life, and the great business also to which, as the field of observation extends, all the sciences of fact devote themselves. “What we call experience,” says Hobbes, “is nothing more than the memory of certain connections of antecedents and consequents. No one can perceive the future, because the future is not yet; but from our recollections of the past we form our conceptions of the time to come.”

When the cause of a fact is investigated, the aim is only to inquire into the fact, or the series of facts, which, according to the laws of nature, are always followed by that fact. Not content with the connections which present themselves at first sight, we investigate and scrutinize the intermediate links which bind together two facts apparently immediate. Upon the presence of a corporeal object [p. 117] follows the vision of that object in the soul. The cause of the vision is the presence of the object. But what is the cause of this connection? Why does a present object excite in me certain visual sensations? This is the same as to ask what facts constantly intervene between the presence of the object and the sensations which we experience in consequence of it: a question to which we can reply by describing the movement of the rays of light which issue from a luminous body; their decomposition at the surface of the body present; their reflection from each point of this surface and their diffusion in all directions; the refractions of the whole of the rays that reach the eyes, and the image of the object formed by them that reaches the retina, to whose delicate shades there correspond a multitude of varied nervous impressions, which produce as many visual sensations, elements of the complex sensation that represents the object. But what does this explanation do but interpose other facts between two distant facts, converting the succession of two terms into a series composed of many, between each one of which and that which appears to follow it immediately we conceive that same uniform and constant succession which was before conceived between the two extremes?

It will perhaps appear that experimental and scientific discoveries do not simplify the knowledge of nature, but complicate it more every day; and that our investigations, far from giving us an account of a succession of phenomena, only succeed in adding to this first enigma as many others as there are intermediary phenomena which we ascertain. What does the theory of vision, for example, do but substitute for the connection between two things apparently immediate a great number of connections as inexplicable as the first was without them? Supposing that we carried the investigation of an intermediate series of causes and effects to the last point to which man is capable of reaching; supposing that we represented to ourselves with the greatest individuality and precision the whole series of phenomena that begins in a given cause and ends in a given effect, we should only have succeeded in unfolding a long chain of causes and effects, each link [p. 118] of which would reproduce the first difficulty in all its force.

Such is assuredly the term toward which scientific speculations tend, and beyond which it is not given to the human understanding to pass, however well conducted and fortunate they may be. But nothing follows from this against their utility and importance; for to ascertain in this manner the procedure of nature is all that we need in order to make it serve our ends, by predisposing the antecedents which, according to the order established in it, lead to our convenience and pleasure.

Moreover, the complication which arises from the predisposition of a causality is only relative to each particular case considered by itself; for if we take into account the results of other decompositions, we shall see the same connections often reproduced in many of them; so that, as investigations and knowledge multiply, the number of the elementary connections which we discover does not multiply in proportion, but rather diminishes rapidly. Thus the affection of the soul preceded by the nervous impression is a phenomenon common to sight with all the senses, external and internal: the nervous impression of an immediate impulse of a corporeal agent upon an organ is a phenomenon common to the sensations of sight, smell, hearing, taste and touch, to the sensations of heat and cold, and perhaps to every kind of sensation; the reflectibility of the rays of light is an attribute of all elastic bodies; their rectilinear direction is a general law of motion; they obey the same laws of refraction in the eyes as in other refracting bodies, etc.

Each of the elementary connections which takes place in one species of phenomena takes place also in very many others. As all the words of a language, however various, resolve themselves into a small number of simple sounds, so all the phenomena of the universe, however heterogeneous and even contrary they may appear, are capable of being decomposed into a comparatively small number of simple connections; and if each phenomenon by itself is complicated by its resolution into its own elements, the aggregate of all the [p. 119] phenomena is infinitely simplified by its resolution into the elements whose varied combinations constitute them. The sciences occupy themselves in investigating these elements and in forming of them, so to speak, the alphabet of nature.

The metaphorical expressions which we use to signify the relation of causality have given occasion to the vulgar, and to philosophers themselves down to the age of Bacon and Hobbes, to figure to themselves in causes a certain mysterious action, distinct from the mere invariability of their precedence of the effects; and this illusion has not been entirely banished from the sciences. It is said, for example, that one phenomenon produces another, brings about another; that water dissolves, that fire burns, expands, volatilizes; and, dazzled by these expressions, we are led to imagine that all this conceals something more than a succession or a series of constant and uniform successions. But, on the other hand, the language of philosophers and of the vulgar themselves shows that when it is a question of explaining a phenomenon, the aim is only to unfold it into other phenomena already known and familiar; and if this is accomplished, the problem is believed to be satisfactorily solved. Imaginary connections, more or less plausible, are sometimes invented for this purpose. The motion of heavy bodies, for example, has sometimes been sought to be explained by the action of a fluid which impels them to the earth; not because the connection between the impulse and the motion is more intelligible than the connection between the want of support and the descent, but because the connection between an impulse and a motion is that which we ordinarily employ to produce motions in bodies other than our own.

Another cause of this error is the very habit which we contract of resolving some connections into others more familiar and elementary. The limitation of our senses does not allow us to see the minute particles of which bodies consist, nor consequently the minute changes which take place in them; whence it comes that we perceive phenomena only in the lump and in a confused manner, and that, what is in reality most complicated appearing to us one and simple, there necessarily escape us [p. 120] many links of the series of antecedents and consequents which constitutes each phenomenon. These hidden links are what we investigate under the name of causes; and the frequent discoveries which we make of them, as well in the ordinary experience of life as in scientific inquiries, while they reveal to us unknown connections, and seem to us thus to explain the action of some things upon others, and to give body and color to the powers and virtues which we attribute to them in abstract language, foster in our understanding a strong propensity to inquire into ulterior causes, that is, new links between those which we already know, and induce us to believe that every connection of phenomena necessarily supposes other intermediate connections, as if there were not of necessity a limit at which phenomena succeed one another immediately, and at which causality and power can no longer signify anything else than the constancy and uniformity of the succession of elementary phenomena.

The relation of cause and effect between two facts which we consider immediate is the mere constancy of the succession of two facts. But when we consider it between two distant facts, separated by one or more intermediate facts, these last form so many elements of the relation which we conceive between the first. In a chain two contiguous links have no other relation to each other than this very contiguity; whereas the relation between two distant links consists of all the intermediate links and of the relations of contiguity between each two of them. Thus between the stroke given to the bell and the auditory sensation which follows it, we conceive a relation of causality composed of these elements: vibration of the bell produced by the percussion of the clapper; vibration of the air produced by the vibration of the bell; organic impression produced by the vibration of the air, and auditory sensation produced by the organic impression; that is, a complex causality, consisting of three intermediate facts and four simple causalities. Our discoveries may convert these last into complex causalities; but even if we knew perfectly the procedure [p. 121] of nature, we should have done no more than multiply the intermediate facts and the immediate, constant successions which take place between these two things. The vulgar prejudice on this point consists in figuring to ourselves all causality as complex, which is evidently absurd.

The variety of the linked facts is what gives to the relation of causality its various aspects and the richness of colors and shades with which the universe displays itself. Son and father, work and artificer, vassal and king, subject and magistrate, slave and master present causality and power combined with different kinds of facts, which are, so to speak, what give its particular coloring to each complex relation; and we have a multitude of abstract nouns which signify the various series and groups of which complex causalities are composed, such as paternity, authority, government, electricity, attraction, magnetism and infinite others. But in reality there is hardly a word in whose signification one or more relations of causality are not incorporated.

From the relation of cause and effect arises the idea of possibility. We call the effect possible with relation to the being in which we conceive the power or faculty of producing it. To fly is possible to the bird, and the bird has the power or faculty of flying, or the bird can fly, are synonymous expressions. But it often happens that possibility or impossibility seem to be considered in an absolute manner, either because we attribute them to a fact without regard to any cause in which the power exists, or because it is supposed that there is no being in which that power exists. “It is possible that all the planets are inhabited by living races”; “it is impossible that the universe should have come out of nothing of itself.”

Finally, the idea of possibility leads to the idea of necessity. Necessity is the negation of the possibility of another negation. To say that a thing is necessary is to say that it is impossible that it should not be.

Power, possibility and necessity, besides the meanings which we have just indicated, admit others peculiar to them, which result from certain tacit modifications of the proper [p. 122] sense. When we say that a thing cannot be done, we are accustomed to mean legitimately or honorably, and when we say that a thing is necessary to us, it often happens that we deny only the possibility of its non-existence in the hypothetical sense of our honor, convenience or pleasure.

II

The constant succession into which we have resolved causality involves in the adult intelligence the idea of necessary succession, that is, of the necessity of the effect, the cause being supposed. But how do we arrive at the idea of the necessity of the effect? Observation and experience cannot have led us to it. We must here recognize a judgment which the phenomenon of a repeated succession provokes, but to which it could furnish no logical antecedent, except because we believe in the stability of phenomenal connections, which we regard as so many laws of nature. This implicit belief manifests itself in man from earliest infancy. We see it even in the limited intelligence of many species of animals. Why does the horse, when the rider raises the whip, quicken its pace? Why does the dog, on seeing the attitude of one who is about to throw a stone at it, flee?

Another judgment provoked by the connections of causes and effects, and likewise not logically justified by experience, is that of the necessity of a cause for every new phenomenon.

We have seen the phenomenon A repeatedly followed by the phenomenon B. The phenomenon A has consequently become a true logical antecedent of the phenomenon B; but the force of the deduction consists in the instinctive belief in the stability of natural laws. In the same manner, when, a new phenomenon being observed, we judge that it has had a cause, the presence of the new phenomenon becomes to us a true logical antecedent of the judgment which regards it as necessarily brought about by a cause. But the force, the bond of the deduction, consists in the instinctive belief that every [p. 123] new phenomenon is brought about by a cause. In both cases the instinctive belief is an implicit principle which authorizes the deduction and which cannot have been the work of experience. The principle of the stability of phenomenal connections, and the principle of the necessary precedence of a phenomenon or series of phenomena to every new phenomenon, are two primordial laws of the human intelligence. All reasoning founded on experience implies them. The first is called the empirical principle, because it is that which most directly authorizes experimental deductions: the other is called the principle of causality.

It must not be supposed that these principles present themselves under a general form from the first development of the intelligence. The greater part of men reason with them without their consciousness so much as glimpsing them. They are two instincts by which man is guided without knowing it. They are two movements impressed upon his intelligence by the Author of nature.

III

From effects we infer causes, as from causes effects, by means of the concatenation of phenomena which we call laws of nature. If we see a motion in a direction different from that which heavy bodies take when left to themselves, we infer that it has been produced by an impulse. If we see a fruit, we cannot doubt that it has been developed and formed on a plant by the ordinary process of vegetation. If we see order, correspondence of parts, means directed to the attainment of an end, we deduce from this the existence of a will which proposed the end, of an intelligence which devised the means, and of a power which put them into action. In this manner we were led to the knowledge of the adorable Author of nature. The wonderful harmony of the universe, where each part seems to have been made to play with the others, and all concur in the conservation and propagation of animate beings; where even the, to all appearance, most [p. 124] minute and contemptible of these presents to the sight a delicate framework of parts, evidently calculated to act together, a system of needs and faculties constantly correlative, a symmetry of form which is like the device of an intelligence that has wished to reveal itself to others, a uniformity of reproduction which in nothing resembles what we can figure to ourselves in the effects of a fortuitous collision of atoms; where each organ of each one of these living beings, each viscus, each muscle, each vessel, each fiber, is a system of machines of complicated but exquisite artifice, full indeed of mysteries for our limited reach, but sure in its effects, expeditious in its mode of acting (which takes place in the greater part of cases without the intervention of the will, and even of consciousness) and endowed to a certain point with the faculty of resisting accidents and of repairing itself; where, for example, the organ of vision, one of those which we know best and probably one of the least complicated, contains refinements of mechanism which have scarcely been able to be imitated even grossly in the most finished instruments of which human industry boasts: this wonderful harmony, these correlations, this order oblige us to recognize an intelligent cause, endowed with a power and wisdom superior, beyond all comparison and measure, to those which man employs in his works.

All the relations of cause and effect are reduced, as we have seen, to constant successions of phenomena; but what is the cause of this constancy? Why does motion constantly follow impulse, and certain sensations certain organic impressions? All the phenomena of the universe being reduced to the last elementary successions, what is the bond that unites in each of them the two contiguous facts? This bond cannot consist in an intermediate phenomenon or phenomena, because, according to the supposition, we have reduced the phenomena to the last elementary successions, and because in such a case the new series would present new successive terms, whose constant relation would reproduce the difficulty in all its force.

[p. 125]

Cause and effect are, in the last result, certain facts which follow one another immediately and constantly: but the understanding cannot conceive an absolutely necessary connection between the phenomena whose constant succession it observes. That the body A, striking against the body B, should communicate to it a part of its force, and make it move in a certain direction and with a certain velocity, is a thing which, speaking absolutely, might not be. For if the connection between such phenomena were of absolute necessity, it would be necessary to suppose in the universe a multitude of causes which, destitute of intelligence and of will, would nevertheless act with the greatest concert, producing jointly this astonishing order in which we discover at every step ends and means, that is, will and intelligence. Consequently, the connections which we observe cannot be of absolute necessity; they suppose an anterior cause which has willed and coordinated them; a cause endowed with will and intelligence to will and coordinate them; a cause moreover whose connection with the effects which it produces is of absolute necessity. Communicated and secondary necessities presuppose a first, absolute necessity; and the power to whose acts the effects are bound by an absolute necessity cannot exist except in an intelligent will which wills the ends and coordinates the means. Now what does the absolutely necessary succession of the effects to the acts of that power in that intelligent will signify? What does the absolutely necessary connection between let there be light and the existence of light signify? It signifies omnipotence, uncreated, infinite power. Infinite power, because nothing less is needed to draw beings out of nothing, and to subject their phenomena to necessary connections, by merely willing it; uncreated power, because, if it were not, the connection between its volitions and the correlative effects would be borrowed, and not of absolute necessity; power, consequently, eternal, and not only sovereign, that is, superior to all other powers, but sole, because all other powers are nothing else than emanations from it.

The harmony of the universe compels us, then, to recognize an all-powerful Author and Lawgiver, whose will has established [p. 126] the connections of phenomena from which the general order results. The power of inferior causes is finite and derived, and that of the first cause is infinite and proper to itself. But to this is reduced the difference between the two kinds of causes. The production of the effects of the first cause is a mere succession, like the production of the effects of the others. God willed that there should be light, and there was light, is a concrete but complete expression of the original relation of causality. The idea of the one power and of the other arises from the idea of the constancy and necessity of the effect, or rather, is this very idea: and although it is evident that the necessity of the immediate effects of the first cause is absolute, and that of the effects of secondary causes derived, we can see in the one and the other nothing but constant successions.

IV

It will not be superfluous to remark that we often represent to ourselves rational deduction under the image of succession: “the earth moves in elliptical orbits; therefore there is a force which makes it vary continually in direction.” We say that the second judgment follows from the first; that it is a consequence of it; that since the one is certain, the other cannot but be so; and it is well known that pues [since] (post), although applied now exclusively to posteriority of reason, signified in its origin posteriority of time. All languages have adopted this image to represent deduction or inference, that is, the intellectual operation which from one judgment draws necessarily another judgment. In demonstrative reasonings the connection between the premises and their legitimate consequence is of absolute necessity.

## APPENDIX I

The idea of causality is an idea of relation. By this alone it is said that it is a product of the activity of the soul; a product in which the soul draws from intuitions and sensations [p. 127] a concept which is not resolvable into mere intuitions and sensations.

But causality is not an elementary relation sui generis; it is a relation compounded of those of succession and of resemblance.

The idealists, fearing to attribute this relative concept to sensation, have believed that they saw in causality something more than a constant succession. An unfounded fear. The simplest succession cannot be known by sensation alone, even though we include under this name pure, absolute intuition. I cannot, then, admit with M. Cousin that by means of sensation alone (even including under this title the acts of pure consciousness, metaphorically called inner sense) we perceive the succession of one phenomenon to another. To perceive two sensations successively is not the same as to perceive the succession of the two sensations, or of the two phenomena represented by them.

“If causality,” says Reid, “were nothing more than a constant succession, night would be regarded as the cause of day, and day as the cause of night.” To appreciate this argument at its worth, let us present it under a general form: motion succeeds to rest; therefore, if causality is nothing more than a constant succession, rest is the cause of motion. The body which is heated passes always from a lower temperature to a higher; therefore the latter is the effect of the former. In the same way, in the moon the waning will be the cause of the waxing, and the waxing will be the cause of the waning, etc., etc. As the being in which every new phenomenon is developed leaves of necessity its state and takes another, the state which is left should always be regarded as the cause of the state which is taken. Dr. Reid might have strengthened his argument by observing that the connection of the two states is not only constant, but necessary by absolute necessity, because to say new phenomenon is to say transition from one state to another. Now would it not be absurd to consider the ceasing state as the cause of the incipient state? Therefore, in the idea of causality, Reid might say, there is something more than the idea of [p. 128] a constant succession, and even something more than the idea of an absolutely necessary succession.

This argument is founded on a distorted understanding of what is called the antecedent phenomenon in the constant succession which constitutes causality. He who seeks the cause of a motion seeks a phenomenon which supervenes upon the rest, and is an indispensable previous condition for the body which is at rest to move. He who seeks the cause of day seeks a phenomenon which supervenes upon darkness, and is an indispensable previous condition for light to succeed darkness. He who seeks any cause whatever seeks a fact which supervenes upon a state of things, and is the previous condition for the transition from that state to another. The cause of every incipient phenomenon is a constant anterior phenomenon, which supervenes upon the ceasing state; which is therefore distinguished from the ceasing state. To give the ceasing state as cause of the incipient state would be to incur a ridiculous tautology; it would be to say, for example, that if day succeeds night it is because night precedes day. It is not, then, to night or to day, but to a supervening phenomenon, that is, to the presence or the absence of the sun, that the notion of antecedent phenomenon, productive of day or night, belongs in the theory of Hobbes and Locke.

Let us see now whether the arguments with which M. Cousin impugns the formula of Hobbes and Locke are stronger.

“I ask,” says M. Cousin, “whether, by the mere fact that one phenomenon succeeds another, and succeeds it constantly, the former is the cause of the latter? When you say and think that fire is the cause of the melting of wax, do you understand merely that the melting of the wax always succeeds the approach of the fire? Do you not believe, does not the whole human race believe, that in the fire there is a something, I know not what, an unknown property which it is a question of determining, and to which the phenomenon of the liquidity of the wax must be referred?”

But to what does this belief of the human race really reduce itself? The something, I know not what, of the constant succession, as the generality of men conceive it, is nothing else than intermediate constant successions. If these are revealed to us, and are of those with which we are familiar, we shall be probably [p. 129] satisfied. It is true that the philosopher would wish to go farther. When he saw the mechanism of the universe laid open before his eyes, and it were possible for him to resolve it into its last elementary connections, he would still not be content; he would wish to discover the hidden tie which forms all those connections. It is to be believed, nevertheless, that the philosopher himself does nothing more in this than let himself be carried away by the ordinary habit of inquiring after intermediate connections in every connection perceived. Imagining that of necessity we must arrive at elementary connections, irresolvable into others, he still insists on interpolating in these a something, I know not what, a certain activity in the causing phenomenon, to which corresponds a certain passivity or susceptibility in the caused phenomenon; occult, indefinable, mysterious qualities, an inheritance from the peripatetic school. But the harmony of nature obliges us to recognize that the qualities which we observe have been coordinated by a first intelligent cause, and that therefore all these powers, all these particular virtues, are emanations from a supreme virtue or power. Was this subject to the necessity of creating an intermediate agency in order to bind, in an elementary connection, the phenomenon A with the phenomenon B, so that A should develop this agency, and by means of it act upon B? And what would this be but to place between A and B an intermediate connection which, with equal reason, would have to be resolved into another and another, to infinity?

If the primitive agency of a first and sole cause is not admitted, an absolute necessity would have to be supposed in each elementary connection, and the universe would then be the concourse of an infinite number of independent causalities, from which the harmonious order that our senses attest could not result.

“Let us suppose,” continues Cousin, “that at this moment I wished to hear a sonata, and that, my volition hardly having taken place, that sonata were heard in the neighboring room: in this it is evident that there would be nothing more than succession.”

I have never been able to make out what this hypothesis of M. Cousin amounts to. If it exhibits to us an isolated case in which the volition has casually preceded the sonata, and not

## PHILOS.     9

[p. 130]

one of an infinity of cases in which the same succession of phenomena has been produced, there will certainly be in it nothing more than a mere succession, not a causality, because causality is not a mere succession, but a constant, invariable, necessary succession, verified by its generality.

“But I wish to produce vocal sounds,” says Cousin, “and I produce them. Shall I here place between my volitions and the sounds I utter anything other than the succession which I before placed between my volition and the sonata? Is it not evident that in the latter case I not only believe that the volition precedes the sound, but believe also that the volition produces the sound, that is, that my will is the cause, and the sound the effect?”

This is the case of a true causality. But what do the words cause, effect, production signify in the vulgar belief, if not constant, invariable succession? What else is it that is generally sought when one desires to know a cause?

Let us suppose, I say in my turn, that someone were to make an instrument placed at a certain distance sound, merely by commanding it, and as it were by a sort of magic, and that the persons present were to hear the sound constantly follow the command. As this succession of phenomena is entirely new to them, they would not at first look upon the command as the cause of the sound; but they would believe the two linked together by means of constant, intermediate successions. As soon as they were shown the hidden spring that moves him who pronounces the command, and the mechanism that propagates this motion successively as far as the vibrations of the sounding body, their curiosity would be satisfied, and, knowing intermediate constant successions which were already familiar to them, they would believe they had arrived at the knowledge of the cause, and would desire to know nothing more. They would stop at those familiar intermediate connections, that is, at mere constant successions, verified by their generality. Such is the way in which the generality of men conceive the relation of causality.

The philosopher himself, when he desires to know why the movement of the hand follows upon the act of the will which wishes to move it, ordinarily seeks nothing else than connections [p. 131] intermediate. If he saw which is, in the animated body, the organ that is in immediate communication with the will; if he determined the first phenomenon that takes place in that organ upon the volition, and the whole series of phenomena that unfold successively in other organs, until they end in the contraction of certain muscles, and if he saw between each two phenomena only connections previously known, he would believe, and not without reason, that he had made most important discoveries of recondite causes which until now have scarcely been glimpsed in a vague and obscure manner; and yet he would have discovered nothing else than intermediate constant successions. Only Ontology aspires to rise higher. But the Ontology which imagines in elemental causality anything other than a necessary succession strives fruitlessly to give substantiality to a supposition.

“Our acts,” says M. Cousin, “are not merely phenomena that appear in consequence of the operations of the will, but we regard them, and other men recognize them, as direct effects of our volitions. Hence moral imputation, juridical imputation, and three fourths of human life and conduct. If there is nothing but succession between the act of the homicide and the death of his victim, farewell to the universal belief of all civil life. All civil life is founded on this generally admitted hypothesis: that man is a cause; as the science of nature is founded on this other hypothesis, that bodies are causes, that is, have properties which can produce such or such effects.”

This seems to me the weakest part of M. Cousin’s reasoning. What constitutes the imputability, the morality, of human acts is the volition in which they begin, and those who have embraced in this matter the doctrine of Hobbes suppose this volition no less than M. Cousin and his school. Whether the assassin puts in action an I know not what, or whether there unfolds, only because he wills it, and by virtue of constant successions established by the Author of nature, a series of movements, of phenomena, whose last term is the agony of [p. 132] the victim, is the same for the responsibility which nature and the laws impose.

In what follows we have the satisfaction of being entirely in agreement with the illustrious chief of the eclectic school.

“Not only is there in the understanding the idea of cause, not only do we believe that we are the cause of our acts, and that certain bodies are causes of the movements of certain others, but we also judge in a general manner that any phenomenon whatever cannot begin to exist without a cause that determines this existence. In this there is more than an idea; there is a principle, and the principle is as incontestable as the idea. Imagine a movement, any change whatever: the instant you conceive that change, that movement, it is impossible for you not to suppose that it has been produced by a cause. The question is not what this cause may be; what matters is to know whether the human mind can conceive a change without conceiving that a cause has produced it. . . . I do not say that there is no effect without a cause; a frivolous proposition, in which one term contains the other, and which does no more than express the same idea in a different manner. As effect is correlative to cause, to say that the effect supposes the cause is to say that the effect is effect. But an identical and frivolous proposition is not uttered when it is said that every phenomenon that begins has necessarily a cause. The two terms of this proposition do not contain each other reciprocally; the one is distinct from the other; and yet the mind sees between them a necessary bond. This is what is called the principle of causality.”

We have laid it down that the principle of causality is instinctive; and that, far from being given to us by experience, all experimental knowledge supposes it(a); but, admitting the instinctive propensity

(a) Some philosophers have pretended to demonstrate the principle of causality

in this manner. If a new phenomenon existed without a cause, its cause would be nothing, nothing would produce it; which is absurd, because if nothing produced something, it would already have a real action, a positive quality, and would consequently be something. According to them, the theorem of causality is derived from this other: Nothing produces nothing. What [p. 133] of human reason to suppose a cause for every new phenomenon, nothing follows from it in favor of this or that particular way of conceiving causes.

The principle of causality always goes united with that other instinctive principle by virtue of which, a connection of phenomena having been observed in given circumstances in a certain number of cases, we extend it to all the cases in which the first of those phenomena has presented itself, or in which, in like circumstances, it will continue to present itself. This principle of the perpetuity of the laws to which we see the phenomenal connections subject is the basis of all the knowledge we acquire by experience, and for that reason we have called it the empirical principle.(a)

“So certain is it,” says M. Cousin, “that the principle of causality does not come to us from the senses and the external world, that without the intervention of this principle the external world, from which Locke would derive it, would not exist for us. In effect, supposing that a phenomenon could begin in time or in space without your being irresistibly impelled to attribute it to a cause; when the phenomenon of sensation appears before the eyes of consciousness, you would not seek a cause for this phenomenon, you would not desire to know to what

is certain is that men, from a very early epoch of reason, have admitted causality, not as a derived truth, but as a true principle, which guided them in their reasonings by a sort of instinct.

(a) Might not the principle of causality be resolved into the empirical principle?

In other terms, are we not led to suppose for every new phenomenon another phenomenon that brings it about, because in the sphere of our observations certain new phenomena are often brought about by certain other phenomena, and because an instinctive analogy makes us extend this bringing about to all new phenomena unobserved and unobservable? I believe that we conceive the principle of causality as necessary. We cannot conceive that a new phenomenon should spring up in time without some cause producing it. The principle of causality is not, therefore, logically derived from any other, and arises spontaneously in the understanding because the Author of nature has so willed it. [p. 134] it refers; you would stop at the phenomenon itself; you would never reach the external world. What is needed that you may reach the external world and conjecture its existence? It is needed that, a sensation being given, you should find yourselves compelled to ask what is the cause of this new phenomenon; and that, in the twofold impossibility of referring this phenomenon to yourselves and of not referring it to a cause, you should find yourselves under the necessity of referring it to a cause distinct from yourselves, to a foreign cause, to an external cause. The idea of an external cause of our sensations, such is the fundamental idea of the external, of external objects, of bodies, of the world. Eliminate the principle of causality, and sensation remains alone in view of consciousness, and reveals to us nothing else than its connection with the I that experiences it(a), without revealing to us what produces it, the not-I, external objects, the world. It is often said, and philosophers say it with the vulgar, that the senses discover to us the external world; not without reason, if it is meant that without the senses, without sensation, without this antecedent phenomenon, the principle of causality would lack a basis from which to reach external causes, and we should never conceive the world; but those would be completely deceived who should believe that the senses themselves, directly, without the intervention of reason,(b) without the intervention of another distinct principle, make known to us the external world. Reason alone knows; it knows the external world, and does not know it at first except as a cause. The principle of causality is therefore, I do not fear to say it, the father of the external world; so far is it from being true that we derive it from the external world, and that it is derived from sensation. When one speaks of external objects and

(a) Not even this are we bound to concede to sensation. To conceive the sensa‐

tion in the I is to conceive a relation of identity; it is to engender, in consequence of the sensation, something that is not sensation.

(b) The psychological formula of reason, “it is the faculty of conceiving relations,”

an intuitive faculty, if you will, but whose acts must not be confounded either with sensation, or with mere intuition, in which the soul confines itself to contemplating an affection of its own, without conceiving it as its own, without conceiving any relation. [p. 135] of the world without previously admitting the principle of causality, one does not know what one says, and falls into a paralogism.”

Our readers will perceive the harmony of this doctrine with our exposition of the phenomena of sensitive perception. We have seen that the objective reference deduced from experience, and above all from tactile experience, supposes a fundamental reference to which touch itself does not attain, the reference of tactile perceptions to a cause distinct from the I. This fundamental reference is given to us by the principle of causality.

It is easy to see that, this principle being admitted as universal and necessary, nothing obliges us to conceive causality as M. Cousin conceives it.

“The result of all this,” says the illustrious leader of the eclectic school, “is that, if it is a question of the idea of cause, we cannot find it in the succession of sensible phenomena; that succession is the condition of the concept of cause, not its principle and logical reason; and that if it is a question not merely of the idea of cause but of the principle of causality, it resists still more the attempt to explain it by succession and sensation. In the first case the antecedent of an idea is confounded with the idea itself; in the second there is made to come from the phenomena of the external world that very thing without which there would be for us neither exteriority nor world; what is confounded is no longer the antecedent with the consequent, but the consequent with the antecedent, the consequence with its principle; because the principle of causality is the necessary foundation even of the slightest knowledge of the world, even of the faintest suspicion of its existence; and to explain the principle of causality by the spectacle of the world, which could only have been given to us by that principle, is to explain the principle by the consequence.”

The concept of succession, it is necessary to repeat, is not given to us by sensation, nor by mere intuition: it is a judgment; it is the work of that special faculty to which we attribute judgments and reasonings; it is the work of reason. Its origin being thus purified, the notions of which it forms a part belong, like itself, to the domain of a faculty higher than sensation [p. 136] and than mere intuition. Sensations and mere intuitions provoke the concepts of succession, occasion them, necessarily precede them, and in this sense produce them, not as elements of them, but as previous conditions. But the concept of succession once engendered, it enters, not as a previous condition, but as a constitutive element, into the idea of cause.

Locke’s error consists not, in my opinion, in confounding the idea of cause with the idea of constant succession, but in confounding with sensations the ideas of relation, products of the intellectual activity, concepts of pure reason: and in this the eclectic school has erred no less than the school of Locke.

When we speak of the concept of succession, of resemblance, of causality, and suppose their existence at an early epoch of reason, we must not imagine that these ideas present themselves to the infant understanding as to the adult understanding, or rather, as to the philosophic understanding. All the axioms, all the principles that direct human reason have been in their origin mere instincts, reasoning tendencies that worked in a practical manner, and that much later (in the great majority of the human race, never) present themselves to the mind as general formulas. Long before the understanding came to say to itself in the abstract, if two or more things are equal to a third, they are equal to each other, it had already said very many times that two concrete things were equal to each other because they were equal to a third thing, also concrete. Observing, for example, that in the two scales of the balance, A was in equilibrium with B, and B with C, we deduced instinctively that B was in equilibrium also with C, without the need of consciousness contemplating that principle under its general and abstract form. But it is necessary to reserve this subject for when we treat of generalization, of judgment and of reasoning. Let us content ourselves with recognizing from now two principles, two reasoning tendencies: the principle of causality, which makes us suppose a cause for every new phenomenon, and the empirical principle, which makes us suppose the constancy of the laws [p. 137] to which the phenomenal connections we observe are subject.

In what we have said hitherto, we have left out of account the intervention of the human will in the phenomenal connections. But before going further, and to complete the notion of causality, it is indispensable to take into account the existence of a particular kind of causes.

Every physical phenomenon may be considered at one and the same time as effect and as cause. As effect it is necessarily linked to the aggregate of antecedents that determine it; and as cause it has the same necessary connection with the phenomenon or phenomena which, according to the laws of physical nature, it is destined to produce.

An act of the will, a volition, is a phenomenon like any other, if it is considered as cause. I wish to move an arm, and I move it; between these two things the connection is as necessary as between the spark that falls upon a heap of powder and the explosion of the powder. But a volition considered as effect does not seem to have, between it and its antecedent, the same necessary tie that exists between two purely physical phenomena. I believe that our consciousness attests to us that volition is free: that in the very act of willing a thing suggested by the antecedents, we can suspend the empire of the will at our pleasure and introduce a new phenomenon, a different volition, which does not seem to be linked with the antecedents in a necessary manner.

There are, then, two kinds of causes. The one kind are blind and slavish, so to speak, because they obey an antecedent that determines in every point the action they exert, without its being given them to refuse or modify it. Thus a body A that is in motion and strikes the body B can act upon B only in the precise particular manner determined by its own mass, by the direction it takes, by the velocity with which it moves, and by other dynamical agencies.

There are other causes, endowed with intelligence and will, which either develop their action spontaneously, or, if an antecedent provokes them, do not submit blindly and servilely to it, but [p. 138] either refuse the action solicited, or modify it at their pleasure. Could I not, for example, execute a movement by virtue of a spontaneous and capricious determination of my will? and, supposing that an antecedent or concurrence of antecedents induced me to move, could I not modify this action at my pleasure, refuse it, or, among various ways of executing it, conducive to the end I propose to myself in it, choose one arbitrarily?

I know very well that many will protest against this division, and will reject the second kind of causes as inconceivable, regarding the element of spontaneity or election with which they are characterized as an effect without a cause, in manifest opposition to the principle of causality. But if, for irrefragable reasons, we find ourselves obliged to recognize that there exist causes endowed with spontaneity and election, in a word, free causes, and that without them the universe cannot be conceived, must we not infer that the principle of causality is not so universal as many believe, or must be understood in a sense different from that in which it is most commonly taken?

Mr. J. Stuart Mill(a) has peremptorily denied the existence of these causes. “Correctly conceived,” he says, “the doctrine called Philosophical Necessity is simply this: that, given the motives which are present to an individual’s mind, and given likewise the character and disposition of the individual, the manner in which he will act may be unerringly inferred; that if we knew the person thoroughly, and knew all the inducements which are acting upon him, we could foretell his conduct with as much certainty as we can predict any physical event. This proposition I take to be a mere interpretation of universal experience, a statement in words of what every one is internally convinced of. No one who believed that he knew thoroughly the circumstances of any case, and the characters of the different persons concerned, would hesitate to foretell how all of them

(a) System of Logic, Book VI, chap. 2. [p. 139] would act. Whatever degree of doubt he may in fact feel, arises from the uncertainty whether he really knows the circumstances, or the character of some one or other of the persons, with the degree of accuracy required; but by no means from thinking that if he did know these things, there could be any uncertainty what the conduct would be. Nor does this full assurance conflict in the smallest degree with what is called our feeling of freedom. We do not feel ourselves the less free, because those to whom we are intimately known are well assured how we shall will to act in a particular case. We often, on the contrary, regard the doubt what our conduct will be, as a mark of ignorance of our character, and sometimes even resent it as an imputation. The religious metaphysicians who proclaim free-will maintain at the same time that it is compatible with the divine foreknowledge; and if it is with this, why not with another? We may be free, and yet another may have reason to be perfectly certain what use we shall make of our freedom. It is not, therefore, the doctrine that our volitions and actions are invariable consequents of our antecedent states of mind, that is either contradicted by our consciousness, or felt to be degrading.”

This argumentation of Mr. Mill turns wholly upon an unverifiable hypothesis. What sensible man can flatter himself that he has penetrated into the most recondite folds of another’s heart, or even of his own? In the motives themselves, what a multitude of little accidents may there not be that are hidden from us, or seem to us insignificant, though they are not so? And an unverifiable hypothesis, how can it be the matter of a universal experience? The general conviction which Mr. Mill invokes in his favor extends no farther than to recognizing the influence of powerful motives which, if in the greater part of cases they dominate the heart, in none sweep it along with irresistible violence. Nor do I see how the persuasion that another is capable of predicting with complete assurance what my conduct is to be in given circumstances can be reconciled with the inner feeling of my own liberty. Nor is it permissible to argue from the divine foreknowledge to the human. The Eternal Being is present to all the instants of the duration of His works: for the Divinity [p. 140] there is neither past nor future, as there are for created intelligences.

“There are few,” continues Mr. Mill, “to whom mere constancy of succession appears a sufficiently stringent bond of union for so peculiar a relation as that of cause and effect. Even if the reason repudiates, imagination retains, the feeling of some more intimate connexion, of some peculiar tie, or mysterious constraint exercised by the antecedent over the consequent. Now this it is which, considered as applying to the human will, conflicts with our consciousness, and revolts our feelings. We are certain that, in the case of our volitions, there is not this mysterious constraint. Those who think that causes draw their effects after them by a mystical tie, are right in believing that the relation between volitions and their antecedents is of another nature.”

In another place I have expressed my opinion about that mysterious I know not what; but that is no reason for affirming that it could not exist without our consciousness perceiving it. What does it matter to explain causality by the mere constancy of succession, if at the same time it is claimed that the universality of that principle extends to the phenomena of the human will in the same manner as to those of pure matter?

According to Mr. Mill, the conviction that we can modify our inclinations if we will is the whole inner feeling of moral liberty of which we are conscious. An individual feels himself morally free if he feels that the temptations do not dominate him, but he them; and if, even when yielding to them, he knows that he can resist them, and that if he tried to shake off their yoke he would need for this no more imperious desire than that which it is given him to develop, if he will. But in this if he will there is meant a volition like any other. Can it develop itself in the soul without an antecedent that necessarily produces it, and in every point determines it? We are free. Is that the unfailing consequence of a certain concurrence of antecedents? Human liberty does not exist.

Let us suppose that human liberty does not exist, and that our volitions are nothing more than phenomena constantly brought about by other phenomena: it remains to inquire whether there does not appear in [p. 141] the universe any other element of spontaneity and election. It is at least certain that the great system of causalities which the universe presents to us begins in a first cause; and it cannot be otherwise than supposed that in it there was a volition which in the production of the universe was spontaneous and free. This volition was, consequently, a fact without a cause that in every point determined it; an exception to the principle of causality. And this exception admitted, it is evident that the principle of causality, in the sense in which it is generally taken, is not necessary with an absolute necessity; and that if it is subject to one exception, it may be equally so to others. In short, it is not a universal principle.

It will perhaps be said that the principle of causality refers solely to new facts, because, as these cannot be conceived to come out of nothing by themselves, it is necessary to assign them an antecedent that determines them. But a volition which produced the creation was necessarily a new fact on the infinite scale of time; and if with respect to the Eternal Being nothing is old or new, because for the Eternal Being there is no before nor after, for human reason there are, and it is to this very chain of successive existences with which human reason is concerned that we assign creation as a beginning. Moreover, if the principle of causality were necessary with an absolute necessity, eternity itself would be subject to its empire.

Setting aside that the stupendous coordination of ends to means in the system of the universe is an unequivocal sign of intelligence and election in the first cause, its spontaneity and liberty are proved by metaphysical arguments which seem to me incontestable.

It is evident that the universe might have existed in another region of infinite space than that which it in fact occupied, because space was as capable of receiving the universe in one of its infinite regions as in any other. If it is where it is, it is because the supreme will chose to place it in that region and not in another, and chose it arbitrarily. If it was to exist, it was necessary that it should exist in some [p. 142] part; and as all the infinite regions of infinite space lent themselves equally to it, the supreme will was bound to choose one arbitrarily: if there is anything in this matter that is necessary with an absolute necessity, it is the absolute liberty of this choice.

If from space we pass to time, it is no less evident that the first cause might have fixed the first moment of the existence of the universe at any instant of the eternal evolution of time, since all the instants lent themselves equally to it. Thus, as it chose an instant which has with the present moment a determinate relation (unascertainable by us, but not on that account the less real), it might have chosen among an infinity of other instants which would have had with that moment very different relations. The foundation of Rome, for example, might in some of them have taken place thousands of centuries ago, accompanied, preceded and followed by the same phenomena that have hitherto unfolded themselves in time and that have yet to unfold themselves. Is it not clear that in the choice of the initial instant of created existences the will of the Supreme Maker has been completely spontaneous and free?

Still more. As in infinite space there is no above nor below, right nor left, terms entirely relative to the perceptions of created intelligences, it is evident that the creative will, in making the universe appear in the region of space in which it in fact appeared, might have given it a multitude of different positions, in each of which all its parts would have had the same reciprocal situation which they in fact had, and the same evolution of phenomena would have been verified without the slightest difference, and its inhabitants might have experienced the same sensations and exercised the same absolute and relative perceptions and the same volitions which they have in fact experienced and exercised and will continue to experience and exercise. The creative will was, then, completely free not only in choosing a particular region of space for the theater of the universe, and in fixing the beginning of its duration at a certain instant of the course [p. 143] of time, but also in assigning to the universe the particular position which it in fact assigned to it in space.

All this seems to me of an irrefragable evidence; in such terms that if there existed but a single material atom moving in a certain direction and with a certain velocity, I believe that this single fact would have sufficed a created intelligence to infer the existence of a will which spontaneously and freely had given that atom its particular movement at a determinate point of time and space.

But a school of metaphysicians maintains that in the chain of phenomena of the universe everything is linked by a bond of absolute necessity that has never begun and will never end. What does this doctrine, however, do but represent to us the eternal evolution of phenomena as a fact without a cause? So that, in order to escape from a first cause, intelligent and free, stamped with manifest characters upon created things, that doctrine entrenches itself in what it calls absolute necessity; in an ideal conception to which no objective reality corresponds; in a cause that without intelligence coordinates; without will is spontaneous, and without liberty chooses.—Why have the phenomena that now unfold before our eyes not unfolded before now, or were they not destined to unfold later? Why have they not the relation of coexistence which they have with a certain determinate epoch of absolute time with another of the infinite ones that we can conceive in it? What reason is there, for example, why the solar eclipse that occurred at a certain hour, month and year, which is a date purely relative to us, should have coexisted with a certain determinate second of absolute time and not another? That system does no more than add to the others the absurd supposition of spontaneity and liberty, no longer in a blind cause, but in a mere ideal conception, in a mere word.

The evolution of volitions in time is not repugnant to the divine nature. Immutable in its essence, it admits nevertheless a variety of actions ad extra [outward], in the way that in a man of beneficent character beneficence may be permanent, notwithstanding the variety of acts in which he exercises it; actions ad [p. 144] extra, successive for us, all coexistent for the eternal substance. The principle of causality is the work of God, it is one of the laws established by God. God could create inert causes, destined to act in all and by all in conformity with the actions received, and free causes capable of modifying these actions, and of acting also spontaneously. The element of spontaneity and election is in free causes an emanation of the sovereign liberty, as the power of created things to produce in given circumstances the particular effects proper to them is an emanation of the uncreated infinite power that embraces all times and places. The empirical principle and the principle of causality are two laws destined to act in a different manner in brute and inert beings and in intelligent and free beings; necessary each in its sphere; but not necessary with an absolute necessity; and it may even be said with truth that the spontaneous and free element is not a fact without a cause, because it has its own, mediately or immediately, in the divine nature, the only cause without a cause, necessary with an absolute necessity.

The liberty of the first cause is original and unlimited; the liberty of the human mind is derived and finite; it is a faculty impressed upon man like all the other faculties which his soul and his body enjoy. A voluntary action of man has consequently its immediate cause in the human mind itself, which has respectively its own in the creative mind. Thus the liberty or free will of man, when it exists, no less than the power or action of each of the created things, acknowledges as its sole source the divine essence, sovereignly free as sovereignly powerful. On the first cause, then, universally depend all the causes that constitute the phenomenal connections.

[p. 145]

## APPENDIX II

## OF THE SUPREME BEING AND OF HIS ATTRIBUTES

There exists no nation, people, or race of men so barbarous as to have no idea of a Supreme Being, though for the most part it be enveloped in fables and gross errors. Nor is it permissible to regard as a fact of little importance this unanimous assent of the human race; above all if it be observed that the ideas which men have formed of the Supreme Being are the more elevated and pure, the further they have advanced in civilization. In vain has it been attempted to deny the fact by turning over accounts of travels, and drawing from them two or three examples of atheistic peoples: more recent accounts show that the earlier travelers had judged precipitately, after a short residence among savages whose language they did not know.

There are observed in the human mind certain instincts which from the first, without its knowing it, guide it in the exercise of its intellectual functions, and which are formulated later in general propositions, to which experience could not have attained. May not one of these instinctive beliefs be that which all races hold in a superior nature, which governs the universe?

Without that belief, moral obligations would lack their most efficacious sanction.

“C’est le sacré lieu de la societé,

Le divin fondement de la sainte équité,

Le frein du scélérat, l’espérance du juste.

Si le ciel, dépouillé de son empreinte auguste,

Pouvait cesser jamais de le manifester, Si Dieu n’existait pas, il faudrait l’inventer.” [It is society’s sacred bond, holy eq‐

uity’s divine foundation, the curb of the wicked, the hope of the just. Should heaven, stripped of its august imprint, ever cease to manifest Him, were there no God, He would

have to be invented.]

So said Voltaire. And in effect, in order that a man may be truly virtuous, that in the most hidden place, and in complete solitude, he may be disposed, if it be necessary, to sacrifice life itself to duty, it is needful that he regard it as

## PHILOS.     10

[p. 146]

a law emanating from God; it is needful that he firmly believe that his actions, even though the world be ignorant of them, are known and appreciated by an infallible judge; by a judge who fathoms the profoundest depths of the soul, and is witness of our most intimate thoughts.

It is objected to this argument that in it the existence of God is presented not as a truth but as a condition of social interest. But man has been formed to live in society, and the principles on which the social order rests are truths inspired, so to speak, by human nature, truths of instinct.

Let us pass to another kind of proofs, which, the existence of the universe being supposed, the existence of any being whatever being supposed, are rigorously demonstrative.

Something exists.

Therefore something has existed from all eternity; because the first existence, the first cause, could not have sprung from the bosom of nothing.

The first cause carries in itself its own necessity, its sufficient reason; without that it would not be first.—In other terms, it has existed of itself with an independent existence, necessary with an absolute necessity.

But might it not be supposed that this universe, this chain of phenomena of which we are spectators, has existed from all eternity; that there is a series of existences, depending successively one upon another, without beginning or end?
