No. None of the links of that eternal chain would exist with an independent existence, necessary with an absolute necessity; since, being brought about by the preceding links, its existence would be necessary only so far as the preceding links determined it; it would not, then, carry in itself its own necessity, its sufficient reason; and if of none of the links could it be said that it exists of itself, and by an independent and absolute necessity, it follows that neither could this be said of the aggregate of all the links, of the eternal chain.

Moreover, if in that concatenation of existences which compose the universe there is an order of causes and effects, of means and ends [p. 147] (and our observations testify to us that as far as they reach there is that order) the previous existence of an ordaining intelligence is necessary. The first cause is, consequently, something distinct from the universe and anterior to it.

Absence of limits in space is an essential attribute of the existence which carries in itself its necessity, its sufficient reason. If anything limited it in space, if it existed in one part of space and not in another, one part of space would contain peculiar conditions of necessity, which were not found in the others, and not only would an independent existence which carries its necessity in itself depend upon those conditions, but moreover a real existence would depend upon a mere abstraction, since space is nothing else; and, finally, space would consist of parts of different nature, some endowed with certain conditions and others not; whereas nothing can be more similar to itself than abstract extension to abstract extension, nothing to nothing. Thus the idea of a first cause limited in space would involve three evidently absurd conceptions.

From the independence of the first cause its eternity also follows, not only because nothing could not have engendered it, but because in time no beginning or end can be conceived for that which exists of absolute necessity. That which existed in one part of time and not in another would not be necessary except relatively to certain conditions of time; it would not, then, carry in itself its necessity, its sufficient reason. Moreover, on that hypothesis, a real existence would depend upon a mere abstraction, since time is not a substantial reality; and, finally, as we cannot conceive a difference between one instant of time and the other instants, we cannot conceive that one instant should develop peculiar conditions of existence which were not developed in the same manner by all the other instants. There is nothing, then, in time that can limit the existence of the first cause. The first cause is eternal.

Infinity, in a word, is in all respects an essential quality of all the attributes of the First, Necessary Being. Necessary, independent existence, and limited existence, are [p. 148] incompatible; because everything that is limited supposes external conditions which determine its limits.

In the phenomena of the material universe we have already seen the intelligence of the First Cause stamped. Created intelligences reveal to us the supreme intelligence in a manner yet more evident, if that be possible. Would it be possible to conceive the marvelous order of the understanding, the activity of consciousness, the laws of attention, of memory, and of reasoning, the development of the mysterious instincts of the soul, destined to put it in relation with the sensible universe, and to raise it above that universe to the sphere of the eternal truths, which experience does not reach? Would it be possible to conceive this other order of phenomena, this other chain of successive existences, coordinated among themselves, coordinated with the material universe, without an anterior, supreme, ordaining intelligence?

Another character of the First Cause, revealed by the universe, is a sovereignly free will. The phenomenal world which we have before us is a complex of particularities. Let us fix our attention on a single phenomenon: on the force of projection with which our planetary system is animated, and which probably is not wanting to any of the orbs with which we see space peopled. Let us confine ourselves to a single accident of this phenomenon: the direction of the force. The actual movements undoubtedly suppose one or more primitive directions, so determined that from them should result these movements which are actually taking place in the universe. But a primitive necessity, destitute of will and of choice, could not produce particularities in this respect, nor in any other: it could not make a movement unfold itself in the direction A B rather than in the direction B A, or in any other direction whatever; all the lines that can be traced in space were equal to it; to develop itself preferentially in one was to act as an elective principle, as a free will.

“Run over,” says Samuel Clarke, “all the things of the world, and there will be seen in them characters which demonstrate in the clearest manner that they are all the works of a free agent.— There is not [p. 149] to be seen in them the least appearance of absolute necessity.— Motion itself, and all its quantities and directions, with the laws of gravitation, are entirely arbitrary, and might possibly have been altogether different from what they now are. There is nothing in the number or in the motion of the celestial bodies that agrees with the absolute necessity of the Spinozists. The number of the planets might have been greater or less. Their motion upon their own axes might have been swifter or slower. Their motion from west to east was visibly a matter of pure choice, since that of the comets testifies that they might have moved, like them, in any other directions whatever. All these things might have been diversified to infinity; if they are in one way and not in another, it is necessary to recognize in the first cause a free agency. The same is inferred from terrestrial existences. What necessity was there that precisely the number of animal and vegetable species that exist should exist? And who would not be ashamed to say that neither the form, nor the structure, nor the least circumstance of terrestrial things could have been otherwise disposed by the supreme cause?”

There have not been wanting those who have attributed motion to a primary endeavor (conatus), inherent in matter, and necessary with an absolute necessity. But it is evident that this endeavor must tend either to unfold itself in a particular direction, or in every possible direction. An endeavor in a particular direction is absurd; because there is nothing in matter that can determine it to move to one side rather than another, essentially and necessarily. And if the endeavor is towards all sides, it could produce nothing but the complete equilibrium and eternal repose of matter.

The determination, the particularity of the phenomena of the universe, proves, then, an elective principle, a free agency. Nor is it repugnant, as Leibniz thought, that the divine intelligence should choose arbitrarily one form, one particularity, among infinite possible forms and particularities. On the contrary, to suppose that the supreme will was governed in all its acts by a sufficient reason, in such manner that among infinite [p. 150] possible universes it could not have chosen at its pleasure, but must produce the one it did produce, would be to convert it into a purely passive being, and make it the slave of fatality. A free agency is not like the balance, which, solicited by two equal weights, cannot but remain at rest. The balance is entirely passive. The same cannot be said of the will. When two modes of acting are absolutely equal and indifferent, the will can determine itself for one of them at its pleasure. If the supreme will lacked this elective discretion, the universe would be inconceivable. Why does it exist in one part of infinite space and not in another? Why is it not placed in an inverse manner, or in any other manner, in the very place which it occupies? Space lent it indifferently all the recesses of its immense capacity; and in each of them the universe might have taken an infinity of positions, all its parts keeping among themselves the same relative situations that we see in them. In general, as Clarke said to Leibniz, there is a sufficient reason for everything; but what we are concerned to know is, whether in certain cases, when the action is rational, there may not be different rational modes of acting, and whether in such cases the mere will of God is not a sufficient reason for acting in one special way and not in another. The sense in which Leibniz takes his sufficient reason cannot be distinguished from an absolute necessity, which inflexibly determines the will; and Leibniz, in demanding that this supposition be admitted, proceeds upon the very point in dispute, and falls into a veritable begging of the question.

The particularities of the universe cannot, then, be conceived, unless we attribute them to an independent elective principle, to a sovereignly free will; and hence it follows by an inevitable consequence, that upon the volitions of the First Cause there necessarily follow, with an absolute necessity, the existences and phenomenal particularities which it wills. In other terms, the sovereignly free will, the divine will, is a creative will; to produce by a simple act of the will is to create: Creatio est productio rei per imperium [creation is the production of a thing by command].

[p. 151]

The succession of created existences upon the acts of the creative will is necessary with an absolute necessity. Created existences, and the laws to which these existences are subject, are not necessary, except because they have been ordained. They suppose a creative command, and prove it.

But a will that produces what it wills by the mere willing is an almighty will. Absence of limits is, moreover, an essential quality of the power of the First Cause, which, as we have proved, is in all its attributes and in all respects infinite.

God is the adorable name of the first cause, necessary with an absolute necessity, immense, eternal, sovereignly free, creative, infinite in intelligence, in power, and in all its attributes.

As first cause, it is one: there cannot be another cause of the same category; because a single principle of existence suffices, and because the superfluous cannot be a logical consequence of absolute necessity. On the other hand, if there were many principles of existence, their natures and their agencies would have to be coordinated among themselves, and, in order that order might arise from their concurrence, they would suppose an anterior, intelligent, coordinating cause: they would not be principles of existence and of order; by admitting them we should have done nothing but place one step more between the created beings that we know and the first fountain of being.(a)

If as immense it embraces infinite space, as intelligent it is simple, unextended. It does not, then, fill space in the manner in which an infinitely extended matter would fill it. For the Supreme Being immensity is as a point.

Furthermore, infinite in intelligence, it does not perceive successively either space or time. To perceive successively is proper to finite intelligences. The Supreme Being sees it

(a) Consequently, there is no ground for saying with Paley that reason does not

make us attribute to the divine essence any other unity than that of plan and design in the system of created things. The First Cause might, according to that, be a congress of gods. [p. 152] all as present. In this sense the idea of Kant is plausible, who regards space and time as correlative to human intelligences, as types to which man moulds his perceptions and knowledge.

Infinite in all its attributes, it has no need of instruments for the exercise of intelligence, as it has none for the exercise of power: it has no need of senses, it needs no organic apparatus. The intelligence that coordinated souls to organs, and organs to objects, perceives intuitively the souls, the organs, and the objects. It perceives intuitively the substances and the forms of spirits and of matter. All the modifications of souls, their most intimate and fugitive thoughts, are present to the divine intuition.

Supreme Intelligence, it is not only the principle of order, but the type of the perfection of order; and since justice, veracity, and beneficence constitute the very essence of the moral order, whose laws the Creator has stamped upon the conscience and the heart of man, it is necessary that the Principle of order be absolutely just, veracious, and beneficent.

Contemplating the emanations of the Supreme fountain of being, we recognize at once that the Supreme Being delights in pouring forth life and happiness.

It pours forth life profusely in the air, on the earth, in the waters; but, however incalculable the number of living creatures that present themselves on all sides to the sight, what is that compared with the millions of millions that people the microscopic world? And even that is nothing. The same profusion of life exists without doubt in all the planets that form the world of which our sun is the center; and in all the worlds of the stupendous number of suns that people space.

The beneficent providence with which it attends to the well-being and happiness of so many living creatures shows itself at once in the correlation of the necessities of life with the means that it has given to all for satisfying them. And it has united animal pleasure and happiness not to this satisfaction alone, but to desire, as a principle of activity, which for living creatures is of itself a pleasure [p. 153] and to hope, which is the anticipation, the perfume, so to speak, of happiness.(a)

And what shall we say of the intense, of the exquisite pleasures of the intelligence, of the imagination, of the moral affections?

It is true that the happiness of living creatures is interrupted by pain, and sometimes by the most acute thoughts. But this very thing gives us occasion to recognize the paternal goodness of the Creator, even with respect to the beings that seem most abject and despicable. What fine instincts for procuring what they need, and for avoiding dangers! Pain is in the plan of Providence a zealous monitor, which continually draws us back from what might harm us. In brutes, on the other hand,

(a) “The air, the earth, the water,” says Paley, “teem with delighted existence. In a

spring noon, or a summer evening, on whichever side I turn my eyes, myriads of happy beings crowd upon my view. The insect youth are on the wing. Swarms of new-born flies are trying their pinions in the air. Their sportive motions, their wanton mazes, their gratuitous activity, their continual change of place without use or purpose, testify their joy, and the exultation which they feel in their lately discovered faculties. A bee amongst the flowers in spring is one of the most cheerful objects that can be looked upon. Its life appears to be all enjoyment; so busy, and so pleased: yet it is only a specimen with which we are familiar by reason of the uses that we derive from it. Any of the winged insects would probably present us with a like spectacle, if we stopped to observe it. We should see in each species special instincts, labors, and offices; and we should find that with each instinct, each labor, each office, pleasure is associated, whether as end or as means. Plants are covered with aphides, sucking their juices, and, as it should seem, doing nothing else in all their life. Other species are in perpetual motion, with every mark of the most animated delight. Large patches of ground are sometimes half covered with these brisk and sprightly natures. Nor are the crowded legions of little fishes that frequent the margins of rivers, of lakes, and of the sea itself, less in number, or less animated and content. They are so happy that they know not what to do with themselves. Their attitudes, their vivacity, their leaps out of the water, their frolics in it, make plain the agreeable emotion which they feel. . . . Imagine the sum of the enjoyments of all these little animals. What a scene of happiness!” [p. 154] diseases are rare; death, unforeseen. Cares, sorrows, and remorse do not embitter their existence, as they do ours. And is it not true that pain sharpens pleasure? Pleasure would be less agreeable, would be blunted, and would become wholly insipid to us, without the alternations which from time to time interrupt it, to make its enjoyment more desired and more lively.

The existence of man is disturbed by pain much more often and more profoundly than that of brutes. If his intelligence procures him delightful enjoyments of which brutes are not capable, it also makes him susceptible of weariness, of vexations, of anguish, of griefs, of remorse, which brutes do not feel. The longing for a good torments him; but scarcely does he possess it, when he undervalues it; and, nevertheless, even when he regards it with disgust, the fear of losing it causes him bitter disquietudes. He sees evils coming from a great distance, and is ingenious in forging them for himself even where they do not exist. He feels himself compressed, so to speak, in his earthly existence; and yet death terrifies him. He aspires to a happiness which this world cannot give him, and to immortality in it.

But, without this mixture of pleasure and of pain, the fairest of the works of God, virtue, could not exist. Virtue supposes temptations, combats, painful privations, sacrifices. Remorse embitters the enjoyments which conscience reproves. It is one of the principal elements which compose the moral order, the world of free agencies.

Furthermore, the Author of nature has placed in no living creature necessities and desires without correlative faculties and objects destined to satisfy them. Would he have departed from this plan in the noblest, in the best endowed of the creatures with which he has peopled the terrestrial globe? His justice and his beneficence do not permit us to think it. There is for man a future destiny capable of satisfying his aspirations. The human soul survives death. And would there be for virtue no more recompenses than the perishable goods which it has found; the perishable goods in which even he who seeks them with eagerness, and he who prefers them to his duty, finds only an ephemeral pleasure?

[p. 155]

The divine beneficence and justice assure us that the moral order must receive its complement and its perfection beyond the grave. The sufferings of man are, then, on the one hand, a means of perfecting, and on the other a pledge of immortality. The divine beneficence, then, shines forth even in them.

It will perhaps be objected that, God being able to do whatever he wills, it would have been more proper to his will to grant to living creatures a pure happiness, in which there should not be a single moment of pain. But this is the same as to say that the Divinity might have made men and the other living creatures happier; an argument that would subsist at any other degree whatever of happiness, unless an infinite happiness had been dispensed to each living creature. If human reason does not attain to deciphering the plan of creation in all its parts, may not this very ignorance be one of the trials predestined for virtue? Is it not this ignorance that makes us feel the need of a revelation, and is it not the first link between reason and faith? If reason leads us to the shore of an infinite peopled with mysteries and enigmas, do we not know at least enough to fill us with confidence in the goodness of that Being, who has not judged it unworthy of his greatness to provide for the wants of his humblest and most brutish creatures?

On the relation of extraposition.

Knowledge of bodies by means of touch.—Reproduction of form: 1st, by the double series of tactile affections and organic movements; 2nd, by any tactile affections whatever that represent a series of movements of the organ; 3rd, by simple visual affections corresponding to the tactile magnitude and figure; 4th, by touch, through the procedure in which it is wont to supply and represent itself: combined experience of simultaneous affections with successive affections.—The idea of extension is distinguished from that of movement: primitive characters of the former.—Objective character of extension: different epochs in the history of the perceptions of tactile extension.—Extension in itself is inexplicable.—Opinion of Destutt de Tracy.—Dr. Brown.—Analysis of the elements of which the idea of extension consists.— The perception of place resolves itself into that of distance and situation.— Concept of space: its successive determinations in relation to the place and volume of bodies.—Touch in concurrence with other perceptive faculties; the cognitions it originates.—Whether space is a real entity; space-nothing considered ontologically.—Whether space has a necessary and absolute existence.—Barrenness of ontological questions.—Examination of Balmes’s opinion on the reality of space.—Samuel Clarke.—Leibniz.—Kant.—Conclusion.

I

Touch is the sense that primitively leads us to the knowledge of the magnitudes and forms of bodies, that is, of their extension; but it does not make them known to us by itself, but through the intervention of other faculties of the soul.

If we perceive by touch that an object is extended, it is because [p. 157] we perceive a series of tactile affections, as we pass one of the organs of this sense over the surface of the object.

The idea, then, of tactile extension is the idea of an external cause, which produces a series of tactile affections, corresponding to a series of movements of the organ. By organ I understand any part of the surface of our body endowed with tactile sensibility, and determinately the inner surface of the hand, which is the instrument we most often make use of in the exercise of touch.

To touch the surface of different bodies, it is necessary that we execute different series of movements. The tactile form and magnitude of each body are consequently represented in our mind by two series: one of the movements of the organ, necessary for touching successively the whole surface of the body, and another of the tactile sensations that correspond to the movements of the organ. So long as the form and magnitude of the body do not vary, we can reproduce this pair of series as many times as we please, and as soon as the form and magnitude vary, another pair of series succeeds it.

It is fitting, however, to make the following observations.

1st. One and the same form may be perceived by means of very many pairs of series. Let us suppose that the body whose form we do not know and wish to ascertain by touch were a small pyramid. We might begin the examination by touch at the base or at the apex; and each of these procedures could not but require a particular series of movements, to which another particular series of tactile affections would have to correspond. But once touch is trained we know the equivalence of the various pairs of series, and we readily reduce them to one another. If, for example, in examining a flower I proceed from the calyx to the petals, I have only to invert the two series that result, and I shall thus represent to myself those that would result from proceeding in the contrary direction. Familiarized with the equivalences of these procedures, I perceive one and the same material form in various pairs of series, and I am free to represent it to myself by means of any of them: in the way that in languages whose [p. 158] syntax admits of transpositions, the sense of a sentence does not vary, whatever be the order in which we place the words of which it is composed.

2nd. The knowledge we acquire of the form and dimensions of the object does not depend on the particular kind of tactile affections that we experience. It is enough that there be produced in us any tactile affections whatever, corresponding to a particular series of movements of the organ, for us to form an idea of the form and magnitude of the object. The various forms and magnitudes are, then, peculiarly represented by the various series of movements of the organ.

3rd. To form an idea of the tactile figure and magnitude of an object, it is not necessary that the movements and affections of the two series from which this idea springs should actually have been produced. For we have already seen that, by virtue of the connections which experience has shown us between visual and tactile affections, it happens that at the mere sight of an object we know its tactile magnitude and figure, that is, the movements that would be necessary to give to the hand in order to touch successively the various parts of an object. Accustomed to deduce the said movements from optical appearances by a sort of computation, we come to supply one sense by another; and habitually representing to ourselves, by the aspect of bodies, their palpable forms and dimensions, we cannot, without much effort of meditation, shake off the prestige which makes us believe them immediately perceptible to sight.

4th. As sight supplies and represents the act, touch is also wont to supply and represent itself.

In the present state of our intelligence touch may lead us in two ways to the knowledge of magnitudes and forms, either by passing a point of the hand successively over all the points of the surface of the object, or by touching them all at once. In the first case, we experience successive tactile affections, which form a series corresponding to that of the movements of the organ; in the second, the tactile affections are simultaneous.

We have only these two means of perceiving forms [p. 159] and magnitudes by touch. It is true that when we submit an object to the examination of this sense, we may perceive them by passing, not a point, but a large part of the surface of the hand over that of the object; and indeed this is the most ordinary way in which touch gives us its information. But it is evident that in such a case we do nothing else than combine the method of simultaneous affections with that of successive affections.

Are both equally fitted to make extension known to us? In the present state of our intelligence we can doubtless make use arbitrarily of the one or the other, or combine both. But it is possible that originally we owed to one of them alone our ideas of magnitudes and forms; that experience then taught us to supply it by the other, showing us a certain correspondence between the two; that, consequently, the secondary procedure does no more than suggest the perceptions of the primitive one; and that in this case, as in that of sight, the suggestions are so rapid that they seem to us actual perceptions.

It is not merely possible but necessary that it should have been so, because the procedure of simultaneous affections cannot by itself lead us to the idea of extension. In effect, if the simultaneous touching of many points leads to this idea, it is because we perceive the magnitude and form of the surface touched, in the magnitude and form of that part of the organ in which the contact takes place. But when our own body was no better known to us than external bodies, when we lacked every idea of magnitudes and forms, how was it possible for us to divine, by virtue of the simultaneous affections of touch alone, that various points of our body were affected by another body, that these points were the one outside the other, and that the substance which affected us must therefore consist of points having a like relation to one another? The mere fact of there being various physical points on the surface of the organ affected can only make known to us that we experience a multitude of simultaneous affections of a particular kind, different from visual, auditory affections, etc., and nothing more. And it is even probable that the idea of multitude would not so much as occur to us, and [p. 160] that from the impressions produced simultaneously on several points of the skin there would result only a confused affection, like that which odoriferous effluvia produce in the sense of smell; an affection which gives no idea of extension or of multitude, although it proceeds from impressions produced on a surface.

We originally perceive extension, then, by perceiving a series of tactile affections corresponding to a series of movements of the organ. Familiarized with the size and with all the modifications of figure that we can give to the hand, and taught to discern the impressions produced on different parts of its surface, we acquire the habit of representing to ourselves, by the magnitude and form of the organic surface simultaneously impressed, the magnitude and form of the surface that is in contact with it. The facility we have of varying the form of the hands, moulding it to that of the body we touch, gives them a particular aptitude for this mode of exercising touch.

The successive examination of touch, according to this, may be supplied and represented by simultaneous tactile perceptions and by visual perceptions. If these and those inform us often of the tactile dimensions and figures of objects, it is not actually or immediately, but by suggesting the successive perceptions of touch. It is true that, familiarized with the suggesting perceptions, the suggestion often fails to manifest itself, at least in a manner sufficiently energetic for us to fix our attention upon it. We then think of tactile extension, now by means of visual affections, now by means of simultaneous tactile affections; in the way that when we learn a foreign language, we at first translate it into the native tongue, and once we have made it familiar to ourselves, we think with it without any need of translating it.

But the idea of extension, it will be said, enters necessarily into the idea of movement; and there is therefore a vicious circle in explaining the former by the latter. In the present state of our intelligence, the idea of voluntary movement, that is, of that which we execute with some of our members [p. 161] or with the whole body, in consequence of determinations of the will, involves, like that of all movement, the idea of a greater or lesser space traversed by the moving body; and the idea of existence has necessarily preceded that of space, which, as we shall see farther on, arises from it. But we can strip the idea of voluntary movement of every idea of extension and of space. Let us place ourselves for a moment in that first epoch of the intelligence in which the apprenticeship of the external perceptions is made. We have no notion either of our body or of external bodies, nor of movement considered as the translation of a body from one point of space to another. We move, nevertheless, obeying an instinct with which nature has endowed all animals. Sometimes the pleasure which in the state of health accompanies the moderate exercise of the forces; at others the uneasiness occasioned by a want or pain, stimulates us to execute movements, fortuitous and irregular at first, and, in proportion as experience instructs us, directed by the will to the satisfaction of our desires.

If there was a first epoch of the intelligence in which the soul did not yet refer tactile sensations to a cause distinct from the I, it is evident that in this epoch the perceptions were all purely intuitive. In this epoch tactile sensations were for the soul mere modifications of itself; and when the touching was voluntary, the soul saw itself producing in itself the tactile sensations by means of sensations of effort, and the sensations of effort by means of volitions. Volitions produce, according to our present way of conceiving, muscular efforts, and muscular efforts sensations of effort. But, in the epoch of which we treat, it must have appeared to us that volitions would produce sensations of effort immediately. Likewise, in our present way of conceiving, tactile sensations are produced by actions of external bodies upon our organs, and of our organs upon the soul. But, in the epoch of which we are speaking, the tactile sensation was a spiritual modification, without reference to any external cause or one distinct from the I. Thus, the perception of

## PHILOS.     11

[p. 162]

tactile extension was an assemblage of merely intuitive perceptions: by the one set we perceived a series of volitions, by the other a series of sensations, namely, of the sensations produced, without our knowing it, by the muscular contractions which we have called efforts. Such is the embryo of the future knowledge of extension.

Let us now infuse into this work of the nascent understanding the fundamental reference of touch, that reference in which we see the tactile sensation as produced by a cause distinct from the I. By means of this reference, we perceive tactile extension by perceiving the correspondence of a series of tactile sensations, produced immediately in the soul by causes distinct from it, with a series of sensations of effort, produced by the soul in itself. This is the second form which the perception of the extended takes in the nascent intelligence.

Noting the various correspondences of these series, we perceive at first in an imperfect and obscure manner, we perceive in the gross, so to say, the various objects that were within our reach, and among them our own body. The immediate empire which the will exercises over the machine we animate, and the double sensation produced by the reciprocal contact of the tactile organs, led us afterwards to distinguish our own corporeal system from all the objects that surrounded it. We were then able to perceive the instrumentality of our body in the phenomena of the tactile, visual, auditory sensations, etc. Those which were before causes of sensations merely distinct from the I, came to be corporeal substances, that is, tangible and extended, which, impressing the organs, that is, other tangible and extended substances, more immediately subject to our will, affected the I. We already perceived extension in the correspondence of two series, one of external tactile sensations, the other of internal sensations of effort. Meanwhile, and by the same procedure which instructs us of the position of the parts of each body among themselves, we came to comprehend the reciprocal position of foreign bodies among themselves and in respect of our own. We could thenceforth [p. 163] perceive voluntary movement as the translation of our organs from some bodies to others, or from some to other of the parts of one and the same body; we could regard the sensations of effort as produced, not immediately by the will, but by organic modifications, obedient to our volitions; and we could now, consequently, perceive tactile extension by perceiving the correspondence of a series of tactile sensations to a series of voluntary movements of the organs.

We may, I think, sketch the history of the perceptions of touch, relative to extension, in this manner: first epoch: we experience series of tactile sensations, corresponding to series of sensations of effort; but both the one and the other sensations are for the understanding mere modes of the I. Second epoch: series of tactile sensations referred now to causes distinct from the I, and corresponding to series of sensations of effort, still considered as mere modifications of the I, produced by volitions, notify us of the forms and dimensions of objects. Third epoch: connections observed between visual sensations and tactile sensations give us the faculty of deducing the latter from the former, and sight becomes little by little representative and divinatory of touch. Fourth epoch: our form, in all the attitudes of which it is susceptible, comes to be perfectly known to us by the visual and tactile observation of our body, and of other bodies of our species; the efforts are referred to determinate parts of our body subject to the empire of the will, and the tactile affections to external causes, and to determinate parts of our body impressed by these causes. Fifth epoch: we now acquire the faculty of knowing the magnitude and form of what is in contact with a part of the surface of our body, by the magnitude and form of the surface impressed; and the simultaneous tactile affections represent to us those that would result from the successive examination of touch. Sixth epoch: the perceptions of sight, being perfected, inform us individually and instantaneously of the placing of bodies in space by means of the varieties of perspective; and [p. 164] all the details of tactile magnitude and form become easier for us to discern and to recollect, by means of the various shades of light, shadows and colors with which nature sets them off to our eyes. I do not pretend that the idea of extension has developed precisely in the order I have just set forth; probably this order has not been one and the same in different individuals; memory can give us no information about what has passed in the earliest gleams of intelligence, above all when it is a question of instinctive procedures which affected consciousness faintly and obscurely. But I do believe that in the embryo of the ideas of magnitudes and forms there could not but have been something resembling the series of epochs or partial evolutions which I have indicated.

We have said that we perceive extension by perceiving the correspondence of two series, one of tactile sensations, the other of sensations of effort. But perhaps it will be asked: what is extension in itself? To this we can only answer: a quality which consists in producing a series of tactile sensations corresponding to a series of efforts. We cannot conceive it or represent it to ourselves in any other way. Extension is a word which signifies this correspondence, and this correspondence is a fact which admits, in my opinion, of no further explanation.

Destutt de Tracy was the first who saw clearly the true origin of the idea which we form of the extended. A body is not extended, says this philosopher, except because it consists of parts such that it is necessary to execute a certain quantity of movement to pass from one to another.(a) Dr. Brown threw a new light upon this doctrine, completely demonstrating the insufficiency of touch to make extension known to us by itself

(a) The perspicacious Berkeley, Bishop of Cloyne, had already caught a glimpse of

this truth. Among various questions which he proposes in his Analyst, that of number XII is this: “Whether it be possible that we should have had an idea or notion of extension prior to motion? Or whether, if a man had never perceived motion, he would ever have known or conceived one thing to be distant from another?” [p. 165] alone. He showed that the sense of effort is peculiarly that which makes us capable of perceiving extension. I believe, nevertheless, that even after the investigations of these two writers, something remained to be desired. For the perfect decomposition of an idea, as for that of a material substance, it is required that its elements be specified with precision, and the mode in which they concur to form the compound.(a)

Breaking extension down to the minimum in which it is possible for us to perceive or imagine it, what is it that we find in it? To what is it reduced? What is its elementary expression? That two corporeal points have such a relation to one another, that a certain effort is necessary for us to touch them successively with a new point of the tactile organ. This is what we give to understand by saying that the one is outside the other, or that they are extraposed the one to the other; a relation which, applying to psychological analysis the language of chemical analysis, we might call the integrant element of extension.

Calling two tactile points A, B, in the perception of their extraposition there is: 1st, tactile sensation of A; 2nd, sensation of a certain special effort; 3rd, concept of succession between the tactile sensation of A and the sensation of effort; 4th, tactile sensation of B; and 5th, concept of succession between the sensation of effort and the tactile sensation of B. Setting aside the terms A and B between which we conceive the extraposition, it results that this relation is composed of three constituent elements: succession, effort and succession. We perceive the extraposition of A and B by perceiving an effort that succeeds the perception of A and precedes the perception of B. This analysis will be charged with minuteness, but it is exact, and I believe that it resolves the idea of extension

(a) Some philosophers have believed they found in the original notions acquired

by touch the concept of a certain resistance, opposed to the tactile organ by the body touched. But it does not seem to me possible to conceive the idea of resistance without the idea of a reaction in one direction or another, nor the idea of direction without the idea of an extension in length. To place, then, in the first notions of the extended the perception of tactile resistance, would be the same as to explain extension by extension. [p. 166] into the ultimate elements to which the understanding is capable of reaching.

Effort is a general word which embraces as many particular modes and species as there are muscles moved and various movements of each muscle. To all these varieties of organic affection correspond varieties of affection in the soul, by means of which we perceive the various modes of extraposition, that is, the various respects of situation that there may be between two tactile points, and which we know how to express by saying that the one is above or below the other, to the right or to the left, behind or before, etc. Extraposition is a genus of which the reciprocal situations of the extraposed points are species.

Aggregates of tactile points variously extraposed among themselves form bodies of various magnitudes and forms. If in an aggregate of points the modes of extraposition are permanent, if there is a constant correspondence between two determinate series, one of effort and the other of tactile affections, the magnitude and form will be constant. And if, making the efforts smaller and smaller, we perceive more and more intermediate terms between those of which these two series originally consisted, and after it becomes impossible for us to continue this procedure with the senses, we carry it forward in the understanding, we shall join to the idea of magnitude and form (which are particular modes of extension, as the various reciprocal situations of two points are particular modes of extraposition) the idea of infinite divisibility, that is, of continuous quantity. I do not think that more is needed to form a complete idea of extension, so far as it is given us to conceive it.

It hardly seems necessary to observe that when I speak of points, I am very far from meaning, I do not say mathematical points, but not even physical ones. I make use of this word to signify small extensions, although they be not the minimum perceptible. What is said of the one applies without difficulty to the others; because for the present case it is the same whether our ideas of extraposition refer at the beginning to simple physical points or to surfaces of some extension, which in the first trials [p. 167] of touch produced confused affections, in which it was not yet possible to perceive distinction of parts.

We must not, then, confound the idea of extension as we draw it immediately from the first essays of touch and of the sense of effort, with the idea of extension perfected by reasoning. The first represents the extended to us as composed of elements which we conceive as extraposed, and nothing more. The second represents it to us as composed of extraposed elements, each of them resoluble into lesser elements, likewise extraposed, each of these into others, and so on to infinity. To extension, as we learn it at the beginning, we apply the idea of discrete quantity; as we learn it later, by comparing and reasoning, the idea of continuous quantity.

II

Aggregates of tactile points variously extraposed form, as we have seen, bodies of various magnitudes and forms. Aggregates of various extrapositions form also the distance and the reciprocal situation of bodies.

A seems to us to be more or less distant from B by the intensity and number of the efforts it is necessary to make in order to experience successively the tactile sensations of A and B, whether the intermediate points through which the organ is carried be tactile points or merely imaginary ones.

But the series of efforts needed to carry the organ from body A to body B is not the same when B is above A as when it is below; when B is to the right as when it is to the left. The varieties of the efforts which transfer the organ from one body to another determine the situation of B with respect to A.

[p. 168]

## III

The perception of place resolves itself into the perceptions of distance and of situation. In a system of objects, the place in which I represent each object to myself is the distance and situation in which it stands with respect to me, or with respect to another object whose situation and distance with respect to me are known to me. If the magnitude and form of the objects enter into the account, we give magnitude and form to places also, and we say that a thing occupies more or less place according as it has more or less volume.

We represent space to ourselves by representing to ourselves all the series of efforts which the will can impress upon the limbs without meeting an obstacle. So long as we move, and so long as, while we move, no resistance is offered to touch, we perceive space. The resistances of which the tactile sensations apprise me limit space on the one hand, and on the other the volume of the corporeal substances that affect touch.

Space conceived in this manner is no more than free space, the space in which our own body and other material substances can move, occupying successively various places. This was the first signification of the word space. But the idea of the small spaces in which we see bodies move led us easily to the idea of a vaster space in which all bodies move, all the parts of which the universe is composed, and in which we may imagine the entire universe to move. The places of things then appeared to us parts of this space; and the idea of real places led us to the idea of possible places. Beyond the limits of this universe we can imagine another, and another, and a thousand, and an infinite number of universes; for beyond the limits of this universe there is nothing, and nothing cannot resist the placing and moving in it of as many universes as one pleases. Nothing was then called space, and space was without limits.

Between the place or space which a body occupies and the volume [p. 169] which it has, there is this difference: we represent volume to ourselves as a quality inseparable from the body, whereas, representing to ourselves the place or space under determinate relations with respect to a fixed point, we consider it as a thing distinct from the body, and when the latter moves, we say that it is transferred from one place or space to another. It is clear that this expression means nothing else than that the body, which before stood in certain relations with respect to a certain point, has now different relations to it. The independent manner of being which we attribute to space, considered as a whole of which places are parts, is the work of the imagination. Space is not truly anything but the capacity for bodies and movements: the negation of all resistance to matter.

We cannot, then, perceive either place or space, or infinite space, except by means of extrapositions, that is, by means of successions either actually perceived or merely imagined. Space and time thus come to have an affinity which at first sight we should not have suspected. The ancient Mythology might have figured this concept by making space the child of time.

It follows from what has been said that our notions of situation, place and space, and consequently that of movement considered as the transference of a body from one part of space to another, could not have arisen in the soul except on occasion of the perceptions of the inner sense of effort, by means of which we perceive diverse relations among the tactile sensations; relations which consist in the order in which these sensations succeed one another, corresponding to those of the sense of effort.

The cognitions which we acquire gradually by means of touch and sight gave to the first notions of situation, place and space, as of size, form and movement, the relief or coloring which they now seem to us to have. Touch supplies, if it is permissible so to say, the materials, and sight adorns them; but it is the inner sense of effort which, combined with the concept of succession, gives the mixture or mortar that unites them. If we do not take it into account, we fall into one of [p. 170] two equally erroneous concepts; either the perceptions of extension and their derivatives are attributed exclusively to touch and sight, and it is believed that these perceptions spring up in the understanding spontaneously in consequence of the visual and tactile affections, and form ideas which do not result from the combination of other ideas; primitive concepts in which there is no composition or aggregate; concepts which cannot be explained or defined. To explain extraposition recourse is had to space, as to explain succession recourse is had to time. Time and space are two fantastic conceptions which have covered the theory of the understanding with a nebulous mysticism, and converted psychological reasoning into an ingenious play of rhetorical figures.

In the same manner, and at the same time, as the perceptions of tactile extension, the perceptions of the smoothness and roughness of the surface we touch are formed; that is, by perceiving a series of efforts and a series of tactile sensations of a certain kind, and perceiving the correspondence of both series. In the perceptions of tactile extension the kind of tactility which we perceive is of no value; in the perceptions of smoothness and roughness this element is of essential importance.

By means of touch we perceive also the hardness, softness, fluidity, flexibility, elasticity and other qualities of bodies; but neither are these perceptions exclusively of touch, because, as we shall see, various perceptive faculties concur in them. To perceive hardness, softness, fluidity is to perceive a greater or less reaction of the material molecules to touch. Each part of a body resists more or less the effort of the organ which acts upon it, attempting to destroy its cohesion with the others. The effort is perceived by a special inner sense, the reaction by the external sense of touch.

To perceive extension it would suffice that the touching should be parallel to the surface of the body touched. For the perception of hardness, softness and fluidity it is necessary that the tactile organ act in a direction perpendicular or oblique to the surface [p. 171] tending to dislocate the molecules. In truth, it is not possible to perceive extension except in company with some one of the three qualities mentioned, because a perfect parallelism between the direction of the movements of the organ and the surface touched is an unverifiable mathematical supposition. On the other hand, the perceptions of these three qualities, if they do not presuppose that of extension, are intimately mingled with it. We must, nevertheless, separate them in the understanding, and decompose them into the elements which respectively belong to them.

The perception of the various degrees of reaction which we call hardness, softness and fluidity supposes that we compare with one another the reactions of the various bodies, and that we perceive between them the relation of more and less. If the reaction has comparatively a considerable degree of force, we say that the body is hard; if a degree less, we say that it is soft; if a very slight degree, we say that it is liquid or fluid.

To the ideas which we form in this manner are joined those of the dislocation of the molecules; that of the variations of form which the body in consequence receives, and that of the tendency of the body to the horizontal in certain cases: cognitions very easy to acquire by means of touch and of sight, associated with the sense of effort, and with the intellectual faculty which engenders concepts of causality. In this manner our ideas of the three qualities mentioned become more and more precise and instructive. In this manner we form also the ideas of flexibility, frangibility, elasticity, compressibility, dilatability, and other corporeal qualities. And, taking one step more, we come to recognize all the qualities mentioned, no longer by our actions upon external bodies, but by the actions of external bodies upon one another.

IV

Space, some philosophers say, is a real, necessary, absolute, eternal, infinite, uncreated being. Let us fix these ontological enunciations.

[p. 172]

If we suppose the whole corporeal universe destroyed, what remains?—Nothing, some will answer; restricting, no doubt, the word nothing to the absence of corporeal beings, and leaving God out of account, and created spirits, and beings which are neither matter nor spirit; for it is not demonstrated, nor can it be demonstrated, that there are none such: beings inaccessible to our senses, and about whose existence or nature human reason can conjecture nothing, beings with which millions of universes and the very universe we know may be peopled, and which may exercise upon it, and receive from it, influences unknown and to us incomprehensible. Taking the word nothing in this restricted sense, those who answer the foregoing question nothing enunciate in substance a tautological proposition: matter being destroyed, there is no matter.

If we suppose the whole corporeal universe destroyed, what remains?—Space, others will answer. But what distinction do we conceive between space and nothing in the restricted sense we have just given it? What attribute can we give to that space which we cannot give to nothing? Space is extended; so is nothing. We consider space as extended, because we conceive in it extraposition of points; intangible, invisible points; in a word, imaginary ones; and the same we can conceive in nothing.— Space is the capacity for corporeal beings and for movements; so is nothing, for nothing cannot resist bodies or movement. Space is without limits; neither is it given us to conceive them in nothing. Beyond the corporeal universe nothing extends in all directions, as interminable, as immense, as it was on the eve of creation.—Space is eternal, uncreated; so is nothing. Can we conceive an epoch at which that interminable, immense nothing began to exist of itself, or by the will of an omnipotent being who drew it out of another nothing? It existed from all eternity, before, fecundated, so to say, by the voice of the Eternal, it produced the universe, and would exist throughout all eternity, if, obedient to the same voice, it should some day reabsorb the universe. But it existed in the same manner as empty space, as a mere negation, as [p. 173] an intellectual concept; and in the same sense we may say that every negation is uncreated and eternal: the not-white and the not-black thus existed from all eternity, before there was light and colors; and would exist again as soon as there should be neither light nor colors. What, then, is space? The same nothing considered as extended, and as a possible receptacle of corporeal beings and of movements.

An objection may be made. Let us resuscitate the corporeal universe, whose annihilation we supposed. The nothing will disappear from around us, and space will nevertheless subsist, empty before, full now: therefore space and nothing are not one and the same thing. I confess that, having regard to the use of words, space and nothing represent different intellectual concepts; but I say at the same time that ontologically, that is, having regard to the objective signification of the words, space is not distinguished from nothing. If they were distinct things, where should we see it better than in the first hypothesis, in the hypothesis of the annihilation of corporeal beings? In this hypothesis it is evident that there are not two things, but one only, which in one respect is called space and in another nothing. We have agreed to call nothing space or nothing so long as the void subsists, and to give it only the name of space from the moment its capacity in potentia passes into capacity in actu. Matter having been resuscitated, then, it will not be proper to say that our body and other bodies are in nothing, but that they are in space. Space is the capacity potential or actual: nothing is the potential capacity.

The existence of space is necessary and absolute. Nothing more evident. If matter does not exist, there exists at least in potentia the capacity for bodies and for movements: if matter exists, that capacity exists in actu. Therefore, on any supposition, space exists. Therefore, the existence of space is absolutely necessary. The same cannot be said of nothing, because in nothing we conceive no more than the potential capacity. From the moment that capacity is exercised, from the moment there are bodies and movements, space ceases to be called nothing, and can only be called space. In the universe there are bodies and at [p. 174] the same time there is space. If we leave bodies out of account, what is the space occupied by them? Nothing. But what is it all about, in all this, but the use of two terms which denote pure abstractions, without any real object? The existence which we figure to ourselves in space is in everything and by everything like the existence which we figure to ourselves in nothing: it is the existence of a pure abstraction; it is an imaginary existence; it is an existence which is not existence; it is nothing.

Sunt verbo et voces, pretereaque nihil. [Words and sounds, nothing more.]

We have entered upon this discussion with the sole object of making manifest the futility of the ontological questions which have been and are agitated in the schools with regard to space, and which may well be matched with the most insubstantial of those that were debated in other centuries by the Schoolmen. We have a certain propensity to clothe with a real being, with a kind of substance, everything that is signified by a substantive. The philosophy of Plato, in great part, is reduced to nothing else. To nothing itself, from the time that, laying aside its proper name, which was an insuperable obstacle,(a) it took the title of space, we have given a shadow of existence, in which some have thought to find something more than the work of the imagination. But the common run of men have spoken a more exact language than the philosophers, calling those spaces which we conceive beyond the limits of the universe imaginary spaces.

For my part I confess that I cannot descry any true existence in those phantasmagorical appreciations of time and space. Time in itself is for me a possible order of successive facts, as space in itself is a possible order of coexistent facts. All my efforts to find in them something real to which my understanding might cling have been vain:

Ter conatus ibi circumdare bracchia collo:

Ter, frustra comprensa, manus effugit imago:

Par levibus ventis, volucrique simillima somno. [Thrice I tried to clasp his

neck; thrice the image, grasped in vain, fled my hands, like light winds, like a winged

dream.]

(a) Nihilum; that is, non hilum, nulla res ne minima quidem [not a thread; nothing, not even the

least].

[p. 175]

V

“Is space a pure nothing?” Balmes asks, and to this question he answers: “He who says extension nothing contradicts himself in terms. If in a room everything it contains is reduced to nothing, it seems that the walls could no longer remain distant from one another, because the idea of distance includes a medium between two objects; and nothing cannot be a medium, it is nothing. To say that nothing can be a medium is to attribute a property to it, and to say that nothing can have properties is to destroy all ideas, it is to affirm the possibility of being and not being at the same time, and consequently to subvert the foundation of human knowledge.”

The soul of this reasoning is the scholastic axiom: Nihili nullæ sunt proprietates [of nothing there are no properties]: an axiom of complete evidence, but whose signification it is necessary to determine. We cannot attribute to nothing any positive quality, negative ones we can. Nothing cannot resist the movement of bodies, is a proposition which attributes to nothing a negative quality, and in which we perceive the same evidence as in the scholastic axiom, because the scholastic axiom contains it. With the same evidence we can say that nothing is not white, nor black, nor solid, nor liquid, nor aeriform. In a word, we can give it all imaginable attributes.

“Supposing an empty sphere,” Balmes continues, “within it there may be movement. Now, if the space contained is a pure nothing, movement is nothing also, and for that very reason does not exist. Movement can neither exist nor be conceived, except by traversing a certain distance: in this its essence consists; if the distance is nothing, nothing is traversed; therefore, there is no movement.” Who does not see here a play upon words, unworthy of so eminent a philosopher? Is it not clear that the possibility of movement within an empty sphere is a necessary consequence, of absolute necessity, of the impossibility [p. 176] of offering resistance, which is inseparable from nothing, and consequently from empty space, which is the very same, the selfsame nothing?

As to the idea which Balmes proposes to give us of space, we believe it sufficiently refuted by the corollaries he deduces from it, among which the following deserve to be noted:

That where there is no body there is no space.

That what is called distance is nothing else than the interposition of a body.

That when every intermediate body disappears there is no distance; there is immediacy, there is contact, by absolute necessity.

That if two bodies only existed in the universe, it would be metaphysically impossible to conceive distance between them.

That a vacuum, great or small, disseminated or heaped together, is absolutely impossible.

That a single body cannot move, because all movement supposes distance, and there is no distance when there is only one body.

That the universe cannot be bounded except in a certain manner, all those figures being excluded in which the shortest line between two points would fall outside the exterior surface.

Balmes himself, alarmed at such strange consequences, fears that some error may lie hidden in the principle from which he deduces them. That principle is none other than the nihili nullæ sunt proprietates, which indeed cannot be admitted in Balmes’s unlimited sense without putting it in contradiction with itself.

VI

Samuel Clarke, fascinated by the ideal existence of space, which he regarded as an ontological reality, and forced by the most imperative evidence to deny to space a substance in which the immense extension that the imagination attributes to it might reside, judged that, since an infinite quality must correspond to a subject equally infinite, space could not be conceived except as one and the same thing with the immensity of God. A like reasoning led him to identify time with the eternity of the First Cause.

[p. 177]

Leibniz powerfully combated the conceptions of Clarke. He denied to space and time not only the character of divine attributes, but that of real things; reducing them, as we have done, to mere abstractions or ideas. Kant thought in a similar way when he made them a priori conditions of all our empirical knowledge; but subjective conditions, that is, proper to the human intelligence; a mould to which it adapts all the notions that experience supplies to it.

Between these a priori conditions and the relations of succession which, as we have seen, belong equally to the conception of space and to that of time; relations which the soul engenders by virtue of the activity proper to it, there is, if well considered, no more difference than that of language, which in the first expression is synthetic and in the second analytic.

Space and time are, then, mere capacities for real existences; and although in themselves they be nothing, there will not for that reason be any contradiction in representing space to ourselves as a sphere of interminable dimensions, and time as a scale of interminable length, referring to the former all the extensions and to the latter all the durations that we can imagine. Far from these ideas being repugnant to the ontological nullity of time and space, they are on the contrary a necessary consequence of their absolute insubstantiality.

## PHILOS.     12

[PDF 194]

On sight as significative of touch.

Phenomenon of vision.—The eye: its physiological conformation for receiving the rays of light.—Convergence of the rays of light.—The optic axis.— Functions of sight analogous to those of touch.—The retina.—Simultaneous perceptions of sight.—Visual extension, or the ocular picture.—Visual dimensions.—Notions we should have by means of sight, without the aid of touch.— The laws of the visible world different from those of touch.—Visual signs that suggest to the understanding the tactile qualities of objects.—Reference of colors to objects placed in determinate situations.—Dr. Reid’s observation on the reference of the visible point to the tactile point.—Ministry of nature.— Experience.—Knowledge of the distances of bodies: movements of the eye.— The two eyes.—Measure of distance by the intersection of the two optic axes. —Observations of Dr. Reid.—Phenomenon of double vision.—Dimension of objects by means of their apparent magnitude.—Fading of colors as a means of estimating distances.—Illusions that objects occasion by reason of distance. —Tactile figures suggested by visual perception.—Appearance of reliefs.— Observation of Dr. Brown.—Judgments on the magnitude and distance of objects.—Universal language of sight.

The eyes are composed of membranes or tunics that give them their globular form, and of transparent substances destined to refract the rays of light.

There are, moreover, in the eyes, as in the whole animal organism, nerves and muscles, which are the organs of sensibility and of movement, and vessels that nourish the eyes, supply their peculiar secretions, and carry away from them whatever is superfluous, or altered and decomposed as a result of the vital functions.

Every visible point seems to emit at each instant, toward each [p. 179] eye, a pencil of rays or luminous straight lines, which by means of various refractions cross each other in the pupil, and pursue their course until they are again reduced to a point at the extremity of the pencil, where they strike a corresponding point of the retina.

What happens with respect to one point of the object happens with respect to all, and to the entire prospect; and as each pencil is tinged with a certain color according to the point from which it proceeds, the total result is a picture of the object and of the prospect, a picture instantaneous but in a certain manner permanent by reason of its continual reproduction; an exact copy of the objects, although inverted, because, the rays crossing each other in the pupil, those that come from above are directed downward; those from the right, toward the left, and reciprocally.

The convergence of the rays of light toward their respective foci is caused by the refractions they undergo in traversing the eye; an effect for which the density and the form of the various refracting substances are admirably adapted. And as visible objects are at different distances, the eye has the faculty of accommodating itself to them by lengthening or shortening the path of the rays of light, so that the focus of each pencil may coincide with a point of the retina.

It should be observed that when we undertake to examine an object attentively, by virtue of habits acquired from the earliest infancy we place the eye in such a manner that the pencil of rays coming from some point of the object strikes more or less the center of the retina, which is that which receives the most vivid impression and produces, consequently, the clearest and most distinct perception. The imaginary line which, issuing from a central point of the retina, terminates at the visible point of which a clear and distinct perception is desired, is called the optic axis. By giving, then, different positions to the optic axis by means of the various movements of the eye, we pass the sight over all the details of the surface under contemplation—a successive examination in which the psychological part of vision begins.

I do not mean by this that, in order to perform vision, the idea of any optic axis passes through our [p. 180] head, for what is so called is nothing but a line devised by physiologists to explain it. But the various movements of the eye furnish us with an equivalent means: these, like all those that concur in vision, were doubtless tried instinctively at the beginning, and, repeated without ceasing, came to be executed with an instantaneous rapidity, without perceptible intervention of the will or of consciousness.

To direct the sight, then, toward an external point is to give the eye the disposition suited to make this point, by impressing the center of the retina, produce in the organ the most vivid and distinct impression; and to study an object or a prospect with the sight is to give the eye successively the dispositions suited to make each point of the object or of the prospect, by impressing successively the center of the retina vividly and distinctly, be perceived in its turn by the soul. These movements of the organ of sight are analogous to those which we execute with the organ of touch in order to perceive successively the various parts of a tangible surface. Sight is truly a kind of touch exercised upon distant objects by means of the optic axis, which is like the staff that in the hand of the blind man in a certain manner prolongs for him the organ of touch, and serves him to explore, although in a highly imperfect manner, the bulks that lie before him.

The retina is pre-eminently the organ of sight, as the olfactory membrane of the nose is the organ of smell; and the rays of light play the part of the odoriferous effluvia, although with a most notable difference. In olfaction the organ does not act upon the effluvia in such a manner that we can conceive relations of extraposition, nor, consequently, any idea of extension; the same is true also of hearing, and would be true likewise of taste, if touch did not constantly accompany it.

It seems to us, in the present state of our intelligence, that by sight we perceive at a stroke the details of a somewhat extended surface; but it is probable that this faculty has been gradually acquired and perfected; and that [p. 181] sight, like touch, learned to perceive a surface simultaneously, deducing from the simultaneous sensations the successive sensations that would correspond to the movements of the organ. So it happens with those kinds of objects upon which sight has been very frequently exercised, of which reading offers us an example; laborious and slow in beginners, because they have to fix themselves successively on each letter; but so easy and rapid after many years of frequent exercise that an instant suffices to perceive all the letters of a word, and perhaps of an entire line. But this faculty of simultaneous perceptions is confined in sight to the objects of which we have just spoken. To acquaint ourselves with the details of an unfamiliar surface, we have to run over its various parts successively, until we stop at the minutest details, or at those which consist of forms already known and familiar. The vividness of the organic impression is then greatest at the central point, and diminishes by degrees in the surrounding parts in proportion to their distance from the center.

The sense of sight is exercised, then, immediately upon the retina, in so far as it is struck by the picture which is formed, as has been said, by the extremities of the luminous pencils. If we take from this picture all tactile significance; if we suppose an epoch of the intelligence in which this picture did not indicate to us situations, distances, figures, or colors of palpable objects, it is evident that, perceiving the correspondence of a continuous series of sensations of effort (sensations correlative to the various movements of the organ, but not accompanied by any idea of this correlation, nor of the organ), we could not but perceive by means of the ocular picture a visual extension, which resolved itself into continuous extrapositions, each of which was made known to us by the effort we made in order to perceive successively two points.

When we say ocular picture, this expression is not to be taken in the sense we give it by virtue of the knowledge we have acquired at a later time. A picture is for us, in the present state of our intelligence, a surface [p. 182] of such or such tactile figure, of such or such tactile dimensions, in such or such a situation within reach of touch; and it is evident that sight alone could never have led us to the ideas of these tangible qualities. What, then, in our hypothesis, is the ocular picture? A complex of causes which at each given moment excited a complex of visual sensations by means of which, and of the organic efforts necessary to make the elementary sensations successively vivid and distinct, we perceived successively various extrapositions, but of causes in other respects unknown.

We must also guard against believing that we gave to the things pictured on the retina the dimensions that we habitually attribute to the tactile objects signified by them. Of what size is that tree in the ocular picture? Sight instructed by touch gives it a height of three or four yards, which is a tactile dimension; but sight by itself could not have given it any dimensions of that kind. The tree appears larger to sight the more of the prospect it takes up, and smaller the less. The compass of the ocular picture, which is constant, is the natural scale of visual dimensions. But this picture, which in the estimate of touch will have a certain number of lines in diameter, has for sight no tactile dimensions of any kind. Its visual magnitude is the fundamental measure of the other visual magnitudes, and there is outside of it no measure to which we can refer it.

If we could separate from the artificial appearance called phantasmagoria all tactile significance, all idea of tactile locality and dimensions, it would be for us the same as the phenomenon produced by the picture on the retina.

This, if I am not mistaken, is the history of the knowledge we should have acquired by sight without the instruction of touch.

Before we had come to consider visual sensations as effects and signs of causes distinct from the I, they must have been for us mere modifications of the I perceived by consciousness; and visible extension could not have been anything else for us than the correspondence of a series of visual sensations [p. 183] considered as mere modifications of the soul, to a series of sensations of effort, considered in the same manner.

Once the visual sensations were referred to causes distinct from the I, and represented by them, we should have perceived, in the variety of the effort necessary to perceive successively two visible points, the various modes of extraposition of these points, or in other terms, their various reciprocal situations, merely visual.

By adding extrapositions, we should have perceived visual surfaces of various sizes and forms, and we should have acquired ideas of merely visual distances and places.

We conceive situations, forms, sizes, distances, and places as relations of various causes, represented by the visual sensations.

The extensions perceived in this manner must have been mere lines and surfaces: objects consisted of two dimensions only, and space was an indefinite surface. But while certain efforts moved the organ, other efforts transported the spectator from one place to another; and to this second kind of efforts there corresponded considerable changes in the prospect; some objects expanded, others contracted; some appeared, others ceased to be seen, or presented themselves anew; as if things came out of nothing and returned to it, grew and dwindled, at our pleasure. Was it not natural that we should thus form the idea of an extension which we penetrated, of a space that spread out in every direction and was peopled with various prospects that succeeded one another with a certain regularity and under determinate connections?

The visible world is governed by laws very different from those of the world which the affections of touch make known to us. In the latter, magnitudes and forms are constant, or variable only within narrow limits dependent upon material agencies; in the former, on the contrary, magnitudes and forms vary extremely, according to the position we take; the tree that now occupies a very small part of the prospect may, if I wish, cover it all: the object that is now a [p. 184] circle will become a more or less eccentric ellipse, and, if I take the fancy, a straight line. In the tactile universe the reciprocal situations of objects are likewise constant, or variable only in subjection to the laws of the real motion of bodies: in the visual universe it is not so: the reciprocal situations of objects vary in subjection to the laws of the apparent motion of bodies, which are very different from those of real motion. Finally, the objects which touch makes known to us, that is to say, bodies properly so called, are impenetrable; each necessarily occupies a space, and does not yield it to another body except by passing to occupy another space; whereas the objects which sight alone makes known to us interpenetrate continually in their movements, now the moving object disappearing beneath the objects it meets, now these disappearing beneath the moving object. Hence it follows that the ideas which we should form by means of sight of the causes of our sensation would be absolutely different from those which we form by means of touch. It is to touch, therefore, associated with the sense of effort, that the idea we have of the material universe is truly due.

Such, if I am not mistaken, are the notions which sight would have formed by itself, without the aid of touch. But it is probable that the variable perceptions of the former sense began very early to signify to us the constant perceptions of the latter.

Everything was prepared by the Author of nature in order that touch might derive from the visual affections an incalculable advantage. The affections of sight are continuous while we are awake, and correspond to tactile phenomena that occupy an immense compass. On the contrary, nothing is more limited than the reach of touch.
