To this is added the different facility of the organic movements, which is much less in the exercise of touch. To give sight a tactile significance was in a certain manner to put wings on touch; to make it capable of traversing in a few moments what otherwise would have required ages of laborious examination, and to subject to it even the objects which without the ministry of sight would have been eternally inaccessible to it.

[p. 185]

Let us now see what kind of signs are those which in vision suggest to the understanding the tactile qualities of the distant objects that by means of light affect the retina.

The first step is to refer colors to distant objects placed in determinate situations. We refer the sensation of color produced by each point of the ocular picture to a tangible point situated in the prolongation of an imaginary straight line which issues from that point of the picture and passes through the center of the eye. The lines that issue from the various points of the ocular picture cross, then, all in a central point of the eye; those that issue from the lower part of the picture are directed upward; those from the upper, downward; those from the right, toward the left; those from the left, toward the right. The reciprocal situation of the points of the ocular picture makes known to us the reciprocal situation of the corresponding tangible points in the prolongations of the various respective straight lines; and it is clear that, in referring the color of each point of the ocular picture to a tactile cause situated in the said direction, we could not recognize as the cause of the various sensations of color the distant points that excite them, if the ocular picture did not present them in a reciprocal situation inverse to that in which touch perceives them.

I express here the connection between each point of the ocular picture and each point of the tactile object by means of the line which, issuing from the first of these two points, passes very nearly through the center of the eye; not because, when we exercise the sense of sight, we think of any line, but because everything happens as if the idea of that line were present to the understanding. By the inner sense of effort we know the position of the organ; from the position of the organ we deduce the situation of the tactile point that corresponds to the central point of the retina, which is that which gives us the most vivid sensation; and from the situation of the points of the ocular picture among themselves, and with respect to the central point, we infer the reciprocal situation of the corresponding tactile points, placing each of them in the prolongation of the straight line that issues from the respective point of the retina and passes, as we have said, through the center of the eye; without [p. 186] its being necessary for this that we think of the central point or of any straight line. The result is the conception of the color and of the tactile situation of the surface under contemplation, and of each of its parts.

At first sight it might be believed that we see each point in the direction which the rays have in striking the retina, because it seems natural that the various directions of the rays should produce different impressions on the retina, and, therefore, different sensations, which the soul would be capable of discerning, as it discerns the slightest shades of color painted by them. Dr. Reid observes that each point of the retina is struck by rays that reach it in different directions, as they form a cone of which it is itself the apex; and that notwithstanding this variety we refer the visible point to the tactile point that lies in the prolongation of a straight line, namely, that which passes through the center of the eye; which, according to Reid himself, is not due to any particular virtue of the rays that pass through the center of the eye, because, if these rays are intercepted, the same image is formed on the retina with the others, and the objective point that sends them is seen in the same direction as before.(a) What is it, then, that makes us place the tactile point in the prolongation of the imaginary straight line? Is it a primary law of nature, an instinct? Of the existence of such instincts in various species of animals there is no doubt, since we see them, before all experience, direct themselves correctly to the tactile objects that present themselves to their sight.(b)

But nature has observed a special plan in the education of man. She has desired from very early to instruct him by experience and by his reason. All that man

(a) Any portion of the rays that form the objective cone may be intercepted, by

placing over the pupil a playing card pierced with a hole, which lets pass only the other portions.

(b) “The chicks of the great family of the gallinaceous birds walk already on leav‐

ing the shell, and are seen running eagerly toward the grain and managing to peck at it; which proves that they know how to make very good use of their eyes and estimate with exactness situations and distances.” Cabanis, Rapports du phyzique et du moral, Second Mémoire. [p. 187] has been able to learn by means of experience, there is sufficient reason to believe he has not owed to special instincts, and the apprenticeship in question does not appear more difficult than so many others which, in the first dawn of reason, have undoubtedly been the fruit of observation excited by necessity, and of a kind of spontaneous analogical reasoning of which consciousness gave no notice.

The intensity of the light and the direction in which it is received cause the color to vary considerably, and for this reason painters diversify with various shades of the same color, and sometimes substitute for it another different one, to indicate the more or less vivid, more or less direct light with which the object and each of its parts is bathed. When we see a garment whose color is uniform, its folds would appear to us of different colors, if we judged of it by the visual sensations which they truly excite. But, instructed by experience, we see in these accidental variations only the undulations of the surface, and attribute to each point its particular and constant coloring, which is that in which we should see it at a short distance and in a sufficient degree of light, in a determinate position. Experience teaches us, then, to judge of the true coloring of objects, which is constant, by the apparent, which is variable; and this variety is an important element in the judgment we form of the reciprocal situation of the various tactile objects, and of the reciprocal situation of the various parts of one and the same tactile object, of its prominences and concavities, and, in a word, of its form.

The situation of visible objects being known, we pass to estimate their distance. Nature, as has been said before, has endowed us with the faculty of modifying the disposition of the parts that form the internal structure of the eye, so that, adapted to the distance of objects, these may be painted on the retina by the rays of light with the greatest possible clearness and distinctness. By contracting some muscles we adapt the refracting apparatus of the eye to the vision of near objects; and by contracting others we adapt it to the vision of distant objects. It is not for us to inquire what efforts we make or [p. 188] what muscles we move in each case; it is certain that from the tenderest age we learn to accommodate the eyes to distances in order to see objects as attentively as possible. The varying distance of the object obliges us to modify the internal structure of the eye, and each modification of the internal structure of the eye is accompanied by particular efforts, from which arise internal sensations of effort that constitute natural signs of distances.

But this way of estimating them does not furnish results at all precise, except when the object is situated between 6 and 7 inches and 15 and 16 feet distant from the eye. Within the first limit vision is ordinarily confused; beyond the second, the differences between the modes of adaptation of the organ are less and less easy to distinguish.

It follows from what I have just said that distinct vision signifies a mean distance of at least 6 to 7 inches. A small object, situated half an inch from the eye, appears to us to be much farther off if we look at it through a little hole made with the point of a pin in a playing card; and for no other reason than that in this way we succeed in seeing it distinctly.

Hitherto we have spoken of the organ of sight as if it were only one in each individual; but we have two eyes, and it is necessary to examine whether, both concurring in vision, the one of them does no more than duplicate what passes in the other, or whether their combined actions add something to what each eye is capable of symbolizing to us by itself. Let us observe at the outset that, if there is no preternatural defect in the organic movements that concur in vision, when one eye moves upward or downward, to the right or to the left, or in any other direction, the other eye executes the same: as if the two were set in motion by one and the same force. Thus when both are open we see them directed constantly to one and the same object; and when one of them is closed, it does not on that account cease to move in the same direction as the other, whether we will it or not; and what makes this phenomenon still more curious is that the nerves and muscles that contribute [p. 189] to produce these organic movements are wholly distinct and have no apparent connection with one another.

Let it not be supposed that this depends on a habit acquired in infancy, for if it were so, when the child begins to see he would move one eye differently from the other, as he does with the arms and the legs, and would gradually learn to give them parallel directions; since habits are formed only by the repetition of the same acts, performed at first with intention and labor, and progressively easier and more rapid. It appears, then, that before all custom there is in the constitution of the animal an instinct which induces it to move the two eyes in parallel.

But this parallelism is not to be understood to the letter, for although the eyes are never otherwise than approximately parallel, there will hardly be a moment when they are so with perfect exactness. When we direct the sight to a point, the two optic axes must meet in it, forming an angle the greater the nearer the object is. Nature, by giving us the faculty of altering, although within narrow limits, the parallelism of the eyes, has thus furnished us, within the same limits, with a means of estimating the tactile distance at which visible objects are situated with respect to us. The intersection of the two optic axes determines the distance of the objective point. To be sure, we do not measure the angle formed by these two straight lines in order to determine by it the distance of the intersection; but according as the distance varies, and consequently the reciprocal inclination of the optic axes, the reciprocal position of the two eyes must vary; and we perceive this varying position by means of the efforts we make to place them and to maintain them in it.

When the object is not very far off, we can by this means estimate the distance with sufficient exactness; but, in proportion as the object recedes, the inclination of the optic axes varies less and less; the two eyes approach more and more to a perfect parallelism, in which we can scarcely perceive differences; and judgments of distance are in this same proportion more vague and more exposed to error. At great distances the [p. 190] two optic axes are sensibly parallel, and however much the distance be increased, the parallelism remains. Hence it is that the sun, the moon, the planets and the fixed stars appear to be situated at one and the same distance, as if they were fixed upon the concave surface of a great sphere, whose centre is the observer.

The individual who loses the sight of one eye loses together with it this means of estimating distances, and at first deceives himself in the judgments he makes of them, even with respect to objects that he can reach with his hand. With one of the two eyes closed it is difficult for us to thread a needle; from which it may be gathered that the inclination of the optic axes, or, in other words, the internal perception of the reciprocal position of the eyes, is the principal indication on which we rely for the estimation of small distances.

The same is deduced from the following observation, which we copy almost literally from Dr. Reid.

“When a picture is seen with both eyes, and at no great distance, the representation appears not so natural as when it is seen only with one. The intention of painting being to deceive the eye, and to make things appear at different distances, which in reality are upon the same piece of canvas, this deception is not so easily put upon both eyes as upon one; because we perceive the distance of visible objects more exactly and determinately with two eyes than with one. If the shading and relief be executed in the best manner, the picture may have almost the same appearance to one eye as the objects themselves would have, but it cannot have the same appearance to both. This is not the fault of the artist, but an unavoidable imperfection in the art.”

“The great impediment, and I think the only invincible impediment, to that agreeable deception of the eye which the painter aims at, is the perception which we have of the distance of visible objects from the eye, partly by means of the conformation of the eye, but chiefly by means of the inclination of the optic axes. If this perception could be removed, I see no reason why a picture might not be made so perfect as to deceive the eye in reality, and to be mistaken for the original object. Therefore, in order to judge of the merit of a picture, we ought, as much as [p. 191] possible, to exclude these two means of perceiving the distance of the several parts of it. This is what, up to a certain point, intelligent persons achieve by covering one of the two eyes and applying a tube to the other; whereby they succeed in clearing away the indication of distance deduced from the inclination of the optic axes, and at the same time in intercepting the sight of other near objects, whose connection with the canvas would cause the illusion to vanish.”

Another notable effect of the concurrence of the two organs is the one I now proceed to set forth.

When the two eyes concur in vision, it happens that, both axes being directed toward one and the same point, which is consequently impressed upon the centres of the two retinas, the vision of that point is single and not double, notwithstanding the duplication of the image; and the same happens with all the points in the field of vision that are situated at the same distance from the eyes as the point to which we direct our sight. If, then, we place a lighted candle at ten feet distance, and direct the two optic axes toward it, and at the same time attend to another candle placed in a different spot at the same distance, we shall likewise not have a double vision, but a single one, of this second candle. What there is in common in both cases is that the object whose appearance is single is depicted on corresponding points of the two retinas, that is to say, either on the two centres, or on points similarly situated with respect to the two centres. Every point of the retina of the right eye is, then, in correspondence or harmony with a point of the retina of the left eye; and the two points either occupy the two centres, or are similarly situated with respect to them.

On the contrary, objects placed either nearer or farther than that to which we direct the two axes, and which consequently, according to the laws of optics, are impressed on points differently situated with respect to the centres of the two retinas, each produce two distinct appearances. If, then, I place a candle at ten feet distance, and, extending an arm, raise a finger between the candle and my eyes, it will happen that, looking at the candle, I shall see two fingers, and looking at my finger I shall see two candles.

[p. 192]

This phenomenon of double vision is not generally noticed, because, in order that it should be, we should have to direct the two optic axes to the object which is doubled, and by that very fact and in that same instant the duplication would cease. It would not, then, be strange that many persons to whom the phenomenon was pointed out as a thing of constant recurrence should assert in good faith that in all their lives they had never observed that duplicated appearance; which nevertheless takes place at every moment, and of which those same persons would be convinced by the experiments I have just indicated. Though it is not easy for everyone to perceive it in the first trials, because we must do ourselves some violence in order to direct the sight to one object and attend at the same time to another. But notwithstanding that this phenomenon of double vision is continually produced, taught by experience, we represent to ourselves a single object when in reality we see two.

As in certain circumstances a single object is invariably seen doubled, so in certain circumstances two real objects are confounded with one another and appear to us as one. Let us apply to the two eyes, in a parallel direction, two similar tubes, and we shall seem to see with them a single object; and if at the extremities of the two tubes there are placed two small pieces of money of the same size and shape, one exactly in one optic axis and the other exactly in the other, we shall seem to be seeing a single piece of money. And if two coins, or any other bodies whatever, of different colour and shape are placed in the same manner at the extremities of the two tubes, the two bodies will be seen at once in one and the same spot, without the one concealing the other, and the colour of both will be that which corresponds to the composition of the two colours.

In conclusion, the central points of the two retinas harmonize naturally with each other, and nature has preordained the same harmony between any points whatever of the two retinas that are similarly placed around their respective centres; in such terms that a single object impressed on inharmonious points appears to us double, and [p. 193] two real and distinct objects impressed on harmonious points appear to us one.

In the ordinary use of sight we pay no attention to the phenomenon of duplication, because we are not wont to attend save to the point to which the two optic axes are actually directed; but we are not on that account to think that the sensations excited by the concurrence of the two organs are in every respect similar to those which the constant simplicity of the visual appearances would produce, or that, the sensations differing up to a certain point, this difference signifies absolutely nothing to the soul; for the effect of the modifications of the soul to which we pay no attention, although so faint and obscure that it is neither noticed nor remembered, is not entirely null, but always contributes in some way to the development of our judgments and volitions. Thus, when, instructed by experience, we were able to give, in certain circumstances, the signification of unity to two visible appearances, it was natural that this duplicity should become for us a sign of the different distance of the objects placed in the field of vision, which had thus to come to represent to us a space extending in length, breadth and depth.

The adaptation of the refracting apparatus of the eye, and the inclination of the optic axes, serve only for estimating small distances; other signs we have of more general application, although the less capable of precision the greater the distance is. One of them consists in the dimension of the apparent magnitude of the object. This apparent magnitude, as everyone knows, is the smaller the more distant the object is. I know by experience the magnitude in which a man or any other object appears at the distance of 10 feet; I perceive the gradual diminution of the figure at the distance of 20, 30, 100 feet, and at still greater distances, until I cease to see it; and in this way the visible magnitude of a known object becomes a sign of the distance. Hence it is that a known object seen through a lens appears to approach us in the same proportion in which the lens increases its dimensions.

“If a man who had never before seen objects through a

## PHILOS.     13

[p. 194]

telescope were told that the telescope which he is about to use magnifies the dimensions of objects ten times, would he not suppose that a man, for example, seen with the telescope, was to be transformed for him into a giant 60 feet in stature? But it is not so. The man appears to him no bigger, but nearer than before. There is no doubt that the telescope magnifies the image of this man upon the retina ten times in diameter; but, as we have been accustomed to see this visible magnitude, when he was ten times nearer than he is presently, and in no other case, this visible magnitude suggests the conception of that distance with which it hath been always connected in the understanding, and the spectator makes no change in his judgment of the real magnitude.”

The fourth means of estimating distance consists in the faintness of the colours, owing to the blue veil, imperfectly transparent, in which the atmosphere envelops objects; to which is added the confusion of the minute parts, and the indefiniteness of the outlines. “Hence it is,” says Reid, “that painters, not content, in order to represent distance, with diminishing the dimensions, make the colours more faint and languid, soften the outline of objects, and disguise the prominences and depressions of the surface. If a painter should make a human figure ten times less than another, having the colours as bright, and the outline and minute parts as accurately defined, it would not have the appearance of a man of ordinary stature at a distance, but of a pigmy or Lilliputian close at hand.”

When an object consists of various colours, placed in some particular manner, its distance is more clearly indicated by the various colours being formed into a single one by insensible gradations. In a tower near at hand I perceive with perfect clearness the joinings of its various parts; the grey of the stones and the white of the mortar that unites them are clearly defined and limited; and the line of separation is distinctly perceptible. When the tower is seen from farther off, the joinings are perceived more obscurely, and the two colours begin to be confounded. And as the distance is increased, the limits that separate the one from the other disappear, and from the two there results a homogeneous colour.

“In an apple tree covered with flowers, which presents itself to me at [p. 195] the distance of twelve feet, I can perceive the figure and the colour of the leaves and petals; through the leaves I descry pieces of branches, some enlightened by the sun’s rays, others shaded; and some of the interstices let me see the blue vault of the sky. When I gradually remove from the tree, its appearance changes every minute; the parts are mixed and confounded; the colours of sky, branches, leaves and petals are gradually diluted into each other, and the colour of the whole becomes more and more uniform.

“Berkeley, in his travels through Italy and Sicily, observed that cities and palaces seen at a great distance appeared nearer to him by several miles than they really were; and he attributes it to the purity of the Italian air, which gave to very distant objects that degree of brightness and distinctness which, in the grosser air of his own country, was to be seen only in those that are near. Hence also the Italian painters give a more lively colour to the sky than the Flemish. Ought they not, for the same reason, to give less degradation of the colours, and less indistinctness of the minute parts, in the representation of very distant objects?

“As, in air uncommonly pure, we are apt to think visible objects nearer and less than they really are, so, in thick and foggy air, we exaggerate their dimensions and distances. Walking by the sea-side in a thick fog, I see an object which seems to me to be a man on horseback, and at the distance of about half a mile. My companion, who has better eyes, or more experience of illusions of this kind, assures me that the object which seems to me a man is in reality a sea-gull. I look again, and recognize my error: the object is suddenly transformed before my sight into a sea-gull at the distance of seventy or eighty yards. The error and the correction are so instantaneous that they seem rather immediate perceptions than suggested judgments. The truth is that my belief is in both cases produced rather by signs than by arguments; by habit rather than by reasonings of which we are conscious. Here is what I imagine to have been the procedure of my understanding. In the first place, not knowing, or not taking into account, the effect of the fog, I seem to perceive in the object those faded tints, that outline [p. 196] indefinite and obscure, which bodies commonly present at the distance of half a mile: the visible appearance is here a sign which suggests to me the idea of this distance. And in the second place, this distance, together with the visible magnitude, signifies to me the tactile magnitude of a man on horseback, which I erroneously attribute to the object. Thus the deception is brought about. But no sooner do I perceive that the object is a sea-gull, than the ordinary magnitude of the species, together with the visible magnitude now presented to my eyes, immediately suggests to me the idea of the true distance, and in the faintness of the visible characters I see no longer anything but the ordinary effect of the fog. The whole chain of signs and ideas seems to me now stronger and better connected than before: the half mile vanishes to eighty yards: the man on horseback dwindles to the dimensions of a sea-gull; I seem to see a new object, and it is not possible for me to recover the former judgments.

“The fifth means of estimating the distance of an object is that which is furnished by intervening or contiguous objects whose distance or magnitude we know. When I perceive that a plain or tract of country lies between me and the object, the dimensions of this suggest to me the idea of the distance at which the object is. Even when we have not traversed the intermediate ground, we can easily estimate its dimensions, by the habit we have of judging of the surfaces that are presented to our sight, and which we measure in a certain manner with our steps; a habit which we acquire early, because it is one of those that most concern us.”

An object placed on the top of a high building appears to us less than on the ground, the distances being supposed equal; because in this second situation the intervening ground suggests the idea of the true distance, and the distance, together with the visible magnitude, becomes a sign of the real magnitude; but in the first situation, the indication of the intervening ground being wanting, the estimated distance is somewhat less than the true one; and this erroneous apprehension, together with the visible magnitude, makes us likewise err as to the real magnitude, and judge it somewhat smaller than is proper.

[p. 197]

“The two first means would never of themselves make the distance of a visible object appear to exceed 150 or 200 feet, because beyond that limit there is no sensible change, either in the conformation of the eye or in the inclination of the axes. The third means is applied especially to objects whose tactile magnitude we know. The fourth is but a vague and undeterminate sign, applied to distances of more than 200 or 300 feet. When some unknown object, situated on the surface of the earth, appears to us to be at the distance of some miles, the fifth means is that which leads us to this judgment.

“Dr. Smith has observed, very justly, that the known distance of the terrestrial objects which terminate our view makes that part of the sky which is towards the horizon appear more distant than that which is towards the zenith. Hence it comes to pass that the apparent figure of the sky is not properly that of a hemisphere, but rather a less segment of a sphere; and hence likewise it comes to pass that the diameter of the sun or moon, or the distance between two fixed stars, seen in such a manner that their apparent distance is small with respect to a hill or other terrestrial object, appears much greater than when no such objects strike the eye at the same time. To this it may be added that when the visible horizon is terminated by very distant objects, the celestial vault seems to be enlarged in all its dimensions. When I view it from a confined street or lane, it bears some proportion to the buildings that surround me; but when I view it from a wide plain, around which rises an amphitheatre of distant hills and ranges, methinks I see a new heaven, whose magnificence declares the greatness of its Author, and puts every human edifice out of countenance; for what are then the lofty towers and gorgeous palaces, and what proportion do they bear to the immensity of the heavens?”

Passing from distance to figure, it is enough to note that one and the same palpable and real form presents to sight innumerable apparent figures, according to the various positions of the object, to perceive that the former can seldom be deduced from the latter with any tolerable exactness; and in reality there are no judgments in which sight more often deceives us than in those which we form concerning [p. 198] the tactile forms of objects whose kind is unknown to us. We proceed with more security when, from the comparison of various visible appearances, taken in different situations, we deduce the palpable form. But reasoning is then a slow operation, a calculation that is very far from those rapid inferences in which the visible, acting as a sign, instantaneously excites tactile conceptions.

The only deductions relative to tactile figure that deserve to be counted among the secondary perceptions of sight are those suggested by the distribution of lights and shadows, which painters call chiaroscuro.

Light reveals to us the reliefs, shadow the concavities; and from the more or less sudden or gradual transition from the one to the other, we infer the smoothness or roughness of the prominences and depressions, and the greater or less sharpness of the salient and re-entrant angles.

Each relief, looked at obliquely, hides from us a greater or lesser part of the surface; a part which, looked at from another place, would become visible to us, another part of the surface disappearing in its turn behind the same relief. Now, the spaces concealed by the projection of the relief upon the background of a near perspective do not coincide exactly for the two eyes, and the lack of coincidence is the greater the less the distance of the object. Hence arises another insuperable obstacle to the illusions of painting. The reliefs figured in a picture are projected, with respect to the two eyes, upon one and the same part of the background of the perspective, and consequently cannot produce in us, when we see it with both eyes, that exact combination of impressions which corresponds to the vision of real solids. This defect is imperceptible when the picture represents distant objects; but in the contrary case it would not be possible, seeing it near with the two eyes, that the projection should appear to us entirely natural.

“As we are not accustomed to think of visible figure,” says Dr. Reid, “and make use of it only as a sign which represents to us the tangible form, as soon as [p. 199] it has done its office we dismiss it from our attention, and its idea vanishes, without leaving so much as a trace in the understanding. The painter, whose office it is to hunt after these fugitive forms and copy them, knows how difficult it is to succeed in this, even after many years of labor and practice. Happy he, if he comes to possess the art of fixing them in his imagination in order to transfer them to the canvas, for then it will be as easy for him to copy the ocular picture formed by nature as any other picture. But how few are they who attain this facility!”

If the knowledge of distance contributes little to that of form, it is not so with the magnitude or size of objects. These two things, magnitude and distance, most frequently suggest one another. Given the magnitude, we estimate by it the distance, and vice versa, given the distance, we estimate by it the magnitude.

A certain illusion, caused at times by a kind of morbid sensibility of the retina, shows the intimate connection of the judgments we form concerning the magnitude and the distance of objects. When I have spent some time reading, especially by artificial light, and in a chamber whose imperfect illumination makes reading somewhat laborious to me, it happens that some minutes after I close the book and rise, I seem still to see the lines and letters, though in a state of motion, and as if climbing confusedly upon one another, so that I can scarcely recognize here and there a monosyllabic word, which escapes me instantly. But in the midst of this confusion the letters, invariable in their form, appear to me larger and larger, as I withdraw from the wall upon which they are projected and on which they seem to me to be impressed. The different distances of the wall, which are known to me, suggest to me different magnitudes of the letters; and the suggestion is so instantaneous that it is impossible for me to distinguish it from the actual perception.

Such are the principal means we have of perceiving the palpable qualities of objects by our visual affections.

It has been judged, with sufficient reason, that if men [p. 200] spoke one and the same language in all the countries of the world, it would be difficult for us not to believe that there is a natural, unlearned connection between our ideas and the words we make use of to express them. “It is not wonderful, therefore,” as Brown observes, “that a similar illusion should take place with respect to what may be termed the universal language of vision. Visual perceptions constitute a language which all understand, since they suggest to all the same ideas concerning the situations, distances, forms and dimensions of bodies; but if we understand this language, it is because we have learned it, as we learn the native tongue, by noting the correspondence between the signs and the objects.”

[PDF 217]

On the relation of identity.—Substantiality.

I. Peculiar character of the relation of identity.—We conceive it first in our own being.—It is revealed in every exercise of memory, and always attests the unity and continuity of the I.—True relation of identity, different from those which language is wont to denote.—Identity of time of two phenomena.—II. Substantiality of the I; knowledge of the substantiality of bodies.— Appendix I. On intelligence in brutes.—Existence of the soul in them.

I

The relation of identity has this singular feature, that we cannot conceive it between two distinct things, but only in one and the same thing considered in two different states, modifications or appearances.

We conceive it first in our own being, in the I, in the substance that contemplates itself. The soul shows itself to us identical with itself, even when it exercises diverse functions. The I that feels, that perceives, that remembers, that imagines, that judges, that reasons, that desires, that wills, is to our consciousness one and the same I, one and the same being, one and the same substance. Thus those who attributed sensibility to the body and intelligence to the soul erred gravely. The phenomena of sensibility are modes of which we have intuition, no less than of judgments or of reasonings, and in [p. 202] all the phenomena of which we have intuition the soul perceives itself as a being always identical.

The exercise of memory involves the judgment of the identity of our being at all the remembered moments of our existence and at the moment of recollection. To experience a recollection is not merely for a past perception to be excited anew, but for the soul to recognize it as its own, perceiving at the same time, between the thing remembered and the things of which it has present perception, the relation of before and after.

The perception of our identity is an essential principle of the constitution of the human soul, by virtue of which it is impossible for us not to consider our various successive or simultaneous affections, not only as simultaneous or successive, but as ours, as states or modifications of a single substance.

To perceive the identity of the I is to perceive unity in something that presents itself to us under different appearances; and to perceive its continuity is to perceive unity in something that presents itself to us under successive appearances.

The continuity of our being is shown to us in the concatenation of our present perceptions with our recollections, as far back as the first epochs of life. If it should happen, then, that at some point of our existence all the earlier perceptions were effaced from memory, and an entirely new store of recollections and knowledge began to be formed out of other perceptions, this point would separate, so to speak, two intellectual existences incapable of identifying themselves in the soul, and in this sense distinct.

But they would not be so in reality. The unity of the being is independent of the intuitive perception of it. The relation by virtue of which we call objects or ideas identical may be known by perception or by reasoning; and it may also exist although we do not by any means arrive at the knowledge of it.

When we conceive that two or more objects are identified, we figure them to ourselves, as we have said, under the image of that unity which we perceive intuitively only in ourselves. But with the word identity (and the same is applicable [p. 203] to the contrary word, distinction) we are wont to signify widely different relations: the identity of substance, which the mind perceives intuitively in all its simultaneous modifications and in the concatenation of its perceptions and recollections, and which we represent to ourselves in the other substances, conceiving them like our own; the identity of person, which we attribute to the intelligence that presents itself under various appearances, as when we judge that the Caesar who conquered the Gauls was the same Caesar who conquered at Pharsalia and who was slain by Brutus and Cassius in the Roman Senate; the identity of the living body, which consists in the continuity of the functions that constitute life, without being impaired by the renewal of molecules that takes place unceasingly in all organized structures; the identity of class, which is the resemblance of characters by virtue of which we impose the same name on two or more distinct entities, and specific identity, which in living bodies is the same as identity of class, together with the faculty of procreating among themselves individuals of the same forms, and capable also of transmitting them by generation.

The identity of time of two phenomena is coexistence with a determinate segment of the infinite scale of time. In time it is easy for us to set up as many standards as we please, to refer existences to them; in space it is not so. There is for us in space no fixed point to which we can refer objects, in order to determine, by means of their distances and situations relatively to that point, their absolute places, because everything within man’s reach is in motion. There are for us no absolute places. If the earth remained motionless in space, the situation and distances of an object with respect to a given point of the earth would constitute its absolute place, and in the identity of that relation would consist the identity of place of one or more objects at different moments. But we know only places relative to a given point, whose motion we disregard while we move with it. Like the places of the things in the ship in which we sail, so are the places [p. 204] of things on the earth, the places of the planets in our planetary system, and the successive places of this system about a center which already seems to be dimly descried; and this very center probably changes its place in vast revolutions around another center, without our being able to say where this successive involution of orbits within orbits, and of systems within systems, comes to an end.

We have noted that the identity of the living body is the uninterrupted continuity of the vital functions. There are other similar acceptations of the same word. When we say, for example, that the river which has its source in a certain place is identically the same that empties into the sea at another, we affirm only the continuity of its course, which may hold good although not a single drop from the source reaches the mouth.(a)

It follows that identity is in the greater part of cases a complex relation. Vital identity, for example, is an uninterrupted series of vital functions; and identity of class is a relation of resemblance, which is resolved many times into a great number of elementary resemblances.

The identities of substance, of life, of person are called individual; a river is also considered as a single individual; the ocean with all its dependencies is another. Between these and the identities of class and species there is a considerable difference: to the former we give unity as their type, and to the latter, resemblance.

II

Properly speaking, we perceive no other substance than that of the individual I, and this serves us as a type for representing to ourselves that which

(a) In geography the continuity of course is wont to be combined with the identi‐

ty of the name which a continuous stream retains in different places, without yielding it to the other streams with which it joins. But the first of these two ideas is necessary and fundamental. [p. 205] by an instinctive and irresistible analogy we attribute to the other intelligent and sensible beings.

Do we conceive substance in bodies? Do we conceive that there is in them something real, though neither intelligent nor sensible, which serves as the seat of the qualities we represent to ourselves in them? We know those qualities only through the corresponding sensations and through the relations which the mind conceives between these; we know them only as causes of sensations that we perceive in ourselves, and of relations which our mind engenders, by a kind of activity proper to it, in comparing the sensations; the idea of substantiality in bodies is thus far nothing other than the idea of causality.

But this power which causes the sensation necessarily exists in something real. Shall we figure this real identity to ourselves in what we call matter? Or shall we place it in the Great Spirit, Creator and Preserver? This has been a hotly contested question in the arena of Philosophy: a question which nevertheless (as I hope to prove later on), reduced to its true dimensions, hardly leaves an appreciable difference between the opinions of the two opposed parties. This is not the fitting place to discuss them.(a)

## APPENDIX I

## ON INTELLIGENCE IN BRUTES

That brutes feel and compare their sensations is absolutely beyond doubt. They have consequently a soul; and that soul is in them, as in man, a simple substance,

(a) This chapter, doubtless, would have been eliminated by the author, who

would have had in view to segregate the parts of its content in order to adapt them successively to the matters which, like those of section 3 of chapter 2, and those of the final section of chapter 9, seem to have been reproduced subsequently with the dismemberment of the [p. 206] unextended, incorporeal. Nor is this opposed to the human soul and that of brutes being of different natures, for there is no reason whatever to deny that God has created widely different species of immaterial substances, with faculties more or less exalted and with different future destinies.

From the immateriality of the soul of brutes it follows neither that it is capable of moral ideas, since even in the human species neither children nor idiots have them; nor that it is destined to immortality, since from the immaterial and simple the immortal does not necessarily follow. The human soul can be annihilated by God; and if it can be annihilated, this annihilation could be subjected to general laws pre-established by the Creator; in a word, God can create substances that are simple and at the same time perishable, because these two things involve no contradiction. Existence is a gift which the Divinity is not obliged to grant unconditionally and irrevocably. We know that the human soul is immortal; but not because it is unextended, but by another kind of proofs, deduced from the moral phenomena of the universe, as we shall see farther on.(a) Appendices first and second of the present chapter. We reserve, therefore, the useful part of it that remains, deduced from the special content which it represented in the primitive plan, and as is shown by the oldest writing and redaction that appears in the original.

(Note by the Editors.)

(a) Pomponazzi, a Mantuan philosopher, wrote at the beginning of the sixteenth

century a book in which he undertook to prove that reason alone cannot make known to us the immortality of the soul, but that we are bound to believe in it, as a revealed truth, set down in Scripture and confirmed by decisions of the Catholic Church. This apparent deference to religious dogma did not deceive Pomponazzi’s contemporaries, who held him a materialist, notwithstanding his repeated protestations of firm adherence to the doctrine of the Church, whom he called his mother.

Had Pomponazzi confined himself to maintaining that from the materiality of the soul its immortality does not follow, it would have been difficult to refute him. It is said that only the composite is destructible, and so it is, if by destruction is understood the dissolution of the parts of which a whole is constructed. As the soul is not a constructed being, because [p. 207] Brutes have incontestably a species of intelligence, into which sensibility enters as one of the elementary faculties, in the same manner as in ours; but sensibility alone is not capable of the intellectual acts which are revealed to us in them, as neither is it of the intellectual acts of which we have intuition in ourselves. The dog would suffice to prove that the phenomena of intelligence in brutes cannot be explained by mere sensibility: the dog, which understands our orders and obeys them; in which, as in us, need and danger develop a wonderful cunning and sagacity; qualities which it owes not to a blind instinct, but to experience, that is, to observation and reasoning, since it acquires them by degrees, learns them, is educated.(a)

Of instinct, by which it has been sought to explain the intelligence

it lacks parts, it is not a being that can be destroyed, in the proper sense of the word destruction. But it remains to be proved that the cessation of being cannot take place except by destruction or dissolution. The human soul might be annihilable and perishable, if God had willed to make it so, because God can give existence under whatever conditions He pleases.

Even had Pomponazzi confined himself to saying that we have no proofs of the immortality of the human soul independent of revelation and of the definitions of the Church, he would have erred grossly. Reason alone suffices to see written in the moral phenomena of which we are witnesses a future awaiting us beyond the sepulchre.

(a) “The shepherd’s dog,” says a modern writer, “is a prodigy of intelligence. At

the master’s first signal he gathers the scattered sheep, separates from the flock those that are pointed out to him, conducts them where he is bidden, and keeps them all perfectly subject to his direction, not so much by active exertions as by the modulations of his voice, which expresses every tone, from that of affectionate warning to that of angry menace. And these are things of every day, seen everywhere in the fields.” The phenomena of a cultivated intelligence are no less visible in the blind man’s dog, in the hunting dog, and even in the domestic dog. What shall we say of his respect and submission to his master, of his fidelity and gratitude? He who attributes these qualities to matter should not put much faith in the philosophical arguments by which the immortality of the human soul is proved. [p. 208] of animals, ideas are held so vague and obscure that we think it necessary to fix them. Instinct does not spring from experience. An animal that feels for the first time the goad of need betakes itself, without preceding observations, without any apprenticeship, to the objects which nature has destined to satisfy it, and makes of them the convenient use with the greatest skill and tact. These instinctive actions often precede the need itself. The bird builds its nest for the future brood which it does not know, and each species has its peculiar architecture, adapted to the shelter and defense of the young, and transmitted from generation to generation through all the ages, without need of teaching or example. Instinct does without experience what reason does with it, but it is not susceptible of improvement except with the aid of experience, that is, of a faculty that observes and reasons; and that only in those species of animals which in the exercise of intelligence are most like man. In the other species instinct is, so to speak, stationary. In the bee and in many other insects instinct is exercised always in the same operations with the most complete uniformity.

Man also has his instincts; intelligence itself has them; without them, as we shall see in its place, reasoning is inexplicable.

But what is instinct in itself? for hitherto we have done no more than set forth its external characters.

In the second place, the determinations of the will are not deliberate and free; the volitions which produce instinctive voluntary movements are forced; they are developed by connections in which the effect necessarily follows the cause. So at least it seems to be deduced from the constancy and absolute uniformity of the acts of a pure instinct, as it shows itself in the dullest species, which are not susceptible of any education or teaching.

In the third place, instinctive volitions necessarily have a cause, and this cause seems to exist in sensibility: the animal has internal sensitive perceptions, produced by peculiar organic modifications; perceptions of uneasiness [p. 209] and of reason; perceptions of a certain need, of a certain appetite, which make it act deliberately and blindly to satisfy it. Nature has pre-ordained the volitions correlative to these appetites, as the movements corresponding to the volitions.

But has the animal knowledge, has it ideas of the objects toward which its instincts draw it, in order to direct its movements to them? If it has them, it doubtless owes them not to experience. Cuvier imagines that it has them; that nature causes them to arise spontaneously in its soul; that there develop in it fancies, visions, dreams, in which it beforehand contemplates the objects that are necessary to it, and even enjoys them; so that when it really sees the objects, it recognizes them, goes toward them, and in them satisfies the appetites that goaded it. But this explanation is a mere conjecture. What cannot be doubted is that when an appetite develops in animals, the correlative object, which before it regarded with indifference, excites sentiments and emotions that give it a charm, a prestige, a power the more impetuous the lower the rank of the animal in the scale of intelligence.

The animal has instincts not only for seizing upon the objects it desires, but for withdrawing itself from those that might injure and destroy it. Upon the perception of these objects there follow in the animal emotions of aversion and horror. The fear that children have of the dark, where at every step they might stumble, fall, strike, hurt themselves, is one of these instinctive affections which keep the animal from danger, without any previous experience having been able to make it known to it.

There is often awakened in the animal a series of appetites and instincts directed to a final end, of which it cannot have an idea, at least by its own experience, or by the example of its fellows. The bird makes the nest without thinking of the brood; it sits in the same manner; hatches the brood, feeds it, encourages it to fly: a series of perceptions and emotions, aided to a certain point by experience in the more exalted species, produces this series of operations, which end in the complete education of the young. When that epoch has come,

## PHILOS.     14

[p. 210]

nature emancipates the offspring and the mother obeys new instincts which make her indifferent to those very ones in which before she displayed her most careful solicitude.

There are in the animal, finally, instincts that seem disinterested, that produce cares and exertions directed, in appearance, to the preservation and welfare of others. But the animal always seeks its individual satisfaction; it is essentially egoistic. Nature has placed the propagation and preservation of the species under the tutelage of individual appetites.

Let us conclude. The phenomena of the intelligence of brutes cannot be explained by sensibility alone; but, even if they could be accounted for in that way, we should have advanced nothing toward denying immortality to the principle that animates them; because sensation is a phenomenon of which we have consciousness, a spiritual phenomenon, and we cannot attribute it to matter without throwing down the barrier that separates it from spirit. What is called instinct is a particular form of intelligence. In the instincts of man there are sensations and perceptions. What is there, for example, in the horror of darkness, which is an instinct in children? The external perception of the object, and the internal perceptions of a painful organic modification, and undeliberated determinations of the will, which in this case ceases to be a free cause. A strong analogy obliges us to recognize the same elements in the instincts of brutes.

[PDF 227]

On the composition of ideas.

Idea of objects in general; perception and idea; what the content of each separately represents.—Memory considered as the faculty of renewing perceptions.—Imagination as the faculty of composition of ideas.—It has a wider extent than memory.—Power of the will in the formation of ideas.— Ideas of spiritual objects.

From the moment that we recognize and distinguish an absolute corporeal quality by means of a sensation, this becomes for us a sign, a representation, an idea of that quality; and the aggregate of partial ideas which represent to us, one by one, the absolute qualities of a corporeal object, constitutes a considerable part of the complex idea which represents to us the whole of the object.

If to perceive the color of a violet is to experience a sensation which we refer to an external object as its cause, to have an idea of this color is nothing else than to recollect that sensation and to represent to ourselves in it a particular quality of the cause that produces it. Having no means whatever of knowing what corporeal qualities are in themselves, we are obliged, in order to think of them in any manner, to think of the sensations excited by them. In this way the sensation becomes the symbol of its cause, and takes the name of perception or of idea: of perception while it subsists, and of idea while it is merely reproduced by memory.

But the total idea which represents to us a corporeal object consists not only of recollected sensations, but of concepts [p. 212] relative, both primary and of higher orders; whether between the sensations themselves produced by the object, or between these and the sensations produced by other objects. Thus in the idea of a flower there enter not only recollections in which the sensations formerly excited by it in our sight, smell and touch are reproduced with more or less vividness, but the ideas of its size and form, which, as we have seen, are aggregates of various relations of extraposition; the ideas of the resemblances or differences, of color and of form, between it and other flowers, etc.

To abbreviate language, we shall consider the perceptions of relative corporeal qualities as the complement of the purely sensitive part of the perceptions of corporeal objects. In this sense we may say that forms, magnitudes and places are perceived representatively by means of tactile and visual sensations, the sensations of the sense of effort being incorporated in these latter and in the former; and that the idea of a corporeal thing is composed of sensitive recollections. We leave out of account, then, the part which active consciousness takes in these ideas, in comparing sensations, conceiving relations and attributing them to corporeal objects.

In the ideas of corporeal beings that have been subjected to the examination of our senses, the recollected sensations are referred to the very causes that excited them in us. There are other ideas in which the sensations are referred to causes different from those that originally excited them. He who has seen a rose can picture to himself many others, although he has not seen them, and although in fact they do not exist. He who has seen only roses of the ordinary color can picture them to himself white, purple, or of any other color of those he has perceived in other objects. The ideas of these new roses consist of recollected sensations, but which we no longer refer to the individual causes that originally excited them, but to different causes, whether real or imaginary.

The idea of a rose consists of all the sensations produced by this flower; that is, of all those which represent its color, form, fragrance, etc. A more complete idea [p. 213] of the same rose will include the sensations by means of which we perceive its successive modes of existence, and the objects which have had or have connection with it, such as the rosebush in all its various states from the seed to the bearing of fruit, the garden in which we have seen this plant grow, etc. When the recollected sensations of which the idea of a rose consists represent to us the same individual object that excited them in us, accompanied by the same adjuncts, the group of recollected sensations that forms the idea of the rose is a copy of the group of actual sensations that formed the perceptions of the rose and of its adjuncts. The faculty which the soul possesses of renewing its perceptions in this manner is called memory in the strictest sense of that word.

On the contrary, when the recollected sensations of which the idea of a rose consists do not represent to us the same rose that excited them in us and the same adjuncts, the group of recollected sensations that forms the idea consists of parts that belonged to different groups of actual sensations. The rose which I represent to myself now is not the same that I have seen blooming in my garden; its idea no longer has my garden for an adjunct, but a forest that I know and in which I am told this flower exists: I join the sensations which represented to me the rose with the sensations which represented to me the forest, and form of these and those a new group. I hear of a rose of the same magnitude, the same form, the same odor, as the roses of my garden, but of a different color, purple, for example. The group of sensations that form the idea of the purple rose is not the group of sensations that form the idea of the rose of my garden: both agree, it is true, in the sensations which represent to me the magnitude, the form, the odor; but the recollected sensation which represents to me the color of the former is not that which was excited in me by the color of the latter, but by the color of a violet, a lily, so that the group of sensations that form the idea of the purple rose consists of sensations that belonged, partly to the group of the perception of the ordinary rose, and partly to the group of the [p. 214] perception of the violet, the lily. The faculty which in this manner picks out the recollections and forms with them new compounds is called in general imagination. The materials of ideas are in reality always supplied by memory. Imagination is nothing else than memory, in so far as it forms new compounds with the elements of perceptions.

The ideas of the imagination are much more numerous than those of memory. All that we do not learn immediately by perception, we learn by imagination, forming, with the elements of previous perceptions, new groups and combinations. Imagination is that which gives form to all the knowledge that we acquire by reasoning or by the experience and testimony of others. For if we learn anything by reasoning, it is because we form new compounds of ideas. If on seeing a field covered with ashes and burnt trunks, we infer the previous action of fire, an inference which constitutes the reasoning, what do we do but represent to ourselves the fire in the act of consuming the forest as we have before seen it consume other things; forming of the representative perceptions of the forest and the representative sensations of the fire a new group? Neither do we understand the language of other men, except in so far as it awakens in us previous perceptions; nor does this language teach us anything, except in so far as it makes us combine our previous perceptions in a new manner.

In all perceptions and ideas, in all the acts of sensitive memory and imagination, the sensations are always referred to corporeal qualities, which we cannot know except as causes of these very sensations. It is true that perception supposes the real and actual existence of the cause, whereas the idea may be representative of causes which we believe do not exist or whose existence we leave out of account. The judgment of the real and actual existence of a corporeal cause, a judgment which accompanies actual perceptions from a very early period and comes to form part of them, then abandons the idea, or perhaps yields its place to the contrary judgment of the non-existence [p. 215] at present, or of the non-reality of the corporeal cause. I picture to myself, for example, a tree of golden apples, and at the same time I believe that no such tree exists. The recollected sensation, no less than the actual, is representative of a cause; but the judgment of actual cause, of real cause, of possible cause, of past or future cause, is founded on a thousand antecedents of observation and reasoning, on a thousand data acquired by ourselves or through the information of others; and varies necessarily with these antecedents and data.

Ideas which are not accompanied by the judgment of the present or past existence of their objects are regarded more properly as the work of the imagination. Imagination in its widest sense is memory forming new compounds with the materials with which perception supplies it. In the strict sense of which I have just spoken, imagination is memory in so far as it forms, with previous perceptions, compounds not only new, but representative of causes to which we do not attribute existence.

If I do not confound the perceptions of the trees I am looking at in my garden with the recollections of the trees I saw yesterday in the park, or with the ideas of trees that I have not seen, and that perhaps do not exist; if the perceptions of the former are accompanied by the judgment of reality and actuality, and the ideas of the others by the judgment that the objects do not now act upon my organs, but acted yesterday, or have not acted and never will act, it is, first, because over the representations of memory and imagination my will has an almost absolute sway, since at my pleasure I make them vanish from the mind, and they yield their place to others, over which I exercise equal dominion. Nothing limits the power I have of varying these shifting scenes (unless in abnormal states of the soul, in which deep meditations or intense passions keep them fixed, even when the will strives to draw them aside): whereas I cannot cease to experience actual perceptions, except by withdrawing myself from the action of corporeal causes upon my organs, by stopping my ears, closing my eyelids, moving away from the object. Secondly, because an [p. 216] early experience taught me to distinguish between the vivid and distinct affections of actual perception, and the confused and feeble affections of renewed perception; a distinction more obvious and easy when we experience actual perceptions and renewed perceptions at one and the same time; and this is one of the causes why in dreams the vividness of the latter is increased, and the soul, occupied by these alone, mistakes them for the former, to which the torpor of a part of the mental faculties doubtless contributes, while another part retains up to a certain point the image. Thirdly, because actual perceptions, the perceptions I have now, do not permit me to associate them with the renewed ones and to judge their objects coexistent and present. The prospect which I have before me cannot coexist with the prospect which I recollect or imagine. Fourthly, because my observations and reasonings, my knowledge of all kinds, have made me form two great theaters, space and time, to which I refer all the objects I recollect and also all those I imagine when I judge them real, giving them a place more or less determinate in these two great orders of existences. How shall I confound the prospect before me with the recollections of Paris or the imaginings of Rome, when these ideas cannot fail to come associated with those of their position on the surface of the earth and their distance from the place I actually occupy?

The ideas of spiritual objects are also recollected perceptions, which belong sometimes to memory and at other times to imagination, more or less strictly understood. The ideas we form of the modes of being, not only of other minds, but of our own, placed in hypothetical circumstances, are all figured, painted, clothed, so to speak, by the imagination.

[PDF 233]

On general ideas.

Origin of general names.—Genus, species, body, being, thing or cause.— Vague ideas.—Formation of the name.—Generalization.—Its principal characters.—Examination of the opinion of Destutt de Tracy.—Two causes of error in the concept of general ideas.—Attributes of an object.—They are distinguished from qualities.—True abstraction.

We have already observed that, since it is impossible to give a distinct name to each existing or imaginable thing, nature, as if to obviate this difficulty, suggested the expedient of giving the same name to similar objects. One object recalled another object which bore a resemblance to it, and the recollection of this second awakened the memory of its name, which, in consequence, was applied to the first, and became common to the two. The same thing happened with new objects that seemed similar to the two former; and as each resemblance observed gave occasion to the formation of another common name, names were in this manner generalized, that is, the individuals to which we applied them were multiplied, and objects were distributed into collections or classes, each of which had for its foundation one or more relations of resemblance, which is as much as to say one or more characteristic qualities observed in them. Each class was thus marked by a general name, which is like the label of the class. Thus a general name is a name applicable to an indeterminate number of individuals that present the resemblances and consist of the qualities [p. 218] observed in them, and a class is the indeterminate number of individuals to which a general name is applicable.

It happened many times that some classes were included in others, as quadruped, bird, fish, in animal; oak, willow, elm, in tree. The including classes were called genera with respect to the included classes, as these were denominated species with respect to those. Thus animal is a genus with respect to man, quadruped, bird, etc., and bird is a species of animal.

Passing from the more obvious resemblances to those that were less so, we gave the name of bodies to all the classes of objects capable of producing sensations, and we were able to arrive finally at the universal class, thing, entity, being, which embraces all that exists and all that can be imagined.

But what is the character of resemblance that belongs to everything that has real or imaginary existence?

Body is the cause of sensations, and spirit is the cause of intuitions by acting on itself, and of voluntary movements by acting on the body it animates. Causation is the common character of both and of whatever can be conceived. For this reason we gave to the universal class the denomination of thing, cause.

The specific name determines the signification of the generic name, that is, it restricts or limits the number of the varieties of which each quality of the object is susceptible. Animal makes the imagination wander over the great number of forms, sizes and colors, organisms, functions and habits of all the animals we have observed or of which we have any knowledge; bird suggests a much smaller number; eagle a number still smaller, and if, our simple names failing us, we lay hold of combinations of words that perform the same office, black eagle will narrow the signification still more, and the eagle that is on that rock will leave it reduced to the individual present.

The vague idea of a simple quality is an aggregate of ideas of the various modifications and degrees that we have observed in it. A vague idea of color is an idea of white, green, yellow, blue, red, black, etc.; a vague idea of color [p. 219] green is an idea of various green colors, as that of the elm, that of the oak, that of the plane tree, that of the willow, that of the sea, that of the emerald, etc.; in the same manner the vague idea of a complex object is composed of the vague ideas of all and each of the elements of which we have observed it to consist. The vague idea which the word tree calls up in the soul consists of the vague ideas of those forms, sizes, colors and other qualities that we have perceived in trees. If any one speaks to us of a tree that we do not know, we attribute to it a set of qualities similar to those of the trees that we know; but this new set is indeterminate. Our imagination wanders over a great number of combinations without fixing on any.

The idea excited by every appellative name is necessarily vague, and the field over which the imagination ranges, when we hear one of these names, is more or less vast, according as we have observed more or less. What comparison can there be, for example, between the number of colors and forms which the word tree suggests to the Laplander or the Kamchadal, and the infinite variety of combinations which this same word recalls to the inhabitant of the banks of the Ganges or the Orinoco?

The idea of an object embraces that of the successive states through which it passes, and the idea of resemblance between several objects comprehends the ideas of the successive resemblances between the various states of them. To say that an object is a tree is to say that it springs from seed, that it grows, that it bears flowers and fruits, that it grows old and dries up: successive states in which it resembles other trees.

The combinations of words which we make use of to designate classes of objects serve as names. The number of common names of which a language consists, however rich it may be, is necessarily limited, and that of the resemblances which we can perceive in things, infinite. Hence the necessity of having recourse to combinations of words to indicate resemblances. It belongs to grammar to expound the laws according to which these combinations ought to be formed, which for the [p. 220] purpose of which we treat may be considered as true names.

The specific name indicates a more lively resemblance than the generic name. The resemblance of animals to one another is less than that of birds; this is less lively than that of eagles; that of eagles is not so great as that of black eagles; and finally, the most lively of all is that which an unalterable individual has with himself.

The specific name is less extensive; in other terms, it is applicable to a smaller number of individuals than the generic name. The greater the resemblance indicated by the common name, the less is the extent of the class. The proper name indicates of itself no other resemblance than that which the individual to whom it belongs has with himself, and in this sense it might be said that in this kind of names the maximum of resemblance coincides with the minimum of extent.

I think that what has been said suffices to enable us to conceive clearly what is the signification of general, common or appellative names (denominations of the same value, which comprehend alike generic and specific names); what the general idea is, and to what the operation of the understanding called generalization reduces itself. If names are signs, if a common name is a sign applicable to many individual objects, and if the idea awakened in the soul by any sign is not and cannot be other than that of the object or objects to which we apply it, it follows that the general idea, or the idea awakened in the soul by a common name, is not and cannot be other than the idea of the individual objects to which we are accustomed to give this name, and the idea, consequently, of the varieties of which each part and each quality of the said objects is susceptible; an idea so much the more complete and exact the better we have observed them. It follows also from what has been said that generalization, or the intellectual process by which we form general ideas, reduces itself to perceiving resemblances and to imposing common denominations on the resembling individuals.

What does man mean? It means Peter, John, Caesar,

[p. 221]

Scipio, Charles, Louis; in short, it is a sign which we make use of to denote any individual of the human species, or some one of them indeterminately. It does not denote a single part or quality, nor an incomplete portion of the parts and qualities that we have observed in the individuals of the human species, but the whole of all the parts and qualities under all the forms and degrees in which each of them is capable of existing. If an inhabitant of Kamchatka, who has no knowledge of other men than those of his own country, sees a negro for the first time, he will probably not judge him to be of his species. Why? Because his idea of man does not comprehend the modifications of color and physiognomy of the African. The color and the form in his idea of man vary within narrow limits, which do not include the swarthy skin, the woolly hair, the depressed skull, the thick lips of the individual before his eyes. The idea which in the understanding of our Kamchadal is like the type or model with which he compares the individuals presented to him in order to judge whether or not they are of his species, comprehends the particular modifications of which each human part and each human quality is susceptible, as his observations have made them known to him; but it goes no farther. Perhaps, noticing the greater number and superior importance of the resemblances of this new object to men, as he conceives them, he will come by degrees to form another judgment. But he could not call him man, without altering his general idea of this class, by including in it the new color, the new form of the hair, the new features observed. The general idea, then, is composed of the ideas of all the parts and qualities that we have perceived in the individuals of the class, or that by reasoning we have deduced from those perceived, or that other men have known by perceptions and reasonings, whose ideas have been incorporated with our own: all under the modifications of which each part and each quality, according to our own or communicated knowledge, is susceptible in them. This is so clear that it hardly deserved the trouble of being inculcated; and yet it is one of the points that have been involved in most obscurity by philosophers.

[p. 222]

Every common name supposes a concept of resemblance between the objects to which we apply it. Green, for example, supposes a certain resemblance of color between the objects we call so, such as grass, the leaves of trees, the rind of unripe fruits, the emerald, the sea, etc. But it is important to remember that the perception of resemblance does not presuppose the perception of common qualities, understanding by such those which would produce in the soul affections in every respect alike, so that we should not perceive the slightest difference between them. I mean, confining myself to the foregoing example, that the perception of resemblance between the grass, the sea, the trees, the emerald, etc., by virtue of which we call all these objects green, does not suppose that there is a common, homogeneous, elementary color, which is repeated with absolute uniformity in all these objects. In effect, one has only to open the eyes to know that their colors, though similar, are not so much so that we do not perceive various kinds of greenness in them. In a word, the colors of these objects appear to us at one and the same time similar and different.

Our consciousness testifies to us that in this resemblance and difference, simultaneously perceived between two colors or any two simple qualities whatever, the perception of the quality is not divided into two heterogeneous perceptions, namely, the perception of that part in which one quality resembles another, and the perception of that part in which it differs. The color of the willow leaf gives me a homogeneous perception. The color of the elm leaf gives me another homogeneous perception. If, comparing these two colors, I perceive them similar and different, it is not because I have a particular perception of that in which the color of the willow is like that of the elm, and another particular perception of that in which the first color differs from the second; for if it were so, we should see in reality two different colors in the willow leaf and two different colors in the elm leaf. The relation is double, notwithstanding that the two affections compared are simple. On the one hand we perceive that the resemblance of the color of the willow to the color of the elm is much greater than the mean resemblance [p. 223] of the class of colors, and on the other hand we perceive that that resemblance is less than complete resemblance.

As the resemblance of complex objects is ultimately composed of resemblances between elementary qualities, what I have said of these applies to the others.
