These considerations being allowed, let me be permitted to discuss the doctrine of Destutt de Tracy on general ideas; a doctrine which he holds in common with many others, and which I believe may be regarded as the most current at the present day. When I feel obliged to depart from the opinion of so many eminent philosophers, I cannot but distrust myself, however powerful the reasons may seem to me that militate in my favor. I must say, nevertheless, that the more I meditate the subject, the more I am convinced that the writers to whom I allude have adopted the doctrine of the schools without sufficient examination.

“Let us suppose,” says Destutt de Tracy, “that a child sees a peach for the first time; that he receives from it the sensations of a certain color and a certain taste; that he recognizes in it a certain form; that he finds a certain soft resistance on taking it, etc. Of all these ideas he forms a single one, which is the idea of that peach and of no other, for let us suppose that he has seen no other fruit of the same species. This idea in this state is individual. The child hears that fruit called peach; but this word, which the persons from whom he hears it pronounced have already generalized, and which for them is the common name of all imaginable peaches, is for the child no more than the name of that single peach which he has seen, and consequently is a proper name.

“After the child has formed the idea of this first peach, others are presented to him which have more or less the same qualities, between which and the first there are certain common characters, but which nevertheless differ in many respects, since there are not two absolutely alike beings in nature.”

Let us halt here. If by common characters are understood those which are repeated uniformly in things, so that in contemplating them successively we cannot perceive in [p. 224] them the least difference, the most superficial observation is enough to recognize that nature seldom produces them, and that, if we attended only to them, we should have taken very few steps in the classification of objects. Confining ourselves to the example of Destutt de Tracy, colors, forms, dimensions, tastes, tactile resistance, all will offer differences if not in two or three peaches, at least in a great number. Destutt de Tracy understands, then, by common characters those which have a certain degree of resemblance, such as are in peaches the various tints of the color, which from green passes by degrees to pale yellow; the spherical form more or less irregular; the consistency, which from the hardness of the green fruit arrives progressively at the softness of the ripe fruit; the taste, which from sour becomes little by little sweet, etc. In short, these pretended common characters are nothing more than resembling characters, variable within a certain limit, determined in peaches and in each class of objects by observations.

“All peaches,” continues Destutt de Tracy, “certainly have not the same colors, the same figure, the same size, the same degree of ripeness; but the child disregards these differences, and considers in the peaches he goes on seeing only what they have in common with the first; he calls them also peaches; and behold, the idea of peach has become general, and is no longer composed except of the characters that agree to all these fruits. This operation is called to abstract. In effect, what the child does in such a case is to pick out from two or more individual ideas all that confounds them, rejecting all that distinguishes them; and in this manner he forms a general idea.”

But if the child disregards all the differences he observes, and we understand by different everything that is not completely alike, one of these three things cannot fail to happen: either the child disregards all the affections produced in his mind by peaches, for surely none of them is produced uniformly by all these fruits, and in such a case he picks out nothing, abstracts nothing, nothing remains to him for the formation of the general idea; or he decomposes the [p. 225] simple affections of its mind, dividing them into two parts, of which one should correspond uniformly to all peaches and the other not; a faculty with which the human understanding does not seem to me endowed; or else, notwithstanding the indivisibility of its simple affections, the quality corresponding to each simple affection is represented to it as divided into two parts, one of which exists in all peaches and the other not, and this would be to say that by means of an indivisible and homogeneous affection of our mind we can perceive in one and the same quality two heterogeneous elements, which is evidently absurd.

And if the child retains for the formation of the general idea those characters which, without being completely alike, are alike up to a certain point, what then is it that he excludes? His general idea of peaches will comprehend all the individual modifications observed, and will leave no residuum whatever.

Let us confine ourselves to color, and suppose it homogeneous in each peach. There is no sensation of color which is produced uniformly by all peaches: the peach passes through an infinity of shades from green to pale yellow, and even among the colors of ripe peaches differences are not wanting to be perceived. The understanding, moreover, lacks the faculty of dividing the homogeneous sensation of color, produced by each peach, into two sensations, of which one should be produced by all of them and the other not. Consequently, the child cannot represent to himself in the color of each peach two colors, one of which should be common to all of them and the other not; for since the idea of color is nothing else than a sensation referred to a certain external cause, the modes of this cause cannot be for us more or less than the modes of the sensation. Does the child, then, reject everything that he finds different in the colors of peaches? In that case peach in general will be for him an object destitute of all color. Will he retain the incomplete resemblances which he observes in the colors of peaches? Will he regard as common characters those which vary within certain limits? Such, in fact, is the sense in which I believe we ought to understand this expression of Destutt de Tracy, common characters. But in this sense the

## PHILOS.   15

[p. 226]

general idea of the peach will comprehend all the modifications of color of which this fruit is capable. In the first case everything is rejected; in the second everything is retained; and consequently, in neither of the two is anything separated, picked out, abstracted.

Supposing that there are several colors in one and the same peach, the resemblance between fruits in respect of color will be complex, and the preceding reasoning will apply without difficulty to each of the elementary resemblances. We shall then compare the grounds of the color, the shades, the spots, etc., and in each of these elements we perceive a series of modifications, as we contemplate the various peaches in succession.

If it is maintained, then, that for the formation of the general idea we retain only those characters which recur with absolute uniformity in the individuals, I say that such characters are mere nothings, and that in the greater part of classes they do not exist. If it is maintained that we retain the characters which, without coming to be confounded, approach each other more or less in the objects to which one and the same name is given, it is impossible for me to conceive what it is that in this case is excluded. And finally, if it is supposed that the qualities which we know by means of simple perceptions are mentally resolvable into others, and that from this resolution the common characters emerge, I say that the human understanding enjoys no such faculty.

Even supposing that common characters, in the sense of complete resemblance, occurred more often than they actually do, an intellectual object consisting only of such characters could not serve as a type by comparing other objects with which we should perceive whether or not they were of the class represented by it. Let us suppose, for example, that all pears had a variable form and color; an object of the same form and color might not be a pear. If its other qualities did not approach those of this fruit, as our previous observations have made them known to us, we should not recognize it as of the same species; we should not give it the same name. To form a sure judgment it would be necessary that we should compare quality with quality, passing over none that appeared to us important, and that we should see whether those [p. 227] of the new object were or were not within the limits which we had observed in pears. That there should be one or two qualities which do not vary at all, or which vary only within very narrow limits, would not dispense us from the comparison of the other qualities which vary within less narrow limits. The general idea of a class is, so to speak, a multiform type, and the conformity of objects with one of the forms of this type, or their disconformity with all of them, is what authorizes us to place them in that class or to exclude them from it.

If from individuals we pass to species, and from many of these form a genus, neither will the generic idea consist of the common characters of the species in the sense of complete resemblance, for since it is difficult to find such characters within a single species, how much more difficult will it be to discover them for a whole genus, composed perhaps of innumerable species? When from many classes we form another, a higher one, what we do is to combine, so to speak, many types, linked with one another by a relation of resemblance, in such a manner that the generic type embraces all the variations of the specific types. The amplitude of the variations of each quality increases by degrees, as the extent of the class increases.

The erroneous conception which has generally been formed of general ideas has proceeded from two causes. The first of them is the equally erroneous conception which is held of the relation of resemblance. It was imagined that this relation consisted in this, that resembling objects were made up of one part which resembled completely in all of them, and of another which did not; whence it was not only natural but necessary to infer that the objects to which we give the same name are made up of common characters which resemble each other completely in all of them.

We have noticed elsewhere that in scientific and artificial classifications an effort has been made, as far as possible, to found the classes on the existence or non-existence of a condition, of a fact. Since in existing or not existing there is room for no different degrees or shades, and the resemblances in this respect [p. 228] are complete and present truly common characters, it may be said of the classes which have been formed in this manner that qualities and attributes run pari passu; but this is not the natural and ordinary procedure of the understanding, and nothing would be more erroneous than to attribute to classification in general what is a mere accident. In the next place, even in these same classes it is not always easy to discern the existence or non-existence of the fact. To possess or not to possess the aggregate of qualities which constitute, for example, man, is a fact, and therefore it cannot be said that one individual is more or less a man than another in the sense of an individual of the human species. But it is often difficult to recognize the existence or non-existence of an aggregate of qualities in the particular degree and form which characterize the class; and from the moment this happens, the classes founded in this manner do not really differ from the others: instead of common characters we then see nothing but partial resemblances or approximations.

The second of the causes indicated is the belief that to the separation of signs in language there corresponds an equal separation of ideas in the understanding. We say sky-blue and dark blue to signify particular modifications of blue, and we say simply blue to signify some one or any of the modifications of this color. It was then reasoned in this way: to each word there corresponds an idea: sky-blue is, consequently, a complex idea, which consists of two elementary ideas; dark blue is another complex idea consisting of an equal number of elements; and just as, to indicate in language the blue in general, we discard the particular signs sky and dark, and leave only the common sign blue, so, to represent this color in general to ourselves in the understanding, we separate the ideas corresponding to sky and dark, and retain only the idea corresponding to the common sign. But the general idea denoted by the common sign is very far from being an element of the particular idea denoted by any of the compound expressions, sky-blue, dark blue, etc. Blue offers to the understanding the ideas excited by sky-blue, dark blue, Prussian blue, etc., either in a distributive [p. 229] sense, as when we say blue is a color agreeable to the sight, which is an abbreviated way of saying, sky-blue is a color agreeable to the sight, dark blue is a color agreeable to the sight, Prussian blue is a color agreeable to the sight, and so of all the other blues; or in an indeterminate sense, as when we are told that a flower is blue, in which case we figure to ourselves in it some one of the modifications, sky-blue or dark blue or Prussian blue, etc., wandering over them all without fixing ourselves particularly upon any one of them.

Those names are properly called attributes of an object which we give it according to its qualities, which is the same as to say, the resemblances which it seems to us to have with other objects. Qualities and perceptions are individual, attributes are not; for each attribute belongs to an indeterminate number of individuals. Let us suppose that the object is a rose. Being, body, vegetable production, organ destined to form the seed, polypetalous, rose-colored, fragrant, etc., are the attributes of this object, and each of them is a common name and supposes a preceding generalization. A jasmine produces perceptions which lead me to give it the attributes being, body, vegetable production, organ destined to form the seed, monopetalous, white, fragrant, etc. Another flower will perhaps receive the attributes being, body, vegetable production, organ destined to form the seed, monopetalous, purple, fetid, etc. Observing the same procedure with other flowers, and then comparing the attributes of the one with those of the others, I find that there are common to all the individuals of the various species of flowers the attributes being, body, vegetable production, organ destined to form the seed: I form, then, with these attributes, picked out from those which belong to the various species, the genus of flowers, which consist therefore of the attributes being, body, vegetable production, organ destined to form the seed. As among the attributes of each individual those of the classes which include it are necessarily found, and as the word attribute was often used to denote not signs of qualities, but the very qualities in which individuals resemble one another, the reasoning went in this manner. Every [p. 230] individual has qualities which are common to it with others; the individual idea comprehends the ideas of all these qualities, proper and common; I discard the ideas of the proper qualities, and there remains a residuum composed of the ideas of the common qualities; this residuum is the general idea of the class; the general idea is formed, consequently, by abstracting, that is, by separating some qualities from others. It seems evident to me that in this reasoning it is supposed that we do with qualities what we can only do with attributes.

The more we generalize a name, the greater the number of individuals to which we apply it, or in other terms, the greater the extension of the class represented by it, the smaller is the number of the attributes of the class. Man necessarily has more attributes than animal, and animal than body, and body than being. What philosophers call the comprehension of a class is properly the number of attributes which belong to it and into which its name is resolvable. When the celebrated ideologist cited above says that names, in proportion as they are more general, signify a smaller number of common characters, and that in this consists their lesser comprehension, he doubtless applies to qualities what ought to be understood only of attributes. Thus what is truly common in the ideas excited by general names is not the qualities, but the attributes. We formed the first generalizations by giving the same name to individuals which presented a certain resemblance among themselves; and it is clear that then there could be no selection of attributes, because every attribute supposes a preceding generalization, and here we are treating of the first generalizations from which the first attributes arose. But from the continual repetition of this intellectual procedure, as languages were being formed, or as each man was learning his own, it resulted that each thing found itself comprehended in several classes, and a multitude of attributes corresponded to it. New generalizations were then proceeded to, and one and the same attribute became resolvable into others. It would be, therefore, an anachronism to imagine a selection of attributes in the first steps of generalization.

[p. 231]

Animals live, feel, and move: here we have at first sight an expression of the characters common to all animals, particularities being excluded. But can we conceive life, feeling, movement, if we do not represent to ourselves individual modifications of these things? Let us confine ourselves to movement. To say that the animal moves is to say that it walks, or runs, or leaps, or flies, or swims, or crawls. If the expression moves does not awaken the ideas of these particular modifications, it awakens no idea whatever of the movement of animals. But the words walks, runs, leaps, etc., are still general; for if, for example, the idea of walking is really awakened in the understanding, it is necessary that we figure to ourselves individual limbs that walk and individual modes of gait. The idea, then, of walking is not abstracted, is not picked out from the particularities of this movement, nor is the idea of movement in general abstracted or picked out from the ideas of walking, running, etc.

I do not on that account deny that a great number of classes are formed upon partial resemblances, which we observe by comparing certain qualities to the exclusion of the others. Attending, for example, to color in particular, we call some things white, others green, others blue, etc. Attending in the same way to figure, we say that one body is a prism, and another body a sphere. Attending exclusively to number, that is, performing the very simple operation of counting, we apply to things or to their parts the general denominations 1, 2, 3, etc., and we say, for instance, that one flower has five stamens, and another ten. To attend exclusively to certain qualities is neither more nor less than to attend exclusively to certain perceptions; and if we limit the sense of the word abstract to this exclusive attention, I find no inconvenience in its use. But this kind of abstraction cannot go further than we reach with perceptions; a simple perception cannot be divided in such a manner that we represent to ourselves in it two elements, of which the one should be truly common to an indeterminate number of things, that is, completely uniform in all of them.

[p. 232]

If abstraction is nothing more than attention directed to a separately perceptible quality to the exclusion of others which accompany it and which are also separately perceptible, there is hardly an act of thought in which abstraction does not intervene. Classifications founded upon complex resemblances which embrace all the parts and qualities of objects require it no less than classifications founded upon the resemblance of a single part or quality, for we do not perceive complex resemblances except by perceiving, one by one, the elementary resemblances. In this sense we may say that whenever we think of an object, we abstract it from the others. If the object is complex and we wish to represent it to ourselves distinctly, we cannot do so except by representing to ourselves its parts and qualities successively, that is, by a series of abstractions. But this is not the sense which philosophers have given to this word. By it they have wished to signify a certain mysterious procedure, a sort of intellectual distillation, by means of which we extract general ideas from individual ones, as in the alembic the essence to which its aroma is united is extracted from flowers. Abstraction in this sense ought to be struck out of the catalogue of the intellectual operations.

General ideas, as I believe we ought to conceive them, involve so great a number of modifications and particularities (and the same may be applied to individual ideas), that if, when we think, each idea had to be unfolded, so that we should contemplate distinctly all its elements and all the faces of which each element is capable, thought would proceed with the utmost difficulty and slowness; at every step it took it would have to drag along a voluminous and complicated train of ideas, and it could not form the most obvious judgment upon the simplest object without making a review of a countless number of objects. But the more familiar to us a group or series of ideas is, the more rapidly it is reproduced. The representations, then, of the various parts and modifications of an object or class of objects, by virtue of their frequent association in the understanding, come to be reproduced with a celerity such that consciousness [p. 233] cannot follow them. In truth, in this case they form a confused whole, of which it is not possible to give an account to ourselves, because we perceive or recollect distinctly only those acts of the soul which have a certain duration and intensity. But ideas too rapid and feeble to leave any trace in the memory may nevertheless excite other ideas whose duration is less momentary, and in this way contribute to thought. So it is when we read. The fugitive ideas of the written characters and of the elementary sounds represented by these characters are for consciousness as if they did not exist; and yet they suggest the ideas of the entire words of which the written phrases are composed, and the ideas of which the sense of these phrases is composed: ideas which exclusively occupy the attention. Habit, then, which by accelerating in this case a certain series of ideas makes them so feeble and fugitive that it is impossible to find any trace of them in the memory, without their ceasing on that account to contribute to thought, doubtless produces the same effect in all those associations of ideas which are often repeated in the soul; and in this case are found the groups of ideas which represent objects familiar to the senses or to the imagination, whether individuals or classes.

It happens then that any element of these groups, which occupies the attention, becomes the sign of the whole group, and the relations of the groups are represented by the relations of these signs. To think, for example, of an individual of the human species, it is enough that we represent to ourselves a part of his visible form. If we are spoken to of a certain park, it is enough that our imagination sketch for us a few trees, whether this sketch has for its original the trees of that very park (as will happen if we know it from our own observations), or whether by way of supplement we represent to ourselves trees of those which we are accustomed to see in other parks, or any trees whatever. And if we are told that such a man was in such a park, the combination of the two signs mentioned, that is, the combination of the idea of a certain human form with the idea of certain trees, is for us [p. 234] the sign of the complex idea of a certain man in a certain park, and in the ordinary exercise of thought takes the place of the entire complex idea, while all the other elements are renewed so rapidly and obscurely that I cannot recollect their existence in the thought. In the same manner, to think about two parallel lines in general, it is enough that I represent to myself two parallel lines of determinate situation, length, color, etc., and to think about mountains in general, it is enough to represent to myself one or two, of determinate sizes, figures, and colors, at a certain distance at which the sight can easily embrace their dimensions. In truth, these ideas which we make use of as signs of the groups to which they belong are not rigorously elementary. Nor is it necessary that they should be. For the ordinary exercise of thought, it is only required that their reproduction be not so faint and confused that we cannot perceive them and distinguish them from one another.

It might be feared that the imperfection of these signs would often lead into error. But latent ideas, or such as leave no trace in the memory, exercise upon other ideas associated with them a certain influence which forestalls or corrects aberrations, if the thought is occupied with objects familiar to it. When Iriarte says in nonsensical décimas:

Some folías were dancing

The sons of Zebedee,

we perceive at once the absurdity of the association by virtue of a most rapid mental procedure, of which we neither had consciousness nor have memory. The wit of a facetious expression consists many times in a subtle relation, so fleetingly perceived by those who hear it, that even by meditating upon it it is not easy to analyze it: it might be said that the intellectual procedure inscius sui [unconscious of itself] is more apt and sure than the intellectual procedure sui conscius [conscious of itself].

In the second place, the easy substitution of one sign for another completely remedies the imperfection resulting from their individuality. There is no danger that I should attribute to trees [p. 235] what is proper only to the elm, if, thinking about trees in general, I represent to myself now an elm, now a pine, now a willow. In an equilateral triangle I can demonstrate the general properties of triangles, provided that none of the steps of the demonstration supposes the equality of the sides, or in other terms, provided that each step applies equally to the equilateral triangle which I have before my sight, and to a scalene triangle which I trace in my imagination.

And in the third place, we can, in case of difficulty, suspend the march of thought, to unfold up to the convenient point the different parts of a complex object, to contemplate each important part or quality under its different faces.

[PDF 252]

On negative ideas.

Negative ideas: they always refer to a universality of entities divided into two classes.—Positive class and negative class.—The content of every negative class is nothing; a sign-idea.—Use of the word nothing in language; in reasoning ad absurdum.—Nothing has different mental objects.—It is opposed to the idea of the infinite.—This is a sign-idea; it is also an element of the argument ad absurdum.

Negative ideas are those which signify classes of objects founded upon resemblances of differences. Thus the negative idea which corresponds to the denomination invisible or not visible represents a class whose individuals resemble one another in differing from visible objects. So also when we say that an object is not a tree, which is to give it the attribute non-tree, it is the expression of a negative idea, which represents in general all the beings that resemble one another in differing from trees.

Every negative idea supposes the universality of entities to be divided into two classes. The idea of the invisible supposes that all that exists is distributed between two great divisions: the one embraces all the objects that affect the sight, and the other all those that differ from these, that is to say, all those that do not affect it.

In proportion as a positive class extends, the corresponding negative class contracts. Much greater is the extension of the classes non-green, non-blue than that of the class invisible; incomparably greater that of the class non-tree than that of the [p. 237] class immaterial or incorporeal. When we say invisible, the imagination represents to itself not only the corporeal substances that cannot be seen, but all immaterial things; and when we say non-white, the imagination ranges, not only over the class of invisible objects, but over that of black, red, blue, yellow objects, etc.

If the positive class includes all entities, as does that which corresponds to the words entity, being or thing, there will be no corresponding negative class; in its place there will be nothing.

But what, it will be asked, is the idea corresponding to this word?

An idea is the renewal of one or more perceptions, intuitive or sensitive, absolute or relative; and since nothing cannot be the cause of intuitions or of sensations, and since, on the other hand, it is not given to us to conceive relation except by comparing intuitions or sensations, it follows that nothing cannot be the object of any idea properly so called. It is necessary that in place of this idea, which we neither have nor can have, there should be something in the understanding that supplies it, and in a certain way takes its place; that is, a sign-idea.

As nothing is the negation of all being, we figure to ourselves in it a subject that has for its attribute a relation of difference with respect to all that is or exists. But we do not really perceive difference except between different things, and this perception is impossible when we put all things on one side and none on the other. The subject, then, to which we attribute that universal and absolute negation is a purely verbal sign, that is to say, the very word negation or difference.

We are accustomed to combine the word nothing with others, forming propositions which all resolve themselves into these: nothing has no positive quality, or nothing is nothing. The contrary proposition, nothing is something, nothing is a thing, is an expression of the impossible, is absurd; and consequently every other proposition in which this is contained is also necessarily an expression of the impossible, an absurdity; and to demonstrate it, it will suffice to convert it into this by a process of [p. 238] rigorous reasoning. If it were said, for example, that the universe had begun to exist without the agency of any cause or principle of its existence, we might reject this proposition as inadmissible, because it would imply in it that nothing can be the cause or antecedent of a real effect, and consequently have a positive quality.

The sign-idea of nothing is employed, then, as an element in a formula of the reasoning called ad absurdum, in which the falsity or impossibility of a proposition is demonstrated by showing that there is implied in it another proposition evidently false.

As in the language of Algebra the expression √−1, which does not and cannot represent any quantity, serves to demonstrate that every expression which contains it is absurd, and is deduced from data whose existence cannot be admitted, so in ordinary language this proposition, nothing is something, serves to demonstrate that every proposition which contains it is absurd, and involves an impossible hypothesis.

But the word nothing is commonly used in another sense. When we say of an individual that nothing pleases him, we do not mean that nothing gives him pleasure, but that all things are to him not-pleasing; so that the negation which seems to be expressed of all things is not in reality understood except of the particular attribute we give them. Nothing in this case involves two unconnected ideas which refer to different mental objects: the first is the idea of all things, and the second the idea of the negation, or of a difference with respect to the predicate of the proposition. Nothing pleases him or nothing is pleasing to him is equivalent to all things are different to him from the pleasing.

Nothing enters also as an element of various metaphorical expressions, in which we fancifully figure it to ourselves as an immense abyss out of which spring the things that receive being, and into which sink those that lose it.

The infinite occupies in the intellectual scale the extreme opposite to nothing.

The infinite is that which has no limits, that which differs from [p. 239] the finite. But this difference cannot be truly perceived by the human intelligence, whose perceptions present it with limits in all the objects it is given to reach. The idea we have of the infinite is, consequently, a sign-idea, and cannot be anything else. We might express it by the formula a + a + a + a + etc.

The infinite is also an ideal sign which we employ for reasoning ad absurdum.

Every hypothesis that involves the proposition the finite is infinite is necessarily rejected as absurd. To prove, for example, that it is not given to us to perceive continuous quantity, we may employ this reasoning ad absurdum. To perceive continuous quantity would be to perceive in a given time infinite successive divisibility; and to perceive in a given time infinite successive divisibility would be to perceive in a given time an infinite number of divisions and of parts, and to have in a given time an infinite number of perceptions, and to attribute infinitude to a finite intelligence.

These and any other kinds of reasoning ad absurdum are really reducible to one, in which every hypothesis is rejected as inadmissible which is transformed into an absurd proposition, that is, one contradictory to an evident proposition. In mathematics this kind of reasoning is frequent and fruitful; in Philosophy it hardly serves except to prove, with more labor than perspicuity, what needs no proof, or what can be satisfactorily proved by direct means.

[PDF 256]

On sign-ideas.

Sign-ideas: in what they are distinguished from other ideas.—Mental representation of objects: it is always imaginary.—Homonymous sign-ideas.— They are little exposed to error.—Two kinds of homonymous sign-ideas.— Other kinds of sign-ideas: metaphorical sign-ideas.—Frequency and spontaneity of these.—The formation of metaphorical sign-ideas is governed by the same principle as the formation of classes and general names.—Cause of error in the use of sign-ideas.—Examples presented by Cabanis.— Metaphorical supposition of the relation of intellectual objects to sensible objects.—Inopportuneness of the sensationalist theory.—Abstract ideas are comprehended among metaphorical sign-ideas.—Different denominations of this idea.—The most correct sense is that which likens it to attention.— Inherence of qualities in objects as modifications of a substance.—Utility of their separation.—Errors arising from abstraction in the philosophical schools.—Abstraction facilitates language.—It is the foundation of many ideas.—Objective representation of abstract names.—Perceptions of the understanding.—Abstraction in the sense of attention.—Abstraction in the sense of generalization.—Conclusions.—Endogenous sign-ideas.—Necessity of signs in reasoning: elucidations.

I have pointed out incidentally some ideas which in the understanding take the place of others that it is not given us to form. I call them sign-ideas. I propose now to inquire what it is that distinguishes them from other ideas, and to enumerate their different kinds.

In the mental representation of an object we often renew perceptions that have not been originally produced [p. 241] by it, but by other objects. When I think of the city of Rome, which I have not seen, if I represent it to myself in any way, it is by renewing the perceptions of the houses, palaces, temples, streets and squares of other cities that I have seen. Probably my imagination presents to me in this way a picture which in many respects will not resemble the capital of the Catholic world; but this picture, however unfaithful it may be, serves me to think of it; and there is no danger of its leading me into error, so long as my judgments are not founded upon the particulars which I figure to myself in Rome, or at least upon any other particulars than those which, by my own reasonings or by the testimony of other men, I have reason to judge true.

I cannot represent to myself abstractly what Rome has in common with other objects of its kind. The idea of this city must of necessity consist of individual details, whether these be purely imaginary or not. But the faculty of substituting some particulars for others is equivalent to the faculty of eliminating them all, and brings it about that when we think of any object which we have not actually perceived, we give it only the attributes that belong to all the objects of the same class, or the particulars which our reasonings, or the perceptions of other men transmitted to us, have led us to conceive in it.

Whenever we think of individual objects that we have not observed, in the exercise of thought we do not confine ourselves to combinations of vocal signs; the mental representations of the objects are composed of imaginary particulars. We think in no other way of the personages, places and events of which history tells us, or which we find described in novels or in books of travel. However minute the description we read of them, it can never be individual; it is the reader who gives it this character. The historian, the poet, the traveler, may indeed narrow considerably the space in which our imagination is to range; but to reach individuality is denied them, because all the descriptive elements of which languages consist are of necessity general. He who describes

## PHILOS.   16

[p. 242]

refers the objects to classes more or less extensive; it is the reader who clothes them with the determinate forms, dimensions and colors which constitute individuality. All readers do pretty much what Don Quixote did when he pictured to himself the figure and features of Roland and of Amadis of Gaul; the only difference is that in reading histories or travels we give no credit to our apprehensions of individuality, as the gentleman of La Mancha did to his. Thus in all acts of thought a great part of the perceptions we renew are furnished by our imagination, which figures things that have not been objects of our observation by means of things of the same kind that have been.

These ideas which take the place of others, representing objects of the same kind as those which would be represented by these others, had we been able to acquire them, form the first class of those I have called sign-ideas. I shall give them the distinctive title of homonymous, which signifies that the object of the substituted idea is of the same kind or name as that of the idea for which it is substituted. And it is evident at once that homonymous sign-ideas are a supplement so much the more perfect and the less exposed to error, the less extensive the class to which the sign and the object signified jointly belong. In representing men to myself, my mind will wander less, and there will be less of the arbitrary in the composition of the signs, than in representing animals; and in this second case I shall likewise wander less and have less to choose from than when I represent bodies to myself; and if I pass to representing things in general, nothing will limit my choice, and to fabricate mental signs that shall symbolize them I may avail myself of all the perceptions my memory has accumulated. The errors in the use of these signs arise from our attributing to the object signified what belongs only to its image: if we think of an individual, we shall perhaps attribute to him the particulars of another; and if of a class, we shall perhaps not give to its characters the amplitude of modifications that belongs to them.

Great will necessarily be the danger of error when, in order [p. 243] to represent to ourselves an unobserved object, we have to go beyond the limits to which our observations have been confined. The savage who knew no more men than those of his own tribe, nor more trees and animals than those of the forest in which he lives, could only imperfectly figure to himself the productions of other climates, or the moral qualities of civilized man; and in the judgments he might form of these objects it would be exceedingly difficult for him to avoid error. This might happen even though in order to form exact ideas of them he needed no more elementary perceptions than those he had experienced in observing himself and the objects that surround him. What, then, if we have to imagine perceptions which we have never experienced or which perhaps it is impossible for us to experience? How will the savage conceive the exquisite pleasure which the contemplation of the masterpieces of the arts gives to civilized man, or that which the discovery of a recondite, fruitful truth, of interesting consequences, gives to the philosopher? In what manner shall we be able to figure to ourselves a color different from all those known, a new sense, an intelligence whose modes of perceiving have no analogy with those of the human intelligence? Conceptions of this kind suppose modes of knowing that have no relation to our intellectual faculties. The signs we are able to employ for such representations take the place of ideas of which feeling is incapable. The words color, sense, intelligence, their signification thus extended beyond the limits of all our possible observations, either excite in the understanding no idea of which we are conscious except that of their material sound, or excite only fantastic images to which we ought to give little credit, and which in the operations of the understanding cannot legitimately serve any other office than that of artificial symbols.

It is important, then, to distinguish among homonymous sign-ideas those which represent objects that we might have been able to know by means of the perceptive faculties with which we are endowed, and which we have previously put in exercise, from those which represent, or rather indicate or symbolize, objects that we cannot know by any of the modes of perception [p. 244] that we have exercised, or that nature has dispensed to man. If we must be on our guard against the fallacy of the former in the physical order, and chiefly in the moral order of ordinary life, the influence of the latter, invested with the enchantments of the imagination, is more to be feared in certain metaphysical discussions, where, however much on the alert we may be, it is almost impossible to guard ourselves entirely against the illusions produced by them.

There is another kind of sign-ideas, founded like the preceding upon relations of resemblance; but in these, unlike the preceding, the sign and the object belong to different classes, and their resemblance is not supposed, but is actually perceived.

When we figure to ourselves an unknown man, arbitrarily combining the features, limbs and moral qualities that we have noticed in other men, we suppose a resemblance between that object and the rest of its class which we have been able to observe, and by virtue of this supposition we employ the latter as signs to represent the former to ourselves. In the ideas of which we now treat the contrary happens: we imagine, for example, that the soul looks at or contemplates intuitively its affections, because we perceive a certain resemblance between consciousness and sight; and notwithstanding the essential diversity which we cannot but find between consciousness and sight, it seems to us that these two faculties resemble each other up to a certain point. Between seeing a thing and having knowledge of it by the reports of others, we conceive the same difference as between the affections by which the soul perceives itself and the affections of the senses which represent to it external objects; and by virtue of this resemblance of differences, sight comes to be in the understanding an image of consciousness.

Such is the character of the second kind of sign-ideas, to which I give the distinctive title of metaphorical, because every metaphor is the expression of an ideal sign of this class. When we say that the forms of objects are impressed upon the memory, we make use, as everyone knows, of a metaphor; and [p. 245] everyone knows also that in this case we represent to ourselves one thing by means of another diverse one, with which, nevertheless, we seem to perceive a certain resemblance, which we express by giving it the name of the sign; but a partial resemblance only, for we perceive well that the name of the sign cannot be applied to the object without losing a part of the signification which language has appropriated to it.

Exactly the same thing happens then as when we say that an able minister is the pillar of the State. As the pillar supports the edifice, the ability of the minister gives firmness and consistency to the State. We declare this resemblance by calling the minister pillar; but to do so we strip the idea of the pillar of the greater part of the partial ideas that compose it. We make use of this kind of signs, not only to communicate our ideas to others, but also to give an account to ourselves of what we think, and in a certain way to help ourselves to comprehend it. We then bring the idea of the sign near to that of the object, and notwithstanding the difference we perceive between them, which does not permit us to confound them, we perceive at the same time a certain analogy which makes us see the one with more clearness, contemplating it, so to say, beside the other.

One of the most curious phenomena is the spontaneity and frequency with which the sign-ideas of which we speak occur to the soul when it stops to observe itself. The names we give to the mental operations have all been originally metaphorical, and it is almost impossible to speak of them except by employing the words and phrases with which we are accustomed to indicate the reciprocal actions of bodies.

The necessities of animal life directed our attention at the outset to the laws that govern the corporeal universe; and when the time came to turn it toward the interior world of which consciousness gives us notice, it was natural that we should refer the one to the other, and that instead of inventing words and phrases which would have been intelligible only to their authors, we should lay hold of the established language, applying it to the new objects of our ideas according to the resemblances that seemed to us [p. 246] to find between them and corporeal objects. Familiarized with the qualities of matter, we clothe with them the spiritual affections, and we do not believe that we perceive them clearly except under the garb of sensible appearances.

In general, we facilitate for ourselves and for others the perception of the less familiar objects by comparing them with those which we have had occasion to observe often. It is well known that all men are inclined to draw their metaphorical signs from that class of things with which they have been made familiar by the locality they inhabit, their habitual exercises, their profession and manner of life. The expressions of the savage who lives by the chase will present a different fund of images from those of the tiller of the soil, the artisan or the mariner.

It follows from what has been said that the same principle which led us to the formation of classes and the imposition of general names is that which suggests to us metaphorical signs. It may be said that every general name was originally a metaphor, and that every metaphor is an imperfect generalization. The transition from one signification to another more general and extensive was an alteration of usage, hazardous at first, to indicate newly known objects by means of an image or resemblance, and which, frequently repeated, finally incorporated the object and the sign in one common class. This, however, could be effected only when there was little distance between the two; in the contrary case one of these two things must have happened: either the name lost the primitive signification, and the metaphorical word, having become familiar, passed into a proper one, of which we have examples in the words soul (originally breath), thought (originally the action of thinking); or the name acquired the new signification without being stripped of the old, and is employed with propriety in both, as has happened in the words reflection, discourse, apprehension and many others.

The cause of error in metaphorical signs, as in homonymous ones, is our propensity to attribute to the object what in reality belongs only to the sign; for although we have them both present in the understanding and it is not possible to confound [p. 247] them, it will happen not infrequently that we carry the analogy much farther than is just.

In the Memoirs of Cabanis on the relations between the physical and the moral in man, notable examples of this fascination of metaphorical sign-ideas are found. I shall limit myself to mentioning one only. “It has been observed,” he says, “that in old age the most recent impressions are easily effaced; those of mature age grow weak, and those of childhood on the contrary recover their vividness and distinctness. This, according to our way of seeing, is explained without difficulty.

“In infancy the softness of the brain makes it susceptible to all impressions, and its mobility multiplies and repeats them without ceasing; I mean those which relate to the objects the child has before his sight, and which interest his curiosity. And as these objects are limited in number, and the relations in which they are considered very simple, everything concurs to give then to the combinations of the nascent intelligence a durable character, to identify them in a certain way with the organization, and to bring them near to the automatic operations of instinct.

“But in proportion as the brain acquires consistency, and the sensitive extremities, protected by denser coverings, find themselves less immediately exposed to the action of external bodies, the impressions become less lively, their repetition less easy, and the communication of the various centers of sensibility less rapid; in a word, all the movements are retarded. At the same time the number of the objects that are considered grows from moment to moment, their relations become complicated, and the universe enlarges itself.

“Thus, then, from the moment that the need of receiving and combining new impressions ceases to be felt, and no object any longer excites the curiosity of the organs and of a sated mind, it is inevitable that the recollections should be effaced in an order the inverse of that of the impressions received, beginning with the most recent, which are the weakest, and ascending to the most ancient, which are the most durable; and in proportion as those with which the memory was loaded vanish, the preceding ones, which were obscured by them, reappear. Very soon, ceasing [p. 248] to exist for us, all the interests, all the thoughts which occupied us in the course of the later ages, only the moments in which we began to feel attract our looks toward themselves and reanimate our failing attention.”

Accepting as purely metaphorical what there is of the material in this exposition, we might regard it as a veracious history of the human intelligence; but if we wish to give it another sense; if the impressions are sensations and perceptions; the organs, senses, and the memory a soft pulp, which consolidates gradually until at last it is incapable of admitting deep and lasting impressions, what is done but to abuse the metaphor and confound the sign with the thing signified? I leave aside the absurdity which the metaphor involves in itself, supposing, as Mr. Pariset observes, the permanence of the first impressions in the midst of a perpetual flux of compositions and decompositions which incessantly renew the molecules of our organs.

By an effect of the same fascination, the relation between intellectual representations and sensible objects was likened to that which exists between a picture and its original, and it was supposed, in consequence, that objects sent to the organs true images of themselves, which were impressed upon a part of the brain called the sensorium, where they were perceived by the understanding. This gross theory has long been banished from the schools; but I do not know whether in that of Condillac and his disciples, on the modifications of the human soul, the interference of that principle of error is not entirely to be perceived, which, by exaggerating resemblances, presents to us as a discovery what is perhaps a simple metaphor. When this is not so, the theory which reduces to sensation all the other acts and affections of the soul can only be regarded as an arbitrary generalization of the signification of a word.

If in giving to a known object the name of a known class the whole signification of this name is preserved, this new use of the name of the class is the exact and rigorous expression of a judgment; and if the resemblance on which this judgment is founded is not immediately perceptible, but is deduced from [p. 249] observations or experiments, skillfully compared, he who first makes it known presents a discovery. In this sense Newton gave the title of gravity to the force which makes the planets describe elliptical orbits around the sun. The class heavy or gravity became more extensive than before, and in this sense was generalized; but it retained all the comprehension it had, all the attributes that belonged to it, and the extension of the class was increased without its comprehension being diminished. The word gravity, applied to celestial phenomena, lost nothing of the propriety of its former meaning.

The contrary would happen if, in applying to an object the name of others, we altered its signification and stripped it of a part of the attributes into which it is resoluble. We should then certainly express a perception of resemblance, and in this sense a judgment; but not the perception of that degree of resemblance which rigorously corresponds to the word, and therefore not the judgment properly signified by it. Applied to the new object, it would represent metaphorically some quality of the latter, and if there were not a great distance between the ordinary signification and the metaphorical, by dint of repetition in the second it would perhaps come to appropriate it; but the first would be altered, losing in comprehension what it gained in extension. Certain objects would seem in consequence to acquire a new attribute; but we should not on that account have discovered anything new in them.

Let us see, then, in what sense it may be admitted that all the operations of the understanding and of the will are sensations. When Condillac and his disciples maintain, for example, that to judge is to feel a relation, they present no new analogy between judging and feeling, between the affection of the soul which arises from the action of a corporeal object upon its organs and serves it to represent that object to itself, and the affection of the soul which arises directly and spontaneously from the simultaneity of two other affections, and consists in perceiving a particular relation between them. Their doctrine, therefore, either exaggerates the feeble resemblance we perceive between these two things, and gives [p. 250] too literal a sense to a metaphor, or is reduced to duplicating the signification of the word, so that it agrees with equal propriety with sensation and with judgment, without our being shown anything new in this second opposition. The same we may apply to simple intuition, to desire, and to the other modifications and operations of the soul. But the word sensation once generalized in this way, what does that pretended theorem of metaphysics tell us, except that spiritual affections are spiritual affections? Nor do I see that this new value of the word contributes anything to improving psychological nomenclature. To take the word sensation in the general sense of thought, including in it even the acts of the will, is to do violence to language without making us advance a step in the knowledge of our mind, and is to confound things which these same philosophers and all men recognize as different. The simplicity which this doctrine of Condillac seems to introduce into the theory of the human mind is wholly illusory.

To the metaphorical sign-ideas we may reduce abstract ideas. But this denomination is used in various senses which it will not be amiss to recall.

As to abstraction, considered as the faculty of drawing from individual or specific ideas, or separating from them, common characters, and of forming with these the ideas which represent species or genera, I believe I have demonstrated by irrefragable arguments that this theory of generalization is erroneous, and abstraction, understood in this sense, a chimera. Considered as the faculty of contemplating certain parts or qualities of objects separately and of classifying them according to the resemblances we discover in them, abstraction exists; but it differs in nothing from what we commonly call attention. Prism, triangle, red, green, are names that represent classes founded upon these partial comparisons, and in this sense may properly be called abstract. Finally, the title of abstraction is given to an act of the soul which considers qualities as distinct from the objects in which they exist, or as if they were, by themselves and separated from all substance, objects [p. 251] that are real; and in this sense those ideas are said to be formed by abstraction, or abstract ideas, which correspond to the words extension, figure, roundness, color, resemblance, virtue, quality, relation, and countless others; and, consequently, names are all divided into concrete, which involve no such consideration, e.g., beautiful, rich, prudent; and abstract, which involve it, e.g., beauty, wealth, prudence.

Let us inquire first, by the use that is made of these names, what their signification is. It is said that a body is round, green, soft, but it cannot be said that it is roundness, greenness, softness, but that it has or possesses these qualities, or that these qualities exist in it. Language attributes, then, to qualities expressed in this manner a being which is not the being of the objects in which we perceive them, and of which it represents them as parts. We picture to ourselves the greenness of the tree as a part of it, in the way that the branches, flowers and fruits are; and by virtue of this fiction, it would shock as much to say that the tree is greenness as to say that the oak is acorn.

But nothing can be more false than such a conception. The existence of qualities is so entirely one thing with that of objects, that it is not possible to conceive it without a substance actually modified by them. Between whiteness and the white, between resemblance and resembling objects, we can apprehend no distinction. The perceptions by means of which we know and recollect any thing whatever are the same by means of which we recollect its modes of being; consequently, the separation of qualities is a false supposition which can exist in the mind only in the shadow of some fantastic image, e.g., that it forms part of another. Abstraction, then, in the sense we are treating of, is nothing else than the apprehension of a fantastic image, and involves a true metaphor. As real and substantial objects are designated by substantive names, to give a quality a substantive name is to represent it as a substance.

Absurd as it may seem, however, to picture to ourselves qualities as distinct from real objects, and in a manner to make them [p. 252] substances, this fantastic separation or substantialization is most useful to language, furnishing it with convenient and precise means of expressing relations which without it would be indicated in a somewhat vague and obscure manner. Since some qualities seem to us to arise and derive from others, it is natural that we should consider the former as actions and particular modes of the latter, and should express, consequently, the relation between these and those by the same means we use to express the relations between real objects and the qualities we refer immediately to them; that is, by making them subjects in their turn, and giving them in that capacity attributes. The virtuous man is respectable offers the same sense as human virtue is respectable; but with this difference: in this latter way of speaking the connection between being a virtuous man and being respectable is expressed with more precision than in the former; because, strictly, a virtuous man may not be respectable through circumstances foreign to virtue, which weaken or destroy its natural effect on the minds of the men who contemplate it. Let us translate abstract language into concrete, I do not say in the writings of philosophers, but in the productions of eloquence and poetry, and we shall see how slow, how encumbered, how obscure the exposition of ideas becomes, and how languid the very descriptions of material objects, and the expression of the affections. And if it is so difficult at times to discard the meaning of a first abstraction, and we cannot do so without great detriment to the clearness, brevity and energy of the sentence, what will it be when we proceed from abstractions to abstractions, and the qualities of abstract objects, and the modifications of these qualities, and the modifications of these modifications, are transformed into new objects to signify a series of dependences and derivations?

Abstraction, according to what has been said, is, in the sense in which we now take this word, a trope, an artifice of language, a fiction which we use to express with facility and vividness relations between the modes of being of things, and perhaps also to aid us in conceiving them. This fiction, however, [p. 253] gross as it may seem, is not without its prestige. From the illusion produced by the use of abstract names (natural, moreover, to men, since we find it in the most barbarous languages) not a few of the absurdities have sprung which have contaminated for centuries the philosophy of the understanding, and from which perhaps the labors of Locke, Berkeley, Condillac and other eminent philosophers have not wholly purged it. Hence the substantial forms of the peripatetic school, qualities to which a certain kind of independent reality was attributed. Hence so many erroneous conceptions relative to space and time.

Abstraction facilitates language and renders it at the same time more expressive. It not only presents with more neatness and clearness the relations of ideas, but heightens and colors them. The abstract world is a world of images, with which we give body to intellectual conceptions, to the point of sometimes mistaking fiction for reality.

The fictitious entities that owe their being to abstraction have been classified like real and substantial objects, according to the resemblances and differences observed in these. Thus extension includes roundness, triangularity, length, depth, breadth, etc. Color embraces whiteness, greenness, yellowness, etc., and sense is divided into these species, sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, sense of heat, sense of effort, etc.

Finally, by virtue of the hypothetical existence of abstract entities, the universal class entity or thing is divided into two great species, that of real entities or substances, and that of abstract entities.

It must not be forgotten that abstract names, setting aside the image or metaphor they involve, represent identically the same ideas, the same objects, as the respective concrete names. Understanding offers the same idea as intelligent; greenness the same as green; extension the same as extended, without any difference. To say that the understanding perceives is neither more nor less than to say that intelligent beings perceive; save in so far as we give to understand an immediate connection between the perceptive and the intelligent [p. 254] The only thing, then, that differentiates these two ways of speaking is that the first expresses in a clearer and more precise manner than the second the dependence or particular connection which we conceive between the qualities of one and the same substance, which is the end for which abstract names were created.

Returning now to the various acceptations of this word, and setting aside as wholly inadmissible the first, in which the abstract and the general are supposed synonymous, we shall make some observations on the two remaining senses. In the one we have just explained, abstraction is a trope; in the other it is the attention we give to certain qualities of objects, setting aside the rest which accompany them in them, although the one and the others be naturally inseparable.

To tell the truth, abstraction in the one sense is frequently accompanied by abstraction in the other, that is, the effort of attention, which contemplates certain qualities setting others aside, is regularly accompanied by the use of the sign which attributes to these qualities an independent existence; but it must not be lost sight of that the one signifies a separation of coexistent ideas, so far as it is possible for us to effect it, and the other is a mere artifice of language.

The abstraction by which it has been sought to explain generalization is an erroneous supposition; the abstraction which consists in giving qualities a fictitious independent existence, representing them with substantives, is a trope; the abstraction in which we confine ourselves to certain qualities, setting aside all the others that accompany them, is a true fact of the understanding. The first is a chimerical abstraction; the second a tropical abstraction; the third an analytic abstraction.

The idea of man is a general idea; but it is not an abstract idea in any of the admissible senses; because man is a concrete object, a substance; and because in the idea of man we do not attend to this or that of the qualities which constitute him, setting aside the others, but to the whole of them together. The idea of the prism or of the sphere, the idea of the white or of the green, is also a general idea, for [p. 255] it embraces all prisms and all spheres, all white bodies and all green bodies possible; and is at the same time an analytic abstract idea, in which we confine ourselves to bodies of a certain figure or of a certain color; but it is not an abstract idea in the tropical sense, because the prism and the sphere, the white and the green, are ideas which have, or in which we can conceive, a real independent existence. Finally, the idea of the understanding is not only a general idea, since it embraces all possible understandings, but an abstract idea in the tropical sense, since it represents under the fictitious image of substance a quality of intelligent beings. By means of it we contemplate this quality setting aside any others that accompany it in intelligent beings.

Attending merely to the terms, it may be said: 1.º that the general does not necessarily suppose the abstract in either of the two admissible senses; 2.º that analytic abstraction does not suppose tropical abstraction either, but does suppose generalization, and 3.º that tropical abstraction always supposes generalization and almost always analysis.

I say almost always because there are a few tropical abstract names which embrace all possible abstractions. The word existence, for example, embraces all the modifications of whatever exists.

The third class of sign-ideas is formed by those which come out of the very depth of the idea signified, and which for this reason I call endogenous.

When we think of a person recalling only his countenance, or of a city, bringing to memory only one of its principal buildings, or perhaps a single one of the façades of this building, of which it may be that we do not distinctly recollect more than one or two details, we represent the whole by the part, availing ourselves of the latter as of an artificial sign. The same happens when, thinking, for example, of fire, we recall only the heat it produces in us, or only the form and color of the flame. Although the ideologists have not mentioned this kind of signs, I am persuaded that any one who observes with some attention the phenomena [p. 256] intellectual, as his own consciousness exhibits them to him, will perceive that their use is very frequent; that we almost never picture to ourselves the whole of the objects of which we think, nor even all their principal parts and qualities; and that if the names of things often figure for them in our minds, they rarely fail to be accompanied by partial ideas which serve as a link between them and the things signified by them.

It is said that we cannot reason except by means of signs, and the proposition seems to me true, understood of signs in general, comprising sign-ideas; because without signs of some kind, the simplest step of reasoning would require the review of an innumerable multitude of details. To affirm something of a class of objects it would be necessary that we should affirm it of its individuals one by one; and even to represent to ourselves an individual, of the human species for example, how many elemental ideas would the memory have to run over! But limited the necessity of signs to those of speech, it seems to me doubtful. It is true that names, by virtue of the close connection which the use of language has established between them and the respective objects, are for the understanding like the qualities or parts of these, and parts all the more important and conspicuous the more we have in them the system of the universe cyphered, according to the relations of resemblance observed among all beings: so that our propensity to make use of names as signs seems to me to resolve itself into the general propensity to employ partial ideas as representatives of complex ideas. But a word after all supposes something corresponding to it in the understanding, though it be no more than a sign-idea. And if we can reason with words, it is by virtue of this correspondence. Ideas are the coin, so to speak, of the understanding; and words are a sort of paper money, which is worth nothing except because in the understanding there is something that corresponds to them, and is represented by them. The reasonings we make by operating on vocal signs suppose, then, a reasoning which is executed by operating on ideas; a reasoning which may not be truly executed, but into which the first can always be translated [p. 257] and which can consequently be effected without it.

The endogenous sign-ideas do not suppose the use of speech; vocal or nominal signs do suppose it, or rather are speech itself. But, although their connection with objects is arbitrary or conventional, their use is not for that reason exposed to more inconveniences than that of the other kinds of signs. Once we have become familiar with language, the division between vocal signs and the natural signs we have called sign-ideas is in reality of little importance. The combinations and resolutions of some vocal signs into others possess in a superior degree the convenience of being perceived with more clearness, being placed, like the signs of Algebra, within reach of the senses; and if they can lead us into error, it is because we have not determined with exactness what they signify, or because it is difficult to preserve for each sign an invariable signification; no small difficulty when the ideas signified involve complex relations susceptible of many modifications.

To the three preceding classes, of homonymous, metaphorical and endogenous, seem to me reducible all the ideas which help us to conceive or express other ideas, or to take the place of those we lack.

## PHILOS.   17

[PDF 274]

On the resemblance between sensible objects and the actual or

renewed perceptions we have of them.

What resemblance there is between bodies and the affections of the soul.— Resemblance between the object and the idea.—Simple sensations have no resemblance to corporeal qualities.—Resemblance of sensations to the resemblance of the causes.—Resemblance of complex ideas to their objects.— Relation and relative quality.—Foundation of the relation.—Elementary relations of resemblance.—Conception of universal resemblance.—General relation of this resemblance.

So long as the soul confines itself to its own affections or to the relations that exist among them, it perceives itself intuitively; but when it refers its affections, which in that case are sensations, to causes distinct from itself, and when, in consequence, it figures those causes to itself under the appearance of its own modes of being, and judges of the relations among them by those which it perceives among its own modes, the perceptions are purely representative. It is important, then, to ascertain in what this representation consists; in other terms, what resemblance there is, or can be conceived to be, between the bodies or causes which affect the soul and the affections of the soul, which, committed to the memory, form the ideas we have of corporeal causes.

The word idea signifies image; a denomination which seems to indicate resemblance between the object and the idea, between the cause of [p. 259] the sensation and the sensation itself. Under this aspect the expression, as we shall see, is not altogether proper. But if we regard the idea not as the image of its corporeal object, but of the perception we had of that object when it was actually acting upon the senses; if we conceive the resemblance not between the idea and its object, but between the perception renewed by memory and the actual perception, the expression is appropriate and exact; for there is indeed resemblance between renewed perceptions and actual perceptions. Perhaps this was not the sense in which this word, of which the schools have since made such abuse, was originally taken.

Between simple sensations and the ideas of the corporeal qualities which we represent to ourselves by means of them, there is not, nor can there be conceived, the least resemblance. When we represent to ourselves the odor of a rose, it is evident that we do not conceive in it a sensation of odor such as we experience in smelling the rose; for to what can a simple sensation be like, if not to another sensation? These sensations, then, when referred to their objects, may be called signs or symbols, but not images of them. They represent them not as a painting does its original, but as the letters of the alphabet do the elementary sounds of a language, with which, when we compare each letter with its sound, they have no resemblance whatever.

We limit this to simple sensations and to the ideas which we form by means of them of the respective corporeal qualities.

As to ideas of relations, we have reason to think—I have spoken amiss: we feel ourselves irresistibly drawn to believe—that the causes of sensations have among themselves relations like those which we perceive intuitively among the sensations themselves.

From the resemblance of the sensations we infer the resemblance of the causes which impress the organs. From the succession or coexistence of the sensations we infer the succession or coexistence of the causes. If one sensation is more intense than another, we infer that the cause of the first acts upon the organs with more force or more intensity than the cause of the [p. 260] second. This is one of the instinctive principles of human reason, which cannot be demonstrated and have no need of demonstration. (a)

Finally, between complex ideas and their objects there is necessarily a certain resemblance, which is not difficult to understand, by appealing to the simile we have just made use of.

In the written word alabanza [praise] four similar letters enter, and the relation of resemblance which we note among them is not merely a symbol, but a true image of the relation of resemblance that exists among four of the sounds which concur to form the word. Although there is no resemblance between any letter and its sound, the relations among the letters of which a written word consists have it with the relations among the sounds of which a spoken word is composed. In the same manner, in the complex idea of the rose the simple sensation of rose color enters as many times as we represent to ourselves parts of that color in the rose; and the resemblance among these sensations of color produced by the rose in our mind is a true image of that which, as to color, exists among the parts of the rose. The relation of resemblance cannot but be like itself, whatever the things among which we conceive it.

When in the quality we attribute to any person or thing another person or thing intervenes in such a manner that, in order to conceive the quality, the existence or conception of the two persons or things is equally necessary, the quality takes the name of relative. Relation and relative quality are expressions of one and the same meaning.

If we conceive, for example, any relation between two objects, it is because the understanding compares them, that is,

(a) The relation between the sensations does not always truly correspond to the original

relation between the causes. It is necessary, therefore, in some cases to correct the instinctive judgment. It seems to us, for example, that the crash of the thunder follows the lightning after a longer or shorter interval. Afterwards we learned that these two things were truly simultaneous in their origin, and that the interval between them was due to the different velocity with which light and sound are propagated. We were able, then, to correct the first judgment. [p. 261] contemplates them at once; regards them, so to speak, side by side. The fact or the idea in which the two related objects intervene, and which establishes a particular bond between them, is called the foundation of the relation. Thus in the relation of father and son the fundamental fact is a generation, and in the relation of grandfather and grandson, of great-grandfather and great-grandson, etc., the foundation is a series of generations: in the relation of resemblance the foundation is simpler, because it reduces itself to a kind of nearness, of affinity, of something indefinable which the soul perceives in the two things when it contemplates them at once, which belongs to neither of them in particular nor to their mere aggregate, and which cannot be explained.

There are in fact, as we shall see, elementary relations which are susceptible of no definition or explanation whatever, however clearly they may be perceived and distinguished, as happens with other affections of the soul. Who can define or explain resemblance? All that we can do is to point it out in the soul, determining the occasion and the conditions of its appearance, and this same is all that we can do with elementary relations.
