We express the relation by saying, for example, that the camellia is like the rose, that John is the brother of Francis, or that the rain fertilizes the fields. But there is among relations a notable difference, which reduces them to two classes. In some the relation can be expressed in two ways, of which the one is merely the inverse of the other: M is similar to N and N is similar to M signify one and the same identical relation, which we may also state by means of a copulative expression, M and N are similar. If F is the brother of G, we can express the same by saying that G is the brother of F, or that F and G are brothers.

But in other relations the inversion cannot be effected except by substituting for the relative word another word of contrary meaning; whence it results that to each of these relations there corresponds a pair of words, called correlatives, which change places in the expression: e.g., Abel was the son of Adam; Adam was the father of Abel. Spain was master of the [p. 262] Indies; the Indies were the dominion of Spain; Caesar conquered Pompey; Pompey was conquered by Caesar. His friends abandoned him; he was abandoned by his friends.

In the same manner, A is the cause of B and B is the effect of A; M is creditor of N and N is debtor of M; P is prior to Q and Q is posterior to P, express respectively identical relations to each of which there corresponds a pair of words whose meanings make us regard the relation in two ways, the one the inverse of the other. In the expression A is prior to B, the relation is considered as a quality of A; while in the expression B is the effect of A, the relation is a quality of B; and yet the foundation of the relation in both expressions is identical.

Qualities are commonly divided into absolute and relative; the former being what may very well be conceived without its being necessary that two terms be set in opposition in the understanding, bound together by a fundamental fact on which both depend: a negative character which seems to be attributed to these words, white, fragrant, spherical.

But in reality there is scarcely a quality that does not involve one or more relations, although only one of them ordinarily occupies the attention.

In fact, the perception, actual or renewed, of a quality apparently absolute supposes that we at least refer a quality of the soul to the soul, if the perception is intuitive; or that we refer a sensation to its proximate or remote cause, if the perception is sensitive. The pure conception of an absolute quality necessarily involves the conception of a relation of identity or of a relation of causality, as has been said in treating of intuitive and sensitive perceptions.

Besides, if I judge that a jasmine is white, it is because I mentally compare it with other objects to which we already give the same title, and because we find resemblance between the jasmine and those objects. This relation lies wholly in the attribute which we give to the jasmine, and I cannot but conceive and affirm it by the very fact of perceiving its whiteness.

It is otherwise when we recognize in a person the quality [p. 263] of son or father, or in any thing whatever the quality of cause or effect, because these words do not include in themselves the term to which the quality which they explicitly signify refers. Every relation supposes two terms, one to which the relative quality is attributed and another to which this quality refers. If we say, for example, that Abel was a son, we necessarily suppose that he was so of somebody, and we do not complete the idea of the relation except by adding of Adam, without which the word would not comprehend the whole relation; and this is what characterizes the words, and consequently the ideas, which are regarded as truly relative.

The word descendant is in itself truly relative, like son or father, and obliges us to think of an ancestor or ancestors from whom the person or persons to whom that title is attributed derive their origin; but from the moment that this person or these persons enter into the attribute to complete the relation, we cease to attend to the latter and no longer consider the word as relative. So it happens, for example, in Heraclidae, which signifies descendants of Hercules.

There is still more, and it is that words whose signification is naturally relative are represented as absolute if we leave the terms out of account. In this case is found, for example, the word resemblance, when we say: resemblance is an indefinable thing; the proposition expresses priority and posteriority at the same time.

The absolute and the relative are, then, variable characters, which depend not only on our manner of conceiving things but on the signs with which we represent them in language. Relation, however, is in itself a product of the soul of a peculiar nature, whether we regard it in its original state of simplicity, or in composition with other elements of the same kind or of different kinds.

Besides, if among the written words alabanza [praise], naturaleza [nature], albor [dawn], we notice that certain elements resemble one another and certain elements differ, these relations of resemblance or difference will not merely symbolize but will copy faithfully, supposing a perfect alphabet, relations of the same kind be-tween [p. 264] the respective elements of the spoken words. And what else happens when, comparing snow with milk, we conceive that they resemble each other in color and differ in temperature, or when, comparing the peach with the pear, we find them alike in the colors of trunk, branches and leaves, and different in the color of the flowers and the flavor of the fruits? These resemblances and differences between the one object and the other are not merely indicated to us, but are depicted to us in the relations which we perceive intuitively between the modes of the soul excited by the one and the modes of the soul excited by the other.

The combinations of simple ideas which represent the whole of the qualities of an object and constitute its complex idea are, then, like the combinations of letters which form a written word and represent a word. In comparing written words one with another, we perceive that, by means of the resemblance of the elements or letters of which they consist, the whole of writing reduces itself to a limited number of characters; and in the same way, in comparing complex ideas one with another, we see them resolve themselves into simple elementary sensations which, though extremely numerous, are nevertheless infinitely fewer than their combinations.

In this manner the resemblance which we notice among the sensations discovers to us the affinity which not only the parts of one and the same object, but the various objects that people the material universe, have with one another. By means of this relation it may be said that the universe is decomposed, like language, into a certain number of elements; that nature, by means of the sensations, has given to each of these elements a sign, as writing has marked with a letter each of the simple sounds of speech; and that, combining these signs and forming with them complex ideas, we represent to ourselves the combinations of the simple qualities with which objects are endowed, with a fidelity proportioned to the care of our observations, which are like the spelling out of the great book open to our senses in the corporeal universe.

Moreover, the order in which the letters succeed one another in a word, [p. 265] and the words in a written sentence, faithfully depicts to us the order in which the elementary sounds succeed one another in the corresponding spoken words. And what else do the relations of succession which we perceive among our sensations do? The series of sensations which a fruit passing through different degrees of ripeness produces in our sight represents to us, and cannot but represent to us, the series of modifications which that fruit undergoes in ripening; and as a written sentence consists of several words, each of which signifies a certain combination of sounds, the complex idea we have, e.g., of a tree consists of a great number of groups of sensations by means of which we represent to ourselves the various states that are developed in it, from the minute seed that germinates in the earth to the gigantic body, composed of trunk and branches, clothed with leaves and flowers, and finally laden with fruits. As the resemblances and differences of the letters of each word, whether among themselves or with the letters of which other words consist, make known to us the composition of sounds that corresponds to it in speech, so the resemblances and differences of the sensations of which each group of those which form the idea of the tree consists, whether compared among themselves or with the sensations produced by other objects, depict the composition of the qualities of each state of the tree. And finally, as the succession of the written words corresponds exactly to the succession of the spoken words, so the successive order which we notice among the various groups of sensations depicts to us the successive order of the various states of the tree.

This is the last point to which the comparison between human language and the language which the corporeal universe speaks to our senses can carry us. The two relations of resemblance and succession are common to both, and in the one as in the other they do not signify but copy relations of the same kind, whether among the sounds of speech or among the qualities of bodies. But sensations represent to us yet another relation. We may notice, for example, that the body A is more or less white than the body B, or that the whiteness of the [p. 266] one is equal to the whiteness of the other. In this case, comparing the sensations received, we notice between them the relation which we are accustomed to declare by one of the words more, less, equal; and we represent to ourselves a relation of the same kind between the causes of the sensations, that is, between the corporeal qualities: a representation which is effected not by means of symbols, but of true images. If each elementary sound of speech were susceptible of a great number of different tones, and we were to represent them in writing by an equal number of apices or accents, the various apices of each letter would be like the various degrees of each sensation, and the various tones of each voice like the various degrees of each corporeal quality. The relations of more and less which we perceive among the sensations do not symbolize but copy relations of the same kind among their causes, in the same way that, in the supposition we have just made, the visual scale of the apices would represent the scale in which the tones strike the ear, and there would be true resemblance between the two.

Not otherwise, then, than as writing represents speech, that is, without there being in the representation any more resemblance than that of certain relations between the elements, does our understanding represent to itself bodies, the laws of nature, the phenomena of the universe, in a word, whatever falls within the reach of our senses; because all this exists for us only in the sensations; in the combinations, resemblances, series and quantities of which we perceive the combinations, resemblances, series and quantities of the objects that people the material world.

But in another aspect there is a great distance between the letters and the sensations. A, B, C, represent to us elementary sounds which we know without the aid of these letters; whereas the sensations of white color or of the odor of jasmine represent to us things which we know only by these very sensations. Nature is for us what, on the supposition of a perfect alphabet, the sounds of speech would be to the deaf-mute who has learned to read.

[PDF 283]

Examination of the theory of external sensitive perceptions, ac‐

cording to the Scottish school.

Simple qualities and compound qualities.—Whether there is correlation in both.—Correlation of extension and color.—Erroneous theories of sensitive perception: whence they originate.—Locke.—Berkeley.—Dr. Reid.— Observations on this philosopher’s doctrine.—Judgment of the existence of an object.—Testimony of Berkeley.—Judgment which we make in the references of sensations to their causes.—Simple sensations, according to Dr. Reid.—Extension.—Final elucidation.

Simple qualities of matter are those which we represent to ourselves by means of homogeneous spiritual affections. Such, e.g., is a color. Compound qualities, on the contrary, are those which are represented to us by means of heterogeneous spiritual affections. Such is extension.

We may conceive in the former, if it is permissible to say so, a structure like that of simple bodies in Chemistry. As the integrant molecule of these consists of a single principle, of the same nature as the whole, so the last element which we are capable of perceiving in a color is always the same color; because the last element that enters into the representative sign with which we form the idea of this color is always a visual sensation irresolvable into diverse spiritual affections, and which does not differ from the aggregate of spiritual affections that represent to us the whole color, save as unity differs from number.

[p. 268]

We may also liken complex material qualities to compound bodies. As in these the integrant molecule consists of several constituent principles, different from one another and from the whole, so the integrant element of the complex corporeal quality resolves itself, by means of intellectual analysis, into a certain number of simple qualities, absolute and relative, which differ from one another and from the whole, and to which spiritual affections of different kinds correspond, each of which, multiplied, would never reproduce the idea of that complex quality. In tactile extension, for example, the integrant element which, added to itself, reproduces it, is the extraposition of two tactile points; a complex relation, in which there enter as elements tactility, the effort necessary to pass from one point to another, and the succession of the effort to the tactility and of the tactility to the effort. To say that tactile extension does not result from the multiplication of any of the elements of tactile extraposition is the same as to say that the ideal sign of that complex quality does not result from the multiplication of any of the simple spiritual affections which constitute the ideal sign of its integrant element.

Do simple qualities suppose complex ones, or these those? It seems impossible to hesitate in this alternative: the compound necessarily supposes the simple. Nevertheless, both propositions may be admitted as true, under different aspects. Let us confine ourselves to color and visual extension. It is impossible for us to arrive at the idea of visual extension without having first formed the idea of color; because visual extension is a series of extrapositions among colored points. But at the same time it is incontestable that, the idea of visual extension once acquired, we cannot represent to ourselves a color without representing to ourselves a visual extension to which it is united. Although nature always presents color to us united to extension, the understanding began by perceiving color alone: it noticed afterwards, by means of the sense of effort, extraposition of parts in visible surfaces, and visual extension thus conceived, there came to be [p. 269] an indissoluble connection between the ideas of these two qualities, and color came to presuppose visual extension necessarily.

If we consider ideas subjectively, if we attend to their generation and development, extension presupposes color or tactility, because the integral element of visible or tangible extension is the extraposition between two colored or tactile points, and because the idea of extension in general cannot but be posterior to the idea of visible or tangible extension. But if we consider the qualities objectively, if we render an account of what they are in themselves, we cannot but confess that there can be no color without a surface on which the rays of light are reflected, nor is anything accessible to touch except what presents a surface, greater or less, that resists it. If, then, in attending to the chronological development of ideas, extension presupposes color, in attending to the logical order, color presupposes extension.

From a failure to understand clearly that extension, hardness, softness and other qualities which are perceived by sight or touch, with the aid of the sense of effort, resolve themselves into simple qualities, absolute and relative; that their ideal signs resolve themselves in the same manner into simple sensations and conceptions of relation; and that, although it is not possible to conceive a resemblance between the simple qualities and the sensations, neither is it possible to fail to conceive it between intellectual relations and external relations, there have arisen, in my opinion, erroneous theories concerning sensitive perception.

Locke divides corporeal qualities into primary and secondary: those he calls primary which serve as a kind of subject to the others, and he regards it as a peculiar character of these that they resemble their ideas. Thus extension, according to him, is a primary quality, and color a secondary quality, because color logically presupposes extension. But his doctrine, as regards mere tactility, which according to him includes tactile extension, seems to me inexact. Tactility is, with respect to touch, what color is with respect to sight: color is a visual tactility, and there can be, or be conceived, no more resemblance between the [p. 270] pure tactility and the elementary sensations of touch than between color and the visual sensations. When Locke places among the primary qualities the extension, hardness, elasticity and other complex qualities of matter, his doctrine is most certain; but when he lays it down that the ideas of the primary qualities of bodies resemble them, and that their models or prototypes really exist in the bodies themselves (Book 2, Chap. 8), he does not give us the expression of this resemblance, nor explain to what extent there can be any between spiritual affections and corporeal qualities: a problem which I think I have resolved in the preceding chapter.

What the illustrious author of the Essay concerning Human Understanding left unexplained, Berkeley judged inexplicable. According to this author, there can be no external things of which our ideas are copies or resemblances. “An idea,” says the Bishop of Cloyne (Principles of Human Knowledge, VIII and IX), “can be like nothing but an idea; a color or figure can be like nothing but another color or figure.” Berkeley believes that on this point the primary qualities do not differ from the secondary, and the impossibility of conceiving any resemblance between our ideas and material qualities is in his view one of the most powerful arguments against the existence of matter.

Dr. Reid, dazzled by the supposed absurdity of a resemblance between the affections of the soul and corporeal qualities, and frightened at the consequences which Berkeley derived from this principle, gave a new theory of perception, in which he pretends to confine himself to a simple exposition of its history. According to him, sensation and perception are two entirely distinct things, two acts of the soul between which no connection can be conceived, except that of the one succeeding the other, by virtue of the fundamental laws of our nature. We smell a body, and upon the sensation of odor there follows at once, by a particular instinct, the notion of the present existence of that body, as the cause of the sensation of odor. We touch a body, we experience a sensation; and as if by a kind of magic there arises at once in the soul the notion or [p. 271] idea of the present existence of that body, and of its extension, its hardness, elasticity, etc. The perception of a secondary quality is limited to regarding it as the cause of the sensation and to giving us notice of the presence of the body; and the perception of the primary qualities gives us besides a clear and distinct idea of them. But in either case the perception, as Dr. Reid conceives it, is an immediate intuition of the corporeal object, and arises in the soul in consequence of the sensation, although it has nothing to do with it; so that the organic impression, the sensation and the perception are three steps in the process by which we are informed of the existence and qualities of matter, but three entirely distinct steps, there being no greater connection between the second and the third than between the first and the second. Since, then, we perceive the primary qualities of bodies immediately, it is not necessary, in order to know them, that there should be any resemblance between them and the mental affections excited by them.

Such is the theory, or, according to Dr. Reid and his followers, the narrative of the facts concerning perception, stripped of all hypothesis. But a slight examination suffices to show that it is full of suppositions not only voluntary but repugnant to all sound reasoning.

In the first place, it cannot be denied that there is an evident connection between the organic impression, the sensation and the sensitive perception: it is not given us to conceive, for example, that the mechanism of the eye which determines the visual sensation could have been adapted to the impression of odoriferous effluvia or of aerial vibrations, and had not been preordained so that the sensations, consequent upon the perceptions, might contribute, together with the sense of effort, to give us the perception and idea of superficial extension, and even, in certain circumstances, the perception and idea of a space spreading out in length, breadth and depth. In the second place, it is altogether inexact that there is no connection between sensation and sensitive perception, when the former is evidently not a sign, as Reid pretends, but an element, a part [p. 272] integral to the second. Such is the result, in my opinion incontrovertible, of what I have said in the preceding chapters, and it suffices to overthrow Reid’s expositions. But other considerations of equal force militate against the doctrine of this illustrious philosopher.

It is undoubtedly more analogous to the ordinary procedure of the human understanding to suppose that ideas so abstract as those of existence and present time do not arise in the soul by virtue of a particular instinct or primitive law of our constitution; that they are due to preceding observations, comparisons and classifications; that we lack them for some time, and that there arrives at length an age at which sensation suggests them, as it suggests other ideas.

This epoch of the understanding being reached, it happens that when a body acts upon an organ and a sensation is produced in the soul, there arises in us the judgment that the affection we experience is not a remembered sensation, but an actual one, and that other minds, placed in the same circumstances, would experience it as ours does. Knowing that to this sensation correspond others of a different kind, as for example to those of sight, hearing and smell those of touch, we shall judge also that, on placing ourselves in circumstances to experience the latter, these will infallibly arise in the soul. On seeing a river, for example, I cannot doubt that I truly see it; that the vision I experience is not comparatively feeble, like those I imagine or recollect, nor subject as these are to the empire of my will; that others will see the river as I do, if they are in the same circumstances as I; and that if I apply to it the organs of touch, certain tactile affections will be produced in me and in them, those, namely, which correspond to a certain slight resistance, a certain mobility, pressure, impulse, etc. . . . It is true that we do not usually pronounce these propositions mentally, because, being familiarized with them, we come from a very early age to pay no attention to them; they nevertheless enter at every step into our thoughts, and are the precise supposition upon which we regulate all the operations of life.

[p. 273]

Such are the complicated elements into which the judgment of the presence of the object resolves itself; elements over which the soul passes rapidly, because they have been made most familiar to it; but which nevertheless exist in the understanding from the time when, in the first epoch of life, observation and that kind of reasoning which we know develops very early in the child gave rise to them.

I ask now: when we opened our eyes for the first time and saw the first object, could the judgment have occurred to us that this vision was neither recollected nor imagined, but actual; that other living beings placed in the same circumstances as ourselves would see what we saw, and that, on applying the organ of touch to the object of vision, we should experience certain tactile sensations? Assuredly not: these judgments into which that of the presence of the object is decomposed could not occur to the soul except at a later epoch, though an early one: when the understanding had already been developed and exercised to a certain point. Reid’s own disciples agree in this. But at this epoch of the understanding, what was needed to form them? It was needed to have observed the affections of the soul, to have compared them, to have noted their natural connections; and nothing more was needed. It was not necessary that they should be infused into us at the moment of sensation, by virtue of a law of nature dispensing us from acquiring them by the ordinary process of observation, since this sufficed to conduct us to them with certainty, and to conduct us early. If one affection of the soul gives rise to the judgment of the presence of the object and another does not, it is because we have learned to distinguish actual sensations from recollections: a distinction no more difficult than that of any other modes of the soul. I cannot see, then, in this element of perception anything but an acquired judgment; nor do I know how the contrary doctrine can be regarded as the simple and naked exposition of a fact.

In the judgment of the presence of the object there is involved that of the existence of causes distinct from the soul which produce the sensations. These two judgments, however, are perfectly

## PHILOS.     18

[p. 274]

distinct and separable: the one bears properly upon the actuality of sensations; the other refers them to external causes, and is strictly that which gives them the character of representatives and converts them into perceptions.

The reference which we make of sensations to causes distinct from the soul is a judgment which is doubtless due to a primitive tendency of the understanding. But we do not on that account regard it as an intuitive perception of those causes; because it is not the same thing to be led by nature to imagine a cause and to suppose its existence, as to perceive it intuitively.

It seems to me, then, that even this part of Dr. Reid’s theory rests upon a gratuitous supposition, in support of which I believe that neither he nor his disciples have alleged any proof; namely, that this judgment is due, not only to an original operation of the understanding irresolvable into others, but to an intuitive perception of corporeal objects.

Of the existence of these judgments in sensitive perception (that of the actuality of the perception, and that which attributes the sensation to a cause distinct from the soul) no one, not even Berkeley himself, has hitherto doubted:(a) what is new in Reid’s doctrine is to consider the representative perceptions of corporeal objects as infused in the act of sensation, and as immediate perceptions, like those which the soul has of itself. But is this to set forth nakedly

(a) Berkeley denies the substantial existence of matter; but he does not deny that

sensations have causes distinct from the being that feels: he finds these causes in the laws to which the Creator has been pleased to subject the production of sensations in spirits; that is, in the will of the Supreme Being; in direct influences of the Great Spirit upon created spirits. Berkeley recognizes likewise (and how could he fail to recognize it?) the difference between actual perceptions and recollected perceptions or ideas. The judgment of the present existence of the object, or of its past existence, or of its future existence; that of its absolute non-existence, that of its impossible existence, are all judgments equally accessory to the actual or renewed perception, and are due to observations and reasonings which the perceptions suggest. [p. 275] the fact, or to disfigure it with a voluntary supposition, and one of the boldest?

It is to be remarked that in the reference we make of sensations to their causes, that perception imagined by Dr. Reid, that primitive intuition of the understanding, irresolvable into other acts and entirely distinct from sensation, teaches us nothing which the experience of touch could not have taught us without it from the earliest epochs of life. It tells us nothing of any of the causes which mediately or immediately affect the organs, and by means of them the faculty of feeling, unless these causes are accessible to tactile observations, or to those of sight as representative of touch, or unless we have associated with the sensation the information of this sense. On the other hand, would it not be natural that this intuition of bodies should always refer to those which immediately produce the organic impression: to the odoriferous effluvia, when we smell; to the vibrated air, when we hear; to the luminous rays in vision? But neither do we perceive these intermediate agencies, nor of the distant causes which determine them do we perceive more than a single quality, the color, the odor, the sound, and this very perception is reduced to a pure symbolization. A delicate analysis, which the greater part of men are loath to credit, has been necessary in order to distinguish in the functions of sight what is truly perceptive from what is not. We believe we really perceive what is only inferred from what we really perceive. So that, even when consciousness appears to testify to us that we perceive, it is possible that we deceive ourselves, mistaking the rapid suggestions of reasoning for the acts of the perceptive faculty. Ought not this to make us cautious not to confound with perception, and much less with intuitive perception, what in reality belongs to other functions of the intelligence?

The various deductive judgments which accompany actual or renewed sensation give it a multitude of complex forms, which we ought not to regard as original affections of the soul. The acts of memory are accompanied by the judgment of the past existence [p. 276] of the object, not, as Dr. Reid pretends, by another primitive law, by virtue of which this judgment and the renewed perception form a whole whose parts have not previously existed separate, but because in the order and connection of our mental representations with one another and with our present existence, we distinguish the work of memory properly so called from the works of imagination, notwithstanding that the materials with which both faculties of the soul work are absolutely the same. Hence it is that the works of imagination are sometimes accompanied by the judgment of the present or past existence of what we imagine. In reading Josephus we picture to ourselves what happened at the siege of Jerusalem, and in seeing the countenance of a man we form an idea of the inward feelings that agitate him. In either case we persuade ourselves that our ideas, though fabricated by imagination, are to a certain extent conformable to the truth of things. Shall we regard these judgments as naturally and essentially attached to the mental representations? To express the certainty of our deductive judgments, we are accustomed to say that we perceive in a man’s countenance whether he is sad or cheerful. But who is there that understands this vulgar expression literally?

According to Dr. Reid, those sensations are simple, that is to say, homogeneous, from which arise the perceptions of extension, hardness, softness and other complex qualities. This is another fundamental error of his theory. Extension we cannot conceive at all except as an aggregate of extrapositions; and we have already seen that each extraposition is composed of diverse elements, to each of which corresponds either a sensation of touch or of sight, or a sensation of effort, or an intellectual relation. As to the ideas of hardness and softness, there is, as this philosopher pretends, no simple sensation that produces them, such at least as we have them in adult age. Let us suppose a man in whom the sense of touch is developed for the first time. This man touches a piece of marble and a piece of wax. The one resists the impression of the finger; the other yields [p. 277] gently to it. If the individual of whom we treat is destitute of all previous notion of extension and of motion, and if the sensations which we suppose him to experience for the first time, in touching the marble and the wax, are not prolonged sufficiently to make him perceive the extrapositions of the particles touched, the constancy of the reciprocal situation of the one and the inconstancy of this situation in the others, the marble on its part and the wax on its, will produce two homogeneous sensations, each of which will represent a simple quality. For this individual hardness and softness will be two different qualities or modes of being, as are, for example, the odor of the rose and that of garlic; but they will be nothing more. He will not figure to himself hardness or softness as the firm or feeble cohesion of extraposed particles, but as a hidden cause, which excites a certain affection in his mind and is represented by this affection as the sound of the a or the b is by one of these two letters, without there being any resemblance between the symbol and the thing symbolized; whereas for us the idea of hardness or of softness is an aggregate of sensations and conceptions, which represents the respective quality as a written word represents a spoken word, and which therefore cannot but have a certain resemblance to the thing represented, that is to say, a resemblance of relations.

“No man,” says this philosopher, “can give a reason why the vibration of a body might not have given the sensation of smelling, and the effluvia of bodies affected our hearing. In like manner, no man can give a reason why the sensations of smell, or taste, or sound, might not have indicated hardness, as well as that sensation which, by our constitution, does indicate it.” This is the same as to say that because the sound a might have been represented by the letter b and the sound b by the letter a, if the inventors of the alphabet had so willed, the word soul or heart might equally well have been represented by one of these two letters. But according to the system of the alphabet, a combination of sounds is represented by a combination of letters, and according to the system [p. 278] of the generation of ideas, complex qualities, complexes of absolute and relative qualities, are represented by complexes of sensations and of elementary relations.

Setting out from so many mistaken principles, it was inevitable to stumble upon the impossibility of complex notions derived from simple sensations; and there was no other expedient for avoiding it than to make sensation and perception entirely distinct: another hypothesis, not only voluntary, but belied by our own consciousness. Mine, at least, tells me that in the perception of visual or tactile extension there enter, besides the conceptions of succession, internal sensations of efforts associated with affections of the external senses; in the perception of hardness or softness, internal sensations of the greater or smaller efforts we make to dislocate the tactile molecules, associated with perceptions of the constancy or alteration of figure; and so of the other complex qualities.

Conceiving them in this manner, the difficulty disappears, and the resemblance which we found ourselves forced to conceive between complex qualities and ideas is perfectly explained, without the most unhappy expedient to which the illustrious head of the Scottish school has recourse for the purpose. Material relations cannot but resemble the relations conceived by the understanding. The resemblance or succession between two sensations is a true image of the resemblance or succession between the corporeal actions which the sensations represent to us. Reid supposes that sensation is a mere sign, by virtue of which there arises in us, by a special instinct, a notion which is not resolved into it, nor has resemblance to it. But if sensation were no more than a sign of perception, nature, in giving us the sign at the same time that she presents to us the thing signified, would have taken a superfluous trouble. Was it not enough that the presence of bodies should immediately produce the perceptions, without the sterile intermediary of sensation, which enters for nothing into them? It is not thus, for example, that visual affections become signs of [p. 279] tactile affections. In translating the former into the latter, we supply the one by the other. Nature, as Reid himself observes, is economical in her works, and employs no particular instinct to give us that knowledge which we can easily acquire by experience, according to the general laws of the human constitution. How much less conformable to this economy of nature is the intervention of a sign, at the very moment when the thing signified is placed before us!

[PDF 296]

Analysis of the acts of memory.

Memory is a faculty of the mind.—Renewal of perceptions.—Morality and beauty in recollections.—Anamnesis.—Memory as a system of signs.— Resemblance is the foundation of the anamnesis equivalent to perception.— Anamnesis in every perception of anteriority.—Anamnesis in all the acts of thought.—Dugald Stewart’s doctrine on the relation of anteriority.

In the preceding chapters I have treated of ideas, considering them only as aggregates of renewed perceptions, but without inquiring into the manner in which this renewal is effected, or into the laws according to which ideas succeed one another and succeed perceptions: matters of sufficient importance to deserve separate treatment.

All ideas are ultimately resolved into renewed perceptions, and the faculty of renewing perceptions is called memory. It is true that the soul renews not only actual perceptions but ideas: not only, for example, the actual perceptions of the tree we saw yesterday, but the idea of a tree we have never seen and know only because we have heard or read its description. But the idea of this second tree is composed, no less than that of the first, of renewed perceptions. The whole difference consists in this, that the first set of perceptions was given to us immediately by the external world acting upon our senses, and the second we have formed ourselves, culling them from the vast store which memory has already accumulated.

[p. 281]

This renewal, it seems to me, may be understood literally; for memory does indeed make perceptions live again, though with more or less vigor and completeness. And sometimes it even happens that, an actual perception or an idea being renewed, an emotion or affection is renewed with it, and the soul again exerts that mysterious influence from which proceeds the organic modification that originally accompanied the perception or the idea. Thus the recollection of a loathsome object excites nausea, and the recollection of a great danger, that emotion of terror and shuddering which the danger itself produced in us when we found ourselves in it.

The perceptions renewed by memory will be, cæteris paribus, so much the more vivid the greater the attention the soul gives to them; and their fidelity, that is, their resemblance to the original perceptions, will likewise be, cæteris paribus, so much the greater the greater the attention the soul has given to these. I say cæteris paribus, because the representations of memory will in general be so much the more vivid the less time has intervened between the actual perceptions and the recollections, as if the power of reviving past affections diminished with time, and their coloring, so to speak, gradually paled and faded away. There are, nevertheless, various circumstances which modify this general law.

We recall, for example, the perceptions of childhood and youth much more vividly than those of mature age. The pastimes and affections of youth are painted in the memory of the old man with a clearness and energy which the reproduction of the events and affairs in which he figured a few years, or perhaps a few days, before does not possess. But the vividness of renewed perceptions will rarely be so great that the soul confounds them with original perceptions; unless in certain abnormal states in which a predominant idea takes possession of the whole soul, and even makes it deaf to the impressions with which the external world shakes the organs.

To me, certainly, it seems that renewed perceptions differ from actual ones only in degree of vividness, and that when, for example, I represent to myself the face of a friend [p. 282] or the façade of a building, the sensations I formerly experienced in the presence of these objects are repeated, somewhat confused and deadened. We recall a sentence or a tune that we know by heart, and we seem to repeat it letter by letter and note by note, without needing so much as to move the lips. A skilful portrait painter recalls the features of a person so distinctly that he can transfer them from his mind to the canvas almost as easily as if he had the original before his eyes. And if, on seeing a painting, we find that it resembles an object which is not before us, is it not because we compare the recollected sensations with the actual ones, in the same way as we compare the actual sensations produced by the painted canvas with those produced by the original, when we have both before our eyes? How is it possible to explain these facts, except by supposing that the acts of memory really renew, to a certain extent, past perceptions?

To what degree the pleasure or pain which originally accompanied perceptions or ideas is renewed with them is a matter on which it would not be easy for us to add anything new to the observations that any man may have made in himself. In general, it is not mere perceptions, but the complex states which we have called emotions, that, when renewed by memory, reproduce the pleasures and pains which originally accompanied them. He who received a wound will recall the physical pain, proceeding from the organic lesion alone, and the moral pain arising from the injury: two elements of so different a nature that they bear no proportion to one another. The recollection of the physical pain will be vivid enough for us to compare it with other pains, and to perceive in this comparison resemblance or difference and relations of more and less; and yet it will perhaps produce not the slightest physical discomfort. On the contrary, the recollection of the injury may have force enough to awaken along with it the emotion of anger, with some of the organic modifications which usually accompany that passion.

Agreeable sensations, renewed by memory, usually come accompanied by a certain degree of pleasure, unless [p. 283] they are embittered by other emotions associated with them, such as those produced by the idea of divine wrath, of the hatred or contempt of the world, and the reprobation of our own conscience, if the pleasure we recall was obtained by unlawful means. The emotions excited by our religious and moral ideas then trouble, so to speak, the pleasure of recollections, and may perhaps predominate over it to the point of stifling it. The same will happen when with the recollection of past happiness the idea of our present misery is associated. We then repeat with Francesca da Rimini: “Nessun maggior dolore che ricordarsi del tempo felice nella miseria. . . .!” [There is no greater sorrow than to recall a happy time in misery] The emotions produced by this comparison take away all its charms from the memory of past joys and turn them into piercing thorns, above all when the transition has been the effect of crime or of a blameworthy imprudence. But where the beneficence of the Creator and His wisdom as author of the moral laws shine forth most is in the feeling of pleasure which the recollection of past thoughts sometimes produces; above all when the soul bears witness to itself of the fortitude with which we have borne fortuitous ills, and of the manly efforts we put forth to triumph over them. How exquisite the inward satisfaction of him who recalls the labors undergone in the discharge of a duty or in the disinterested defense of a just cause! Memory is the instrument of the rewarding or avenging conscience; it is for the just man a fountain of satisfactions and consolations; it is a baleful torch, by whose light the guilty soul beholds the foulness and the pernicious consequences of its acts, without its being possible for it, do what it may, to put it away from itself, or to stifle the bitter emotions with which this spectacle torments it.

In the acts of memory we must distinguish various elements: the first is constituted by the renewed perceptions; the second, the intuition or act of consciousness which perceives them, and the others consist in a judgment which recognizes the renewed perceptions as such, distinguishing them from those which are wont to be excited by present objects.

As it is necessary to give a particular name to the pure renewed perception [p. 284] in order to distinguish it from the other elements which enter with it into the constitution of the acts of memory, I shall be permitted to call it anamnesis, a word which in Greek signifies the same as recollection, but to which we may give, in our language, where it has never been in use, a conventional meaning. Anamnesis, in the sense in which I use it, is not all that which forms the thought when we remember or imagine something, but merely the renewed perception, which, separated from the peculiar judgments that accompanied it, occasioned by the presence of the object, serves as the matter or substance of recollection. Anamneses in this sense are not precisely recollections, but integral parts of recollections, of imaginations, and of every kind of ideas.

Anamnesis is a sign, a representative affection, which performs the office of the original affection whose image it is, and which has disappeared from the soul, leaving anamnesis in its place. But the soul, which in the acts of memory has only this sign present, ordinarily thinks only of the thing signified; that is, of the object of the original affection.

All systems of signs are founded upon memory, and memory itself is a system of signs. When we employ the idea of the individual as representative of the class, the idea of a part as representative of the whole, the idea of a name as representative of a thing, we do no more than substitute for certain signs others, which are like ciphers or abbreviations of the former. What an artificial fabric is that of thought! We have ideas which are employed as signs of other ideas; the class, so varied and numerous, of sensations forms an immense collection of signs which symbolize the qualities of matter; and all the acts of memory, and consequently of imagination and of reasoning, are composed of anamneses, which replace and represent actual affections. And as this last system is the foundation of the others, it was necessary that the signs of which it consists should be the most obvious and natural of all.

But although the soul, when it exercises memory, does not ordinarily think of the signs, sometimes the contrary happens. The [p. 285] first way of contemplating things past is that which I should express by saying: at daybreak there were red clouds. In such a case the soul would seem to have distant realities before its sight. And if, instead of expressing myself thus, I were to say: I saw red clouds at daybreak, I should not then picture to myself the object in itself, but in the original perception, as in a distant painting. On the other hand, when I say: I remember that there were, or that I saw, red clouds, I fix my sight on the anamnesis, as on a painted canvas which I am viewing close at hand. But the picture which in the first of these two expressions, I remember that there were red clouds, represents to me distant real objects, seems to me in the second, I remember that I saw red clouds, a faded copy of another painting in which real objects were represented to me as present. But all these ways of speaking are used as equivalents, or as purely verbal shades of meaning, to which the soul pays no attention. In all of them the object of the anamnesis is identified with the object of the original perception.

Could not the soul experience the anamnesis without the idea of such an identity occurring to it, or in other terms, without conceiving any relation between this new modification of itself and another, earlier one? Whence comes it that the soul does not believe it has in the anamnesis an actual perception, but the representation of a perception which it does not now have and which the anamnesis reproduces for it, though in an incomplete, deadened and confused manner?

The soul recognizes in its new mode of being a copy of another, earlier modification, just as in a corporeal object situated at a certain distance we recognize the same man, the same tree, the same house which stood a few paces from us and which we could reach with the hand. As the confusion and indistinctness of vision suggests the idea of the object’s being distant, so the indistinctness and confusion of the anamnesis produces the idea of the perception’s not being actual. There is, however, a considerable difference in the two cases. When I recognize in a distant tree the same tree in whose shade I sat, I compare the tree which I see with the tree which I remember. But when I believe I see in the anamnesis the [p. 286] representation of a thing of which I formerly had, and no longer have, an actual perception, it is manifest that I cannot compare the anamnesis with the perception, because the perception no longer exists except in the anamnesis itself, and comparison supposes that the objects on which it turns are at the same time present to the soul.

The anamnesis is a copy of the perception; a copy ordinarily confused, abridged, and sometimes imperfect and faulty. The abbreviations and errata of this copy make it happen at times that when we believe we remember an object, when, for example, on seeing a man we judge him to be the same whom we saw yesterday on the promenade, or last week in the country, we are deceived or waver in this judgment. But regularly this is not the case with objects of which we have a tolerable knowledge. We then compare the copy with the original, and from the degree of resemblance between the two we infer that the object is one and the same. Reading both, if I may be allowed to return to this simile, we find in them one and the same meaning.

Admitting, then, as an indisputable fact, that in the recognition of an object the anamnesis coexists with the actual perception of which it is the image, are we not authorized to believe that this same coexistence takes place in the original perception of the object, whenever this lasts some time? Let us suppose that a second suffices for the perception of an object to leave in the soul that impression, whatever it may be, from which proceeds the faculty of renewing it. If the perception lasts but a single second, the anamnesis will succeed it, and this may occupy the mind vividly, provided that the perceptions or recollections of other objects do not call for attention more imperiously. If the actual perception lasts one second longer, the anamnesis already formed will coexist with it and become more vivid and distinct. The same will happen with more reason in the third second, in the fourth, and in the whole space of time during which we suppose the actual perception to be prolonged. The soul will thus be affected in two different ways by one and the same object, and will know it by means of these two kinds of affections. The anamnesis will in this way become an equivalent [p. 287] of the actual perception, will signify the same as it, and will take its place whenever, in the series, whether fortuitous or voluntary, of our ideas, the soul returns to think of the object.

It seems clear to me that every perception somewhat prolonged coexists with its own anamnesis. At first sight these two kinds of affections will appear incompatible. To say that we experience at one time the perception and the anamnesis, is it not to say that we remember what we have present? But the incompatibility is apparent, not real. The word anamnesis suggests the idea of the absence of the object, because when we have it present and know it by means of vivid and distinct affections, it is not natural that we should take notice of those abbreviated signs with which memory works, equivalent to actual affections, but comparatively weak and confused, which nature has destined to supply their place, and which begin to have an effective value only from the time that they fail us. It is impossible to explain, without this coexistence, the recognition of an object previously perceived. Admitting it, then, in one case, what reason is there for not giving it place in the other? In reality, a prolonged perception is a series of perceptions, and all of them, except that which forms the first term of the series, are so many recognitions.

But the soul, it will be said, does not observe in itself this duplication of affections, this coexistence of the original and the copy. We might answer that we are not accustomed to pay attention to those affections of the soul which do not call us, either by their novelty, or by the relation they have with our inclinations and desires; and that the anamnesis, while the perception lasts, says nothing to the soul which the perception does not say to it at the same time, and in a much more expressive manner. But, in reality, we perceive and observe the nascent anamneses which coexist with the original perceptions. Let us suppose that an object which we perceive for the first time varies in its qualities, that it passes, for example, from the color white to red: how do we perceive the alteration of the color? By comparing the new actual perception [p. 288] with the anamnesis of the preceding perception. And if the preceding perception has left an anamnesis when it is followed by a different perception, it is necessary to admit that it has left one also when it is followed by a similar perception, or in other terms, when it remains similar to itself. If in the first case we know the alteration by the dissonance, so to speak, between the perception and the anamnesis, in the second we know the constancy by the harmony between these two kinds of affections.

Nature, in destining anamneses to replace perceptions, wished to bind them to the latter as promptly and as intimately as possible. Not content with having given us these images of the primitive modes of the soul, she placed them, in the very act of forming them, beside their originals, that the resemblance might be more obvious and the connection closer; so that the mind might believe it contemplated one and the same object, whether it perceived it actually or memory represented it.

This, however, would not suffice for our referring the anamnesis to the very object of the original perception, if in the latter we did not give the object a mark of individuality by virtue of its relations with other objects. The man whom I saw yesterday on the promenade presented himself to me under a certain relation of place, of time, and of various other circumstances, which serve us to distinguish him from other men and from any other objects, and give a mark of individuality to the original perception and to its object. By attaching these characters to the anamnesis, we give the recollected object the same relations and clothe it with the same particulars as before, and the concept of identity between the object we perceived yesterday and that which we recollect now arises spontaneously.

In resemblance consists the equivalence of the anamnesis to the perception; but this resemblance is weak: the anamnesis, as has been said before, is an imperfect copy in which the coloring is pale and the details confused. If we have experienced an original affection, A, and afterwards experience another original affection, B, of the same kind, but less strong and vivid, memory, in comparing the anamnesis of [p. 289] A with the actual perception of B, will pronounce that B is not entirely A; that the heat, for example, experienced yesterday and recollected now, was more intense than the heat which we experience now. And yet the anamnesis A is an affection much weaker than the actual perception B. Were the relation of intensity which we conceive between the two heats the contrary, the heat represented by B would seem to us stronger than the heat represented by A, not with the whole excess of intensity which there would really be between the actual perception B and the anamnesis A, but with a considerably smaller excess. And if the heats appeared to us of equal intensity, we should judge them such, notwithstanding the great difference which in this respect there must always be between an anamnesis and an actual affection. Although these judgments are not entirely exact, the error is confined within tolerably narrow limits when no great time has intervened between the anamnesis and the perception. It is clear, then, that in comparisons of this kind the natural weakness of the anamnesis is taken into account; just as in the comparisons of the tactile magnitudes of visible objects the apparent diminution of magnitude produced by distance is taken into account.

Let us now suppose a series of successive affections, A, B, C, D, etc., which leave the anamneses a, b, c, d, etc. The first affection A being ended, we perceive anteriority between a and B: anteriority purely objective, because subjectively, that is, referred to the soul which experiences it, a and b coexist. The affection B being ended, there succeed it the anamneses a and b, accompanied, by virtue of the laws of memory, by the idea of the relation of anteriority between a and b, and we perceive another relation of the same kind between b and C. The affection C being ended, there succeed it the anamneses a, b, c, accompanied, by virtue of the laws of memory, by the ideas of the relations of anteriority between a and b, b and c, and we perceive another similar relation between c and D; and so on successively. In this manner memory represents to us the succession of our spiritual modes, that of things past, and time. Just as between two affections we perceive something elemental, indefinable,

## PHILOS.    19

[p. 290]

which makes us say: this is like that, a perception from which are derived all our ideas of qualities, so between two affections a and B, of which a is a deadened and confused copy of a preceding affection A, and B is a vivid and distinct actual affection, we perceive something to which we give the name of anteriority, if we consider it in A, and of posteriority if we consider it in B; and this perception, from which are derived all our ideas of duration and time, as of extension and space, is no less simple, nor more susceptible of being explained and defined, than that of resemblance.

I am inclined to believe that the perception of anteriority always supposes an actual affection and an anamnesis; that two recollected affections are not represented to us as successive, except because we recollect together the relation perceived between them, when one was actual and the other renewed; and that when this is not the case, the knowledge of the succession of things past is not perceptive, but deductive or communicated. The same, of course, is to be understood of the relation of posteriority, which is the same as that of anteriority under another aspect; and as to the relation of coexistence, I believe that we always perceive it between two actual affections: that two recollected affections are not represented to us as coexistent, except because we recollect at the same time the relation of coexistence which was perceived between them, when they were actual; and that in other cases the knowledge of the coexistence of things past is not acquired by perception, but by reasoning or testimony.

All the acts of thought, whether they turn upon real objects or upon objects which we hold to be imaginary; upon those which we know by our own observations or reasonings, or upon those of which we have only notice through the reports of others; upon the past, the present or the future; consist of perceptions or of anamneses or of both at once, and all that is not perception is anamnesis. When we represent to ourselves the summit of the Caucasus or of Chimborazo, the waters and banks of the Vistula or of the Marañon, which we have never visited, we work no less with anamneses [p. 291] than when we call to mind the church or the promenade where we were yesterday. The ideas which we form of objects that we have never perceived are composed of those same materials which perceptions furnish us; the soul then does nothing else than combine them in a new way, substitute for the relations formerly suggested by them other new ones, and represent to itself by means of them objects different from those which originally produced them.

The judgments we form concerning the past, present or future existence of the objects we imagine are deductive or communicated; and it is even most usual for the testimony of others to be combined with our own deductions. We know that the sun will rise or set tomorrow at such an hour, because we so infer it from the laws which this luminary observes in its apparent periodic movements; and when we represent to ourselves its future rising or setting, we substitute, in the anamneses with which we make these representations, some relations for others. We know of the past existence of Rome, because an infinity of historians and travelers have spoken to us of Rome; from which we necessarily infer the anteriority, or at least the coexistence, of Rome with respect to the histories and travels in which it is spoken of; and we judge that Rome exists at present, because we infer it from the preceding judgment, and from the absence of any testimony that has made us aware that that city no longer exists. In short, when we represent to ourselves fictitious objects, when the imagination of poets creates enchanted gardens, battles or loves, we form judgments which warn us continually, and perhaps importunately, of the fallacy of the objects that occupy the soul. Reason then tells us that the objects we imagine are not and have never been perceived in the manner in which our imagination paints them to us; and that if there were rational or sentient creatures in the place and time, whatever they may be, in which fancy sets them, they would not on that account have had perceptions corresponding to our imaginations; because we have not formed these by deducing some judgments from others, or by appropriating the observations of other minds, transmitted by language, but by combining and [p. 292] adding anamneses at the will of another’s imagination. From the free and capricious manner in which the imagination then acts, we infer the non-existence of the imagined objects.

We must distinguish the judgment of anteriority which recognizes the anamnesis as such, and forms an essential part of all the acts of memory, from those accessory judgments which we form concerning the determinate anteriority, posteriority or coexistence, and the real or imaginary, certain, probable or doubtful being, of the objects we represent to ourselves by combining anamneses: judgments which, as we have said, are either due to our own reasonings, or have been derived by us from other minds, by means of language.

Dugald Stewart supposes that “the remembrance of a past event is not a simple act of the mind; but that the mind first forms a conception of the event, then judges from circumstances, of the period of time to which it is to be referred,” a supposition which appears to him “agreeable to fact;” “for if we have,” he says, “the power . . . of conceiving a past event without any reference to time, it follows, that there is nothing in the ideas or notions which memory presents to us, which is necessarily accompanied with a belief of past existence, in a way analogous to that in which our perceptions are accompanied with a belief of the present existence of their objects; and therefore, that the reference of the event to the particular period at which it happened, is a judgment founded on concomitant circumstances.”

It is evident that the judgment I make of the more or less determinate epoch of a past event, e.g., my voyage to England, does not arise from the elemental anamneses of which the mental representation of this fact by itself consists, since it is founded on a multitude of other facts which, according to the information memory gives me, preceded, accompanied and followed it. But from this judgment’s being accessory it does not follow that that is so too which makes me consider the anamnesis as a perception which was and is no more; and that, as the illustrious philosopher cited says, there is nothing in memory which is necessarily accompanied with the judgment of anterior existence. On the contrary, to refer a past fact to a certain particular epoch supposes [p. 293] that we have already formed a scale of time, and this supposes that we have perceived elemental relations of anteriority. If we had not had the immediate perceptions which we express by saying this is before and that after, we should never have arrived at forming an idea of the duration of things, or of time. But should we have perceived the elemental relations of anteriority, if these did not arise spontaneously from the anamneses? Memory is not memory, except because we are capable of perceiving elemental relations of anteriority between the recollected perceptions and the actual ones.

If Dugald Stewart has meant that the notion of anteriority may be separated from the anamnesis which originally produced it, we agree; for it is evident that in my ideas of imaginary objects, or of objects known only by our reasonings or through the reports of others, we combine anamneses, stripping them of the relations of time which originally accompanied them and substituting for these relations others, which may be entirely different: thus, for the relation of past time we may substitute that of a future epoch. But if Dugald Stewart has meant that in its origin the concept of anteriority does not arise from the anamnesis necessarily, by virtue of one of the primordial laws of our intellectual constitution, his opinion is inadmissible. The anamnesis suggests of itself the concept of anteriority, but we are allowed to make use of it for the representation of past, present or future objects, or of imaginary objects, substituting for the fundamental judgment various others according to circumstances.

To say that we owe to the anamneses our first notions of time is to say in other terms that if we had not had anamneses, and if these had not excited relations of succession, the idea of present time could not have occurred to us either, when we experience actual perceptions. Our actual perceptions are not, then, necessarily accompanied by the judgment of present existence. We had first actual perceptions which, being recollected, and before we had had recollections and served the apprenticeship of memory, we could not form the idea of time. How, then, [p. 294] was it possible for our first actual perceptions to give rise to the judgment of present existence?

As from the coexistence of the anamneses of some objects with the actual perceptions of others there arose spontaneously the simple relation of succession, so from the coexistence of some actual perceptions with others there arose spontaneously the simple relation of coexistence. By comparing perceptions with recollections, we were able to call present that which we knew by actual perception; past, that which we knew by anamnesis; and future, that which seemed to us to have with the present the same relation that we conceive between the present and the past. From the time we made this distinction, actual perceptions suggested to us the judgment of present existence, which we extended to all that which, by means of reasoning or by the testimony of other men, we judged to coexist with our actual perceptions. And this fixed point being established, we extended the compass of the past to all that which, according to the reports of memory or the deductions of reasoning or the communications of other minds, we believed anterior to this point, and the compass of the future to all that which we conceived posterior to it.

Anterior, posterior, coexistent, express simple relations, objects of immediate perceptions. Past, present, future, presuppose the general notion of time, which we form by aggregating elemental relations of succession.

Dugald Stewart holds it as indubitable that we are endowed with the faculty of representing to ourselves a past event without referring it to any epoch: a thing which seems to me incomprehensible, if every epoch is meant, excluding even the most indefinite and vague. Although the precise epoch of the destruction of Jerusalem be not fixed, I do not think it possible for us to represent this event without the idea of an indefinite epoch anterior to the present moment occurring to the soul; and this necessity is still greater when we represent to ourselves a fact of which we have had actual perceptions, because then the concatenation of the one with the others determines with more or less precision the epoch of the fact.

[p. 295]

It sometimes happens that we represent to ourselves the past, the future, the imaginary, with a degree of vividness which approaches that of actual perceptions. We attend so much the less to the judgment of non-actuality, the more vivid the mental representation is; yet without this judgment’s being on that account wholly effaced, unless we dream or find ourselves in a state of frenzy like that of Don Quixote, when he took the little figures of Master Peter’s puppet-show for real personages. The non-actuality which we attribute to the anamnesis supposes that we distinguish it from actual perceptions. When, therefore, this difference ceases to exist, because the vividness of the mental representations is as great as that of actual perceptions, or when through some hindrance of the intellectual functions we are not capable of perceiving it, though it exist, it is not strange that the element of non-actuality should disappear altogether, as happens in dreams and in deliriums.

[PDF 312]

On the suggestion of recollections.

Two causes of the suggestion of recollections.—Influence of the association of ideas on language.—Language according to Dr. Reid.—Artificial signs and natural signs.—Language is not a human invention.—Elements of language. —Artificial signs.—Aptitudes of the human voice.—Writing is a system of artificial signs.—Painting as the primitive art of writing.—Mimetic characters and tropic characters.—Influence of language on ideographic writing.— Chinese writing.—Cyriologic characters.—Structure of words.—Phonetic signs.—Opposition or contrast as a cause of association of ideas, according to Dr. Brown.—Contrary qualities relate to objects of one and the same kind. —There are no other principles of association of ideas than the two causes of suggestion already stated.—Final verification.

Recollections do not arise in the soul by chance. Present perceptions suggest recollections, and some recollections suggest others, by virtue of certain connections which may, in my opinion, be reduced to two: the resemblance of objects, and the simultaneity or coexistence of their perceptions or ideas.

An object brings to our memory other objects like it. On seeing a lake, the idea of the sea occurs to me; in thinking of a battle, we pass naturally to thinking of other feats of arms. It happens also that if two or more perceptions or ideas have been united in our mind, one of them renews the others for us. The sea, for example, makes me think of ships; ships, of commerce; commerce suggests to me the idea of England; England reminds me of Nelson; Nelson, the [p. 297] battle of Trafalgar; the battle of Trafalgar, Spain; and so on in succession. There is no perception, no recollection or imagination, that does not awaken a throng of ideas linked together, now by the tie of resemblance, now by that of simultaneity; but among them all we give our attention only to those which most concern us by their relation to our needs, our passions, our studies, our tastes. The sea, for example, suggests a thousand diverse ideas which resemble it, with which it has coexisted in our mind; and of these the philosopher will fix perhaps upon the causes of the ebb and flow; the religious and contemplative man upon the grandeur of the works of the Creator, among which the sea is one of the most conspicuous to our eyes; one will recall a naval battle, another a shipwreck; a merchant will remember the expeditions he has dispatched overseas, and a mother will think of the absent son who crossed the ocean to visit distant regions.

The influence of these two causes of association shows itself plainly in all systems of signs and particularly in speech. An object B recalls its like A; this recalls to us its name, the idea of which has coexisted with that of the object A in the soul; we then apply that name to the object B; the same happens with the objects C, D, E, which we contemplate in succession; and by virtue of the resemblances observed among them and of the laws of association of the memory, the name of the individual A comes to be a general denomination which comprehends them all. In this way is formed the nominal classification of objects, the basis of the significant systems which we call idioms or languages.

“By language I understand,” says Professor Reid, “all those signs which mankind use in order to communicate to others their thoughts and intentions, their purposes and desires. And such signs may be conceived to be of two kinds: First, such as have no meaning but what is affixed to them by some express or tacit compact or agreement among those who use them; these are called artificial signs: Secondly, such as, previous to all compact or agreement, have a meaning which every man understands by [p. 298] the principles of his nature; these are called natural; and the same denominations are applied to language, according to the kinds of signs of which it consists.

“I think it is demonstrable that, if mankind had not first had a natural language, all the ingenuity and reason in the world could never have arrived at the invention of an artificial one. For this supposes a certain compact, by virtue of which an arbitrary meaning is affixed to each sign. There must, therefore, have been compacts before all artificial language. But what compact can be conceived among men except by means of signs or some language? There must, then, have been previously a natural language, in order that the artificial might be formed.

“Had language in general been a human invention, as much as writing or printing, we should find somewhere in the world nations as mute as the brutes. But what do I say, brutes? Even these have natural signs by which they express their own thoughts, affections, and desires; and understand those of others. A chick, as soon as hatched, understands the different sounds whereby its dam calls it to food, or gives the alarm of danger. A dog or a horse understands, by nature, when the human voice caresses, and when it threatens him.

“The elements of this natural language of mankind, or the signs that are naturally expressive of our thoughts and affections, may, I think, be reduced to three kinds: modulations of the voice, features, and gestures. By means of these, two men who did not speak the same artificial language could communicate their thoughts, ask and refuse, affirm and deny, threaten and supplicate, traffic, enter into covenants and alliances: which it would be easy to confirm by facts of undoubted credit.”

In natural language the influence of the two laws of association of ideas is no less manifest than in the others. A particular affection, anger, for example, produces a particular intonation of the voice; this intonation becomes the sign of that affection, because the idea of anger and the idea of that intonation [p. 299] of the voice have coexisted in the soul, and consequently the one of them naturally recalls the other. We stretch out our hands to seize or grasp the bodies of which we have need or desire; the idea of this gesture coexists, then, often with the idea of need or desire, and the stretching out of the hands becomes, consequently, a sign of desire, of petition, of entreaty.

It is not necessary to imagine that men devoted themselves deliberately to the study of artificial signs and established them by a formal convention, assigning to each object an absolutely arbitrary sign. Men passed by imperceptible degrees from the idiom of nature to the conventional, and found themselves speaking an artificial language without knowing it, as Mr. Jourdain talked prose.

This step was taken without difficulty by means of the two laws mentioned. What more obvious way of indicating any object that has a voice or is capable of emitting a discernible sound, than to imitate that voice or sound with our own? Hence arose signs which, although not so rigorously natural as the accents, countenances, and gestures with which needs and passions are expressed, could be understood without a formal convention. A murmur, a roar, by means of various modifications and accompanied by various countenances and gestures, would denote the tempest, the thunder, the sea, the torrent, the gentle brook, a tiger, a bull, an angry man, the precipitate descent of a body, etc. One sound suggested the idea of another similar sound, and this second suggested that of the object which was distinguished by it, that is, another idea which had coexisted with its own. If in the infancy of languages the meaning of the imitative signs was ever obscure or equivocal, the natural ones would come to serve them as interpreters. Those first semi-artificial signs, difficult to the voice and disagreeable to the ear, would be softened gradually by the suppression of some elements and the addition of others, and would little by little come to form combinations of vocal and articulate sounds. But this metamorphosis, however slow, supposes that some sounds were rejected and others admitted.
