There was, then, [p. 300] a kind of choice, which, made by chance by one individual and adopted by others, constituted a tacit compact, in the preliminaries of which nature served as mediator. It is probable that a great number of signs were formed in this way, and that the analogies between sounds and the other qualities suggested others, in proportion as we came to need them.(a)

A like procedure led to writing. If the invention of the alphabet, if the idea of decomposing all the words of a language into a small number of elements, giving to each element a sign, thus fixing the most fugitive of the accidents of matter and chaining thought itself, furnishing every man with means of communicating with all the points of the globe and with all the generations that are to succeed him: if this grand idea could have been conceived and carried out by one man, what glory would have seemed to us proportioned to the merit of such a discovery, whether we weigh the importance of the object or appreciate the effort of ingenuity necessary to accomplish it? But in the age that preceded writing, less than in any other, was it possible that there should have been an understanding capable of so sublime a reach. Writing could be only the result of a multitude of small gradual inventions, to which a great number of centuries, and probably of nations, contributed, and which will not be altogether complete until we possess a perfect alphabet, such as no nation has, or perhaps ever had.

Painting was probably the point from which men set out

(a) The human voice seems to have been purposely destined as the instrument of

a system of artificial signs. Its advantages consist: 1.º in the infinite variety of modulations of which it is susceptible; 2.º in the brevity and ease of the movements with which we can produce it; 3.º in being equally perceptible in light and in darkness; 4.º in not being easily intercepted. Gestures would be of no use in a dark room; the interposition of an object between the gesticulators would produce the same effect. [p. 301] in search of this marvelous art. The necessity of fixing oral traditions, so easily altered and lost, led to an appeal to painting from a very early time. Employed as a means of instruction and as a monumental art, it was natural that its language should be perfected and spiritualized, giving less part in it to the eyes and more to the understanding. It is rarely within the reach of painting to confine to determinate persons and motives, times and places, the actions which it puts before the sight. A combat transferred to canvas will show the arms and dress of the combatants, at most their age and some trait of national physiognomy; but it will hardly make known who the individuals were, what cause they upheld or opposed, or the precise place and time of the event: circumstances often important. Sometimes, nevertheless, painting might find means of indicating with more or less clearness even these particulars. A pyramid, a mountain or tower of a certain form, the confluence of rivers, any other local feature capable of being presented to the sight, would have supplied an indication as opportune as it was intelligible. Was it a question of individualizing a country? Its natural or industrial productions, or some notable physical feature, skillfully introduced, would have been made understood without trouble. The seasons and the hours furnish an infinity of characters of which all painters have availed themselves. And as in pictures destined for instruction neither regularity of design, nor beauty of coloring, nor any other of the qualities which constitute the excellence of a painting destined only to recreate the imagination was to be sought, the principal figures, and above all the accessory indications, would be reduced to the number of strokes and lines absolutely necessary to awaken the ideas of the objects. To indicate water, for example, use would be made of a horizontal line gently undulating; fire might be represented by another undulating line, but vertical; a pyramid, by a simple triangle; and so of the other objects. And as these alterations in the forms were not to be introduced all at once, their signification could easily be retained and transmitted from one age to another, [p. 302] Here we have arrived at the first epoch of the transformation of painting into writing. While the principal part of the picture preserves the character of a true painting, another part of the objects which the artist exhibits is reduced to simple outlines, presenting only a remote likeness to their originals. These first letters, if we may use so early this name, were, therefore, to a certain extent mimetic or imitative: signs which recalled objects by the resemblance they bore to them.

It is easy to conceive that the number of mimetic characters would go on continually increasing, and the accessory indications gaining ground upon the purely pictorial part. After these signs, which we may call natural, inasmuch as they were imitative of the objects they represented, came others, in which something more conventional and arbitrary began already to appear, and in which, taking for model the figurative procedure of speech, men conceived the idea of representing an object by its concomitant, the whole by the part, the end by the means, the thing contained by the container, the abstract by the concrete; in a word, the tropes of ordinary language were transferred to painting. A cradle, for example, would mean birth; a sepulchral urn, death; a flower, spring; an ear of corn, summer; a crown, royal dignity; a censer, the priesthood; a ring, marriage; a tongue, speech; a footprint of the human foot, the road: as in some Mexican hieroglyphics, an arrow, swiftness; the laurel, victory, and the olive peace: as in the emblematic representations of the Romans and of modern nations. These characters are called tropic; and when the analogy between the sign and the thing signified was obscure, and known only to those who were initiated into the secrets of the art, there was formed the enigmatic writing, reserved to the learned or to the priests. Thus the circumference of the circle was an emblem of eternity, because it has neither beginning nor end.

These signs awakened at first the ideas of certain objects, by means of the relation of resemblance which they bore to them. A few strokes thus represented the palm or the olive. But the idea of this object would serve only to introduce another [p. 303] idea that had coexisted with it in the understanding. The palm which crowned the victor became in this way a sign of victory. The olive, the first of trees, as Columella calls it, probably denoted agriculture and the arts of peace.

The introduction of tropic signs marks the second epoch of writing. The enigmatic signs, which differed from these only in that the resemblance to the thing signified was remote and obscure, may be considered as a sort of cipher employed by those who had an interest in concealing certain kinds of knowledge, either to profit by their exclusive possession, or to give importance and win respect, by means of this mysterious apparatus, for what, if divulged, would fall into contempt.

As the tropic characters multiplied, it became necessary that certain conventional rules should be established for their explanation and for the representation of complex ideas; and the understanding of them became more and more difficult. Preliminary instruction, then, came to be necessary, both to comprehend the meaning of these characters and to express ideas in them; in other terms, there was now an art of reading and writing. But that writing differed notably from ours. The former represented ideas immediately; ours indicates the sounds which we use to declare them in speaking, and is properly a system of signs in which another system of the same kind is translated.

It is natural that language should exercise a certain influence upon ideographic writing. The analysis of thought by means of speech having once been made by men, it could not fail to serve as the basis of the new idiom destined to speak to the eyes as the other to the ear. The grammar of both, if one may say so, must have been in great part the same, and the translation of the one into the other obvious and easy. It was possible, however, that the optical idiom, cultivated through a long series of centuries and applied particularly to the sciences, should acquire an ideographic literature, and not only be considerably enriched in signs, but even become susceptible of beauties and elegances of which we cannot form a conception. Who can deny [p. 304] that there may be a kind of visual poetry? The poetry we know is nothing more than the art of exciting agreeable series of ideas by means of words. Why may there not be an art which makes use of other kinds of signs to excite thoughts and fancies which delight and enchant us? The delicacy or energy with which the conceptions of a great poet would be made known in this kind of composition by means of lines, strokes, and colors might at times be capable of being introduced into the vulgar language, in the way that we often find it difficult, if not impossible, to render in one language the grace, sublimity, or tenderness of the passages we admire in another.

As the signs are more and more simplified, as naturally happens when frequent use is made of them, the natural or tropic resemblance which they must at first have had with objects comes in the end to be lost: third epoch. Such is the state in which Chinese writing now is. The connection between the ideas and the characters appears altogether artificial.

But however great the perfection to which we suppose this system of signs to have been carried, it still lacks the indication of proper names, without which, how would it have been possible for the reader in the greater part of cases to identify the individuals symbolized in this language with the individuals represented by those names in the spoken tongue? It was necessary, then, to find a way of expressing the material sounds of speech; and as in our writing sounds suggest ideas, it was natural that in the symbolic writing which preceded it ideas should suggest sounds. If a proper name was significant of a general idea, or could be resolved into two or more parts each of which was so, the symbolic expression of these ideas could serve to indicate the material composition of that name. Such was the device adopted in the Mexican hieroglyphics. For example, to mention the king Ilhuicamina, whose name is divided into two words, face and water, the painter traced the image of a head and the symbol of water. Axajacatl means arrow that breaks the sky: the king so called was represented by the signs corresponding to these ideas. The city of Macuilxochtl (five flowers) [p. 305] was a flower above the sign of the number five: the Quanhtinchan (house of the eagle), a house from which the head of that bird peeps out. The Chinese, the Egyptians, and other nations availed themselves of this kind of characters, which, because they first represented the sounds of which proper names consisted, were called cyriologic, from kyrios, proper, and logos, word.

The Mexicans had come as far as this; but their writing, if so it may be called, still lets the infancy of the art be perceived. The purely pictorial part, which had disappeared in Chinese and Egyptian writing, occupied a considerable space in the Mexican, which may be regarded as a series of pictures (though of most imperfect design, being destined exclusively for instruction) with brief ideographic and cyriologic inscriptions.

The cyriologic characters represent certain objects by means of the resemblance they bear to them; these objects recall their names, by virtue of the suggestion of coexistence; and one of these names, or a series of names, recalls, by means of the same relation, other objects. Thus, in one of the Mexican hieroglyphics I have just cited, certain colored strokes present to the sight the image of an arrow that breaks the sky; these objects recall the sounds Axajacatl, associated with them in the speech of the Mexicans, and the sounds suggest the idea of the prince whose name they compose.

This means of representing spoken words having once been introduced into writing, it was easy to extend it from proper names to common and general ones, which consisted of significant parts whose symbols were already familiar. Of such words, divisible into other words, there are usually very many in some languages, and in the primitive idioms their number could not fail to be much more considerable. The convenience, then, of indicating an idea by indicating the name which represents it in ordinary language must undoubtedly have induced men to increase more and more the number of the phonetic characters, that is, those representative, not of thought, but of the voice (phone). But in any case the decomposition of

## PHILOS.   20

[p. 306]

words into significant elements could not extend beyond a comparatively small number of cases. How, then, were the words to be represented which did not lend themselves to such decomposition? Let us suppose that we had found ourselves obliged to indicate this word árbol [tree], which in Castilian is irresoluble into significant elements. What should we have done? The device which occurred to several peoples was to divide the word into two or three parts, each of which, though it signified no idea by itself, should at least form the beginning of some significant word. Árbol is divisible into ar, bol. Ar and bol are the beginnings, respectively, of the words arco [bow], bola [ball]. Supposing that these ideas were represented by the mimetic signs C, O, the material structure of the word árbol would be represented in this way, C O.

Here, then, we have men analyzing already the material structure of words in order to transmit ideas: fourth epoch of the art. Certain characters represent certain objects by means of the relation of resemblance; these objects recall their names by means of the relation of coexistence; and combining parts of these names, we form another name which, by means of the same relation, recalls another object.

The analysis of the material structure of words would lead by degrees to monosyllabic writing, in which each syllable would be represented by a simple character, as is used today among the Manchu Tartars and the inhabitants of Corea. The number of syllables of which all the words of a language consist, although great compared with that of the truly elementary vowels and articulations, is not so great but that it might be possible, without great difficulty, to symbolize each syllable with a sign of its own, which would already constitute a complete system of phonetic writing. The alphabet of the Manchu Tartars, whose language is singularly artificial and rich, is composed of fifteen hundred monosyllabic characters.

The Spanish language has about the same number of syllables, and according to this system there might, for example, be represented in it the syllables a, ca, o, ra, ser, by the ideographic signs which denoted respectively a [p. 307] bird, a chain, an oval, a branch, a serpent, objects whose names begin with the aforesaid syllables. This expedient applied to all the syllables that compose the language, we should have come to possess a writing of some fifteen hundred characters, more or less, with which all the syllables, and consequently all the Castilian words, could have been represented. In this system the characters bring to memory the ideas or objects; these recall their names, and their names recall the respective initial syllables.

But the reader, once familiarized with them, would soon associate the characters with the syllables without thinking of the objects or of the names. Behold, then, the ideographic signs converted into signs simply phonetic, or immediately representative of the sounds of speech: the fifth epoch of the art.

There remains but one step, which is to diminish the number of these characters by carrying the decomposition of words down to the elementary sounds,—a step most easy to take if, as some peoples of Asia did, the vowels are left out of the writing. In such a case the ancient phonetic characters, reduced to a small number, would be the true consonant letters, some of simple value, like our b, p, m, others of double value, as were in Greek the letters zeta, xi, psi (ds, cs and ps); and some perhaps of more complicated values. To perfect this alphabet there remained only to add the signs of the vowels, and to substitute for each double or triple consonant the signs of the respective simple sounds, as some do in Castilian by substituting cs for the x. To arrive at perfection the Greeks perhaps lacked nothing more than to complete this last analytic process by banishing all the double consonants. The Latins had an alphabet somewhat less perfect. Both, nevertheless, possessed the most convenient and simple system of writing known to antiquity: an inestimable inheritance, which they transmitted to the peoples of modern Europe, and which passed with these to the New World.

The foregoing exposition shows not only the influence of the two laws of association in writing, but also the [p. 308] slow and almost imperceptible steps by which we have arrived at the point where we now possess this art. The same has happened in the formation of language. These inventions, which, considered in their final result, astonish us and give us so high an idea of man, resolve themselves into a series of elementary inventions, each of which has cost an almost insensible effort of attention and of ingenuity, and yet has been the work of centuries. We owe them not to the meditations or the ingenuity of privileged individuals who created them and raised them to their present state, but to the general perfectibility of the species, to the faculty of transmitting and accumulating ideas.

The apprenticeship of the sense of sight reduces itself, as we saw before, to the formation of a system of signs; but in the art of seeing each individual has nature for his sole master. If each individual not only acquires it, but creates it for himself, and carries it in the tenderest age and in a few months to almost all the perfection of which it is susceptible, let us bear in mind that we begin to practice it from the first time we open our eyes; that we exercise it without ceasing, so long as we are awake; and that it was employed at the outset upon the objects of our first necessities, which excited attention with the irresistible goads of pleasure and pain.

Not only in systems of signs, but in familiar conversation, we see at every step the influence of these two relations of resemblance and simultaneity. One subject leads to another, and although the tie that unites them is not always perceived, because each individual has his own peculiar groups and associations of ideas, it is not seldom glimpsed, and even makes important revelations to us. By these intermediate ideas, which show through without being expressed, we come to read in the soul of the person with whom we are speaking the thoughts which he would be least disposed to communicate to us. Let us suppose that an event known to few, a conspiracy, a murder, a robbery, closely associates two ideas, A, B, which lack every other apparent connection. An individual who, the first of these two ideas being touched upon in conversation, should pass suddenly to the second, or to any other naturally suggested by it, might give to some of the [p. 309] persons present who were informed of the circumstances of the event, strong indications of participation in it.

Tacit intermediate ideas are those which demand the most care and caution from one who is trying to dissimulate what he thinks.

Over the communication of the other ideas the will has absolute sway. In these it is not so. They run with such velocity that they scarcely excite attention, but they leave traces which, without our being aware of it, may reveal their existence.

Indications of this kind, since they have all the air of being involuntary, are those which most flatter the self-love of those who hear us, and which best captivate their benevolence, when the esteem or affection they inspire in us is allowed to appear in them. The art of flattering with grace and delicacy reduces itself to presenting the flattery indirectly, in such a manner that it may seem a revelation, not only sincere, but involuntary, of what we think.

Some reduce the connection of resemblance to that of simultaneity or coexistence. According to them, when one thing suggests another like it, it is because the common parts or qualities of the two suggest the peculiar parts and qualities of the second, with which they have coexisted in the understanding. But resemblance, as we have seen before, does not suppose that there is any part or quality common to the things in which it is perceived.

Dr. Brown believes that when the resemblance is incomplete its suggestive influence may easily be resolved into that of contiguity. This and other authors give the name of contiguity of place or of time to the same species of connection to which the name of simultaneity or coexistence seems to me to correspond rather, being understood by it only that of ideas in the understanding. In effect, two contiguous things will not suggest one another if this relation has not been perceived beforehand by the understanding. It is not, then, the contiguity of things outside us, but the coexistence of their ideas, that associates them in our memory in such a manner that, thinking of one, we pass naturally to think of the others.

[p. 310]

To prove that incomplete resemblance is resolved into contiguity, Dr. Brown makes use of this example. As raiment or dress forms an important part of the complex perception of the human figure, the mode of dress of an age may bring to our memory some one of the celebrated personages who flourished in it. A ruff, such as we have seen in the portraits of Queen Elizabeth of England, will perhaps make us recall that princess, although the person in whom we see it has no other resemblance to her. But in this case the two principles of suggestion act successively, without being resolved the one into the other. The ruff of the person before us makes us recall the ruff we have seen in the portraits of Elizabeth; and this second ruff brings to our memory the features, the name, the character and the deeds of that queen, in a word, the complex idea which represents her to us. In the first suggestion one object recalls another like it; in the second one idea awakens others that have coexisted with it, forming a complex representation.

Others with more appearance of foundation, and among them the same distinguished philosopher, add to the two suggestions mentioned that of opposition or contrast. “The palace and the cottage,” says Brown, “the cradle and the grave, the extremes of indigence and of opulent and voluptuous splendor, are not connected only in the artificial antitheses of the orator, but naturally suggest one another. Of all moral reflections, none are so common as those which turn on the instability of honors and distinctions, the sudden reverses of fortune, the frailty of beauty, the precariousness of life itself; and all of them spring from the suggestion of contrast, because this instability is nothing else than the transition from one state to its contrary. When we see the victorious emperor moving along in all the splendor of majesty and conquest, we must have thought of some unexpected disaster before we can moralize on the vanity and transience of earthly triumphs and glories. If, when we see health and youth, beauty and joy in the countenance of a person, we lament the [p. 311] brief and precarious duration of these blessings, it is because the ideas of old age and of the unfortunate accidents to which the life of man is continually exposed have first been excited in the soul.”

But these contrasts and moral reflections occur to the understanding only because history and our own experience have often made us observe them in life. Why, when I see the triumphal procession of an emperor, does the idea occur to me of a revolution that may precipitate him from the throne and perhaps drag him to the scaffold? The triumphant one recalls to me other personages who, flattered by fortune with the same lot, have ended their career in exile, in chains or on the gibbet. A victorious prince recalls other victorious princes; and in the complex idea of some of these, whose image presents itself to us more naturally by the celebrity their very misfortunes have given them, victory, power and pomp appear beside dethronement and a disastrous death.

Much of the energy of that perpetual propensity to hope, which neither the greatest adversities nor the very prolongation of misery can wholly subdue or stifle, is due, according to the same philosopher, to the suggestion of contrast, which continually presents to the imagination, now the idea of past felicities, now the prospect of a happy state which perhaps awaits us in the future. If the former aggravates the pain of loss, the latter revives and nourishes hope. Nor is it unbecoming the goodness of that Almighty Being, whose providence adapted the marvelous faculties of man to the various situations of life, to have made him capable of conceiving hope where he most needed it, preparing for him this internal source of consolation in the very excess of unhappiness. The painful reminiscences of the past and the salutary summonings of conscience arise, in great part, from the suggestion of contrast, which in the understanding of present anguish leads to thinking of the sweet peace and serenity lost, and which, although it cannot restore innocence, can at least, by means of the images which [p. 312] it places before our view, soften the heart to repentance, which is almost innocence under another form.

There is a passage in the panegyric of Pliny which expresses with considerable energy the action of the suggestive principle of contrast upon the guilty conscience. Merenti gratias agere, facile est; non enim periculum est, ne cum loquar de humanitate, exprobari tibi superbian credat; cum de frugalitate, luxuriam; cum de clementia, crudelitatem; cum de benignitate, livorem; cum de continentia, libidinem; cum de labore, inertiam; cum de fortitudine, timorem. [To thank one who deserves it is easy; for there is no danger, when I speak of humanity, that he may think pride is cast in his teeth; when of frugality, luxury; of clemency, cruelty; of kindness, malice; of continence, lust; of labor, sloth; of fortitude, fear.] In this allusion to times that had scarcely finished passing, what a horrible picture of that despotism, still covetous of the praises of virtues whose very name must have caused it dread; and what a pitiful picture of the servile cowardice which, prostrate on its knees, paid the perilous tribute of adulation; cum dicere quod velles periculosum, quod nolles, miserum esset [when to say what you wished was dangerous, what you did not wish, wretched]; of that reign of terror and flattery, of confiscation and blood, in which, mourning and misery showing themselves on every side, there was added to so many bitter feelings the hard necessity of feigning joy; when informers spied upon countenances and slandered looks and gestures; when the citizen, precipitated into poverty, feared to appear sad, because life still remained to him; and he whose brother had perished beneath the dagger of an assassin dared not put on mourning, because a son was left him! But in the long catalogue of praises that were paid to enthroned crime, the suggestive principle of which we speak could not but have frequently exercised its influence, and, in spite of the artifices of the orator to veil beneath the magnificence of language that frightful form of virtue which he was obliged to put before his eyes, must many times have awakened in the tyrant’s conscience the feeling of what he really was, by the irresistible contrast of the picture of what he was not.

It is not difficult to see that in the first of the foregoing examples the suggestion of contrast is resolved into those of resemblance and of coexistence. An unfortunate situation recalls others; these recall in turn the fortunate and [p. 313] perhaps unexpected issues that ended them. Moreover, the hope of the unfortunate is nourished by their very sufferings and by the longing to see their lot improved. When we desire a thing ardently, we think of all possible means of attaining it and exaggerate their efficacy.

In the same way I believe we may explain the summonings of conscience. The soul agitated by remorse longs for inner serenity; and cannot think of it without picturing to itself the happy time when it enjoyed this inestimable blessing, the companion of innocence.

Brown’s third example will lead us to consider the suggestion of contrast in a more general and comprehensive manner. He who bestows praises on another necessarily appeals to the testimony of the conscience of the praised, which can find in it only what really exists, deeds and crimes, virtues or vices. If the praises are not deserved, the flatterer does precisely the same as if, praising an ugly man as handsome, he should place a mirror before him. The praises of clemency will bring to the tyrant’s memory his acts of rigor and cruelty; those of fortitude and valor will recall to him his pusillanimity and cowardice; in a word, each quality will suggest its contrary; for such is the natural effect of the two primordial laws which govern the suggestions of memory. Contrary qualities bear upon objects of the same kind: their ideas consist, therefore, of common elements which suggest one another, and suggest the peculiar elements grouped with them. What does the flatterer say to the merciless tyrant when he gives him the title of clement? You have pardoned injuries; you have held out a generous hand to the prostrate enemy; you have not wished to purchase an easy and perhaps lawful vengeance with the orphanhood and mourning of an innocent family; the tears of repentance have been able to do more with you than the memory of offences. Such are the ideas which the word clemency awakens in the mind; such is its meaning. But in the mind of the tyrant who hears his panegyric, these groups of ideas set in motion other groups which in part consist of analogous elements: enemies pitilessly immolated; offences slight, punished [p. 314] with proscriptions and tortures; innocent families buried in grief and misery, to content a vengeance that delights in tears and blood.

We have no need, then, of a special bond of contrast to explain the effect of undeserved praises on the conscience of the person to whom they are paid. We shall remark in passing that the contrasts of which Brown speaks are not so easily awakened in the conscience of the powerful, whatever be the tie of suggestion that produces them. The maxims instilled into princes from the cradle and the intoxication of absolute power often cause language not to excite in them the same ideas which would necessarily present themselves to them if they could view their conduct with the same eyes as other men. In a prince steeped in the principles of the divine right of kings, of the sacrosanct character of the authority with which he is invested, and of the grave guilt of all offences committed against it, a guilt which his ministers and favorites have an interest in magnifying, what effect will the praises of clemency and benignity paid him by the flatterers have? He will judge himself deserving of them. The atrocious penalties imposed for imaginary or slight faults will seem to him dictated by justice; and if in the family of the wretch who fell into his disfavor a drop of blood remains to be shed, he will think himself to deserve the title of benign and pious. The despot brutalized by the servile submission of those who surround him applies not to his actions the same rules of morality, nor gives to words the same sense, as other men.

On the other hand, when the connection is as intimate and as obvious as Brown supposes, it would be the greatest of blunders in a panegyrist to excite it. Court flatterers are not accustomed to attribute to their heroes the virtues contrary to the vices from which they suffer, but those which can be conceded them without departing much from the truth, those which their heroes feign or which have a certain affinity with their vices. The parasites of Alexander would not extol his sobriety and temperance. Those of Nero might praise his magnificence, his liberality, his good taste.

[p. 315]

Contrary ideas consist in part of common elements, I mean, of resembling ones. We may, then, represent them by A B and A C: A will represent the common elements; B and C the peculiar elements. If, then, one of two contrary ideas is excited, the part A of the complex A B will recall the part A of the complex A C, by virtue of the suggestion of resemblance; and the part A of this second complex will recall the part C of the same, by virtue of the suggestion of coexistence; the total idea A C being excited in the soul in this manner, as if the one complex suggested the other directly.

But as the part A of A B suggests the resembling elements of contrary ideas, it may suggest by resemblance or coexistence any other class of ideas, and the part B may make an equal number of suggestions. We do not tend more to the contrary ideas suggested in the manner I have described than to ideas of any other class suggested either by resemblance or by coexistence. The inclination of the mind in passing from the idea of a pygmy to the idea of a giant is no greater than to those of other pygmies, or to those of persons who resemble the first in color, in features, etc., or to those of persons or things that we have seen beside him, or that have been otherwise associated with his idea in memory. It is circumstances that make us, in certain cases, give the preference to the suggestions which lead us to contrary ideas. If we have seen a giant, the deviation from the general type of the human species which we see in the stature of the pygmy will make us think of that contrary deviation. But if we have seen another pygmy, it is probable that the idea of this one will excite a preferential attention. If the pygmy is an albino, and we have seen in other men this sort of degeneracy, we shall pass to think of them. The black eyes of the pygmy will recall to a lover the black eyes of his beloved. In a word, each idea suggests a multitude of others either by resemblance or by coexistence; and the mind prefers among them all those of the objects that have made upon it a stronger or more recent impression, or that have a closer relation with our tastes, our passions, our character and our intellectual habits.

[p. 316]

The relations of resemblance and of contrast are, if I am not mistaken, the only ones which it is not necessary to have known beforehand between two objects, in order that the one may recall the other. Since the bond of contrast reduces itself in part to that of resemblance and in part to that of coexistence, and since the property which contrast has of making the understanding pass from one object to another, although the contrariety between the two has not been previously noticed, it owes to the relation of resemblance which it involves, it seems to me that we may lay it down that the relation of resemblance is the only one that does not suppose previous knowledge for the suggestion of ideas: I mean, that A suggests its like B, although we have never stopped to consider the resemblance of the two objects, and that this power of suggesting without need of previous coexistence in the mind is exclusively proper to the relation of resemblance.

I believe it can be demonstrated with evidence that the principles of association or suggestion of ideas reduce themselves to the two facts, and cannot be more or fewer. The suggestion of resemblance is that in which A awakens the idea of B, by virtue of the resemblance of A to B, although A and B have not coexisted before in the understanding; and the suggestion of coexistence or simultaneity is that in which A suggests the idea of B, by virtue of both objects having at some time coexisted in the understanding.

Let us suppose that M recalls the idea of N: this cannot but be by virtue of some particular relation between M and N, such as that of resemblance, of contrast, of contiguity of place or time, of causality, etc. Leaving aside the relations of resemblance and of contrast, of which the second, as we have seen, has the first for one of its elements, the following reasoning may be applied to every species of relations. Let us confine ourselves to contiguity of place. If the contiguity between A and B causes me, thinking of A, to remember B, it can be only because this relation of A to B is known to me by means of my perceptions or my reasonings, or by information from others; and it is evident that in whichever of these three ways the suggestion may have been effected, [p. 317] it supposes that the ideas of A and B have coexisted before in the understanding. A coexistence of which no notice is had cannot bind two ideas. Can A suggest the idea of its cause B, without our having known beforehand that B is the cause of A? What may sometimes happen is that the intellectual process by which we pass from the effect to the cause is so instantaneous that causality seems to us a simple bond of association. A fruit suggests to me the idea of the flower that preceded it, although I have not perceived the species of flower that precedes this species of fruit, nor ever thought of it. But it is evident that the suggestion is preceded by a most rapid reasoning. Fruits proceed from flowers, says the soul; therefore this fruit proceeds from a flower: the fruit makes me think of the class fruits by resemblance, the class fruits makes me think, by previous intellectual coexistence, of the class flowers, which my memory represents to me as the principles or primitive forms of fruits; and the class flowers makes me think by resemblance of the individual flower from which the fruit that I have before me has proceeded.

[PDF 334]

On attention, or on the degree of force or vividness of

perceptions.

Constant multiplicity of the perceptions experienced by the soul.—Powerful exercise of thought.—Faculty of attention.—Consciousness as a perceptive faculty.—Whether all the affections of the soul produce consciousness.— Vividness or faintness of perceptions.—Every intuition decreases in force with respect to its proximate cause.—To notice, to perceive, and to be conscious.—Laws of attention.—The force of attention.—Duration of attention. —The effort of the will.—Exercise of the organs that cooperate in the exercise of the will.—Coexistence of other interesting affections.—Novelty or strangeness of objects.—Relation of the object to our interests, passions, and habitual states.—Predisposition to the recollection of objects that affect us agreeably or painfully.—Relation of the object to our disposition, temperament, or organic constitution.—Link of resemblance and link of coexistence. —Instincts peculiar to age and sex.

There is no moment at which our organs are not impressed by an infinity of stimuli, producing external and internal sensitive perceptions. There is no act of the soul that does not produce intuitive perceptions. There is no perception, no recollection, that does not awaken an infinity of anamneses, through the two links of coexistence and resemblance of which we treated in the preceding chapter. We must, then, experience at every moment an infinity of actual perceptions and of recollections. Add to these the combinations, whether fortuitous or voluntary, of reasoning and imagination, in which resemblance and coexistence take, so to speak, peculiar movements and directions [p. 319] peculiar to them. And if we bear in mind that there is no modification of the soul that does not affect consciousness, and that the intuitions themselves must produce other, ulterior intuitions, and these perhaps others and others in succession, like the successive echoes of a voice reverberated in a group of mountains, we must admit that the soul experiences at every instant an incalculable number of intuitive and sensitive perceptions, actual and renewed.

This, nevertheless, takes place in such a manner that we scarcely notice it. Certain actual perceptions or certain recollections, by virtue of the degree of force they possess, render the coexisting affections as nothing. A vivid perception does not allow us to attend to the other perceptions, and much less to the recollections that are awakened at the same time in the soul. Recollections are naturally weaker than perceptions, and yet they acquire such a degree of force and vividness, through the connection they have with our needs, affections, or caprices, and exert so much power over the mind, that they in a manner tear it away from the senses and make it deaf to the warnings and reports it receives from them. When we are in one of these distractions, what we see and hear is as if we neither saw nor heard it. We neither notice it at the time, nor is it possible for us to recollect it afterwards.

By means, then, of the varying force of actual or renewed perceptions, the great number of coexisting affections which the soul experiences at every instant does not embarrass the exercise of thought, which occupies itself with a small number of them at one time, and commonly passes from some to others with order and choice; a faculty as marvelous as it is necessary, without which our mind, assailed on all sides by objects and plunged in a perpetual tumult of sensations, anamneses, and intuitions, would present the image of chaos.

That the force or vividness of perceptions or of ideas is susceptible of different degrees is a fact we cannot doubt. However little we have lingered in the contemplation of mental phenomena, we cannot have failed to observe the varying force of what we call noticing things, attending to them, heeding, fixing the mind, making a stand upon them, [p. 320] from the exclusive attention which, concentrated on a single object, renders the perceptions and anamneses of the others as nothing, down to the obscure and distracted perception that informs us cursorily of objects in which we take no interest, and to the fugitive recollection that scarcely leaves a trace in the mind. A multitude of intermediate degrees separate these two points, which are the ordinarily observable extremes. But there are extraordinary states in which an imagination so engrosses the soul that the difference of intensity between the anamneses which compose it and the actual affections becomes truly null; as happens in febrile delirium or in the raptures of exalted devotion. And there are also, as we shall see, unobservable though frequent states in which the consciousness of certain spiritual affections is either absolutely null or vanishes at the very moment of its production, leaving no trace of itself or of them in the memory.

By the word attention is commonly signified either the effort of the will that seeks to concentrate the whole soul upon a single thing, or the vividness with which, by virtue of this effort, the idea of that thing is produced in perception, which may also be produced by other causes, acting in entire independence of the will, and even in spite of it. I limit the use of the word attention by itself to the second sense. Attention may be voluntary or not.

It is well also to recall that consciousness is in all cases the true and only perceptive faculty. The soul never perceives anything but itself, nor can it perceive the modes of being of bodies and of other minds except by perceiving its own. In every perception there is, consequently, a spiritual affection or a relation between two or more spiritual affections, which affection or relation of affections is the immediate object of the perceptive faculty.

Recollections consist, as we have seen, of intuitions and of anamneses, and form, consequently, a species of perceptions, in which consciousness has for its object affections that are an imperfect and faded copy of other preceding [p. 321] affections. In actual perception, which is perception properly so called, consciousness has for its object original affections; in recollection, renewed affections.

We may recollect not only actual perceptions but recollections. In this case the anamnesis which was one of the elements of the first recollection is an original of which the anamnesis that is one of the elements of the second recollection serves as the image.

The vividness of perceptions or of recollections consists in the vividness of the actual or renewed affections which are the immediate object of consciousness. If the effort of the will quickens the perception or the recollection, it does so by increasing the intensity of the spiritual affection which the soul contemplates in itself.

It may perhaps be doubted whether all the affections of the soul produce consciousness. As to those which we can remember, there is no doubt that they produce it, because we can remember only what we have actually perceived, and in every perception there is necessarily intuition. This, however, is not without difficulty. If all the affections of the soul produce consciousness, and the very acts of consciousness produce a further consciousness, and the acts of this a third, and so on infinitely; there is no moment of time, while we are awake, in which the soul does not experience an infinite number of affections, taking the word infinite in its literal sense; which is absurd. Might it not be said that the force or vividness of the intuition is always much less than that of the spiritual affection which immediately produces it, and that, therefore, the force of the successive intuitions decreasing in a rapid progression, it soon comes to vanish altogether? There is nothing in this hypothesis that is belied by the observation of intellectual phenomena. On the contrary, we know that the perceptions of corporeal objects, which require only first intuitions, engross all our attention in the earliest years, and that even in adult age the greater part of men rarely stop to think of any others. The general plan of nature is that the affections of the soul which have

## PHILOS.     21

[p. 322]

an immediate connection with our bodily well-being call and draw us at first much more imperiously than the others.

Let us now take into consideration certain facts which suppose mental processes that we do not notice as we perform them, and of which, once performed, we cannot recollect anything.

When we read aloud, we perceive successively the written characters; each perception suggests certain volitions, and these produce the movements necessary for the vocal organ to give the corresponding sound; and while these perceptions or volitions succeed one another with inconceivable rapidity (for an ordinary reader can recognize thirty or forty letters in a second, and there is scarcely one whose pronunciation does not require the concurrence of several muscles), the soul appears to be entirely occupied with the sense of what it reads, and the memory ordinarily preserves no trace of them. The same happens in all the other operations that have become habitual to us. In walking, we regulate our movements in consequence of a multitude of perceptions that inform us of the rises and falls of the ground, of the various windings of the road, of the bodies that present themselves in our way, and of other particulars; and all these perceptions, and the volitions and movements that consequently take place, will not perhaps prevent our being at the same time absorbed in a profound meditation, which seems to leave us able to notice nothing else. What a difference in this respect between the adult and the child who is essaying his first steps! The different stages of the operation present themselves successively to the soul with a velocity ever greater, according to the frequency with which we have exercised them; until at last they are so rapid that we can no longer notice or recollect them. When we walk through places familiar to our sight and at the same time meditate profoundly on something, the material objects that surround us make so little impression on our mind that we could perhaps not affirm the existence of any one that we had just had before us; and yet it is so certain that we perceive them, that if in place, for example, of the familiar shrub on which we do not stop to look, there were a wild beast in our path, the strangeness of the object alone, even without the idea of [p. 323] danger, would immediately suspend the intellectual process that was occupying us. We have, then, true perceptions of the objects that present themselves in our path, and, what is more, we distinguish in them the familiar from the strange, and what concerns us, by the good or ill that may result to us from it, from what does not concern us. The judgment we form of the strangeness or the importance of objects excites attention and quickens the affections with which we perceive them. If we form contrary judgments, and are occupied in a profound meditation, we notice neither them nor the perceptions that give rise to them, because the superior vividness of other affections effaces from the mind those perceptions and judgments as they are produced.

When we attend a dramatic representation, it sometimes happens that, vividly interested in an incident, we believe we perceive nothing else. Yet there is no doubt that very many other perceptions then take place: we have before us the orchestra, the boxes, the spectators, the lighting; the magnificence even of that part of the spectacle which has no relation to the drama contributes to the pleasure we feel; and nothing heightens it so much as that which the other spectators experience at the same time, and which perhaps we enjoy only through their silence. The existence, then, of these perceptions in those very moments in which our attention seems absorbed by what the actors do and say is indubitable: the much greater degree of force with which other perceptions are produced is what prevents our noticing the former.

Let us see the part that consciousness has in these fugitive modifications of our mind. We have already seen that every perception and every recollection is an act of consciousness. Volitions, on their part, suppose consciousness of the spiritual affections that determine us to them. There is no mental act of which intuitive perception is not a necessary element, nor any act of the will that does not suppose it. Consciousness is the bond that links all the affections of the soul and gives them unity and concert. But if the force of intuitions is always considerably less than that of their proximate cause, and if in cases similar to those I have just mentioned the sensations produced [p. 324] by certain objects are so fugitive and slight that at the moment after they have taken place we find no trace of them in the memory, is it not natural to conclude that the consciousness of them is much feebler still, and exists only in the degree indispensable for the execution of the respective mental processes, vanishing immediately without leaving a trace of itself? According to this, to notice a thing, to heed it or make a stand upon it, denotes the intuitions that have sufficient force for their objects to remain for some time present to the soul; and not to notice, not to heed, not to make a stand, denote that very feeble and almost evanescent consciousness which attends the exercise of the mental processes with which we are familiarized.

But in the explanation of the facts just mentioned it is supposed that the understanding, when a series of operations becomes habitual, suppresses none of them, or that between habits to be acquired and habits acquired there is no other difference than that of the velocity with which the various stages are executed. Now, let A, B, C be three affections of the soul, of which A excites or suggests B, and B, C. We know that it is a law of memory that affections which have frequently coexisted suggest or recall one another. But if we suppose that the series A, B, C is often reproduced in the soul, it will come about that its terms, succeeding one another more and more rapidly, coexist at last. A will be able, then, to suggest C, without the need of the intermediate B. The sight of the sea recalls to me a distant port; the idea of the port makes me think of a neighboring city, and from thinking of the city I pass to thinking of a person I knew in it. If this series of affections is often reproduced in the soul, will it come to pass that the sight of the sea immediately recalls the person to me? Is it not, then, probable that in habitual processes the soul omits some of the acts which it was necessary for it to execute in order to acquire them? Generalizing this consequence still further, it seems we might admit that the sensation, for example, of a letter comes, by force of habit, to excite by itself the volition of the corresponding movements of the vocal organ without the intervention of consciousness. And there are even those who believe that [p. 325] in habitual operations the volition itself is one of the acts that are suppressed, and that the sensations immediately excite the muscular movements.

I have no difficulty in admitting that when a series of ideas is frequently reproduced in the soul, the succession becomes ever more rapid until it ends in true coexistence; that in this way terms of it which were at some distance from one another come to touch, so to speak; and that, in consequence, the less important links of the chain vanish and are effaced. But I do not believe we are authorized to extend this law of memory, if we can consider it such, to the point of supposing that a muscular contraction of those which serve voluntary movement is excited immediately by a sensation, without a volition that acts immediately on the nerves and muscles, and without a consciousness that determines the will to influence the body in a particular manner. When we read, it often happens that we correct misprints by mentally substituting for the characters or words written those which the legitimate pronunciation and the context require. But if the sensation were immediately linked with the movement, how could we pronounce other characters and words than those which are traced on the paper? This correction supposes not only that the movements of the vocal organ are directed by the will, but that the will itself is determined by consciousness, and that while we truly perceive the letters, other operations of the understanding recognize the misprints and suggest the emendations. This is the same thing that is observed in other mental phenomena of which we have already spoken. If, when walking through places we are accustomed to see, a strange object startles us, it is because even the most familiar objects, which leave no impression on the mind, are perceived by consciousness. The distinction between what is strange and what is not is the cause of our making a stand upon some objects and not upon others; and to distinguish the one from the other supposes that we perceive them all, although the perceptions leave no trace in the memory except when we dwell somewhat upon them.

[p. 326]

It is commonly said that in such cases we have no consciousness of what passes in the soul. In this common way of speaking the word consciousness denotes something more than the elementary and almost evanescent intuitions produced by certain weak and fugitive affections of which no trace remains in the memory.

But, admitting, as seems to me certain, that the affections of which habitual processes consist produce a certain degree of consciousness, it is not therefore necessary to believe that every affection of the soul, however slight and rapid it may be, is perceived by the intuitive faculty. We saw above that such a principle, taken in all its latitude, is absurd; because intuition is an affection of the soul like the others, and if every affection produced intuition, every first intuition would produce a second, a third, and so on infinitely. To get over this difficulty we have appealed to a supposition which, besides being necessary, appears confirmed by the observation of mental phenomena: namely, that every intuition is considerably weaker than its proximate cause; from which it follows that the force of successive intuitions decreases rapidly until it comes to be too weak to produce a further intuition. But this explanation supposes that the modifications of the soul must have a certain degree of force in order to produce consciousness, and that consequently not all of them produce it.

All that is marvelous in the tricks of the juggler consists in his executing certain movements with a velocity such that they escape the observation of the spectators. Notwithstanding the inconceivable rapidity of the process, consciousness without doubt presides over it; the slightest movements of his fingers are regulated by perceptions and volitions; but in the spectators an equal exercise of the intuitive faculty cannot take place, because they lack the preceding habits which give such facility and velocity to the mental operations of the other.

The facility with which the mental operations of which habits consist succeed one another is the work of long practice, and if in them a very rapid sensation produces consciousness, it is not therefore [p. 327] to be believed that as much happens even in cases of a different kind. The movements which the perceptions of the juggler suggest and regulate with a marvelous rapidity acquired by force of practice excite in the sight of the spectators, probably, sensations too fugitive and feeble for consciousness to inform itself of them and for the memory to recall them.

The velocity of these movements may also be such that the impressions produced on the retina and in the nerves lack the force sufficient to excite sensations. At times they will be too rapid for the sensation to produce consciousness and memory, but not so much so that the organic impression fails to affect the soul; and at others the rapidity with which they succeed one another will be such that not even a sensation is produced. In the common way of speaking, to notice, to perceive, and to be conscious are synonymous expressions; but in rigorously exact language we ought to distinguish notice, which is a perception strong enough to produce in us the faculty of renewing it at a greater or less distance of time, from perception and consciousness in general, which admit all the different degrees of force, from that which accompanies habitual processes up to that of the most intense and profound attention.

Let us now examine the laws of attention; the causes that influence the different force of perceptions and ideas, or which make one perception or idea predominate over the others that coexist with it.

In every perception, in every idea, there is, by that very fact, a spiritual affection present to consciousness. In the greater or less force of these affections consists always the greater or less force of the perception or the idea, or in other words, the greater or less attention we give to it. Let us see, then, what circumstances influence the force of the affections.

The first of these circumstances is the natural force of the affection, that is, its energy in so far as it depends on external causes, and not on the particular activity or susceptibility of the subject. If we experience, for example, an external sensitive perception, the attention we give to it will depend in [p. 328] great part on the natural vividness of the sensation, corresponding to the force of the organic impression produced by the external stimulus. Thus it is that, other circumstances being equal, the sensation caused by the sound of a trumpet will call us much more imperiously than the murmur of the wind gently rocking the trees.

2nd. The duration of the affection. We have already seen that a spiritual affection may be so rapid and fugitive that it does not come to be perceived by consciousness, and that even apart from this extreme case its existence may be so transitory as to leave no trace in the memory. In proportion as the initial affection is prolonged, its force grows, until it reaches the maximum determined by the whole of the influencing circumstances. But from this point duration acts in the contrary sense. The prolonged affection grows weak.

3rd. The effort of the will. We have, for example, several objects in view: we experience, in consequence, a multitude of visual sensations. If there is no motive to call our attention toward any one of the objects present, we shall experience a confused and feeble perception of the whole, so that we shall scarcely be able to give an account of the prospect when we cease to have it before us, and it will be difficult for us to pronounce yes or no upon the existence of many of the particulars that compose it. But if in the midst of that inattention and indifference there comes upon us a desire to experience a vivid perception of any one of the said objects, it is enough for us to will it. In consequence of this act of will, the sensations that represent the object become much more vivid and distinct than the others, which in the same proportion are deadened and vanish. “It is,” says Brown, “as if the other parts of the prospect had been but the doubtful colouring of enchantment, which had disappeared, and left to us the realities on which we gaze; or rather, as if some instant enchantment, obedient to our wishes, had dissolved the surrounding objects, and brought closer to our sight the objects which we desired to see.”

The attention we give to corporeal objects is accompanied [p. 329] by the direction of the organs, adapting them in such a way that the action of objects produces the organic impression most favorable to the vividness of the sensation. But the effort of the will can, even without the aid of the organs, increase the vividness of the spiritual affections on which we desire to fix ourselves; and thus it is that the will exerts as powerful an influence over the anamneses as over actual affections. I speak, of course, of the organs that serve for sensitive perception; for in the present state of our knowledge concerning the correspondence between the soul and the body, it is impossible to determine to what extent the cooperation of certain organs in the intellectual functions is necessary. It might be, for example, that to each degree of vividness of a spiritual affection there corresponded a certain particular organic modification, and that the will, in order to obtain that degree of vividness, had to act immediately upon the organs, producing that modification; so that in the effort of the will the mind should not act upon itself directly, but by means of the organs.

4th. The coexistence of other interesting affections. This circumstance acts, as a rule, negatively, diminishing the vividness of an affection by the coexistence of others; the sound which we scarcely perceive in the bustle of the day will perhaps affect us vividly in the silence of the night. It appears that the energy of attention at the disposal of the soul is a constant quantity, or one that varies only within certain limits; so that if many objects share it among themselves, even if only transiently, the quantity of attention we give to each of them is feeble. I speak of the affections that in some way interest us; for those that in no way call attention readily yield their place to the others and are as if they were not.

But there are cases in which the coexistence of other affections increases the vividness of those with which we perceive or recollect a particular object, and makes more energetic the feelings that accompany them. This happens when there is a certain affinity or harmony among the various affections, so that all [p. 330] conspire to one end. In this way the apparatus of a festival contributes much to the vividness of the perceptions of the principal objects. The example of theatrical representations, cited above, proves it.

5th. The novelty or strangeness of objects. This, as regards material beings, needs illustration. The impression made upon the soul by unforeseen relations and rare coincidences is a phenomenon of the same kind. That a man should perish tragically on the same day of the year on which some time before he committed a great crime; that two famous captains, of whom the one conquered the other and made him pass from the throne to exile, should have been born in the same year; that a proscribed tyrant, fleeing from popular indignation, should pass through the same places and the same lodgings through which some years before, in the same month and day, a celebrated victim had been conducted by his order to the dungeon: these are coincidences that make a strong impression, and once learned, take possession of the memory forever. For this reason one of the chief means of retaining a thing in it is to link it to some relation which, by some uncommon peculiarity, fixes itself easily in the soul. Of all the numbers with which the ratio of the diameter to the circumference can be expressed, 113 and 355 are the easiest to retain, because they consist of three doubled figures forming an arithmetical progression.

6th. The relation of the object to our passions, interests, or habitual studies. This is a law of memory which we see confirmed at every instant of life.

As there is scarcely an object that has not an infinity of relations, whether of resemblance or of coexistence, with other objects, it is easy to account for the facility with which our soul passes from one object to another, although at first sight there seems to be no connection whatever between the two. For if A has no point of contact with P, yet among the innumerable objects that have it with A, it is not difficult that there should be one that either has it with P immediately, or has it with some one of the innumerable objects linked with P; and in case it is not so, the soul may pass from A to B by means of a [p. 331] common link; from B to C in the same manner; and so successively until it arrives at P. Every object sets in motion an infinity of series of ideas to which the soul does not attend and of which it has scarcely any consciousness, because it fixes itself only on the links that interest it. Now, if an object excites a lively passion in us, everything that has relation to it becomes by that very fact interesting to us, and furnishes a multitude of intermediate points for passing from other ideas to that of the favorite object; and as the permanence of this, or its frequent reproduction, links it with new objects, the number of the series that lead to it increases at every instant, until the case arrives that no object of actual or renewed perception presents itself to us which does not lead us swiftly to the contemplation of that thing to which the dominant passion gives a superior importance, and which by this means takes possession of the soul and does not leave it free for a moment. But even without this, the idea that produces lively emotions in us is accompanied by strong, and consequently durable, organic affections; and these organic modifications continually awaken that idea. The death of a beloved person, for example, produces in us emotions of grief, which profoundly affect our organs: the organic affection subsists even when the recollection of the deceased person is transiently dislodged by other objects; and the internal perception of the organic affection is a continually repeated warning, which produces that recollection anew, and which, even when we sleep, evokes the beloved image, and gives to the anamneses the force and power of actual perceptions during the interregnum of the senses.

7th. By reason also of contemplative or imaginative habits, there are persons in whom the sight of certain objects sets in motion agreeable series which never awaken in other men. The sublimity and beauty of natural scenes, at the sight of which the landscape painter and the poet are in ecstasy, make as a rule little or no impression on the soul of the merchant or the artisan. The sound of bells always affected Rousseau in a singular manner. Skeley, every [p. 332] time he came upon a lagoon or pool, stopped to contemplate it; and the proof of the peculiar susceptibility of his imagination at the sight of this kind of objects is found in his own poems, often adorned with aquatic scenes and images.

8th. We recollect with greater vividness and facility the objects that have affected us agreeably or painfully in the earlier periods of life. The scenes we see make us think often of those of the games, diversions, and pleasures of our childhood and youth; and in reproducing them it seems as if the soul were again experiencing the same affections as then; and there are recollected, as Rousseau often observed in himself, not only the times, places, and persons, but all the surrounding objects, the temperature of the air, the odors, a certain local impression belonging to each spot, which has made itself felt only in it, and whose vivid reminiscence transports us anew to it. “For example,” says the same author, describing one of these vivid recollections, relating to events and scenes of his early youth in the house of Madame de Warens, “all that was rehearsed in the hall of the chapel-master, all that was sung in the choir, all that was done there, the noble and handsome dress of the canons, the ornaments of the priests, the mitres of the cantors, the faces of the musicians, an old lame carpenter who played the double-bass, a fair-haired little abbé who played the violin, the tattered cassock which the chapel-master put on over his lay dress after taking off his sword, and the fine surplice with which he covered the tatters to go to the choir, how proud I was to take my place with my flageolet in the orchestra gallery, where I sang a little bit of recitative that had been composed for me, the good dinner that awaited us and the excellent appetite we brought to it, all this collection of objects, vividly pictured, has produced in my memory a hundred times as much delight, and more, than in reality.” Indeed, there are objects which, when perceived, affect us little or not at all, and when recollected cause us an exquisite pleasure, because we have associated them with the feeling of happiness with which the soul was then penetrated, and almost always we exaggerate, the imagination assisting the [p. 333] memory, which puts into these recollections something of its own.

9th. Objects that have a particular relation to our disposition or temperament or organic constitution affect us in a more vivid manner. There are persons who are naturally cheerful or melancholy, prone to anger or to fear; dispositions which appear to have their origin in the radical conformation of the organs, and which influence in a very notable manner the intellectual operations. One and the same object makes an impression on some men and not on others, and, what is more, produces in different individuals the most diverse impressions. The man of melancholy temperament fixes himself by preference on the sad side of the objects that surround him, or rather, has the fatal gift of finding a sad side in all objects. Among the series of ideas which each object awakens, those impress him with most vehemence which figure to him causes of weariness and heaviness, faded pleasures, real or imaginary accidents that lessen the value of goods and disenchant life. Thus the specters that a fearful man believes he sees in the dark are composed of the real lineaments of the things present, perceived with an extreme vividness in so far as they agree with the sketch of the frightened imagination, which completes the fictitious object and gives it bulk with its own conceptions, reinforced also by the tendency of the soul, and by the absence of other visible objects that might attenuate or contradict them. The organic predisposition may be strengthened or counteracted by the notions we have learned in infancy, by the mental or physical occupations in which we have exercised ourselves, by the accidents of fortune that have befallen us in life, and by various other moral influences.

10th. But not only the constitution of the organs, but also their passing states, influence the degree of vividness of perceptions and ideas. The use of spirituous liquors, fever, the nervous weakness that is wont to follow a long illness, good or bad digestion, the organic affections produced by a strong emotion of joy, sadness, anger, or terror, arouse in the soul different dispositions, each of which [p. 334] makes it fix itself by preference on a certain class of perceptions and ideas; and thus give to thought a rapid or slow course, a dark or brilliant coloring.

11th. There are men in whom the ideas excited by the link of resemblance are stronger than those excited by the link of coexistence; and in others the contrary happens. But even descending to the modifications of these two general causes of association, different susceptibilities are found in different individuals. In some the connection of causality is more powerful, in others that of contrast. This power of certain modes of association with respect to certain men, due without doubt to their radical constitution of soul and body and to their early education (taking this word in its most comprehensive sense, which embraces all the physical and moral influences capable of impressing the individual from the time he opens his eyes to the light), constitutes in great part the various mental dispositions for the study of the sciences and arts, the various kinds of memory, understanding, imagination, and wit.

12th. The different ages and sexes develop certain instincts that give a particular force and predominance to certain objects. Instinct acts by arousing, in the presence of these objects, agreeable or painful sensations, which depend on our organic predisposition and imperiously call attention toward them; the perception of the objects becomes then most vivid, and is followed by inclinations and desires of effort and movements, which, at first uncertain and vague, go as if groping toward the satisfaction of some need of animal life, until, enlightened by experience, we employ with choice and discernment the means adequate to satisfy it.

Such are, in my opinion, the various causes that determine attention, and such is their influence upon the different phases and physiognomies, if it is permissible to say so, of the human mind. The subject is most vast. Each one of the causes enumerated might furnish matter for a long and curious investigation. But this undertaking is far beyond my powers.

[PDF 351]

On matter.

Objective reference is a principle of the intellectual constitution.—Principle of the constancy of the order established by nature.—Idea of the nature of matter.—The situations and places attributed to causes.—The inmost nature of external causes is unknown; it is possible only to represent to oneself their qualities and relations.—First idea of the living being or body.—Origin of the idea of animus, anima, spiritus.—Materialism.—Spiritualism.— Universal spirit.—School of Berkeley.—Materialist objections.—Relation of the uncreated spirit to finite existence.—Objection founded on the idea of the eternity of matter.—False comparison of the doctrine of Berkeley with Pyrrhonism.—Dugald Stewart.—Sterility of the question concerning the real existence of bodies.—Necessity of setting sensation apart whenever the nature of external causes is considered.—Doctrine of substance according to Berkeley.—Importance of the principle of causality.—Sense of the word matter according to Berkeley.—Real being in the cause of sensations.— Appendix: sensation without substance.—Material substance.—Frivolity of the question.

When men symbolize in their sensations causes independent of their own substance, converting the subjective into the objective, they obey a principle of the constitution of the understanding which induces them to refer every phenomenon to some antecedent thing or cause, on the existence of which it is necessary that the phenomenon should follow, or, as the Castilian language expresses it with a philosophical propriety, it is necessary that what they observe should happen. This is, as we have seen, one [p. 336] of those principles which observation, though indispensable in order that their development may take place, is not sufficient by itself alone to produce in the mind; for to have observed a great number of constant and uniform connections, that is, a great number of causes and effects, does not authorize us to deduce that everything, everything that is produced in time, must have a cause. And yet, if we give attention even to the reasonings of the ruder part of mankind, we perceive that although they are not capable of expressing the principle of causality in a precise manner, they discourse and conjecture by supposing it. Their most absurd errors, their grossest explanations of natural phenomena, proceed no less upon this supposition than the theories of the philosophers.

Hand in hand with this principle goes the other, in which we suppose the constancy of the order established by nature. Having observed several times that, in given circumstances, the phenomenon B has followed the phenomenon A, we infer that the same relation has existed and will always exist between them. And so irresistibly are we induced to think thus, that it would suffice to have observed such a connection once, to infer its constant repetition, if we could be sure of having perceived all the circumstances necessary for the production of the effect, or in other terms, all the elements of the antecedent phenomenon. So that if we multiply observations and experiments, it is not because we doubt that the order observed once must always be reproduced, but in order to assure ourselves that we have known the antecedent phenomenon with the whole accompaniment of conditions that determine its action. And our errors in this kind of reasonings always proceed from this, that, in this appreciation of the antecedent phenomenon, some condition has escaped us, some circumstance, in short, some part of those that essentially constitute it.

Men suppose, then, the existence of causes for their sensations, as they suppose it for everything, and they suppose also a constant uniformity in the action of the causes of sensations, as they suppose it in the action of every kind [p. 337] of causes. Let us see now how they conceive the nature of the causes of their sensations, or in other terms, the nature of matter.

The comparison of what passes in my body with what passes in other animated bodies makes known to me, within these, the mental states which consciousness reveals to me in myself. I know, then, that they feel and perceive as I do, and I am not long in discovering that the causes of the sensations which I experience will act in the same manner upon them, if they place themselves in the same situation as I.
