But to know this is the same as to know that these causes stand with them in the same relation as with me, and are consequently not one and the same thing with them, as they are not with me. These causes, moreover, have such a relation among themselves that I can touch them only successively; and for this successive touch the production of certain efforts and movements is necessary. I attribute thus to these causes a determinate order of relative situations, and I circumscribe them to certain places. Each elemental cause is a particle of matter; what I call bodies are aggregates, more or less complex, more or less permanent, more or less heterogeneous, of these causes, and more or less variable in their forms, in the place they occupy, and in their other qualities and states.

The cause, then, of sensation, matter, is something whose individual actions are circumscribed to certain localities determined by the order of the tactile affections, an order which consists in the series and kinds of the efforts necessary to pass from some affections to others. Of the inmost nature of this something we know nothing; we can only represent to ourselves its qualities and the relations it has with itself, that is to say, a material particle with other material particles, by the different sensations it produces, and by the relations which these have among themselves and with the sensations. Between the simple qualities and the homogeneous sensations there is no resemblance, nor can any be conceived; between the relations of the material causes and the relations we perceive in the sensations, we not only suppose a resemblance, but by an original principle of

## PHILOS.   22

[p. 338]

our nature we are irresistibly induced to do so.

What is now, in the eyes of the philosopher, a complex mass, a manifold being, consisting of innumerable material atoms, was, in the eyes of the nascent intelligence, a being as individual as each man considers himself to be. The unity of existence which each man attributed to himself he attributed also to the other complex masses that act upon his senses: to the tree, to the flower, to the stone.

It seems to me that the first step taken by the imagination, excited by the appearance of the corporeal universe, was to figure to itself in each of these complexes a certain entity endowed with sensibility and consciousness, such as each man figures to himself in other men. Being, living thing and body were then synonymous words, comprehending at once the faculty of experiencing sensations and the faculty of exciting them.

The difference of phenomena between the complexes truly animated and those which are not so, or which at least give us no indications of being so, strikes the eyes of the rudest man, and does not escape many other species of animals, even of those which, in the scale of intelligence, are at a considerable distance from man. But the gradation of these phenomena from man and the animals that approach nearest to him, down to those that scarcely give signs of sensibility, softens the contrast, so to speak. We have a certain propension to figure to ourselves in inanimate bodies, not so much the absolute privation as the lowest degree of animation; that species of sensibility and of life which we conceive in an animal profoundly asleep, and which we can hardly, without an effort of reason, refuse to the corpse itself. In the infancy of the understanding, whether we consider it in the individual man or in humanity at large, reason followed imagination with blindfolded eyes. And it must be borne in mind that the primitive development of the human intelligence ought not to be compared with that which takes place now in individuals, accelerated and forced, if not by some other kind of education, by the mere use of the vulgar tongue, in which is enveloped no small part [p. 339] of that intellectual inheritance of past generations. It was, then, natural to conceive a kind of individuality, animation and life in all corporeal complexes. And of this we have a by no means obscure indication in the ancient cosmogonies and mythologies, and in the superstitions which often take possession of the human mind, even after it has emancipated itself from its primitive rudeness and barbarism.

The divisibility of all complexes, as causes of sensation, and the indivisibility of certain complexes as endowed with sensibility and consciousness, led us to distinguish two orders of phenomena and two kinds of beings: beings capable of feeling and of being felt, and beings endowed only with this second capacity; two vast departments of nature, to which we consequently attributed different modes of being. Being and body, under this aspect, were still synonymous words; the whole universe, including the Divinity, was composed, according to the manner of conceiving of men, of animated and inanimate bodies. Such has been, and it may even be said still is, with few exceptions, the metaphysics of the human race in all ages and among all peoples.

One of the first attempts of Philosophy to explain the difference between animated bodies and those which are not so, was to suppose in the former the addition of a principle which the others lacked. As everything was body or matter, that principle of life and of intelligence which escaped the immediate observation of the senses seemed to be only a kind of matter lighter and subtler. Hence the expressions animus, anima, spiritus, with which the Latins signified it, and which still subsist in the modern languages of Europe. The hypothesis of the materialists, who figure to themselves in man and in the other living things a corporeal principle from which proceed the phenomena of life and of intelligence, reproduces today, under more abstract terms, the rude conjectures of nascent Philosophy.

This explanation amounts to supposing in the animated body the difference which we perceive in the universe; to supposing that life resides in one part of the living thing, which rules and sets in [p. 340] motion the others, but without there being any difference of nature between this and those. The difficulty, then, remained standing, and to resolve it recourse was had to the supposition of an animating principle, distinct from matter; and as to the nature of the latter, the greater number, giving it the title of substance, figured it to themselves, in my opinion, as endowed with a kind of imperfect animation, and, so to speak, slumbering; because everything that we call being, thing or cause, either exists feeling, or exists being felt, and if we wish to give a kind of substantial existence to what we know only as capable of being felt, we slip unawares into supposing in it a kind of life.

But a third kind of philosophers, conceiving the material elements as mere productive causes of sensations, denied them every kind of real existence, independent of spirits. According to them, the universe is peopled only with spirits, and spirits do not constitute partial elements of certain existences, but the whole of all the existences we are capable of perceiving. Each material element is a mere influence of the Almighty Spirit, which produces at every instant certain sensations in the spirits that are within the reach which this Great Spirit has been pleased to give it; and all these particular influences are nothing else than developments of general laws originally established by the Creator, according to which the sensations of created spirits were and are to succeed one another in a certain order, alterable up to a certain point by the volitions of these same spirits, and for the most part independent of them. And there is no doubt that these general laws and their continuous and successive development suffice to explain all the phenomena of sensitive perception, all the actions which external causes exercise upon us, and all those which we exercise upon them. According to this way of seeing, the external things or causes represented by the sensations are immediate influences of one sole substance, namely, the uncreated, infinite substance, which embraces all times and fills all the reaches of space; time and space are mere series of influences, [p. 341] and the reality of the external universe consists in the constancy of the relation with respect to each percipient individual, and in its uniformity with respect to all.

Such is, if I am not mistaken, the substance of the doctrine which has been impugned by arguments that, in my way of seeing, prove only that its adversaries have not succeeded in considering it from its true point of view.

What! it will be said: are the influences of the almighty will white and black, cubical and square? Do we feed and clothe ourselves with influences? Or shall we say that the eternal mind, the immediate cause of the sensations, is perceived by the senses, and, like the Proteus of the fable, takes now one color, now another, now this figure, now that, so that the physical universe becomes one and the same thing with the Divinity?

Indeed, the school of Berkeley might answer, we do feed and clothe ourselves with influences; there is nothing absurd in this. Does anything else happen in the materialist theory? The whole difference consists in this, that you suppose in them a certain intermediary between the Supreme Cause and created spirits, and we deny the necessity of any such intermediary. The various actions which you attribute to material substances have been, according to you, deposited in them by the first cause; but did Omnipotence need this previous deposit? Was not the establishment of constant laws sufficient, determining the order, the combinations, the results of all those actions which you attribute to a I know not what, of which you have not, nor can have, any knowledge whatever? The influences are certainly white and red, square and cubical, because they produce in a certain order certain visual and tactile impressions; what matters it whether they produce them from an intermediate seat in which they reside, or from a first cause which has diversified and preordained them from the beginning? Is there in this second supposition anything repugnant to the purest and most sublime idea we can have of the Divinity? How can it be supposed that they materialize the divine knowledge who deny the existence of matter?

It seems that against this theory of matter there might protest [p. 342] those who do not recognize a creating power, a first intelligent cause; those who recognize in the universe nothing but matter, and explain the order by a blind necessity, by virtue of which each material particle exercises by its own virtue and nature certain actions upon the other material particles; and who hold all matter to enjoy a substantial existence, uncreated and consequently eternal. The school of Berkeley flatters itself that it proves the existence of matter not only to be unnecessary for producing the appearances of the universe, but impossible in itself. If this were so, it would furnish the most efficacious of arguments against absolute materialism and against atheism; but in this respect it fails. Absolute materialism cannot be combated except on its own ground; the weapons of Berkeley do not reach it.

According to the doctrine of the antagonists of Berkeley, two dramas are performed at one and the same time in the universe: the one passes, so to speak, behind the scenes, beyond the reach of created spirits; the other is performed in our understanding and is a translation of the first. But in the theory of Berkeley it is alleged that we have no motive whatever for thinking that the one drama which our faculties permit us to witness, that which is enacted in ourselves by means of the sensations, is the translation of any other; it is even maintained (in which I think his partisans go too far) that it is impossible that it should be.

It is evident that in this theory the sensible appearances are neither more nor less than what they would be in the contrary system; the means of ascertaining them are absolutely the same, namely, observation, experiments, reasoning; that this doctrine does not tend in the least to weaken our persuasion of the permanence of the established order, so far as it can be perceived by the human understanding and direct our intellectual actions, our affections, our reciprocal communication, all our operations; and that if the whole human race were to adopt it in good faith and act accordingly, there is nothing to fear that it would change its conduct in any respect: the individual would experience the same necessities [p. 343] than before, and would make the same efforts(a), that is, would put forth the same volitions, to satisfy them; society would subsist on the same footing; the moral relations would remain unalterable, and scientific discoveries would lose nothing, either of their certainty or of their importance. The pain of a burn is no less grave an evil to him who believes it produced by a non-spiritual substance acting immediately upon the organs, than to him who regards it as a sensation brought on by other sensations, according to a certain natural order; the voluntary determinations that would be aroused in both to escape the pain, and the effects of those determinations upon sensibility and consciousness, would be exactly the same. What, then, has the doctrine of Berkeley in common with the ravings of that philosopher of antiquity who doubted of everything, and consequently of his very sensations and of the natural connections among them, and who, placed on the brink of a precipice, found no more motive for moving in one direction than in another, because the consequence of his efforts seemed to him equally uncertain in every direction? But it is to be believed that there never was a philosopher who professed so absurd a doctrine, and that the doctrine of Pyrrho was ill understood by the ancients, as that of the Bishop of Cloyne has been generally by the moderns. If posterity had no other knowledge of the opinions of this illustrious philosopher than what is given by the writings which have impugned them, it would perhaps take them for a mere repetition of the ravings imputed to the disciple of Anaxarchus.

“There never was an individual,” says a justly celebrated writer, “who, unless he were mad and desirous of destroying himself, would not change his direction to avoid a precipice or to give passage to a cart; but there have been philosophers of the subtlest genius who have seriously doubted of the existence of the precipice and of the

(a) It is clear that in the system of Berkeley there are no true efforts, considered

as organic modifications, because there are no bodies nor organs; there are only sensations of effort. [p. 344] cart, and have succeeded in maintaining this paradox by specious arguments. Sensation, they say, proves nothing but sensation; to go further is the work of judgment. Considered in itself, sensation cannot deceive us; judgment, on the contrary, is liable to a thousand errors. But to infer, from the fact that judgment may be deceived, that it always is so when it refers our affections to external causes, is what constitutes the peculiarity of this system, and, I add, its futility and fallacy. It is true that these philosophers, in attempting to establish this Pyrrhonism, acknowledged that it would be absurd to act as if matter did not exist; so that their discovery, if it came to be proved, would be perfectly useless, and, notwithstanding that it were true, we should have to act in all cases as if it were not, under pain of immediate destruction.”(a)

(a) I know not why Dugald Stewart has regarded as slight the resemblance be‐

tween the Indian doctrine of the Vedanti and the system of Berkeley. “The fundamental tenet of the Vedanti school,” according to Sir W. Jones, “consisted, not in denying the existence of matter, that is, of solidity, impenetrability, and extended figure (to deny which would be lunacy), but in correcting the popular notion of it, and in contending, that it has no essence independent of mental perception, that existence and perceptibility are convertible terms, that external appearances and sensations are illusory, and would vanish into nothing, if the divine energy, which alone sustains them, were suspended but for a moment.” I believe I perceive in this exposition (setting aside a word here and there which perhaps does not exactly represent the ideas of the Vedanti) something that much resembles the ideas of the Bishop of Cloyne: I believe, above all, that I see in them the unsubstantial existence of matter, and the material affections reduced to mere determinations of the divine energy, such as I have endeavored to explain them in this chapter.

“I had yesterday a conversation,” says Sir J. Mackintosh, judge at Bombay, “with a young Bramin of no great learning. He told me, that besides the myriads of gods whom their creed admits, there was one whom they know by the name of Brim, or the great one, without form or limits, whom no created intellect could make any approach towards conceiving; that, in reality, there were no trees, no houses, no land, no sea, but all without was Maia, or illusion, the act of Brim; that whatever we saw or felt was only a dream, or, as he expressed it in his imperfect English, thinking in one’s sleep, and that the reunion of the [p. 345] I believe that the question relating to the real existence of bodies is altogether futile, inasmuch as its resolution would never lead to any practical or speculative consequence. But I believe also that the discussion of it may contribute to illustrate the nature of our sensitive perceptions, upon which the arguments for and against necessarily turn. In the preceding passage, for example, as in almost everything that has been written against the opinions of Berkeley, we see confounded two things which it is necessary to distinguish carefully in order to form a clear notion of sensitive perception; without which it is not possible to contemplate from its true point of view the doctrine of the Bishop of Cloyne. No one certainly who is in his sound judgment can doubt that a violent blow will be followed immediately by pain and perhaps by death; but one thing is the constant, necessary, indubitable connection of certain spiritual affections with others, to which is inseparably attached now pleasure, now pain, sometimes the multiplication of the sentient being, and sometimes its destruction; and another thing is the nature of the causes which make them arise in beings that are spirits. Berkeley, to whose system I believe this passage alludes, never thought of weakening the credit we give to the testimony of the senses, that is, to the judgments we deduce from our sensations, relative to their permanence and correspondence. When, on seeing an object, I think I perceive that it is of cylindrical figure and of a blue or straw color, I do no more than judge in consequence of the sensations I experience; that on approaching the object I shall not see in it edges or borders; that touch will not find them either; that the color perceived in the circumstances in which I find myself will be equally so if I contemplate the object in a stronger light or at a shorter distance, and that the sensations of other men who are in the circumstances that I am will resemble mine. These

soul to Brim, from whom it originally sprung, was the awakening from the long sleep of finite existence.” This exposition differs much from the preceding and from the theory of Berkeley. [p. 346] judgments are almost always confirmed by experience; sometimes, however, they deceive us. The object which from afar seemed to me cylindrical, examined near at hand by sight and touch, may be a prism; the cloth which by candlelight seemed to me black may by daylight be blue or purple. Now these judgments, which are those that guide us in life and in the study of physical nature, are not considered more fallible in the anti-material system than in any other. What Berkeley denies is that the sensations are produced by beings that have a real existence, distinct from that of the intelligent being who established and preserves the laws of physical nature, according to which the sensations are linked together, correspond and succeed one another in a certain manner. But this is manifestly a point on which we cannot ask information of the senses, because it lies beyond their reach.

Although the reality of bodies in the system of Berkeley refers only to the correspondence of the sensations, the difference between real and fantastic bodies is absolutely the same in it as in the others, and we arrive at the knowledge of it by the same means. He who doubts whether an object he has before his sight is real or fantastic goes to touch it, and if he cannot submit it to the examination of touch, he will look at it from various points. If it tells nothing to touch, or if it disappears from sight in circumstances in which, according to the laws of the physical universe, it ought to strike it, he will hold it for a phantom, for an optical illusion; if the contrary happens, he will judge it a veritable body. The disciple of Berkeley will do the same without apostatizing from his school: his judgments, in consequence of these operations, will be similar and he will express them in the same words.

Berkeley maintains that this notion of material substances is the work of philosophers, and that the common run of men recognize no other reality in bodies than their own sensations. If a man of the vulgar were told that the sun did not really exist, he would no doubt believe that it was meant to tell him that this luminary was nothing more than an impalpable appearance. The sensations of touch are the last criterion of the real existence of [p. 347] bodies. Let the system of Berkeley be explained to persons of good sense, and in the greater part of cases it will only succeed in making them believe that Philosophy is a vain art of proving chimeras and absurdities sophistically. Is it possible that so clear a thing should be denied? Can I doubt of the existence of this tree, of this stone, of this flower which I am seeing and touching? Can it be conceived that all these objects which surround me are mere appearances, against the concordant testimony of my senses? So almost all would express themselves. It seems, then, that men see the existence of bodies in the reality of the sensations, and especially in that of the sensations of touch: for them to deny the one is to deny the other.

But although men express themselves almost universally thus, the partisans of material substantiality interpret this language in a different way from Berkeley. I touch it; it exists: these are two propositions that say one and the same thing, according to Berkeley. I touch it; therefore it exists, is, according to Reid, a reasoning suggested by a special instinct. But an intuitive metaphysical idea that served in no way to guide men in the investigation and use of the objects of their needs, seems to me a thing altogether opposed to the ordinary reserve of nature, which furnishes us only those cognitions that interest our preservation and well-being, and to acquire them has given us in the perceptions, aided by the principle of causality and by the empirical principle, all that we need. A purely theoretical truth, suggested by a particular instinct, would have to be regarded as a most singular fact in the history of the understanding.

There are principles inherent in human reason without whose aid it is impossible to make use of the understanding and to conduct ourselves in life. Such is the belief in the stability of the laws of nature, the foundation of all physical and moral laws, and of all those judgments and reasonings in which by the experience of the past we foresee the future and adjust our operations to it. Such is the principle of causality, which makes us suppose for every phenomenon, for every new existence, a cause. The belief in the substantiality of bodies is not [p. 348] one of these principles, because it is necessary neither for the exercise of reason nor for the conduct of life.

The word matter may be taken in two different acceptations, and it is not improbable that the obscurity in which the question is enveloped arises in great part from philosophers not having sufficiently distinguished them. The existence of the cause of the sensations, as something distinct from ourselves, is admitted by all: by the Bishop of Cloyne no less than by the professor of Glasgow. Berkeley denies only that the sensations are produced by causes which have a substantial existence, separate from that of the Supreme Being, author of the laws of nature, according to which the affections of spirits succeed one another; and, limiting to this determinate sense the word matter, he denies consequently its substantial existence. But those who allege that his doctrine is repugnant to the common sense of men, that is, to one of the primary principles or truths of which I have just spoken, suppose, in my opinion, that Berkeley denies the existence of matter, not in this determinate sense, but in the general acceptation of cause.

There is in reality no repugnance between the anti-material theory and the principle of substantiality, which makes it necessary to conceive in every action an agent, in every accidental quality a substance, in every influence a real being that influences. The causes of the sensations have variable characters; they present themselves to us under different modifications. These modifications exist doubtless in them. If the material causes are nothing but pure influences of the divine energy, the modes of the material causes are modes of acting of the divine energy, and exist therefore originally in the divine substance, under the form of general laws.

Let us suppose that in the imagination of men there were a universal propension to figure to themselves the causes of the sensations as real beings, circumscribed to the places in which we experience them. There can be nothing more universal than the propension of men to refer, not the cause of the sensations, but the seat of sensibility, to their whole body; [p. 349] nor is there any apprehension which it is more difficult for us to dismiss, or which more often enters into the expression of our thoughts. Nevertheless we shall not therefore say that such an apprehension is suggested by a particular instinct, unless we admit erroneous instincts. Equally common among men has been the idea of universal materiality. Shall we admit it, then, as an instinctive truth? Supposing that men represented bodies to themselves as veritable substances, in the sense which philosophers give to this word, are we obliged to see in this tendency of the imagination an instinct in which nature reveals to us a metaphysical truth, and will it be temerity to cite it, as Dr. Reid says, before the tribunal of reason?

Dr. Reid imagines that, the substantiality of matter being taken away from the understanding, the sun, the moon and the stars disappear, leaving the world in darkness; the terraqueous globe sinks beneath our feet and returns to the bosom of nothing; our very friends and relatives abandon us, and each individual is reduced to a solitary existence, and even that not entirely secure. What more fitting illustration can be given of the ideas of the Bishop of Cloyne than the declamations and sarcasms in which his antagonists accuse him of destroying from the foundation the certainty of all our physical knowledge, and of tearing from us the sensitive perceptions? If even in the conceptions of these philosophers the distinction between the sensations and matter is so obscure, how much more must it be in those of the vulgar? For my part, I find it difficult to persuade myself that, if the external cause of the sensations were seen stripped of the attire of signs with which the fancy adorns it, and in that absolute nakedness in which the understanding must contemplate it, so much importance would have been given to the question of its substantial existence. What matters it whether these shadows, which glide into the imagination however much it strives to seize them, be veritable substances, or mere influences of an intelligence acting according to certain general rules upon inferior intelligences?

Let us observe that the existence of other spirits like [p. 350] our own has nothing to do with that of matter, considered as a real and independent being. We deduce the former from irresistible arguments of analogy. Considering objects as mere groups of influences, all the resemblances we observe in them subsist; and from sensible resemblances we cannot but infer the two intellectual phenomena which are revealed to us in them. A certain group of influences which I refer to the place where I am seems to me extremely like certain groups of influences which I refer to different places; is it not natural that I should represent to myself in these groups entities like that which my consciousness perceives in that one? My volitions produce a thousand modifications in the first group, and I see like modifications produced in the others; ought I not to attribute them to volitions of the same nature as mine? Let the degree of force which analogies of this kind ought to have be estimated, from their incalculable multitude and their continual repetition; let there be added that which results from the commerce between spirits by means of the modifications which some produce in the sensations of others, a commerce which comes to be so easy and rapid that each individual seems to himself to perceive directly the mental affections of those with whom he converses. As the substantiality of matter enters in no way into these analogies, we may express them in the very language of the people, giving to the word body the signification which Berkeley gives it; nay more, supposing we were to express them in another language, what would we take from their force by that?

It seems at first sight that, the substantiality being taken away from matter, the physical universe is a great void, peopled with vain appearances in nothing different from a dream; but if it be admitted that this long dream is in all its parts consistent with itself, and that all sentient beings dream it at one and the same time, it matters little that it be so called. This word excites in us the idea of falsity and illusion, because the apprehensions of the sleeping man are rejected by the same man when awake, as irreconcilable with all his other apprehensions, anterior and posterior, and with those of other men. Let this contradiction cease and the difference [p. 351] between reality and the dream will be reduced to nothing. The dream, moreover, might be alleged as a proof that our sensations do not necessarily suppose the substantiality of bodies. But, after all this, we have no motive for considering the theory of Berkeley otherwise than as merely possible. Its necessity, inferred from the fact that there can be no resemblance whatever between our ideas and the qualities of matter, we have already seen to rest upon an unsubstantial foundation.

## APPENDIX

Those who deny the existence of matter as substance do not deny that our sensations have causes different from the substance that feels. They recognize causes; they do not dispute about their existence, but about their nature. According to them, the causes of the substances are certain general laws established by the Creator.

Those who believe in the substantial existence of matter suppose the existence of general laws which determine the qualities and agencies of that supposed substance, and produce in this way the same order, the same varieties of sensations, that in the system of Berkeley are produced without the intermediary of the material substance.

The whole difference is reduced, then, to a mysterious, unknown intermediary, which some suppose and others reject: an intermediary that may be wanting without being missed; an intermediary that explains nothing; that is needed for nothing. The question could not be more frivolous or more sterile.

Why, then, have we dwelt so long upon it? Because it was necessary to reduce it to its just value, in order to show its frivolity; and because at the same time we hoped to bring into greater relief the true character of the sensitive perceptions, at least as I conceive them.

[p. 352]

Is it not singular that Cuvier, the man who has most conversed with matter, who has most dwelt upon contemplating it under all its relations, under all its forms, should have doubted of its existence? “The impression of external objects upon the I,” says Cuvier, “is the production of a sensation, of an image, of a mystery impenetrable to our mind; and materialism is a hypothesis so much the more venturesome, as it is impossible for Philosophy to give any direct proof of the actual existence of matter.”

But although the theory of Berkeley might in strictness be admitted as a possible supposition in the eyes of Philosophy, it is incontestable that it is opposed to some of the most essential dogmas of Catholicism and of almost all the Christian churches.

## CHAPTER I

On knowledge.

Experimental knowledge.—Knowledge a priori.—Principle of causality, of substantiality, of contradiction, of sufficient reason.—The empirical principle as the basis of certainty in experimental judgments.—The necessity these principles imply.—Erroneous judgments originating in sensible connections: how to avoid them.—Knowledge of the relations between sensations and their causes.—Conditions of all experience.—Conditions of knowledge a priori, according to Kant.—Principle founded on the stability of the laws of nature.—Relation of this principle to that of the divine omnipotence.—Analytic judgments.—Synthetic judgments.—Doctrine of Kant.—Victor Cousin.— Dugald Stewart.

The ideas, then, that do not come to us directly from observation, come to us indirectly from it by means of the faculties we have enumerated, aided, if one will, by certain instincts which to my mind all reveal themselves in the natural mobility of the imagination.

But to form an idea is not the same as to pronounce a judgment. To form the idea of a centaur, of a hippogriff, is not the same as to affirm its existence.

It is incontestable that in all our knowledge there are involved many judgments, and among them some of the most important, which nascent experience, confined as it is to the observation of individual facts, could not have [p. 356] given us.

When I refer certain olfactory sensations to the same cause that produces in me certain tactile sensations; when I refer, for example, to the flower I hold in my hand the fragrance that my smell perceives, I form a strictly experimental judgment. But even judgments of this kind, individual judgments, the first source of experience, presuppose certain instincts, which, generalized, are converted later into principles, into primary laws that preside over all the acts of the intelligence. Such is the principle of causality, which makes us refer every phenomenon to a cause; such the principle of substantiality, which does not allow me to conceive a quality, a modification, without a support, without a substance in which it exists; such the principle of contradiction, by virtue of which I cannot conceive that a thing both is and is not at the same time; such the principle of sufficient reason, by virtue of which I conceive that of everything that is, there is a reason why it should be what it is and not something else.

There is a peculiar principle constitutive of that experience which is truly such, which consists in generalized observations. When I see that sealing-wax, rubbed with a piece of wool, acquires the property of attracting the light little bodies that lie near, and, having made this experiment several times with the same result, I judge that in all of them the rubbing of the wax and the wool has produced and will produce the same effect, I take a great step beyond the limits of observation, for it is evident that I could not think thus if I did not proceed upon the principle of the stability of the laws of nature; upon the principle that I have called empirical, not because it is so itself, but because upon it is founded the generalization of all empirical results, the metamorphosis of an observed phenomenal connection into a constant phenomenal connection, into a necessary phenomenal connection. My observations doubtless make known to me, as far as they reach, the stability of certain connections; but to extend it beyond the actual sphere, and even the possible sphere, of my observations, and even of the observations of the whole human race, and even of the observations [p. 357] of all finite intelligences; to judge that it holds always, and that it is impossible for it to fail, is what neither perception, nor memory, nor imagination can lead us to, without the aid of a spontaneous tendency or instinct to judge so; nature suggests this judgment; our reason accepts it, and we reason with the empirical principle, making it not so much a premise as a supposition of all our judgments on matters of fact. We may formulate it thus: Given the cause, the effect necessarily follows; that is, given the antecedent phenomenon, the second phenomenon necessarily develops.1

“A thing cannot both be and not be at the same time” is the formula of the fundamental judgment called the principle of contradiction; a principle not only beyond the reach of observation, but necessary with an absolute necessity for all judgments, for all reasonings, for all knowledge. Suppose for a moment that such a principle did not exist: nothing could be proved, nothing could be judged, nothing could be known. The principle of contradiction is evidently a primary, universal, irresistible virtue, which not only admits of no proof, but does not permit anything to be proved or admitted without it.

The principle of causality is also necessary with an absolute necessity. To begin to exist and to have no cause are ideas that repel each other. Whether the principle of causality is derived from this other, “nothing produces nothing,” and is therefore not a true principle, that is, a supreme truth not derived from another; or whether this second principle, as it seems to me, is nothing but the first, expressed in a different manner, is a question of little importance. We cannot but admit the absolute necessity of the principle of causality, whether we resolve it into

1 M. Cousin has shown in the most luminous manner that the certainty of empir‐

ical judgments is not wholly due to experience, without the concurrence of the empirical principle; at least when they are general, that is, when they carry an observed connection over to all analogous observable cases. (Course of the History of Modern Philosophy. Year 1816–1817: section VII.) [p. 358] another which we cannot cease to admit without falling into contradiction, that is, without supposing that what is, is not, or what is not, is; or whether we find directly in it itself what compels us to accept it.

Another universal principle, and of absolute necessity, is that of sufficient reason, which we may formulate in this way: “nothing can be that has not a reason for being;” a principle which seems to coincide with that of the relation of causality, from which, however, it is distinguished, as the logical antecedent is distinguished from the efficient cause. Suppose, for example, a line B, from whose extremities, as centres, I describe two circles with a radius whose length is that of the line C; the line which joins the intersections of these circles has evidently each of its points at an equal distance from the extremities of the line B, and divides it into two equal parts; for any contrary supposition would lack sufficient reason, that is, logical antecedent, by virtue of the perfect symmetry of construction with respect to the extremities of the line B. The principle of sufficient reason is, with relation to logical dependence, what the principle of causality is with respect to phenomenal connections.

The principle of substantiality is also of absolute necessity. Given a modification, a phenomenon perceived, it is impossible for us not to suppose for it a support, a subject, a substance, a thing modified. Having perceived intuitively in ourselves the substantial I, we make it an image, a sign-idea, of all other substances.

There is a certain tendency of the understanding, likewise superior to all experience, and necessary to the representative value of what we know by means of the senses. By the principle of causality we refer our sensations to causes distinct from the substance that feels. But in sensitive perceptions there is something more than this vague reference. By the relations between sensations we feel ourselves inclined to represent to ourselves relations of the same kind between their causes. From the resemblance of sensations we infer the resemblance of their causes. From the succession of sensations, and from their more and less, we infer the [p. 359] succession and the more and less of their causes. This, however, is a tendency, an instinct rather than a principle. Thus it is that, obeying it blindly, we might often deceive ourselves; and in fact, not a few of our erroneous judgments relative to the phenomena of the material universe proceed from our yielding to this propensity without examination. Two similar sensations may sometimes be produced by dissimilar causes: the same water at the same temperature will give us, in certain circumstances, the sensation of heat, and in others the sensation of cold. What today produces an intense sensation may produce tomorrow a weak one. We have two successive sensations A, B; their causes may be simultaneous; the cause of A may perhaps be not prior but posterior to the cause of B.

But how shall we guard against this class of erroneous judgments, suggested by a tendency, by an evident instinct of the understanding in the exercise of the senses? We cannot avoid them except by means of observations, that is, by means of the senses themselves, comparing and reconciling their reports. Between the thunder and the lightning there seems to us to be a longer or shorter interval. But the observation of a great number of facts reveals to us that sound is propagated with much less velocity than light, and, this knowledge acquired, we are on our guard against judging these phenomena successive, even when the respective perceptions are so.

The special relation perceived in the sensations supposes a foundation, a special relation in the causes, but not precisely the same relation: to deduce this second relation from the first is one of the objects of the physical sciences. They tell us (confining ourselves to the preceding example): the sensation of sound, in so far as it represents an aposcopic phenomenon, does not give sufficient ground for believing that the aposcopic phenomenon is simultaneous with the sensation (understanding by simultaneous that in which it is not possible for us to perceive an interval): the plesioscopic phenomenon, that is, the impression of the air on the organs, is what coexists with the sensation; and we are not authorized to deduce from plesioscopic simultaneity the aposcopic [p. 360] simultaneity. On the contrary, there is always an interval, greater or less, sometimes perceptible, sometimes long, between the plesioscopic phenomenon and the aposcopic phenomenon; from which it follows that two sensations whose causes are simultaneous, or seem to be so, may have aposcopic causes between which there is a perceptible and sometimes a long interval. We must, then, before yielding to this instinct, which translates literally, so to speak, the relations of the sensations into relations of material causes, appraise the report of the senses and reduce it to its genuine significance.

Here there are several degrees to be distinguished. First, the relations between plesioscopic phenomena, although they have their foundation in aposcopic phenomena, do not suppose in them relations of the same kind. Thus the light that comes to us from a distant prism may make upon our visual organs an impression like that of the light that comes to us from a cylinder. In the second place, the relations between our organic impressions, although they have their foundation in plesioscopic phenomena, do not precisely suppose relations of the same kind in them: different predispositions in the organs may give rise to different organic impressions, notwithstanding the similarity of the external actions that affect them. In the third place, the relations between our sensations, although they have their foundation in organic impressions, do not precisely suppose relations of the same kind in them; for example, it is very possible that different predispositions of the soul may occasion different sensations, notwithstanding the similarity of the organic impressions. When many causes concur in the production of an effect, varying and diversifying it, it is necessary, in order not to deceive ourselves, to take them all into account.

Experience (and under this name we understand not only that which the senses form, but that of the inner, spiritual world, which the I contemplates in itself); although experience, by itself alone, that is, reduced to mere observation, could not have given us our first knowledge, our first knowledge has doubtless come to us with it; all knowledge [p. 361] chronologically prior to that nascent experience is a chimera. But at the same time it is incontestable that there is in the understanding a great number of judgments and of knowledge which are logically prior to experience, which are not logically derived from it, either by an immediate derivation or by a further derivation, because there can be no experience which does not imply them. “Every new phenomenon supposes a cause” is a principle that could not logically have come out of experience. But without an experience it is impossible that this principle could have sprung up in the understanding. Let us distinguish, then, with Victor Cousin, the psychological antecedents and the logical antecedents of human knowledge.

Judgments and knowledge are called empirical or a posteriori which are logically derived from experience, the principle of the stability of phenomenal connections being supposed; a principle which (we repeat it) is not in itself empirical, and to which we have given this name only because it is contained implicitly in all our empirical knowledge. Suppose the principle did not exist: experience would be of no use to us, it would be completely sterile; or rather, what we call experience would not exist, for it is nothing but the knowledge of the general laws of the universe, deduced from observations by means of the empirical principle, which supposes the stability of phenomenal connections; the general laws of the universe would be for us neither general nor laws, if we did not judge them stable.

We shall call non-empirical or a priori judgments and knowledge those which are not logically derived from experience. Kant attributes to them these two characters: universality and necessity; characters which, as Cousin observes, are not identical. Necessity supposes universality; but universality does not suppose necessity. But if necessity supposes, implies universality, we may omit the one of these two characters, the one that is necessarily implied in the other. Non-empirical or a priori judgments are, then, those which we conceive as necessary with an absolute necessity.

The necessity characteristic of non-empirical judgments is [p. 362] an absolute necessity; in purely universal judgments we conceive a kind of necessity, but not an absolute one; it is not necessary with an absolute necessity that unsupported sublunary bodies should fall; we can very well conceive a different order of things. The necessity of empirical knowledge arises from the principle implied in it, the stability of phenomenal connections. This principle being supposed, and the connection determined with its essential conditions, we hold it to be necessary. But its necessity is derived from that of the principle.

Is the principle of the stability of the laws of nature in itself a knowledge a priori in Kant’s sense? I believe we must answer that it is. But can we not conceive that phenomena might succeed one another fortuitously; that there might be no stable connections between them? That would lead us inevitably to the destruction of all empirical knowledge. The Author of nature might have established laws different from those we know; so be it. But without the existence of certain laws, those we know or others, empirical knowledge would not exist. The certainty of the empirical principle is not due to experience; on the contrary, the certainty of experience is due to the principle that dominates and governs it, the principle that in this sense we have called empirical, an abbreviated expression meaning the principle of empirical connections.

But is it necessary with an absolute necessity that phenomenal connections should be subject to constant laws? Let us suppose two phenomena exactly determined in all their circumstances and conditions, the phenomenon A and the phenomenon B. Might it not be that sometimes the phenomenon A should be followed by the phenomenon B, and at other times not? Is there in this a manifest repugnance? The affirmative seems to me evident. From the moment we made that supposition there would be neither causes nor effects; for the stability of phenomenal connections enters into the idea of cause, in whatever way the cause may be conceived. Thus the empirical principle, if it is not the very principle of causality, necessarily coexists with it.

That the Creator has subjected phenomenal connections to [p. 363] constant laws is a principle a priori and of absolute necessity. But, 1st, the Creator was able to choose at his pleasure between these or those laws, and the choice that has taken place is a fact, or rather a kind of facts, which we can reach only a posteriori; 2d, supposing a phenomenal connection perfectly known, supposing perfectly known one of these laws established by the Creator at his pleasure, the connection ought not even so to seem to us necessary with an absolute necessity: the Creator can suspend it, as he could establish it; acting without doubt in this suspension in conformity with other rules of a higher category, to which he willed from the beginning that these same laws should be subordinated: there is in this nothing derogatory to his infinite wisdom; nothing that ought to seem imperfection or inconsequence. Phenomenal connections, even if we were sure of knowing them perfectly, ought not, then, to be regarded as necessary except in a highly restricted sense; since, absolutely speaking, they might fail. They are necessary in so far as they conform to the general order, which is within reach of the limited human intelligence; they are contingent in so far as this order was in the beginning elective, arbitrary, and in so far as this order is subordinated to another, vaster order, which we only dimly descry, and which from time to time modifies or suspends the first.

In every judgment there is a relation, and in every relation two terms. The idea of one of the terms may carry the relation so involved in it that it is not possible to conceive it without the relation. Judgments of this kind are called analytic, because to form them it suffices to decompose the idea of one of the terms, among whose elements is necessarily found the relation that is the object of the judgment. When we say that bodies are extended, we draw from the idea of body the idea of extended, because we cannot conceive an unextended body; if we analyze the idea we have of bodies, we shall find in it, as a necessary element, the extraposition of their parts. And as analytic judgments do no more than unfold, explain an idea, Kant gives them also the title of explicative or illustrative. They add nothing to the idea; but they unfold it, explain it, and in this way illustrate it.

[p. 364]

They add nothing to the idea; but they unfold it, explain it, and in this way illustrate it.

At other times the relation is not necessarily comprised in one of the terms. “Unsupported sublunary bodies fall” is a judgment of this kind. It is true that it is a law of nature that unsupported sublunary bodies should fall. But this law might, absolutely speaking, not exist: there is no repugnance between the idea of unsupported sublunary bodies and the idea of not falling. If an unsupported sublunary body did not fall, it would not on that account necessarily cease to be an unsupported sublunary body. Relations of this kind add to the ideas of the terms something that was not in them; and from this addition results a new idea, a new compound. The judgments that express it are called for that reason augmentative and synthetic.

It is easy to see that analytic judgments rest upon the principle of contradiction: to say that a body is unextended would be the same as to say that a body is not a body. The truth of synthetic judgments does not rest upon this principle. Does it always rest upon the principle of empirical connections, as when I say that unsupported bodies fall? Or are there synthetic judgments whose truth is independent of experience? Let us examine.

Cousin cites as one of them this: “Every change, every new phenomenon, every new existence supposes a cause.” If the repugnance of the understanding to conceive a change without a cause is not resolved into the principle of contradiction, as it seems to me, in that case it must be admitted that there are synthetic judgments in which the understanding adds to a term a universal and necessary relation, independent of the principle of empirical connections. Kant calls them synthetic non-empirical judgments, synthetic judgments a priori.

Kant believes that every analytic judgment is a non-empirical judgment, a judgment a priori; and he believes at the same time that of synthetic judgments some are empirical a posteriori, whose truth rests merely on the principle of empirical connections; and the others empirical a priori, whose truth has not for its foundation [p. 365] experience, like the judgment of which we have just spoken, there is no change without a cause.

I believe we may admit without difficulty that every analytic judgment is independent of experience, and supposes it only psychologically; while every synthetic judgment is regularly the child of experience, limited in so far as it arises from observations, and general only in so far as it has been extended by the principle of empirical connections. Regularly, I say; because I think it necessary to except the existence of synthetic judgments a priori, reduced, as I conceive, to the principle of causality, to that of sufficient reason, and to that of empirical connections. The negation of any one of these three judgments, although the understanding cannot conceive it without manifest repugnance, does not seem to me to involve contradiction.

“The true distinction” (we copy Victor Cousin), “the true distinction that divides our knowledge into two diverse classes is that of the necessary and the contingent;” that of those which we conceive as necessary with an absolute necessity, and that of those which, with respect to our intelligence, are fortuitous and contingent, because their existence does not involve the principle of contradiction, nor is it repugnant to the understanding to conceive it.1 “This distinction is not founded on hypothetical classifications. . . . Traced by the hands of nature in the depths of human thought, there are no subtleties of reasoning that can efface it: it resists all the efforts of analysis, which finds itself forced to stop before it, as before an impenetrable wall. Let experience be generalized, let it be fecundated with the principle of empirical connections; the results will always be consequences that partake of the nature of their origin.”

“The principle of contradiction and the principle of sufficient reason are indispensable for all reasoning; the principle of

1 This phrase is not Victor Cousin’s. But it is necessary. The principle of causality,

that of sufficient reason, that of the stability of phenomenal connections, are not resolvable into the principle of contradiction; and yet they are necessary with an absolute necessity. [p. 366] contradiction serves to establish each of the steps of the reasoning, and the principle of sufficient reason to unite them, to establish the legitimacy of the consequence.”

“Will it be sought to resolve these two principles into other principles logically anterior? Vain effort! If it were a question of deducing the principle of contradiction from another principle, it would be necessary that we should not suppose the second known, and the first would therefore lack subsistence, since it might be and not be. In the same way, in the reasoning made to resolve the principle of sufficient reason, one must proceed either on the supposition that the antecedents of that reasoning do not necessarily bring their consequences with them, or on the supposition that they do: in the first case the legitimacy of the deduction will be disputable; in the second one will proceed upon the very principle that is to be proved, and the reasoning will be a vicious circle.”

“Even supposing that necessary principles could be legitimately deduced from contingent principles, this deduction itself could not be effected without the intervention of the principles of contradiction and of sufficient reason, that is, without supposing two irreducible principles, two principles which must be admitted without proof, because there is no possible proof without them.”

## APPENDIX

Dugald Stewart reduces to two classes the implicit judgments without which every judgment of reason is impossible.

The first comprises what he calls the primary elements of human reason. Such are: the constant judgment of our own identity, that which distinguishes original affections from anamneses, and that which gives to the anamneses the representation of their originals.

Dugald Stewart believes that without a reprehensible latitude in the use of words we cannot say that we are conscious of our own identity, which is the identity of the present [p. 367] self with the former self, a concept that involves the idea of time and consequently presupposes the exercise of memory. I confess that the force of this argument is wholly hidden from me. Is not the relation of personal identity simple when the soul perceives it by comparing its present affections with its recollections? Can the soul acquire it in a more direct manner?

“The judgment of our personal identity is involved,” says Dugald Stewart, “in every thought, in every action of the soul, and may be justly regarded as one of the simplest and most essential elements of the understanding. It is impossible to conceive an intellectual being to exist without it. But universal as it is among the individuals of our species, nobody but a metaphysician ever thinks of expressing it in words, or of reducing into the shape of a proposition the truth to which it relates. With respect to the rest of mankind, this judgment is not so much a knowledge as an indispensable condition for the exercise of our faculties. And for the very reason that it is one of the last elements at which it is possible to arrive in analyzing our intellectual operations, it would be contrary to all philosophy to suppose that a metaphysical discussion could throw the least ray of light upon this subject. All that can be done is to state the fact.”

By consciousness we acquire the knowledge of all the present modifications of our mind; our sensations, perceptions, recollections, judgments, reasonings, desires, fears, feelings, volitions, passions, etc. But does it perceive the presence of the affections in an immediate manner, as it perceives in certain sensations the quality of being agreeable or painful? The simultaneity of its present affections with the intuitions that represent them is a relation that the soul perceives in an immediate manner; but this, in my view, is not yet to perceive their presence. The comparison of recollections with present affections is what leads us to the distinction of the modes of being of our I into present and past. And only after these two classes are formed is it possible for us to refer to one of them the modes of being we are experiencing, and which constitute [p. 368] the immediate object of consciousness, and to the other the modes of being we have experienced, and which we perceive representatively in our recollections. We perceive presence, then, not only by perceiving the simultaneity of an affection with its intuition, but by perceiving the resemblance of an affection to a class of affections which have a certain peculiar character, a certain vividness, determinateness and congruence that distinguish them, and whose particular idea belongs, like all others, to memory.1

Without the confidence we place in the testimony of memory, it would not be possible to carry on a complicated and long discussion or argument, because the force of the deduction is founded on the certainty of the premises, and on their progressive and legitimate concatenation; and of the one and the other, as regards all the links of the discussion except the last, we have, at the time of deducing the final consequence, no other guarantee than memory. In a mathematical demonstration it often happens that we refer to propositions previously proved; which puts in a still clearer light the faith we give to the attestation of memory; and shows that in this class of knowledge, justly considered the most certain of all, the authority of the laws that govern human reason in the ordinary occurrences of life is tacitly recognized. Reject the testimony of memory as unworthy of full confidence, and mathematical certainty is destroyed at its foundations, as completely as if the truth of the axioms laid down by Euclid were denied.

Axioms form the second species of implicit judgments. Such are: “the whole is greater than any of its parts;” “two things which separately are equal to a third are also equal to each other;” “if equal quantities are added to equal quantities, the results of this addition are equal quantities;” and others of a similar nature. But I see no reason

1 Observe that a recollection is really a present and actual affection, although

representative of an earlier affection. [p. 369] for speaking of mathematical axioms exclusively. The same office is performed in reasoning, and there is the same ground for considering as implicit judgments various others which have no connection with the idea of quantity; e.g.: “the same thing cannot both be and not be at the same time;” “if one thing is prior to another and this is prior to a third, the first is prior to the third;” “if two objects are identical with a third object, they are identical with each other;” etc.

I observe also that all these axioms are true reasonings reduced to the form of a simple proposition. To say that if A=B, and B=C, A=C, what is it but that from these two propositions: A=B, B=C, the third A=C is legitimately derived? And what is this but to establish as a general rule that all reasonings that conform to this model, A=B, B=C, therefore A=C, are good and legitimate? In the same way, to say that the whole is greater than any one of its parts, what is it but to say that if A=B+C, A>B; and that all reasonings that can be reduced to this type, A=B+C, therefore A>C, conform to a general law that cannot deceive us? And to say that if equal quantities are added to equal quantities the results are equal quantities, what is it but to establish as legitimate this form of reasoning, A=B, C=D; therefore A+C=B+D? Recognizing likewise that if A is after B, and B is after C, A is after C, we establish this formula of reasoning: A after B, B after C, therefore A after C. Finally, when we say that a thing cannot both be and not be at the same time, we say in other terms that if A is B is a proposition that cannot be doubted, and if from the supposition C is D it results that A is not B, the supposition C is D is necessarily false; and we establish as sure this form of reasoning: A is B: if C were D, A would not be B; therefore C is not D. In short, axioms are nothing but formulas of reasoning that carry with them an irresistible evidence. When it is said, therefore, that they are judgments that are necessarily involved in our reasonings, it is said in substance that our demonstrative reasonings, to be correct, must

## PHILOS.   24

[p. 370]

conform necessarily to certain formulas; formulas that vary according to the kind of relation attended to in judgments.

Locke and Dugald Stewart have demonstrated that axioms are not principles, in the sense of premises or fundamental knowledge from which other knowledge is derived in the demonstrative sciences; and Dugald Stewart has shown that if the various theorems are like the stones that form the edifice of a science, axioms are like the mortar or cement that unites them and makes of them a solid and consistent whole. This is very easy to conceive, once axioms are considered as formulas of reasoning. These formulas do no more than represent certain intellectual procedures, and affirm their legitimacy as a fact of human reason, which it is impossible for us to disregard.

On the other hand, it is incontestable that an axiom or general formula of reasoning, placed alongside a special reasoning included in it, adds no light or evidence to it. I am no more convinced when I say, “The whole is greater than a part,” or in other terms, if A=B+C, A>B, than when, confining myself to concrete things, I affirm that the body is greater than the head, or the house greater than the parlor. All men, and philosophers themselves, reason almost always in the second way; and among persons who dispute in good faith it will rarely happen that it is necessary to have recourse to an axiom to settle the question. All that can be done by this means is to make manifest which of the two disputants conforms to the general formulas of reasoning, and which infringes them. D’Alembert has said very well that, far from axioms occupying the first place in the sciences, there is not even any need to enunciate them.

Axioms, however, are not, as this illustrious philosopher has said, the expression of one and the same idea by means of two different terms. When I say that “the whole is greater than a part,” the terms whole and greater than a part, or A=B+C and >B, do not express one and the same idea. What D’Alembert has said of axioms applies only to the hypotheses signified [p. 371] by definitions, and to judgments in which the identity of two objects is affirmed: concepts, the one and the other, to which cannot be attributed the sterility from which axioms suffer, since from the former, as from their true sources, all the mathematical sciences flow, and the most luminous physical theorems are often propositions in which a relation of identity is affirmed. What an immense series of theorems is not derived from this definition: the circumference of the circle is a line that returns upon itself, and whose points are all equally distant from another point? And what discovery more important and fruitful than this: the force that makes unsupported sublunary bodies descend perpendicularly is the same force that holds the moon in her orbit?

Dugald Stewart counts among the primary elements of human reason the propensity to suppose an efficient cause for everything that begins; but I believe that this kind of implicit judgment belongs more properly to the class of axioms. What Dugald Stewart calls primary elements of the intelligence belong properly to the thinking subject, axioms to the object thought of.

Dugald Stewart counts besides among the primary elements of human reason the belief in the substantiality of bodies, which is not an axiom. Here, then, if it were so, is an objective primary element, an act of consciousness that informs us of what passes outside the soul . . . what do I say? . . . of what passes beyond the reach of the senses.

We have proved that the theory of Berkeley presents nothing absurd except to those who have not stopped to examine it. The substantiality of bodies cannot be proved, and we are compelled to believe it: therefore this belief is a primary element of human reason. Such is Stewart’s argument. But it is false that we are compelled to this belief, as we are compelled to believe that the whole is greater than a part, or that a thing cannot both be and not be at the same time.

Common sense is alleged in favor of the substantiality of matter. So (metaphorically) is called that fund of intelligence that belongs to all men, and of which no one [p. 372] who is in his senses can divest himself, though he would. The primary elements of reason, the axioms, the truths that have complete certainty and are within reach of all, are the peculiar objects of common sense; a denomination to which some give a more extensive meaning than others, and of which much abuse has been made in modern times, because the limits within which the jurisdiction of this irrecusable tribunal ought to be confined have not been traced.

But give common sense whatever extension you will, can it inform us of what lies absolutely beyond the perceptive faculties of man? Has the vulgar the remotest idea of the subtle difference that exists between the conception of Reid and that of Berkeley as to the mode of existence of matter? There is nothing more manifest or more natural in the vulgar than the belief in the motion of the sun; a belief that would be universal today if scientific observations had not banished it from the understanding of a small number of men; that belief was doubtless universal at another time; even today it is indubitable to an immense majority of the human race. Could not common sense, then, three centuries ago, have been alleged in favor of that belief with more foundation than it is now alleged in favor of the substantial existence of matter, as philosophers conceive it? Confessing themselves ignorant of what matter is in itself, what authorizes them to pronounce that it is something entirely distinct from the supreme activity and from created sensibility? Is there not in both things a rash judgment, a deduction that nothing legitimates? In reality the vulgar conception, which, misinterpreting the report of the senses, calls real the apparent motion of the stars, is much less absurd than the philosophical conception of substantiality, concerning which the senses neither depose nor can depose; for which the philosophers themselves give us no more guarantee than common sense, which is nothing else but their particular sense; and which, in short, is needed for nothing either in the study of nature or in that of practical life.

[PDF 388]

On judgment and its various kinds.

Definition of judgment.—Dr. Reid.—Dugald Stewart.—Difference between knowledge and judgment.—Division of judgments: perceptive judgment; deductive judgment; testimonial judgment.—Ideas that determine judgments. —The proposition.—Elements of which it is composed.—Negative propositions.—Relation of the subject to the attribute.—Supposed doctrine concerning judgment.—Absolute quality recognized in judgment.—Double aspect under which judgment is considered.—Certainty: its different kinds.— Absolute certainty.—Kinds of evident judgments.—Intuitive judgments; deductive judgments.—Definition.—Description.—Definitions of thing and of name: an arbitrary distinction.—Conditions of true definition.—Division and classification.—Requisites of true division.—Designation of classes, orders, genera; groups, families.

I

It is commonly said that judgment is “that act of the soul in which one thing is affirmed or denied of another”; but since in negative judgments a relation of difference is really affirmed, and since difference, by making its term negative, is converted into resemblance,1 I believe that we may consider all judgments as substantially affirmative.

The defect of the foregoing definition, according to Reid, lies in this, that although by affirmation or negation we express our

1 To say that gold is not transparent is to say that gold differs from transparent

bodies, or that it is of the class of non-transparent, that is, opaque, bodies. [p. 374] judgments to others, judgment is nevertheless in itself a solitary act of the soul, to which this outward affirmation or negation is not essential; and therefore, the definition being admitted, it must be understood of mental affirmation or negation only, and if so we do nothing but substitute for the word judgment another expression perfectly synonymous. To say that we affirm or deny mentally is the same as to say that we judge: the first expression is neither clearer nor more significant than the second. Consequently, what is given as a definition of judgment is not truly one: it does not explain it; what it does is to point it out; as if, on asking what amber is, one were to answer here it is.

“All that can be done,” says Dugald Stewart, “is to describe the occasions on which we judge, so as to direct the attention of others to what then passes in the mind. When we give our assent to an axiom; when, after perusing the demonstration of a theorem, we assent to the conclusion; when we pronounce concerning the truth or falsity of any proposition, or the probability or improbability of any event, the power by which we are enabled to perceive, or think we perceive, what is true or false, probable or improbable, is called in logic the faculty of judgment. The same word, too, is frequently used to express the particular acts of this power.”

To affirm or deny mentally one thing of another is to affirm or deny mentally a relation between them. The soul can affirm or deny nothing but relations. But although it is not possible for the soul to judge except upon conceptions of relation, it often happens that it conceives relations without affirming or denying them. The imagination is incessantly occupied with conceptions of relation upon which the soul pronounces no judgment whatever.

There is a certain difference between knowledge and judgment. Knowledge is the power the soul has of renewing a judgment. If I have once judged that tobacco is narcotic, so long as I have the power of renewing this judgment by means of memory, I have knowledge of the soporific virtue of tobacco. Thus a man of much knowledge is one who [p. 375] has the power of renewing a great multitude of judgments, which he uses to direct his intellectual operations and his conduct in life. Knowledge is possession and judgment is use. And just as possession always begins with occupation, knowledge has in all cases begun with judgment.

Judgments are of various kinds. A perceptive judgment is one that we form by means of present perceptions or of perceptions that we recollect. Such are the judgments we form about the color of the objects we see or have seen, about the dimensions of the objects we measure or have measured, about the states in which our soul is or has been. I feel cold, this flower is fragrant, last night I was at the play, are perceptive judgments.

A deductive judgment is one that we deduce from preceding judgments or from definitions, by means of reasoning. Such is the following: “In the circle every perpendicular drawn from the circumference to the diameter is a mean proportional between the two segments of the diameter.” For this we neither perceive at present, nor have ever perceived, but deduce by reasoning from the nature of the circle, that is, from its definition. Deductive judgments also are these: “The orange blossom is fragrant; the lily is white.” For by these propositions we mean that all orange blossom is fragrant, and every lily white; which it is clear we neither perceive nor can perceive, but infer (by virtue of the principle of the stability of the laws of nature, which guides us instinctively) from the constant observations we have made of the fragrance of the orange blossom and of the whiteness of the lily.

A testimonial judgment is one that we owe to the testimony of other men who have formed it by their own observations or reasonings. Such are those we pronounce on the situation and qualities of places, of which travelers give us information; on past events which historians transmit to our knowledge; on scientific truths which we have attained not by our own observations or reasonings, but by the communication that has been made to us of those truths by [p. 376] those who have learned them by observing or reasoning.

Strictly speaking, the judgments that constitute primary and secondary sensitive perceptions are deductive; for all of them are the fruit of an early experience, that is, have been drawn from observations by reasoning. The primitive reference which makes us refer the sensation to a cause distinct from the self is the only one that, in sensitive perceptions, seems to have a better title to be considered as not deductive; but in reality it is so. If an instinct dictates it to us, it is by impelling us to deduce it from the intuitive perception of the sensation, by means of the principle of causality, which is another of those that instinctively guide us.

Testimonial judgment is likewise reducible, and far more clearly, to the deductive. For if I believe, for example, that Cadiz was a Tyrian colony, it is because I judge that the testimony which the ancient writers give us of it is worthy of credit. “Trustworthy ancient writers relate that Cadiz was a Tyrian colony: therefore Cadiz was a Tyrian colony.” Such is the mental formula of all testimonial judgments.

II

Judgments, according to what has been said, presuppose ideas between which we perceive relations.

There are ideas that faithfully represent objects by means of renewed perceptions. They form the first stock of memory. But there are objects which we cannot reach in this way; objects of which we have had no perceptions; of which we consequently cannot have ideas of our own, and which we represent to ourselves by means of other ideas, which serve us as signs or images, and take the place of the proper ideas we lack.

The imagination figures to us individuals whom we do not know, and even individuals whom we know not to exist, combining at will, not only features, limbs, forms, colors of individuals of the same class that we have seen, but features, [p. 377] limbs, forms, colors that we have seen only in other classes of objects. Its mobility being excited, it figures to itself new classes of beings by means of new and capricious combinations of anamnesis; it figures monsters, genii, gods. It takes one step more. It conceives classes of beings that it cannot represent even in this way; classes of beings that have no forms accessible to human intelligence: beings whose existence reason sometimes affirms, sometimes denies, sometimes believes merely possible. And what does the imagination need for this last effort, to conceive beings different from all we know? It needs only, as the question itself says, the relation of difference.
