It figures to itself beings between which and all those that it knows there is the same relation as between white and black, for example, as between the animal and the stone, between spirit and matter. The idea of difference is, to be sure, in this case not an adequate idea; because every adequate idea of relation supposes two terms that we know, and here the one of the terms of the difference is entirely unknown; but the differences we have formerly perceived serve us as images to represent those that we do not perceive, nor are given to perceive.

By means of sign-ideas, and supposing only the natural possibility of the imagination, the soul rises to the ideas of being in general, of the possible, of the infinite.

III

Judgment expressed in words is called a proposition; but not every proposition expresses a judgment. It is easy to recognize the propositions that express judgments, because in them something is affirmed or denied. “Cicero was the first of the Roman orators,” “there was no play last night,” are propositions that express judgments. There are others in which the verb expresses merely a wish, a condition, a simple conception that is neither affirmed nor denied.

“May Heaven make you happy!” is a proposition that signifies [p. 378] a mere wish. In this sentence: “If you bear your labors with resignation, they will in the end be bearable to you”: the incident proposition, you bear your labors with resignation, signifies a condition whose reality we leave out of account. Finally, in this sentence: “I fear that war cannot be avoided,” the incident proposition war cannot be avoided is a pure conception that is neither affirmed nor denied; the judgment that accompanies it belongs properly to the verb fear.

Sometimes the principal part of the proposition is wrapped up in a single word, followed by others that, if we adopted the ordinary procedure, would be the government of the verb. “Woe to thee!” “Oh vanity of human things!” are equivalent to “I grieve for thee,” “I marvel at the vanity of human things.”

Let us confine ourselves to simple or compound propositions that declare judgments. “God exists” is a simple proposition in which the existence of God is affirmed: “I fear that war cannot be avoided” is a complex proposition in which fear is affirmed as a state of the self. Logicians decompose them into three elements: subject, which is the thing of which something is affirmed or denied; predicate, which is what is affirmed or denied; and copula, which is the verb to be or another of similar signification, which, whether expressed or wrapped up in another verb, links the predicate with the subject. In “God is infinite,” the subject is God, infinite the predicate, and is the copula. If the proposition has no expressed copula, the verb is resolved into two elements; copula and predicate. Thus lives is resolved into is a living being; loves into is a lover or is loving.

But it is much simpler and more exact to consider the proposition as composed of only two elements, the subject and the attribute. The verb to be is a true attribute; the most general of all, because it comprehends all the other verbs, as the word being or thing comprehends all substantives. All verbs that do not signify pure existence signify modifications of existence, as all substantives that do not signify being in general signify particular species or forms of being. There is, then, no more reason for decomposing these verbs in the manner commonly done; for decomposing [p. 379] I read into I am a reader, I live into I am a living being, God into divine being, man into human being, body into corporeal being, and in short any substantive that does not signify being in general into the substantive being or thing and an adjective: a wholly gratuitous decomposition, and moreover vicious, because it complicates language instead of simplifying it.

In negative propositions the negation is a part of the attribute. “Corporeal pleasures do not satisfy the soul” is equivalent to “corporeal pleasures are not satisfying to the soul,” “or corporeal pleasures are incapable of satisfying the soul”: the subject is the entire class of corporeal pleasures, and the attribute the class of things incapable of satisfying the soul: “No man is exempt from falling into error” is equivalent to “every man is a being not exempt from falling into error,” or “every man is a being liable to fall into error”: the subject is the entire class of men, and the attribute the class of beings liable to err. “Nothing earthly lasts” is equivalent to “every earthly thing is a thing not durable,” or “every earthly thing is perishable”; the subject comprehends all earthly things, and the attribute the class of perishable things.

The subject is almost always less extensive than the attribute. Propositions that signify identity, such as these: “Man is a rational animal”; “the circumference is a curve that returns upon itself and in which all the points are at an equal distance from another point,” are the only ones in which the attribute is not more extensive than the subject. Both have in them the same extension.

The subject represents sometimes an individual and sometimes a class. The attribute in propositions not significant of identity always represents a class.

The attribute always has less comprehension than the subject, except in identical propositions; because except in these the attribute of the proposition is no more than one of those that belong to the subject. In identical propositions the subject and the attribute signify one and the same thing with different words; all the attributes of the subject are therefore attributes of the attribute.

[p. 380]

IV

Those who say that the object of judgment is always a relation of resemblance or of difference between two ideas have stopped, so to speak, at the surface of this operation of the soul, and have not made it sufficiently known.

To judge that a thing is green or is not green is to reduce it to the class of objects that I call green, or to exclude it from it, because between that thing and the green objects I find or do not find all the resemblance that these are accustomed to have among themselves. To indicate a quality it is necessary to indicate a resemblance, if the quality is positive, or to indicate a difference, if the quality is negative.

Nevertheless, as the affection by whose means I know greenness is an absolute affection, an affection that does not arise from the juxtaposition of two other affections, greenness is an absolute quality. To judge, then, that a thing is green or is not green, is to recognize in it an absolute quality as the foundation of the resemblance or difference that we declare between it and green objects. But how does the soul acquire the knowledge of this absolute quality? We have already said that it does not see it directly, that it symbolizes it by a sensation, referring the sensation to it as its effect, and representing the cause by the effect. The judgment, then, that we pronounce on the existence of the absolute quality is in this case the expression of a relation of causality. In every judgment in which we affirm the existence of an absolute quality in a material object, there is a conception of a relation of causality, besides the conception of resemblance or difference which I make use of to express the other conception. When I say that an object is green it is as if I said that a certain cause which I do not know produces in my soul an affection like that which the objects I call green produce. I indicate a relation of causality by a relation of resemblance, and it is manifest that of these two relations the more important is the first, of which the second is no more than a sign. The sign is important, doubtless, because upon its [p. 381] good or bad application depends the truth of the judgment. If I should judge, for example, that a certain object I have not seen is blue, the error of this judgment would consist in believing that the object produces in the sentient beings who see it the same effect as that produced by the bodies called blue; but the impropriety would arise, not from the bad choice of the sign, but from having attributed to the body in question an effect that it does not produce in sentient beings, a quality that it does not possess. Thus this conception, which regards the relation of causality, is that which decides the truth or error of the judgments we make on absolute corporeal qualities. The same applies to relative qualities.

To judge that the phenomenon A is followed by the phenomenon B is to reduce the relation I conceive between the two phenomena to the relations that I have designated in language by the denominations before, after, posterior and anterior, or other equivalents. This reduction means that the relation now conceived is similar to the relations of the class that are signified by the words before and after. Consequently, the resemblance does not now turn upon an absolute quality, as in the foregoing example, but upon a relative quality, because the means by which I know the before and after of any two phenomena whatever is a spiritual modification that arises from the comparison or juxtaposition of two other modifications. Modifications, as well as the qualities of corporeal objects, are what prepare the judgments that turn upon spiritual modes or qualities. When I say that I am sad I express immediately a relation of resemblance, but in reality what I propose to indicate is a state, a particular modification of the mind; a modification which I refer to my own substance; I make use, then, of a resemblance as of a sign to express a certain spiritual state, and to express it as a modification of my own substance, as a modification with which I identify myself.

We see, then, that there is indeed in every judgment a relation of resemblance or difference which is an immediate object, but not the essential object; which belongs rather to the proposition, and [p. 382] so to speak, to the rind of the judgment, than to the intellectual act in itself. There are in judgment two affirmations: that of a quality, which is in itself absolute or relative, but which is always known to us by a conception of relation; and that of the resemblance or difference of the being in which we conceive this quality with a certain class of beings, whose name, by virtue of that conception, we give to it.

This resemblance or difference, which is the immediate signification of the proposition, is certainly not the most important object of the judgment. When I say that the glass A is green, or that the tower B is taller than the palm C, I represent to myself the greenness of A, or I represent to myself the heights of B and C and at the same time a relation of more and less between them; and the same is represented to himself by him who hears me. The proposition says materially that the glass A, by virtue of the absolute quality that I conceive in it, resembles a certain class of objects, and that the pair of objects B, C, by virtue of the relative quality that arises from the perceptions of B and C, resembles a certain class of pairs of objects; but this idea of resemblance is a means, not an end; its office is only to excite the idea of greenness and of the more and less of height; it makes in the understanding only the slight impression necessary for us to conceive a certain absolute quality in the first case, and a certain relative quality in the second; and once this office is performed it disappears.

This double aspect under which we consider judgment is of great importance in the theory of reasoning; because the reasoning process is subject to diverse laws, according as we attend to the relation of resemblance, whose idea is like the rind of the judgment, or to the quality, whether absolute or relative, which constitutes its principal object, and whose idea is like its kernel and its true substance. The rules of the syllogism refer to the external relation of resemblance; geometrical demonstration and various other kinds of reasoning more fruitful than the syllogism turn upon diverse relations, and are subject to laws different from those of reasoning.

Only, then, in considering the external form of judgment can it be said that its object is a relation of resemblance or of difference.

[p. 383]

But even under this aspect we may say that the object of judgment is a relation of resemblance, because, as we have already observed, the expression in which the subject is excluded from the class signified by the attribute includes the subject in the class of objects that differ from the attribute, and thereby makes it resemble them. To say that the soul is not extended is to say that it is non-extended, that it is inextended, that it resembles inextended objects. Further on we shall see how much the theory of the syllogism is simplified in this way, the syllogism being, as we have said, a reasoning that turns upon the superficial relation with which we formulate judgments.

The faith we give to our judgments is called certainty, and is of different kinds and degrees.

Absolute certainty is that which we give to judgments that involve necessary relations of absolute necessity. To this class belong in the first place the evident judgments that of themselves irresistibly carry the assent of the soul, and in which there is no need of any demonstration or proof for us to know the absolute necessity of the relation contemplated. When we see a compound object and compare the magnitude of the whole of it with the magnitude of one of its parts, it is impossible for us not to perceive that that whole is greater than that part; and we generalize this judgment by saying that “the whole is greater than the part.” This is not a consequence that we draw from the observation of various particular cases by virtue of the principle of empirical connections, as when, after observing that all the jasmines presented to us have an agreeable odor, we affirm that the jasmine is fragrant, an expression equivalent to saying that every jasmine is so, has been so and will be so; but a general judgment comprehending all the analogous particular judgments that present themselves more or less distantly to the soul, as “my body is greater than my arm,” “this house is greater than that hall,” etc., and representative of all the possible particular judgments in which a whole is compared with one of its parts.

Reciprocally, the judgment I make in saying that my body is greater than my arm is not a consequence of the judgment [p. 384] general, “the whole is greater than the part,” but the same judgment under a general form. And it may even be said that the evidence with which we perceive in a given compound the relation of more and less between the whole and the part is clearer and more forcible than the evidence with which we perceive it in general by means of the particular judgments, which are produced abbreviatedly and rapidly in the soul. Thus it is that, in order to perceive a general relation clearly, we have to formulate it by attending to some specific or individual applications.

These general judgments of necessary relations, whose truth cannot be proved by deduction, and whose proof, if there could be one, would give no more light to the understanding than they of themselves offer it, are called axioms; and we have already seen that all our reasonings involve them, not precisely as principles from which we deduce consequences, but as implicit truths without which the exercise of reason is impossible. If we admitted, for example, that two quantities which separately are equal to a third may be unequal to each other, this alone would suffice to convert the mathematical sciences into a labyrinth of contradictions, in which the understanding could see no light nor take a step.

The intuitive perceptions that reveal to us the operations already examined of our self constitute another kind of evident judgments, which are as particular as the others are general. The consciousness that forms them is incapable of error. When the soul gives itself notice of what passes in it, it is not given it to doubt the veracity of its testimony. To suppose that I could deceive myself when I perceive in myself a desire would be to contradict oneself in terms. And yet it is indisputable that we sometimes believe we perceive in the soul things that really are not. We believe, for example, that we immediately perceive the colors of a body, when we do no more than perceive a certain affection in our mind, and refer it to a certain external cause. We believe we have general ideas that represent to us something that is repeated uniformly in the individuals of the genus, when we have only ideas of individuals, ideas of individual resemblances, and ideas of names. What does this prove [p. 385] but that we sometimes mistake the enchantments of the imagination for the testimony of consciousness? Truly intuitive judgments cannot deceive us, but we are not always sure of recognizing them. This is one of the most frequent causes of error among psychological writers. Thus it is that we see them defend opposing systems, each invoking in favor of his own the authority of the inner sense, which is what we call consciousness.

Intuitive judgments are judgments of necessary connection. If I perceive that I desire, I necessarily desire. On the other hand, judgments in which a necessary connection between two ideas is perceived are by their nature intuitive; because relations between ideas cannot be perceived except by consciousness. In both, therefore, the evidence is intuitive. Absolute evidence, metaphysical evidence, intuitive evidence, are synonymous expressions. Mathematical evidence is intuitive evidence applied to relations of more and less.

But not every judgment of absolutely necessary connection is evident, because it often happens that this connection does not show itself at first sight, and is susceptible only of being proved demonstratively by reasoning. Such are the necessary connections like 7+8=15, and the theorems of geometry and of algebra. There are, then, two things that produce absolute certainty, evidence and demonstration. The title of certainty is sometimes given to demonstrative truths, but with less propriety.

All evident judgments are perceptive; but not every perceptive judgment is evident. The judgments that accompany sensitive perceptions are subject to error. I hear a musket fired and shortly after I hear a cannon fired. If I judge that the cannon shot was posterior to the musket shot, I may err; because the order in which I experience the sensations may often be different from the order in which the movements have occurred that, setting the air in vibration, produce them in my ear. If I limited myself to judging that the sound of the cannon has affected my ear after the sound of the musket, my judgment would not be susceptible of error. When from this relation

## PHILOS.     25

[p. 386]

of priority between the first and second sensation I infer the same relation between the two remote, aposcopic causes, between the cannon shot and the musket shot, my judgment may be erroneous, because I deduce from the order of the sensations a consequence which almost always conforms to the facts, but which sometimes fails. The judgments, then, that accompany sensitive perceptions, and that often suffer from error, are not properly perceptive, but deductive. If we call them perceptive judgments it is because we include in perception certain intellectual processes that properly belong to reasoning.

I perceive the smell of a rose, and I judge that there is near me a rose whose effluvia strike my sense of smell. This judgment seems more closely bound up with the sensation, and yet it is fallible. Other causes may affect my smell as the rose is wont to affect it. If I limited myself to judging that the odor I perceive is like that of the rose, there would be much less danger of erring. What makes me fall into error is the inferring, from the existence of a sensation that may be produced by various causes, the existence of a particular cause; and consequently, it is not here perception but reasoning that errs.

But even when considered in their first and genuine indications, the judgments that constitute sensitive perceptions may not be exempt from error. It smells of roses is a judgment not entirely sure; the recollection of the smell of a rose may be unfaithful or obscure, and the resemblance, consequently, fallacious. The more part memory has in these judgments, the more danger there is that they will lead us astray.

In the judgments that constitute or accompany sensitive perception, or what is the same, in the judgments that constitute primary and secondary sensitive perceptions, there is never evidence. When of two bodies that I am looking at I judge that the one is larger than the other, it will often happen that the intellectual representations of their sizes evidently yield the relation A>B; but the sensitive perceptions do not turn upon relations of spiritual [p. 387] modes, but upon relations of corporeal modes; and as the relations of spiritual modes may represent with more or less fidelity the relations of corporeal modes, nothing authorizes me to believe that the relation which my understanding perceives necessarily exists in the corporeal universe. And even if we believed ourselves authorized to think so, that relation would not be directly perceived but deduced; it would be proved to us by virtue of its conformity with the laws of nature, but could not be called evident: and what is more, could not be called demonstrated, because demonstration requires a series of evident relations.

But although the judgments that we make by the ministry of the senses, aided by the principle of empirical connections, are never evident, they may nevertheless be most certain, such, for example, as these: sublunary bodies, left to themselves, fall: fire placed near wax melts it: air resists the motion of bodies, and gradually diminishes their velocity. For these judgments to lead us into error it would be necessary that some of the laws that govern the material universe should fail, and that the principle of empirical connections should deceive us. It happens sometimes that natural laws are not formulated with sufficient precision in our understanding, because we have not exactly determined their conditions; and when in reality nature is uniform in its mode of acting, it may nevertheless appear to us that a phenomenon contravenes a natural law because it does not fit our formula. Physical certainty, the certainty with which we accept empirical connections, will therefore be more or less strong, according to the assurance we have of knowing all the conditions, all the elements of a natural law. It will also happen that in the applications of a perfectly known natural law to a particular case that presents itself to us, we are sometimes deceived, because, not knowing the fact sufficiently, we erroneously suppose that the law is to be applied to it.

But however great physical certainty may be, it will never attain the force of absolute certainty. Most certain is the individual judgment I form that this body which I am [p. 388] touching produces or is capable of producing in all individuals who bring their tactile organs near it, sensations similar to those that it produces in mine; and for it to cease to be so there would need to be an infraction of the physical laws of the universe. But this infraction is not for my understanding absolutely impossible, as is the non-existence of the necessary relations of ideas, or as is the non-existence of pain in my soul when consciousness assures me that I feel it. The constancy of the physical laws is not of absolute necessity. Physical certainty, the certainty with which our understanding accepts the universality of empirical connections, admits very different degrees; not because the physical laws are more or less constant, but because it often happens that our ideas do not formulate the general laws and the particular facts with complete fidelity. The less the danger that the formula may not be completely faithful, or that the particular fact may not have been observed in all its important details, the less weak is the certainty of the judgments we pronounce on material phenomena; but however strong it may be, it will never have over the understanding a certain empire like the certainty of evidence or demonstration.

But although physical certainty, taken in a general sense, is susceptible of different degrees, it must be observed that we are accustomed to take this expression in a particular sense, understanding by it the maximum degree of confidence that we can give to our judgments when they turn upon corporeal qualities, or upon the phenomena of the material universe. The other degrees are given the title of possibility.

I have spoken thus far of the empirical connections that we hold to be infallible; as to those others to which we do not give this character, it is plain that they are never accompanied by physical certainty but by a simple possibility. That upon a certain appearance of the clouds rain should follow, or that the application of a certain remedy should have in a given case the effect for which it is generally applied, are not invariable connections, and the degree of faith we give them is proportioned to the constancy with which they are realized. The principle, nevertheless, of the greater or [p. 389] less confidence that we give them is always one and the same: the stability of the laws of nature, which we suppose in one case sufficiently known for us to determine its affinity, and in others suspend until we dispel the obscurity or vagueness of the conditions and modifications with which they present themselves.

The certainty of our judgments relative to spiritual phenomena has no particular name. In these judgments, as in the others, it is a question of phenomenal connections, well or ill observed; in them the certainty is of the same nature and susceptible of the same gradations of possibility as in the relations of material phenomena. There would be no inconvenience, therefore, in considering the certainty relative to psychological phenomena as a species of physical certainty; nor would the use of the term in this sense have anything improper in it.1

Definition is a species of proposition, by whose means we determine an object, in such a way that its characteristic qualities are made known, and, once known, it is not possible to confound it with another.

If the object is real, definition represents a judgment or a set of judgments. In the first case, the definition has more properly this name; in the second it is ordinarily called description. When it is said that “consciousness is a faculty by which the soul perceives itself,” a definition properly so called is given, whose attribute consists of two elements, the first a genus in which the defined species is comprehended, and the second a difference, which separates it from all the other species comprehended in the genus: Faculty of the soul is the genus: by which the soul perceives itself is the difference. Here is a description: “the tiger is a mammal, quadruped, carnivorous animal; it walks on the tips of its toes, and is armed with strong claws; it has a round head and its skin is transversely striped with black, on a ground above white, beneath tawny; it is one of the

1 Physic in Greek is nature in general, not precisely corporeal nature. [p. 390] strongest and swiftest of quadrupeds, and the cruelest of all.”

If the object of the definition is a conception of the understanding, to which we do not attribute a real existence, concrete or abstract, or of whose real existence we take no account, the definition does not represent a judgment, but an ideal supposition. “The circle,” according to the geometers, “is a plane surface bounded by a line whose points are all equally distant from another point, called the center.” The object of this definition is a pure conception of the understanding, because in it is supposed an exact equality of distance, and a perfectly plane surface which cannot be perceived by the senses, nor perhaps exist in nature.

There are two kinds of definition, according to the logicians: definition of things, and definition of names. Definition of things makes known to us an object; definition of names the signification of a word. But when the definition determines an object, what is done? It determines the idea of the object. And when by the definition the signification of a word is determined, what is done? Nothing else can be done than to represent the idea represented by the word, that is, the idea of the object to which the word corresponds. Thus, whether I try to define the circle, or to define the name that signifies it, I shall always have to determine the idea I have of the object, and the whole difference would consist in this, that sometimes I shall present the definition in this way: the circle is a plane surface, etc., and at other times in this other: the word circle means a plane surface, etc. There is no more ground for admitting these two kinds of definition than for admitting these three: definition of thing, definition of idea and definition of name.

The first rule of a good definition is that there be no superfluous word. If, for example, in defining the circle we should say: that it is a plane surface bounded by a curved line whose points, etc., it might be said with reason that the word curved is redundant, because a line whose points are all equally distant from another point is necessarily curved. We ought not, however, to admit this rule when the word, [p. 391] although it could strictly be omitted, facilitates the determination of the object and contributes to the clearness of the definition.

The definition must, in the second place, be clear. If clearness is indispensable in all the procedures of reasoning, it is so above all in definition, whose office is to make known with all the exactness that is possible the objects with which the reasoning deals, and which are supposed to be unknown from the moment it is sought to define them.

The third rule is that the definition must agree with the whole of the thing defined, toti definito [to the whole of the thing defined], as the logicians say, that is, that it must embrace all its forms, all its modifications, all the individuals contained in it. The following definition, for example, would offend against this rule: “reasoning is an operation of the understanding in which, by the comparison of two relations, we perceive a third relation”; for, as we shall see hereafter, there are reasonings in which from a single relation we infer another.

The fourth rule prescribes that the definition agree with the thing defined exclusively, or, as the logicians express it, soli definito [to the thing defined alone]. If we were to define the human soul as a substance that feels, we should violate this rule, because the soul of brutes feels. The same would be the case if we said that the human soul is an intelligent being, because the soul of brutes is so to a certain extent, and because God also is, and in a degree infinitely superior to that of human intelligence.

The fifth rule is that the thing defined must never enter into the definition, either tacitly or expressly. This we should violate if we said, for example, that a straight line is that line which maintains an invariable direction; because invariable direction and straight line are one and the same thing. This rule, however, is a practical consequence of the second; for, the idea that is defined being supposed unknown, the concept that contained it would not be clear, nor the definition that expressed this concept.

As definitions always proceed, and cannot but proceed, by genera and differences, there is added to the preceding rules this one, that the genus be proximate and the difference exclusive.

[p. 392]

The proximate genus is the least extensive of those in which the object defined is contained; and the exclusive or proper difference is that which separates it from all other objects. But the proximity of the genus is not to be understood to the letter, but only so far as it contributes to the clear determination of the object; and the propriety of the difference is a necessary consequence of the rule requiring that the definition apply only to the thing defined: soli definito [to the thing defined alone].

The best definitions are those that point out that quality of the object from which all the others are derived. Such is the preceding definition of the circle. Such, it seems to me, is also that which makes reason consist in the faculty of conceiving relations.

Failing a condition of this kind, we may fix upon that or those from which the most remarkable and characteristic qualities are derived. And this is the only thing that can for the most part be done in psychology and in the physical sciences.

To say that matter is an extended substance would perhaps suffice to circumscribe the idea so that it should agree toti definito et soli definito [to the whole of the thing defined and to it alone]. But the designation of other qualities that are never wanting to matter and that often figure in corporeal phenomena, such as impenetrability and inertia, ought not to be considered an idle redundancy. Only from a superstitious respect for the rules of the school could this definition be condemned: matter is an extended, impenetrable, inert substance. If the definition does not enable us to form a sufficiently clear idea of the thing defined, although it satisfy the other conditions, it does not fulfill its object, which is to make it known by means of its most important characters. Thus, description would often be preferable to simple definition even when the latter were possible. Simple definition suits better the sciences that deal with intellectual and positive concepts, like mathematics; description, the sciences of fact.

It is believed that it is arbitrary on the part of the writer to assign to a word whatever signification he pleases, provided that the value once given it be always preserved; and that consequently definitions cannot be censured in which we depart [p. 393] from the usual signification of words. When it is a question of determining a thing, a fact, a phenomenon, it is clear that if the definition is to be true, it cannot be arbitrary, save as to the choice of the character or characters determinative of the object, supposing that this presents several, or can be considered under different aspects. It happens also that, in classifying a multitude of objects for a certain determinate end, we can give more or less extension to a class, and define it in different ways. But this arbitrariness is reduced to very narrow limits, and it is rare that more than one good definition of a thing can be made, at least with respect to the particular end we propose to ourselves. I shall give an example.

There is great variety in the definitions which grammarians give of the different classes of words. But if it be considered that the classification of words in grammar has for its object to show their different offices, it is clear that the definition of the substantive, the adjective, the verb, etc., must confine itself to pointing out the peculiar and characteristic positions of each of these classes of verbal signs. What shall we say, then, of the definition commonly given of the substantive, a word that serves to name or point out things? There is no word that does not signify an idea, and that does not consequently point out a thing. Neither is the definition good which is given of the substantive, saying that it signifies real or imaginary substance: green involves the idea of substance as much as body does; as soon as we say green we figure to ourselves a green thing. And, on the other hand, what is the concept to which the imagination cannot join the idea of real or imaginary substance? The definition would always be vague, and therefore obscure. In reality, the several classes of words do not differ from one another by their signification, but by their connection and mutual dependence in language. The substantive is a word that serves to signify the subject of the proposition and the term of the complement: the subject of the proposition, as in “greenness is pleasant to the sight”; the term of a complement, as in “spring covers the earth with greenness.”

What is the adjective? It is not, as many say, a word [p. 394] that signifies quality; greenness signifies quality, and is nevertheless used as a substantive. It is a word that explains or modifies immediately the signification of the substantive: “white bodies”; “the white color”; “the white lily.”

What is the adverb? It is a word that modifies a modification or explanation of the signification of the substantive: “hopes too flattering”; “news manifestly false”; “service ill rewarded”; “oh, merits late recognized!”; “the ancient philosophers did not know the true way of studying nature.”

As a rule there is no room for arbitrariness in definition except when it is a question of determining the peculiar signification which we give to an unknown or doubtful term. It is not permissible to depart from the common use of the language, nor from the acceptation which a fixed and universally received nomenclature assigns to the technical terms of a science. But it happens that a new idea has to be expressed by means of a new term, and it then falls to him who introduces it to define it, making known the signification in which he takes it. There are, besides, words whose value is not well determined by general use or by that of scientific writers; and it is not only convenient but even necessary to declare that which each one gives to them, in order to avoid verbal disputes in which the contradiction is only apparent, originating in the various acceptations of one and the same word. And this is the only point of view under which a difference can be conceived between definitions of words and definitions of things. Every definition is, at one and the same time, a definition of a thing, of an idea, and of a word; and it depends only on circumstances whether by means of the definition we propose to make known an object, to set forth a new and peculiar concept, or to fix the signification of an ambiguous word; purposes all of which are always reduced to determining an object, because every word signifies an idea and every idea corresponds to an object.

We think it necessary also to say something of division and classification.

There are objects in which many species are included, or which can be presented under many aspects, whose differences it is [p. 395] important to know. Hence the necessity of dividing them. And not seldom it is necessary to subdivide each member of the first division, and then each member of the second, and so on until we stop at the ultimate species or aspects, whose distinction is of importance.

Classification is a single division or a series of divisions.

The first requisite of every division is that it be complete, that it exhaust its object. Such is that of corporeal beings into organized and inorganized. That of the organized into animals and vegetables: that of animals into vertebrates and mollusks: that of vertebrates into mammals, birds, reptiles and fishes.

The second rule is that each of the members completely exclude the others. Thus in the last of the preceding divisions, no mammal is a bird, nor a reptile, nor a fish. But this requisite is at times extremely difficult to obtain in the classification of natural objects, because the extremes touch. Nature passes by imperceptible degrees from one type to another, and the precise point at which one type ends and the next begins cannot always be fixed.

The third is that in all the members regard be had to the absence, presence or modification of a single quality or character, or of the same group of qualities or characters. The last of the preceding divisions satisfies this requisite fairly well: the characters that distinguish mammals, birds, reptiles and fishes are taken from the most important functions of animal life: nutrition and reproduction. But the observance of this rule is not always possible.

It is easy to gather that a complex classification demands the observance of these rules in each of its steps, because each of them is a division. But, besides, it is desirable that, if possible, the subdivisions of the same order be founded on analogous characters. This requisite is wanting in the system of vegetables of Linnaeus, who, subdividing the classes, attends now to the number of the pistils, now to the form of the ovary, now to that of the fruit, now to the adherence of the bark, [p. 396] etc. And yet the classification of plants by that illustrious naturalist is universal and generally admired; and, considering its object, which is to facilitate the knowledge of the name of each plant, it has not been possible to improve upon it; the magnificent variety of the productions of nature does not lend itself to the narrow and paltry distributions of artificial methods.

Classification may be abused by extending it to minute particulars, which by their number or by the difficulty of distinguishing them, far from aiding the understanding, embarrass it, overload the memory excessively, and produce perplexity. Compositum est quidquid in verum et rectum est. [Whatever is composed is in what is true and right.]

In complex classifications the members of the first division are usually given the title of classes; those of the subdivision are commonly called orders; those of the next, genera; those of the last, species. If other steps are necessary, they are given the title of groups, families to the members of the immediately succeeding subdivisions, always ending in the species, which nevertheless admit of some varieties.

[PDF 412]

On reasoning in general.

Definition of reasoning.—Two antecedent judgments or premises.— Different deduction in reasonings.—Syllogistic procedure: its deductive force.—Procedure of empirical reasoning.—Inductive or analogical reasonings: their various kinds.—Analogy of cause and effect: examples.— Difference between empirical and analogical reasoning.—Analogies that proceed from effects to causes.—Inference of resemblance between certain parts or qualities.—Analogies from ends to means, and from means to ends: examples.—Relation of cause to effect in all kinds of reasonings, empirical and analogical.—Essential procedure in all reasoning.

Reasoning is an act of the understanding in which from one or more judgments we deduce another judgment.

It is generally believed that in all reasoning there are two antecedent judgments or premises. But this is not so: in this intellectual operation: “spirit is not extended; therefore what is extended is not spirit,” it cannot be doubted that the two propositions express two different judgments; the subject of the first is spirit; the subject of the second is extended; the attribute of the first is extended; the attribute of the second is spirit. The relation between spirit and the unextended is not the same as the relation between the extended and the not-spirit. On the other hand, it is evident that the second relation supposes no other antecedent than the first, and that, the first being admitted, it is impossible to reject the second. Consequently, the intellectual act which the two propositions express is a true reasoning in which from a single judgment another judgment is deduced.

[p. 398]

Deduction is not made in the same manner in all reasonings. In the reasonings called syllogisms, the deductive procedure is this: A is contained in B; B is contained in C; therefore A is contained in C. To say, for example, that man is an animal is to say that the class man is contained in the class animal; to say that Peter is a man is to say that the individual Peter is contained in the class man; and to say that Peter is an animal is to say that the individual Peter is contained in the class animal. The force of the deduction in reasonings of this kind is founded on the necessity of the relation between A and C, the relations between A and B, and between B and C, being supposed.

The deductive procedure in the syllogism may also be considered in another way, but this is only an inversion of the preceding. The quality of man comprehends the quality of animal; Peter comprehends the quality of man; consequently Peter comprehends the quality of animal: A comprehends B; B comprehends C; therefore A comprehends C. The two formulas are in reality one: in the first we attend to the extension of the terms, and in the second to their comprehension.

The syllogism belongs to the class of reasonings which I shall call demonstrative, in which the consequence is derived from the premise or premises by a necessary deduction of absolute necessity. If matter is extended, it is necessary, of absolute necessity, that what is not extended should not be material either; and if A is equal to B, and B to C, it is impossible, with every kind of impossibility, that A and C should not also be equal to each other. Thus, in the syllogism, the inclusion of A in B and of B in C being conceived, we arrive irresistibly at the inclusion of A in C.

In the consequences which we deduce from physical observations the intellectual procedure is different, and likewise different is the motive of the confidence which we place in the reasoning. A piece of salt being immersed in water, the salt dissolves; and from this I infer that whenever salt is immersed in water, it dissolves. The intellectual procedure is this: in all the cases in which I have been able to observe salt immersed in water, it dissolves: therefore it has dissolved and will dissolve in all cases: the dissolution of salt in water is for me a law of nature.

[p. 399]

The force of the deduction in reasonings of this kind, which we call experimental or empirical, is not founded on the necessity of the relation deduced, the antecedent relation being supposed; for it is clear that from the fact that a thing has happened in the cases of which I have been a witness, it does not follow necessarily that the same must have happened and must happen in all similar cases; necessarily, I say, in the sense of absolute necessity, such as that the whole is greater than the part, or that 2 and 2 are 4; things which cannot fail to be, because a whole not greater than its part, or 2 and 2 not equal to 4, would be concepts involving contradiction, concepts from which the understanding recoils. The deductive force of empirical reasoning is founded on the supposition of the invariable constancy of the laws that govern the physical universe. But although it is of absolute necessity, as I conceive, that the universe be governed by constant laws, it is not so that it be governed precisely by the laws that in fact govern it. The Author of nature might have subjected it to other laws, and can also suspend those which he has once established. Thus, however great the certainty which this reasoning inspires in us, it does not equal the certainty of self-evident truths, nor the certainty of the truths which are derived from these by rigorous demonstration, that is, by one or more demonstrative reasonings. And this inequality would subsist even supposing that we could be sure of knowing perfectly the facts whose connection we suppose constant, an assurance which is not always complete.

Empirical reasoning proceeds in two ways. First: it generalizes a fact: I see that fire in a particular case melts snow; therefore it has melted and will always melt it. Second: generalizing the fact, I then apply it to the particular cases comprised in it: I know that fire brought near wax melts it; if I suppose, then, in a particular case the nearness of the wax to the fire, I deduce that in that case the wax must melt. Such, and no more, are the two forms of true empirical reasoning, authorized by the stability of the laws of nature.

[p. 400]

Nothing is simpler or surer than empirical generalizations and particular applications. With regard to the former, the difficulty consists in determining with exactness a phenomenal connection, that is, the first phenomenon called cause, and the subsequent phenomenon called effect. The reason is that phenomenal connections are seldom presented to us separate: ordinarily we see them knotted and confounded one with another; one and the same cause seems to bring about various effects; and several causes seem to concur in the production of one and the same effect. The reasoning procedure which distinguishes and separates the two phenomena and formulates their essential elements, purified of everything accessory and foreign, is complex and difficult.

With regard to the particular applications of a general law, the difficulty consists in ascertaining whether the particular case is truly comprehended in the law. The resemblance between the particular case and the cases presented by the law may be only apparent; and sometimes it is not easy to verify it, except by means of tedious comparisons and judicious deductions. These reasonings, which serve now to establish a generality with certainty, now to determine the particular circumstances of a general law, are called inductive or analogical, and are of various kinds.

The first kind of analogy is that which proceeds from the cause to the effects. It also generalizes facts, but its generalizations go much farther than the limits of purely empirical reasoning, and to inspire full confidence they need to be verified. I shall give an example.

A rod which is introduced into water appears to us broken, and an object seen through a glass prism does not show itself to us in the true place which it occupies, but in another and different one. If a peseta is placed at the bottom of a cup of water and is seen obliquely, it will appear to rise in the water; if spirit of wine is used instead of water, it will appear to rise more; if oil, still more. But in none of these cases will the apparent place be to the right or to the left of the true place, but in one and the same vertical plane with it and [p. 401] with the eye of the observer. This phenomenon, due to the bending of the rays of light that come from the object to us as they pass from one transparent medium to another, was called refraction of light; and in each combination of two media it appeared to conform to this law: “the angles of incidence and of refraction are in a plane normal to the surface of separation of the two media, and the sines of these angles have a particular relation to each other.” From which it was deduced that whenever light passes from one transparent medium to another, the phenomenon of refraction takes place in the same terms.

The deduction, however, extended to all possible combinations of two media, was not sufficiently safe. In each particular combination the relation between the two media is one; and no reason is discerned why, so long as this subsists, the production of effects should vary. Every generalization of a particular fact in which the media did not vary may therefore be regarded as rigorously empirical. But when the formula is generalized to all possible combinations of two media, was it lawful to affirm with the same assurance that none of the relations in which the two media might come to stand to one another would thwart the production of the phenomenon, as the formula represented it? Nothing would contribute to securing this confidence. Analogy gives no more than a certain degree of probability; and only by diversifying the combinations of media in numerous experiments, and seeing the phenomenon reproduced in all, could the danger of error be seen gradually to diminish, until at last it seemed to vanish and we believed ourselves authorized to raise the general analogical deduction to the rank of empirical truths and to consider it as the exact expression of a law of nature. In the present example it did not happen so. Observations showed that in crystallized substances the phenomenon is observed in a singular manner. It was therefore necessary to correct the formula, limiting it to transparent bodies not crystallized, and only with this reservation could it be admitted as an empirical deduction.

In effect, there are transparent solid bodies, such as rock crystal, which, interposed between the object and the eye, have the singular

## PHILOS.   26

[p. 402]

property of doubling the image of the latter, so that instead of one object we see two, the one beside the other; such bodies, in a word, produce the phenomenon of double refraction. It was observed that of these two images one was in the normal plane and the other not; the rays of light which make us see the second undergo an extraordinary refraction. It was observed that double refraction was always produced by a crystallized body; that is, by some of those substances which naturally affect regular symmetrical forms, and which split or break more easily in some directions than in others: which is not the case with glass. Was it not natural to infer that in the crystallized bodies which had not been submitted to observation the phenomenon of double refraction would be produced equally, with the two images, ordinary and extraordinary, as in those which it had been possible to observe? Not doubting the double refraction of rock crystal in a certain number of cases, we infer experimentally that rock crystal produces the same phenomenon in all cases. And observing afterwards the double refraction of other crystallized substances, with the two images, ordinary and extraordinary, as in that of rock crystal, we infer analogically that all crystallized substances produce it in the same terms. Two pieces of rock crystal present to us a complete resemblance of agency as to the production of the effect; of crystallized bodies of different kinds we cannot say as much. Thus, the second generalization cannot be adopted with full confidence; and in effect, when submitted to many and varied observations, it was seen that it was not exact.

M. Fresnel demonstrated that, certain postulates being given, all the circumstances of double refraction could be satisfactorily explained, and deduced from them by rigorous mathematical calculation: that they explained, first, the absence of double refraction in transparent crystallized bodies; that in the second place the presence of the two images, ordinary and extraordinary, produced by certain crystallized substances was explained by them; and in the third place, that according to those [p. 403] postulates, in most of these substances both images ought to be extraordinary, that is, both appear outside the normal plane; an unexpected conclusion, contrary to what seemed to be deducible from the first observations, and which was fully confirmed by experience.

We have here an example of the difference between rigorous experimental reasoning and analogical reasoning from causes to effects; we have besides an example of the certainty to which analogical deductions may be raised when submitted to varied experiments and observations, and progressively corrected. We see likewise another important circumstance. The calculation shows an exact correspondence between the modifications of the cause and the modifications of the effect, and makes known to us in this way that the general formula represents the facts with exactness. The force of the deduction is so much the greater as the number of various cases to which we see it constantly extend is the larger, and the more complete the correspondence between the formula and the facts subjected to the same conditions; until at last it ostensibly reveals the character of a true natural law.

There is, then, considerable difference between experimental or empirical reasoning and the analogy from causes to effects. The first proceeds with a certain security, the second gropingly, provoking new investigations that may verify it. It might be said that experimental reasoning is nothing else than the analogical reasoning which proceeds from causes to effects, raised to the highest degree of force, to physical certainty. Thus it is that at times what we have called empirical may not be so; the generalizations to which we think ourselves fully authorized may be excessive if carried beyond certain limits, or not excessive if exactly defined; and at other times the contrary: a powerful analogy may be the exact expression of an invariable phenomenal connection.

There are other kinds of analogies in which the procedure is different from that which concerns empirical reasoning. In the analogy which proceeds from effects to causes, the procedure is inverse. We see, for example, a human footprint stamped in a [p. 404] soft soil; and we gather that the print has truly been produced by the foot of a man, because it resembles the print which the foot of a man always produces on a soft surface. If the resemblance between the print we see and the true footprint of the human foot is complete, we shall give our confidence to the inference; but we may still be deceived, because the same print may have been produced artificially. But if we see not merely one footprint but many, if we see them follow one another without interruption from one end to the other of a great field covered with snow, placed at the distance at which human steps usually leave them, equal in dimensions, similar in form and with the symmetrical differences that correspond to the right foot and the left, we infer then with an immense probability, scarcely inferior to physical certainty, that the feet of a man have stamped them on the snow. In the reasoning which proceeds from causes to effects, there is no danger of erring when the cause and its mode of acting are perfectly known: if I hold a piece of lead in my hand and let it go, it will fall infallibly: for the deduction to deceive us, it would be necessary that a law of nature should be infringed. But in the analogical reasoning, which proceeds from effects to causes, the same cannot be said: effects most closely similar may be produced by diverse causes, without any law of nature being infringed. Only when we are sure that an effect cannot be brought about except by a certain kind of causes, can the analogy which proceeds from effects to causes be raised to complete certainty.

We have seen above that empirical reasoning generalizes within certain limits, and then applies the generalization a priori: from the resemblance of causes it deduces the resemblance of effects in particular unobserved cases. The analogy which from effects ascends to causes also applies, particularizes a general cause, but applies a priori. From the resemblance of effects it infers the resemblance of causes.

We also infer at times, from resemblance as to certain parts or qualities, resemblance as to other parts [p. 405] or qualities. I observe, for example, that a new star moves around another in elliptical orbits, similar to those which the planets and satellites describe around their respective centers. From this resemblance I deduce (if I have not been able to observe it) that the new star has also a motion of rotation upon itself, in the same manner as the planets and satellites in which I have been able to make the observation. This kind of analogy is usually the weakest of all; and yet observations have often confirmed it. When it is founded, not on an imperfect or obscure resemblance, but on a great number of well-marked and determinate resemblances, it may carry assent irresistibly along with it. Who, after having minutely studied the external form of an animal, and recognized by it that another animal is of the same species, will fail to infer with entire confidence that the internal conformation of the second is similar to that of the animal which has been observed first, although for judging so there be no other foundation than the resemblance of the external forms?

There are other analogies which proceed from ends to means, and from means to ends. We see, for example, that the planets have motions of rotation which alternately show them and hide from them the sun, and motions of translation around the sun, which, by the inclination of their axes to the planes of their orbits, make them experience a series of vicissitudes in which heat and illumination increase and decrease by degrees, this series being constantly reproduced with the most invariable uniformity, as happens on the earth. If from this we deduce that on the earth, as on the planets, day and night and the different seasons are due to two motions, the one around its axis, and the other around the sun, from the resemblance of the effects we infer the resemblance of the causes. And if, going farther, we judge that on the planets, as on the earth, these alternations have relation to the development and the needs of the organized beings that inhabit them, from the resemblance of the means we infer the resemblance of the ends.

I have observed that the quadrupeds which feed on the flesh of other quadrupeds are armed with sharp claws and [p. 406] teeth, suited to seize the prey and devour it. If I know that an unknown quadruped feeds in the same manner as others, I conclude with considerable probability that it is provided with the same means. Zoology in itself is a science founded in great part upon these correlations of means to ends and of ends to means, in which analogy certainly inspires us with confidence, as empirical reasoning does.

We may reduce analogical reasoning to these five kinds: it proceeds either from causes to effects, or from effects to causes; from means to ends, or from ends to means; or from a partial resemblance to another and greater resemblance. In the first kind the principle that serves as the type of the reasoning is the stability of phenomenal connections; in the other four the principle is simplicity, the unity of plan, which we often see in the works of nature; a principle less sure than the other, and to which nevertheless we cannot at times avoid having recourse.

All reasonings are reduced to these three kinds: demonstrative, experimental and analogical. We shall observe lastly that, notwithstanding the difference of deductive procedure in empirical reasoning and in the various analogical reasonings, the understanding is directed by all these courses to one and the same term, which is the connection of cause and effect. Empirical reasoning supposes the cause determined, and deduces from it with the utmost certainty the effect. The analogy which proceeds from causes to effects establishes the cause innocently by virtue of an apparent resemblance; and if it comes, by any of the modes which I have set forth, to determine and circumscribe the cause, the result is the knowledge of a connection of causality, in which we can now deduce the effect from the cause, and from the modifications of the cause the modifications of the effect. Suppose now that we proceed in the contrary direction, from the resemblance of the effects to the resemblance of the causes. If this deduction has the characters which authorize us to regard it as conclusive, the result is the same as before, a connection of causality. If from the ends we infer the means, or from the means the ends, and we have ground for giving entire faith to the inference, we shall also have arrived at a connection of causality [p. 407] for means are causes, and ends effects. Finally, if from a lesser resemblance we infer a greater resemblance, the inference will be founded on our seeing the inferred resemblance as an effect of the known resemblance, or seeing it also as the effect of a new cause, whether we determine it or not. Were it not so, the inference would deserve little faith. To the three kinds mentioned, the demonstrative, the empirical and the analogical, all possible reasonings are reduced.
