On demonstrative reasonings.

Deductive procedure in demonstrative reasonings.—The syllogism.— Doctrine of the Schoolmen.—Figure of the syllogism.—Galen’s syllogism.— The mood.—Conversion of the different moods of the syllogism.—Rules of Aristotle.—Apparent difference between affirmative and negative propositions.—Conversion of the universal proposition.—Conversion in the syllogism of the perfect mood, according to the Schoolmen.—Observations on the use of the syllogism.—Rules 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th.—Reduction of the syllogism by the Schoolmen.—Disjunctive syllogisms.—Procedure of induction: opinion of Wallis.—The enthymeme.—The sorites.—Other demonstrative reasonings.—Instinctive procedure in reasoning.—Deductive procedure in the mathematical sciences.—Conclusions from the foregoing.— Legitimacy of reasoning.—Causes of error.—Fallacy or sophism: in what it consists.—Argument of Zeno.—Argument reductio ad absurdum.—Examples relating to economic arguments.—Supposed rule to which it has been sought to reduce all reasoning: Condillac.—Explanation of Dr. Brown.—Vain attempt to reduce the syllogism. Conclusion.

I

In demonstrative reasonings the deductive procedure is varied, according to the kind of relation attended to.

When we attend to the relation of resemblance which serves as the foundation of classes, the procedure of reasoning, then called syllogism, must conform to the axiom: “if of three things the first is contained in the second, and the second in the third, the first is contained in the third”; that is, “M is contained in N, N is contained in P, therefore M is contained in P”, [p. 409] Take, for example, this syllogism: “Virtue is worthy of love; economy is virtue; therefore economy is worthy of love.” In the second judgment it is affirmed that the class economy is included in the class virtue; in the first it is affirmed that the class virtue is included in the class worthy of love; and in the third it is drawn as conclusion or consequence from these two premises, that the class economy is included in the class worthy of love.

In another way: “economy has the quality of virtue; virtue has the quality of being worthy of love; therefore economy has the quality of being worthy of love.” The regulating axiom is the same as before, though applied in an inverse way: M contains N; N contains P; therefore M contains P. The relation attended to in the procedure of reasoning is also the same; for to say that “virtue has the quality of being worthy of love” is to say in other words that virtue is contained in the class of things that are worthy of love.

The verb to be in the syllogism signifies, then, the same as to contain or to be contained; to contain, if we attend to the comprehension of the words; to be contained, if we attend to their extension.

II

We are going to give a very brief idea of the doctrine of the Schoolmen on the syllogism; afterwards we shall inquire whether it serves any purpose for the investigation and demonstration of truth.

The syllogism consists of three terms bound together by the verb to be, called the copula. Of these three terms, the two of the conclusion are called extremes; the predicate the major extreme, and the subject the minor extreme. The term that is compared with one of the extremes in one of the premises, and with the other in the other, is called the middle. When the verb to be is not expressed, it is understood to be implied in another verb; as in this proposition: “birds fly,” which is as if we said: “birds are flying beings.” Of the two premises the one is called major [p. 410] and the other minor, according as the term compared in them with the middle is major or minor. According to the scholastic form, the major is always the first of the three propositions of the syllogism, and the minor the second.

The position of the middle constitutes the figure of the syllogism. If it is the subject of the major and the predicate of the minor, the syllogism is of the first figure;1 if the predicate of both, of the second;2 if the subject of both, of the third.3

There is a certain kind of syllogisms of which Aristotle did not treat, in which the middle serves as subject to the subject of the conclusion and as predicate to the predicate; the subject of the conclusion is the major extreme, and the premise in which it is found is the major; consequently, the predicate of the conclusion is the minor extreme, and the premise in which it is found is the minor. Here is an example: “Governments in which the representatives of the people make the laws are democratic governments; some governments that have a king are governments in which the representatives of the people make the laws; therefore some democratic governments are governments that have a king.” These syllogisms were regarded as of the indirect first figure; but we find simpler the

1 Calling S the subject of the conclusion, P the predicate of the same, and M the

middle, the first figure is:

M, P, major;

S, M, minor;

S, P, conclusion.

2 The second figure may be represented thus:

P, M;

S, M;

S, P.

In this figure there are only four legitimate moods.

3 It may be represented thus:

M, P;

M, S;

S, P.

It has six legitimate moods. [p. 411] idea of their inventor Galen, who considered them as of a different figure.1

The mood of the syllogism consists in the quality and quantity of the propositions. Quality consists in their being affirmative or negative. Quantity in their being universal or particular. The universal is that in which the subject signifies an entire class, as man, every man. The particular, on the contrary, is that in which the subject signifies part of a class, as some men. If the subject is a determinate individual, the proposition is singular, and reduces to the universals. A determinate individual, designated by a proper name, e.g., Alexander, or by a phrase that takes its place, e.g., “the son of Philip,” “the Macedonian conqueror,” is a class that reduces wholly to the individual. The universal affirmative proposition is represented by the letter A, the universal negative by E; the particular affirmative by I, the particular negative by O.

The Schoolmen disregarded negation for the identity of terms: they considered as one and the same term man and not-man, they fly and they do not fly: a first erroneous consideration that made them needlessly complicate the theory of the syllogism. There contributed also to this complication, and gave rise to that false conception, the essential difference they supposed between affirmative and negative propositions. We have already said that negation is a part of the attribute or predicate: man is not infallible is as much as man is not-infallible. And what things can be less identical with each other, or rather more opposed, than to be liable to deceive oneself and not to be so?

They also disregarded, for the identity of terms, the partitive adjectives certain, some, many, etc. According

1 It may be represented thus:

M, S;

P, M;

S, P.

It has five legitimate moods. [p. 412] to them, some men, many men, and every man, were an identical term.

The legitimate moods belonging to the said figures are those comprised in these four verses:1 Bárbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio; Baralipton, Celantes, Dabitis, Fapesmo, Frisesomorum; Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco; Darapti, Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison.

The first four belong to the first figure; the next five to the fourth, that is, the first indirect; the next four to the second, and the last six to the third.

Here is, for example, a syllogism in Ferio: “No innocent thing is censurable; some pleasures are innocent; therefore some pleasures are not censurable.”

Example in Baroco: “Everything material is extended; some beings are not extended; therefore some beings are not material.”

Example in Darapti: “Every man is a biped; every man is an animal; therefore some animals are bipeds.”

In Fapesmo: “Birds have feathers; horses are not birds; therefore something that has feathers is not a horse.”

All the moods of the second, third and fourth figure are called imperfect.

In reality, the perfect syllogism, the true syllogism, has only one form: S is contained in M; M is contained in P; therefore S is contained in P;2 or, according to the order that Aristotle and the Schoolmen have preferred: M is contained in P; S is contained in M; therefore S is contained in P. The moods Bárbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio, are one single identical mood: M, S, P, are positive or negative; S particular or universal; M and P necessarily universal, because a predicate cannot but be so. The syllogism has in this type three terms. “Is not P” is equivalent to “is not-P” or to “is — P,” the negation being represented

1 The first vowel of each word represents the major; the second, the minor; the

third, the conclusion.

2 S the subject of the conclusion; P the predicate of the same; M the middle. [p. 413] by the sign —. —P ought not to be considered the same thing as P. And the same distinction must be recognized between the universal and the particular, between men and some men, between S and S/r.1 From which it results that in all the imperfect moods there are more than three terms. Take, for example, this syllogism in Fapesmo:

Aves, pennatæ; [Birds, feathered;] Equi, non-aves; [Horses, not birds;] Aliqua pennata, non-equi. [Something feathered, not a horse.] We shall have six terms: aves and non-aves; pennatæ and aliqua pennata; equi and non-equi [birds, not-birds; feathered, something feathered; horses, not-horses].

The business now is to reduce all possible syllogisms to the moods of the first figure, which are reduced, as we have seen, to M, P; S, M; therefore S, P; these three letters signifying three absolutely invariable terms. The object of the reduction is to demonstrate the legitimacy of the deductive procedure. For this purpose recourse is had to conversions.

That transformation of the proposition in which, the truth of the judgment remaining, the subject becomes predicate and the predicate subject, is called conversion; for which Aristotle gave three rules: the universal affirmative is converted into a particular affirmative; the universal negative into a universal negative; and the particular affirmative into a particular affirmative. For example: aves, pennatæ; aliqua pennata, aves. Pisces, non-pennati; pennata, non-pisces. Aliqui homines, nigri; aliqua nigra, homines. [birds, feathered; something feathered, birds. Fishes, not feathered; feathered, not fishes. Some men, black; some black, men.]

But it is evident that conversion is a true reasoning composed of two propositions, antecedent and consequent: “Every man is an animal, therefore some animals are men.” “No stone feels; therefore nothing that feels is a stone.” “Some animals lack limbs; therefore some beings that lack limbs are animals.” To those of Aristotle another conversion was afterwards added, which is the following: “every bird has feathers; therefore no being that lacks

1 The particular term being represented by a fraction in which the denominator is an inde‐

terminate quantity r. [p. 414] feathers is a bird”: Omnis avis, pennata; igitur omne non-pennatum, non-avis [Every bird, feathered; therefore everything not feathered, not a bird]. The subject and the predicate of the antecedent become predicate and subject of the consequent, preceded by negation; and the universal affirmative proposition is converted into a universal with two negations.

I believe we can generalize the doctrine of conversions, establishing first that if “A is B” (a universal proposition, in which A or B or both may be affirmative or negative), it follows necessarily that “not- B is not-A”; or, expressing ourselves as in algebra, “—B is —A”; from “every bird has feathers” it follows that “no being that lacks feathers is a bird.” Consequently, “—A is B” will be converted into “—B is A”; from “the impure is abhorred by God,” it follows that “the not-abhorred of God is pure.” Likewise “A is —B” will be converted into “B is —A”; from “spirit is inextended” it is necessarily deduced that “the extended is not spirit.” Finally, “—A is —B” will be converted into “B is A”; from “no being that has not feathers is a bird” it is a necessary consequence that “every bird has feathers.” It is here clearly manifest that the difference between affirmative and negative propositions is something that does not go beyond verbal signs; and that even in language the negative may often be given the appearance of the affirmative; for to say, e.g., that a being has not feathers is as much as to say that it lacks them or that it is featherless.

In the second place, we can establish that if “A is B” (a universal proposition), at least a part of the beings comprised in the class B, let us say B/r, are necessarily A: that is, “B/r is A.” If the corporeal is extended, it follows of necessity that at least some of the extended things are corporeal. Consequently “—A is B” will give “—B/r is A,” and from “—A is —B” will result “—B/r is —A.” In effect, from “inhuman actions are reprobated” it follows that “a part of the actions that are reprobated are inhuman”: from “birds have no udders” it follows that “some beings that lack udders are birds”; and finally, from “the inextended is corporeal” it is deduced that at least “a part of the incorporeal is inextended.”

[p. 415]

If we now represent the particular subject by A/r, we can establish in the first place that from “A/r is B” it follows that “B/r is A”: “if some men are black,” it is necessary that “some black beings are men.” From which it is deduced that if “—A/r is B,” “B/r is —A”; and if “A/r is —B,” “—B/r is —A.” This is evident, and shows that even the particular negative proposition is convertible. In effect, if “some mammals have no hair,” it is necessary that “some of the beings that have no hair are mammals.”

In general, the universal proposition is convertible, either by changing the quality of both terms, or by changing the quantity of the predicate: if “A is B,” “—B is —A,” and “B/r is A.” And the particular proposition is convertible by changing the quantity of both terms: if “A/r is B,” “B/r is A.” When the quantity of the proposition is changed, it is converted per accidens, according to scholastic language; and when it is not changed, it is converted simpliciter.

Simpler: every universal proposition is convertible, either by changing the signs of both terms, or by particularizing the predicate. “A is B,” therefore “—B is —A”; “A is B,” therefore “B/r is A.” Every particular proposition is converted by particularizing the predicate and generalizing the subject, because the predicate cannot but present itself under a general form: “A/r is B”; therefore “B/r is A.” Our nomenclature corresponds in general to that of the Schoolmen: to convert by changing the signs is in general what they call converting simpliciter, and to convert by particularizing the attribute is in scholastic language to convert per accidens. There is one case only in which this correspondence does not hold. According to them, “A/r is B,” therefore “B/r is A,” is converting simpliciter. But it is plain that they have not fixed upon the essential characters of the two kinds of conversion: the first is effected by the change of signs, that is, by transforming + into —, and — into +; the second takes place, so to speak, in the coefficients of the terms, converting the general predicate into a partial subject, and the partial subject into a general predicate.

Returning now to the syllogism, we shall observe that, according to the [p. 416] Schoolmen, every imperfect mood can be reduced to one of the four perfect ones, and the rules for making these reductions are indicated by the consonant letters of the word that represents it. The perfect mood to which the imperfect syllogism is reduced is that whose name has the same initial: Baralipton, for example, is reduced to Bárbara, Camestres to Celarent, Disamis to Darii, Ferison to Ferio. If in the name of the imperfect mood the letter p is found, as in Darapti, the proposition designated by the preceding vowel is converted per accidens, and if in the name the letter s is found, as in Disamis, the conversion is made simpliciter. If the letter m is found in the said name, as in Frisesamorum, the order of the premises must be inverted; and if the letter c (not initial) is found in it, it means that the syllogism is irreducible, as in Baroco and Bocardo, and that its legitimacy can be proved only by the principle of contradiction.

Examples. Baralipton: It means that the premises remain invariable; that the conclusion is drawn from them according to Bárbara, and that this conclusion must be converted per accidens. “M, S,” “P, M,” “S/r, P,” is converted to Bárbara in this way: “M, S,” “P, M,” therefore “P, S”; therefore, converting per accidens, “S/r, P.”

Celantes: It means that the premises remain invariable; that the conclusion is drawn from them according to Celarent, and that this conclusion is converted simpliciter. “M, —S,” “P, M,” “S, —P.” It is reduced to Celarent in this way: “M, —S,” “P, M,” therefore “P, —S”; and hence “S, —P.”

Fapesmo: The letter p, which follows the first vowel a, indicates that the first premise must be converted per accidens; the s, which follows the second vowel e, means that the second premise is converted simpliciter, and the m denotes that the premises must change places; which done, there results a syllogism in Ferio: “M, S,” “P, —M,” therefore “S/r, —P.” It is reduced to Ferio in this way: “M, —P,” “S/r, M,” therefore “S/r, —P.”

Camestres: “P, M,” “S, —M,” therefore “S, —P.” It is reduced to Celarent by converting the minor and the conclusion simpliciter, and inverting the premises: “M, —S,” “P, M,” “P, —S”; and [p. 417] therefore, “S, —P.” But, with the leave of the gentlemen Schoolmen, the reduction is made more simply by converting the major simpliciter: “—M, —P,” “S, —M,” therefore “S, —P.” But to which of the four direct moods does the reduced syllogism belong? To none, because in none of them are the two premises negative. Nevertheless, it conforms exactly to the perfect type: If —M is contained in —P, and S in —M, it is necessary that S be contained in —P. Which proves that Bárbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio, are not all the possible direct moods.

Disamis: “M/r, P,” “M, S,” therefore “S/r, P.” It is reduced to Darii by converting the major and the conclusion simpliciter, as the Schoolmen say, or by particularizing the attribute, as I should say; and changing besides the order of the premises: “M, S,” “P/r, M,” therefore “P/r, S,” and consequently “S/r, P.”

Baroco and Bocardo cannot be reduced, according to the Schoolmen, except per contradictionem [by contradiction], that is, by showing that he who, the premises being granted, denies the consequence, contradicts himself. This kind of reduction they apply to all the imperfect moods; for example, to Baralipton: “M, S,” “P, M,” therefore “S/r, P.” If the consequence is denied, I take the contradictory of it, which is “S, —P,” because if, e.g., it is denied me that some men are black, it is claimed that all men are of a different color from black, that is, not black. Now, if “S, —P,” and “M, S,” it results necessarily, according to Celarent, that “M, —P,” and consequently “P, —M,” a proposition contradictory of one of the premises granted.

But, forgive me again, gentlemen Schoolmen: Baroco and Bocardo are most easily reducible, as your worships are about to see.

Baroco: “P, M,” “S/r, —M,” “S/r, —P.” I convert the major by changing the signs, and I have the syllogism: “—M, —P,” “S/r, — M,” “S/r, —P.” Can anything be simpler? But to what direct mood shall we refer it? To none of those designated by the school. And yet its conformity with the type of the perfect syllogism is evident. To save the honor of the Peripatetics it might be said that considering not M, but —M, as the middle (a most just consideration, because it is not M but

## PHILOS.     27

[p. 418]

—M the term with which both extremes are compared), and prescinding, consequently, from the negation involved in it, the major is universal negative, the minor particular affirmative, and the conclusion particular negative: that is, it is reduced to Ferio.

Bocardo: “M/r, P,” “M, S,” “S/r, —P.” I convert the major and the conclusion, particularizing the attribute, and change the order of the premises: “M, S,” “—P/r, M,” therefore “—P/r, S,” and consequently “S/r, —P.” If one chooses to consider not P, but —P as one of the extremes, the reduction will turn out to be to Darii.

As the imperfect moods are all reduced, by means of conversions, to the four perfect ones, and as the four perfect ones conform immediately to the formula: “M is contained in P,” “S is contained in M,” therefore “S is contained in P,” it is clear that all the figures and all the moods of the syllogism are reduced to a single deductive procedure, combined with those very simple reasonings to which the title of conversions has been given.1

The scholastic verses would represent the reductions much better, emended thus:

Bárbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio; Baralipton, Celantes, Dabitipte, Fapesmo, Fripesomorum; Cesare, Casenter, Festino, Fasonto; Darapti, Félapo, Dipámiter, Datipi, Dopamopto, Feripon.

1 In a reasoning in Bocardo, like the following:

“Some birds do not fly;

Birds have feathers;

Therefore some beings that have feathers do not fly”:

the deductive procedure may be analyzed thus:

Some birds do not fly,

Therefore some beings that do not fly are birds;

Birds have feathers,

Therefore some beings that do not fly have feathers,

Therefore some beings that have feathers do not fly.

[p. 419]

Whence it is seen that in the second figure all the conversions are made by changing the signs; and in the third by particularizing the attribute; an elegant generalization, which recommends my theory of conversions.

III

We shall add some observations on the use of the syllogism.

1st. It is not necessary that the logical subject of the proposition should coincide with the grammatical subject. When we say: “In every science the principles must precede the consequences,” the logical subject may be science, as if we said: “every science is a concatenation of truths in which the principles,” etc., and it may be also the consequences, as if we said: “the consequences must, in every science, be set forth after the principles.” Consequently, the same must be said of the predicate.

2nd. The reciprocal inclusion of the terms that signify a relation between the subterms requires that each one of the subterms of the consequence be contained in the analogous subterm of the premise. From “the consequences of every principle must be set forth after the principle itself,” it follows that “all philosophical notions that are not psychological must be set forth after psychological notions,” because the subterm philosophical notions is included, with respect to psychology, in the subterm consequences, and the subterm psychological notions, with respect to all other philosophical notions, in the subterm principles. This is a case of extensive containment; but the same might be applied to the comprehension of the terms, which is the same relation considered in an inverse way.

3rd. The premises are sometimes expressed by a conviction: “The bat has no feathers; therefore, if it is an essential character of birds to have them, the bat is not a bird”; which is as if we said: “every bird has feathers; the bat has none; therefore it is not a bird”: a syllogism of the second figure, which is reduced to the type by converting the major per signa [by signs].

[p. 420]

4th. He who should say that universal propositions sometimes have a lesser extension than they appear at first sight to have, “All pass from England to France by the Strait of Calais,” would only mean that “all who pass from England to France” (subject) “do so by the Strait of Calais” (predicate).

5th. Generally, in order to discern the true subject and predicate, and the quality and quantity of both, it is necessary to attend to the sense and not to the material structure of the proposition; but in any case we may, the sense remaining invariable, give the proposition the scholastic form, in order to fix the terms with precision and remove all doubt.

6th. We should lose ourselves in a labyrinth of minutiae if we had to exhaust the subject. The forms in which one and the same judgment may be expressed are innumerable, and without altering the sense they disguise the terms of the syllogism. But the observations to which they would give rise would be so minute and varied that they would become superfluous for every man endowed with moderate reason; and those who had not received this gift from nature could neither study nor understand them.

IV

The Schoolmen reduce to the syllogism several kinds of reasonings in which there are complex propositions.

In conditional syllogisms they establish two moods: that which they call modus ponens: “if A is B, C is D; A is B, therefore C is D”; and that which they call modus tollens: “if A were B, C would be D; C is not D, therefore A is not B.” These deductive procedures are of irresistible evidence, and although Aristotle calls them syllogisms, it is manifest that they differ much from the preceding in their structure. Moreover, the relation they concern is not that of resemblance, which serves as the foundation of classes, but that of necessary connection between two facts. “A cannot exist without B; A exists; therefore B exists”; or else: “B does not exist; therefore A does not exist.”

[p. 421]

Disjunctive syllogisms have this form: “either it is A or B”; “it is A”; therefore “it is not B”; or else: “it is not A”; therefore “it is B.” The relation with which the reasoning deals is likewise one of necessary connection, but reciprocally negative: “A is necessarily connected with —B, and B is necessarily connected with —A”; “A exists”; therefore “B does not exist”; or else: “A does not exist”; therefore “B exists.”

Some have called this syllogism a dilemma; but the dilemma is properly an argument in which from two contradictory hypotheses there results an identical and therefore absolute apodosis; for example: “Every man who discharges badly an office which he serves voluntarily is guilty; for he is either capable of discharging it or incapable: if capable, he is guilty because he does not fulfill his obligations, though he can; and if not capable, he is guilty, because he takes upon himself obligations which it is not possible for him to fulfill.” The deductive procedure is this: “A exists or A does not exist; if A exists, B exists, and if A does not exist, B exists also; therefore absolutely B exists.”

The Schoolmen have wished also to reduce to the syllogism induction, a kind of reasoning in which from several particular propositions a general conclusion is drawn of the same existence as the premises; for example: “In the equilateral triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles”; “in the isosceles triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles”; “in the scalene triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles”; therefore “in every triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles.” If the enumeration of the particulars is incomplete, and the conclusion is more extensive than the premises, the induction is not rigorous, and the reasoning is experimental or analogical, but never demonstrative.

Wallis, cited by Stewart, thinks that rigorous induction (that which proceeds by complete enumeration, which is the only kind that can be treated of here) is a syllogism in Darapti, which he unfolds in this way: “Europe, Asia, Africa and America are inhabited by men”; “Europe, Asia, Africa and America are all the known continents”; therefore “all the known continents are inhabited by men.” We do not know how one can [p. 422] apply to Darapti a syllogism whose conclusion is universal. But induction is so far from being a syllogism in Darapti that it is not even a syllogism. It is evident that in it two different relations are combined: that of classifying resemblance in one of the premises (“Europe, Asia, Africa and America are inhabited by men”), and that of identity in the other premise; for the enumeration would not be complete, nor the induction demonstrative, if in this premise it were not indifferent to use one of the terms as subject and the other as predicate, or vice versa, their quality and quantity remaining the same; a conversion which does not belong to the true syllogism.

There is also an identical dilemma, which proceeds by complete enumeration of all possible suppositions, and which may be figured thus: “All possible suppositions are A, B, C, D”; “in any of these suppositions E is F”; therefore “absolutely E is F.”

The enthymeme is a syllogism in which the major or the minor is omitted because it is supposed to be conceded; for example: “In all the sciences one must proceed from the known to the unknown”; therefore “in Philosophy one must proceed in the same way”: the minor is passed over in silence: “Philosophy is a science.”

The sorites is a chain of syllogisms in which the predicate of the first judgment is the subject of the second; the predicate of the second, the subject of the third; and so on; for example: “The soul thinks”; “what thinks is simple”; “the simple is spiritual”; “the spiritual, immortal”; therefore “the soul is immortal.” Between the second proposition and the third, the conclusion is passed over in silence: “therefore the soul is simple.” And between the third and the fourth the conclusion is likewise passed over in silence: “therefore the soul is spiritual.” The sorites takes the name of prosyllogism when the intermediate conclusions are expressed.

V

There are demonstrative reasonings which deal with relations different from that of classifying resemblance, and which nevertheless [p. 423] seem to fit the formula or fundamental axiom of the syllogism.

“A is after B”; “B is after C”; therefore “A is after C.” If in place of after we put before, greater, less, or any other of the words or phrases which grammarians call comparatives, the reasoning will keep the same form and the same conclusive force.

Manifest is the resemblance between the form of these reasonings and that of the syllogism: “A is contained in B”; “B is contained in C”; therefore “A is contained in C.” The analogy, however, is merely apparent; the quantities, qualities and conversions of the propositions, the figures and moods of the syllogism, have here no application whatever. Certain deductive procedures suit one single kind of relation, and certain others another; and the soul, guided by a marvelous and inexplicable instinct, always chooses the one that suits the relation which engages it; an instinct which no analysis could supply, and which makes unnecessary the study of the laws to which each procedure is subject. To each deductive procedure corresponds a fundamental axiom which expresses or formulates in a general way the course of the understanding, but which in reality does not guide it. The procedure is instinctive; the axiom is the procedure itself generalized.

If we pass to other relations, the essential difference between the deduction which is proper to each of them and the syllogistic deduction will be still more marked. In the relation of identity, for example, the course of the understanding is: “A is B,” “B is C,” therefore “A is C”; but in such a manner that the terms are reciprocally convertible without any alteration of quality or quantity. We cannot resist the force of this reasoning: “A is B,” “C is B,” therefore “A is C”; and yet we cannot reduce it to any figure or mood of the syllogism. The same happens in reasonings which deal with the relation of equality.

In every expression, the terms which signify identical things or equal quantities are reciprocally convertible. Wherever we find the term A we may substitute it for the term B, and conversely, provided that the two signify [p. 424] the same being, or, in the case of quantity, denote equal quantities. If (a + b)/n = c², and a = a′, then (a′ + b)/n = c². Such is the deductive procedure of which continual use is made in the mathematical sciences.

There are reasonings in which the predicate of the conclusion is not found in either of the premises, because it is contained partly in one and partly in the other: “John is the son of Peter”; “Peter is the son of Anthony”; therefore “John is the grandson of Anthony.” Grandson, that is, son of a son, is not contained in either of the two premises considered separately; but it is contained in the two premises at once, partly in one and partly in the other. The reasoning could not be more conclusive; its demonstrative force is perceived at once; and yet it is altogether irreducible to the syllogistic formulas.

I believe what has been said suffices to prove: 1.º That the deductive procedure is various, according to the relation on which the understanding fixes; 2.º That the deductive procedure conforms in each relation to an axiom or general proposition of intuitive evidence, a mere formula of an intellectual operation which of itself carries assent with it; and 3.º That the syllogistic rules, besides being inapplicable to a great many kinds of relations, are unnecessary to direct the understanding even in the kind of relations to which they are applicable, because they do no more than put before us under various forms an axiom, an evident truth, in which we should nevertheless place no confidence, if we did not place it, without them, in the intellectual operations which it symbolizes.

What constitutes the legitimacy of reasoning is that the intellectual procedure which forms it conforms to an evident formula, which cannot be proved and needs no proof; so that, the premises being supposed, it is not possible to refuse assent to the conclusion.1

1 Under this aspect the words Bárbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio, are the expression of

one and the same axiom: If “N is P” and “M is N,” “M is P.” And the other words cannot be considered as true axioms which cannot be proved, because they are in fact proved. Their reduction to the perfect type is their proof.

[p. 425]

But the truth of the conclusion does not depend solely on the legitimacy of the reasoning: on the contrary, the more legitimate the reasoning, the more inevitable it is that the vice or defect of either of the premises should affect the conclusion. If a premise is hypothetical, the conclusion is necessarily so; if merely probable, the conclusion is only probable; if false, whatever is legitimately deduced from it must be false.

Hence it follows that when from certain premises we deduce a proposition mentally, there are two dangers of error: the one consists in the illegitimacy of the reasoning; the other in the vice or defect of the premises.

It seems that we may always be sure of the legitimacy of the deductive procedure by referring it to its peculiar formula, or to the axiom which represents it. There are, however, circumstances which may disturb the understanding in this operation. There are reasonings which present themselves to us as legitimate, and which have only the appearance of it. In all of them the fallacy consists in our referring the intellectual procedure to an axiom that does not suit it, or in some one of the terms of the reasoning varying in signification.

If, for example, one should reason in this way: “man is an animal, the horse is an animal, therefore man is a horse,” the fallacy would consist in applying to the reasoning of classifying resemblance, whose formula is “A is contained in B, B is contained in C, therefore A is contained in C,” the formula “A is C, B is C, therefore A is B,” which is proper to the reasoning that deals with identical things or with equal quantities.

If one should reason in this way: “When we say what we feel, we speak the truth: when men say that the sun moves around the earth, they say what they feel; therefore when men say that the sun moves around the earth, they speak the truth,” the fallacy would consist in the speaking the truth of the conclusion being something other than the speaking the truth of the major. In the major, speaking the truth consists in the intention of faithfully representing our thoughts by means of words, which is what is called moral truth; but in the conclusion speaking the truth consists in the exact conformity [p. 426] of the ideas represented by the words with the reality of things, which is what is called real or absolute truth.

In the preceding examples the fallacy or sophism presents itself at first sight. But at other times it is difficult to find in what it consists.

Let us examine the celebrated argument by which Zeno proposed to prove that there was no motion in the universe. “If a body moves, it moves either in the place where it is, or in the place where it is not. Not in the place where it is, because so long as a body is in a place, it does not move. Nor in the place where it is not, because motion is a modification of the body, and a body cannot be modified except in the place where it is. Therefore nothing moves in the universe.” Will the preceding deduction be legitimate? The conclusion is manifestly false, but does its falsity depend on that of one of the premises, or on the illegitimacy of the deductive procedure?

Let us call A the place which the moving body occupies before the motion begins, B a contiguous place in the direction of the moving body, C another place which follows the second in the same direction, and so on. The moving body does not move in A, nor in B, nor in C, in sensu diviso [in the divided sense], that is to say, motion taking place in each of these places; but it moves in A, B and C, in sensu composito [in the composite sense], that is, A contributing with B, and B with C; because motion consists in the body’s passing from one place to another, and in each place’s becoming successively that of the moving body. Zeno therefore argued de sensu diviso ad sensum compositum [from the divided to the composite sense]; he applied to the reasoning which deals with a relation in sensu composito a formula which does not at all suit it. If A and B express all the possible places in which a body can be found, supposing that it exists, and it is proved that the body is found neither in A nor in B, it will be necessary to deduce that the said body does not exist. But if A and B contribute in such a way to the existence of a thing that this is realized neither wholly nor partially in A or B separately, in this case from the non-existence of the said thing in A and its non-existence in B we are not authorized to infer that it absolutely does not exist. In the first case the reasoning is legitimate, because there is no passing from the [p. 427] divided sense to the composite, as in the second. The fallacy, then, of Zeno’s argument lies in the deductive operation, and consists in applying to the matter of the reasoning a mode of procedure which does not suit it.

The same holds of the argument by which it is sought to prove that no number of grains can ever form a heap; nor any number of drops of water a lake; nor the multiplication of an insensible weight, carried to whatever point one pleases, a weight which the weakest man is not able to carry, etc. “If a portion of water,” it is said, “is not a lake, the addition of one drop will not make it a lake; consequently, the addition of another drop will not either; nor the addition of the third; nor that of the fourth; and so on to whatever number one pleases. Therefore no number of drops of water, however great, will ever come to form a lake.”

When a conclusion is absurd or manifestly false, and it is not possible for us to doubt the premises, the deductive procedure is vicious; and conversely, the conclusion being manifestly false, and the deductive procedure manifestly legitimate, it is of necessity that one of the premises is false. Hence the argument called reductio ad absurdum, which consists in proving that a proposition is false, because from it there necessarily follows an absurdity, or at least a proposition of whose falsity we cannot doubt.

Here is an example: “The value of things,” says the celebrated economist Say, “is the measure of their utility.” By the value of a thing this writer understands the quantity of other things which we are disposed to give for it, or for which we can exchange it. The utility of things, according to him, is that quality which makes them fit to satisfy the various wants of men.

But if the value of things were the measure of their utility, it would necessarily follow that value and utility would be proportional to each other, and that as value increased or diminished, utility would increase or diminish, and conversely: which is absolutely false.

When a machine is invented and brought into general use that facilitates the [p. 428] manufacture of an article, the value of the latter infallibly falls; and we cannot say that its utility is then diminished. A cotton fabric is not now less useful than in the last century, because by virtue of the mechanism which has facilitated its production it is worth a great deal less; nor are the books, which, thanks to the printing press, are sold today at so low a price that even the most indigent class of society can procure them, less useful than the manuscript copies of the twelfth century, which by reason of their high value were only to be found in the libraries of convents and in the houses of great lords. On the contrary, the cheaper a commodity becomes, the smaller the quantity of things for which we can exchange it, the less it is worth, the more the number of its consumers grows, the greater is the amount of well-being, convenience and pleasure which it produces, the better fitted it is to satisfy the wants of men; in a word, the more useful it is. If, then, when the production of an article is facilitated, its value decreases and its utility is increased, what clearer proof can there be that neither is value regulated by the utility of the article, nor utility by value?

Taxes produce an effect contrary to that of machines. A commodity burdened with taxes is worth more than when free, since it is regularly exchanged for a greater quantity of money or of other articles. Who will say on that account that a commodity burdened with taxes is more useful than when free? On the contrary: since the rise in price diminishes consumption, the immediate effect of every tax is to diminish the total of the well-being, convenience and pleasure of society, to make the article taxed less fit to satisfy the wants of men. If, then, with taxes the value of the taxed commodities is increased, and if their utility is not increased with them, but rather it may be said to decrease, neither is the utility of things proportioned to their value, nor their value to their utility.

“That price is the measure of the value of things,” says Say, “and their value the measure of their utility, does not warrant the absurd consequence that by forcing up their price their utility is increased.” But the consequence is legitimate; the absurdity lies in the premises.

[p. 429]

VI

Attempts have been made to reduce to a single rule the legitimate procedure of all reasonings, but with little success.

Condillac holds1 that all reasoning reduces itself to a single intellectual operation: that of drawing from one judgment another judgment contained in the first. According to this doctrine, repeated by a great number of philosophers, there is no legitimate reasoning except when the conclusion is contained in the premise or premises.

He has taken for an example algebraic reasoning. Let the premises or data be:

x−1=y+1

x + 1 = 2y − 2. From x − 1 = y + 1 I infer that x = y + 2, and from x + 1 = 2y − 2 I infer that x = 2y − 3. From x = y + 2 and from x = 2y − 3 I deduce that y + 2 = 2y − 3; from this judgment I deduce that 2 = 2y − y − 3 = y − 3; and from this other I draw as a consequence that 5 = y. Finally, from x = y + 2 I deduce that x = 5 + 2 = 7.

The conclusion’s being included in the premises is here nothing other than its being deduced from them in accordance with certain mathematical axioms. In the first two deductions, the regulating axiom is that “if to equal quantities equal quantities are added or taken away, the sums or the remainders will be equal.” In the third, the regulating axiom is that “two quantities which separately are equal to a third are equal to each other.” In the fourth and fifth, the deduction is in conformity with the first of the preceding axioms. And in the sixth, I substitute for the term y the term 5, because terms which denote equal quantities may always be substituted one for the other.

From this it follows that what Condillac calls the including of one judgment in another, or, according to common language, the including of the conclusion in the premises, is nothing other than the adapting of the reasoning to a certain regulating rule, suited to the peculiar relation which

1 Logique, chap. VII. [p. 430] the understanding contemplates, and which is not always one and the same, even when the relation is constant.

If from the relation of equality we pass to the others, we shall find in like manner that the including of the conclusion in the premises is neither more nor less than its being deduced from them in conformity with a particular axiom or type, suited to the relation with which the reasoning deals; in a word, that the including of the conclusion in the premises is neither more nor less than its being legitimately deduced from them. If Condillac meant to give us a rule that should embrace all legitimate reasonings, it is manifest that he has not attained his object; his pretended rule is a general term, which signifies the same as legitimate deduction. He has done in substance nothing else than found the legitimacy of reasoning on the reasoning’s adapting itself to the law which ought to govern it, without determining this law.

The explanation which Dr. Brown gives of reasoning suffers from the same blindness as the preceding one of Condillac. “When, after having said that man is fallible, I add that he may therefore err, even when he thinks himself least exposed to error, I do no more than state what was involved in the notion of his fallibility. If I add to this, he therefore must not expect that all men will think as he does, even on points which appear to him to have no obscurity, I affirm what is involved in the possibility of his and their erring, even on the clearest points. When I add, He should not therefore dare to punish those who merely differ from him, and who may be right even in differing from him, I unfold what was already contained in the absurdity of the expectation that all men should think as he does. And when I infer from these antecedents that a law which punishes as a crime this or that opinion is contrary to justice, I do no more than draw a special injustice from the general injustice of one man’s wishing to punish another because in his way of thinking he differs from his own.”

Such is the exposition of reasoning according to Dr. Brown. The legitimacy of deduction consists, according to him, in unfolding [p. 431] the comprehension of a term. From Peter’s being a man, I infer that Peter is an animal, because the animal is comprehended in the man. But what is this except to repeat the scholastic doctrine, and to reduce all reasonings to the enthymeme, which is a true syllogism? In the enthymeme, as in the syllogism, from two relations present to the understanding a third is deduced; and if one of the premises is passed over in silence, because it is supposed to be known, it none the less influences the legitimacy of the conclusion. Brown seems to attend exclusively to the comprehension of terms; but we have already seen that, with respect to the theory of the syllogism, comprehension and extension express under inverse forms an identical relation. So convertible is comprehension into extension, that Brown himself has passed unawares from the one to the other, when from the general injustice of one man’s wishing to punish another because he does not think as he does, he infers the injustice of the legislator who imposes punishment on those who follow this or that particular opinion different from his own.

Brown, then, does no more than reduce all reasonings to the enthymeme, and his doctrine is, from this point of view, as inexact as that of those who pretended to reduce all reasonings to the syllogism. This reasoning: “Man is fallible; therefore man may err even in the things which seem to him least exposed to error,” is, according to the scholastic doctrine (which, though scholastic, is here none the less most true), a syllogism in which the major has been passed over in silence and is supposed to be admitted: “every fallible being is liable to err even in the things which seem to him least exposed to error.” But the truth is that of the two premises of this reasoning, the only one that can raise doubts, or that at least needs elucidation, is the one which Brown has omitted; an inconvenience to which enthymemes are often exposed. The argument ought rather to be presented in this way: “every fallible being may err even in the things which seem to him least exposed to error; therefore man may err,” etc. It is clear that the defenders of intolerance will not deny that man is fallible, but that by the very fact of being so he may err even in the things which seem to him clearest and most evident; an assertion which would indeed overthrow all the [p. 432] truths of common sense, and reduce human reason to an absolute skepticism.

If Brown wishes the syllogism always to be presented under the forms of the enthymeme, he gives us in this not a rule of logic but of rhetoric. To express the two premises when one of them can easily be supplied is not to reason badly, but to give to the reasoning declared in words a redundant and pedantic form.

Brown’s rule is in reality not so clear and precise as that which was received in the schools; but the rule of the schools is likewise not applicable to any other kind of reasonings than the syllogism. It is true that the Schoolmen have striven to reduce all possible modes of reasoning, at least all modes of reasoning demonstratively, to their favorite mold; but their efforts have been fruitless. In vain have they tried to transform the reasoning by substituting one axiom for another: the axiom which they have tried to eliminate always subsists; naturam expellas furca, tamen usque recurret [though you drive out nature with a pitchfork, she will ever return]. The reasoning that deals with the relation of equality has been transformed by some thus: “If A and B are separately equal to C, A and B are equal to each other; A and B are separately equal to C; therefore A and B are equal to each other.” Setting aside that the conditional syllogism is irreducible to the common syllogism, I ask: what does this transformation do, except to give the axiom of the mathematicians in the major, under a special form, in order to authorize the consequence by it? And if I admit the major, is it not clear that I make in it the same reasoning which it was sought to legitimate by reducing it to the syllogism? The transformation has not altered, then, the structure of the mathematical reasoning: all it has done has been to hang upon it a pleonastic corollary.

Others have said: “Whatever is equal to C is equal to B”; “A is equal to C”; therefore “A is equal to B.” But if I admit that whatever is equal to C is equal to B, it is because I conceive that B and C are equal; and this reason is irresistible to me only because I know that “if two quantities are separately equal to a third, they are equal to each other.”

[p. 433]

In whatever way we may choose to make the reduction, this axiom always enters into one of the premises; and this axiom does no more than give us, in general terms, the very syllogism we are trying to reduce.

Let us conclude, then, that the type of each reasoning depends on the matter about which we discourse. Men, adapting intuitively to each matter the deductive process that suits it, seldom go astray. But if there should ever be doubt as to the legitimacy of the deduction, the best way of dispelling it would be to have recourse to an intellectual experiment, applying the deductive process to an analogous familiar matter. If from incontestable premises we deduce an absurd or manifestly false conclusion, the deductive process is vicious.

The fallacies which belong exclusively to the premises are of innumerable kinds, and as they are not peculiar to demonstrative reasoning, we reserve them for a later place.

## PHILOS.     28

[PDF 449]

On the matters to which pure demonstrative reasoning applies.

Demonstrative reasoning in the facts of consciousness.—Psychology.— Ontology.—Theodicy.—Mathematical demonstration.—Necessity of memory in all reasoning.—Demonstrative process in mathematics.—Intuitive evidence and deductive evidence.—Particular deductive processes in matters of quantity.—Analogy in the hypothetical sciences.—Certainty in the mathematical sciences.—Conclusion.

I

Demonstrative reasoning is ordinarily mingled with the experimental and the analogical. So it happens, more or less, in all the sciences which deal with the facts of consciousness and of the senses.

Psychology refers continually to the phenomena of which consciousness is the witness, phenomena which present themselves to us with such rapidity and complication that it is exceedingly difficult to conceive them well and to submit them to an exact analysis. Such a writer flatters himself that he translates for us the testimony of consciousness, who in reality translates for us only his own imaginings, and instead of giving us the history, gives us the romance of the human mind. To nothing can the character of a demonstrative science suit less than to the exposition of minute facts, complex in a high degree, fugitive, which are seen under a thousand false colors in passing through the prism of the imagination, whose presence is indispensable in all intellectual operations. Psychology is a science of difficult and fallacious observation: the truths which a sure intuition [p. 435] reveals to us are few, very few, and the consequences which by demonstrative reasoning we can deduce from them do not carry us far. To be convinced of this, it suffices to turn our eyes to the multitude of psychological theories that have divided the schools since Plato’s time. How many disputes there have been on the nature of sensitive perceptions, on the activity of the soul, on generalization, abstraction, ideas, memory, judgment, reasoning!

Ontology, which treats of the general ideas of existence, time, space, cause and effect, the finite and the infinite, matter and spirit, substance and accidents, is in great part psychology itself; because it is for psychology to ascertain what general ideas are, showing in what manner we form them and what they strictly signify; because it is psychology that, scrutinizing the origin of our complex conceptions, can give us the element of time and the element of space, the intellectual forms of causality and of infinity; because it is psychology that traces the limits of intuition and of the senses, the only perceptive faculties of man; because it is psychology that discovers in the depths of thought the primary elements of reason, and the eternal types of reasoning. Thus the basis of Ontology is the analysis of thought into its primitive materials, the exposition of those facts of consciousness which dominate all the intellectual operations. The principles constitute a property, an inseparable element of the mind, and the consequences deduced from them inspire the less confidence the farther they are removed from their source.

Theodicy, or natural theology, is a branch of ontology. It starts from the great fact of the existence of the universe, and from the linking of causes and effects, to raise us to the first of all causes, to the fountain of being; it traces the attributes of the Creator by examining his works; and from these attributes and from the examination of what passes in created intelligences, it deduces the destiny of man, so far as it is given to human reason to know it. Mingling attentive observation with a small number of demonstrative processes, it reads in the fluctuating phases of the [p. 436] phenomenal universe, the eternal order, the characters of the uncreated activity, and the concatenation of means and ends in which the destinies of man are written.

Thus philosophy is in all its branches, like physics and chemistry, a science founded on facts which observation records and demonstrative reasoning renders fruitful.

There are no sciences of pure demonstration but those which rest, not on facts internal or external, objective or subjective, but on precise and invariable hypothetical definitions.

II

In mathematical demonstration, each of the conclusions of the successive reasonings must spring from some necessary, intuitive connection between it and the respective premise or premises. Let us take, for example, the demonstration of the theorem, “The sum of all the angles of a polygon is equal to as many times two right angles as the polygon has sides, less two.”

A. Let straight lines be drawn from the vertex of one of the angles of the polygon to all the other angles, except the two neighboring ones.

B. The polygon will be divided into as many triangles as it has sides, less two: (a consequence intuitively necessary from the hypothesis A).

C. Each angle of the polygon will coincide with one angle or with two or more contiguous angles of the triangles comprised in it; and each angle of the triangles will coincide, either with the whole or with a part of some one of the angles of the polygon: (a consequence intuitively necessary from the hypothesis A and the proposition B).

D. Therefore the sum of all the angles of the polygon is equal to the sum of all the angles of all the triangles comprised in it: (a consequence intuitively necessary from the proposition C).

E. But the sum of the angles of every triangle is equal to two right angles: (a theorem for whose truth we now have memory as warrant).

[p. 437]

F. Therefore the sum of all the angles of the polygon is equal to as many times two right angles as there are triangles comprised in it: (a consequence intuitively necessary from the propositions D and E).

G. Therefore the sum of all the angles of the polygon is equal to as many times two right angles as the polygon has sides, less two: (a consequence intuitively necessary from the propositions B and F).

B and C are intuitively necessary consequences of A, as D is of C, F of D and E, G of B and F; that is to say, they emanate from their respective premises by a legitimate deductive process, which irresistibly compels our assent, because we could not deny it without incurring a manifest contradiction. The intuition which is proper to demonstrative reasonings is not, then, properly in the premises, but in the deductive process.

In the preceding example is shown the part which memory has in reasoning, as we have said before; not only by the theorems or propositions whose truth we admit because memory attests to us that we have formerly found them true, but also by the continual exercise of this faculty in the transition from one consequence to another: in deducing, for example, the proposition D, I admit the truth of its premise C, without need of recalling the necessary connection of C with the propositions A and B, and therefore by virtue of the sole testimony of memory, which assures me of the truth of C. The faith, then, which we give to every demonstration, to every discourse (so I call any chain whatever of reasonings), would fall to the ground from the moment we regarded the testimony of memory as unworthy of credit.

It cannot be denied that in a long discourse, in a long chain of reasonings, memory might at times waver, and make us fall into grave errors, making us regard as demonstrated what in reality was not. To guard against this inconvenience, a continuous and fatiguing effort of attention would be necessary, if we could not to a certain extent spare ourselves this effort, by availing ourselves of abbreviated signs, which condense, so [p. 438] to speak, the terms of the relations, and fix them in an unalterable manner. Suppose we were required to find two numbers whose sum should be 79 and whose difference 25. Calling the greater of the two numbers x and the less z, would not those two data be represented to us with more clearness if expressed thus: “x plus z is 79,” “x minus z is 25”? And should we not then perceive intuitively, as a consequence of these data, that the first term of the first proposition, added to the first term of the second, is x plus z plus x minus z, that is to say, twice x; that the second term of the first proposition, added to the second term of the second, is 79 plus 25, that is, 104; and that, therefore, twice x is 104, and x is the half of 104, that is, 52, and z, consequently, is 79 minus 52, that is, 27?

But if, besides this concentration of the terms in precise and brief phrases, we write the propositions adopting the conventional signs of algebra, the discourse, before purely mental, becomes a mixed operation, in which the eyes direct with entire safety the steps of the understanding. A. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . x + z = 79 B. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . x − z = 25 C. Therefore . . . . . . . . . . . 2x = 104 D. Therefore . . . . . . . . . . . x = 104/2 = 52.

But by virtue of the proposition A,

z = 79 − x.

Therefore, by virtue of the proposition D,

z = 79 − 52 = 25.

From the moment we place the intellectual operations under the guarantee of sight, attention labors much less to direct them aright, the danger of the slips of memory vanishes, and the results are susceptible of complete certainty.

[p. 439]

## III

It has been said that in mathematics the propositions are always identical, so that the subject and the predicate designate in them one and the same object, and all may be represented by the formula “a is a.”

But in the first place the relation of equality must not be confounded with that of identity. To say that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles is not to say that the three angles of a triangle are two right angles. Definitions designate relations of identity, and may be represented by “a is a.” But the same is not true of theorems which deal with quantities.

However, as the deductive process which is exercised upon the two relations of equality and of identity is exactly one and the same, there is no inconvenience in regarding equality as a species of identity: Ἐν τούτοις, says Aristotle, ἡ ἰσότης ἑνότης: “in these things equality is identity.” So, then, in matter of quantity, “a is b” will have for us the same signification as “a = b.”

In the second place, it is not entirely exact that mathematical theorems are propositions in which it is only affirmed that a quantity is equal to itself, and that, for example, the quadrature of the parabola or the binomial theorem do no more than transform that as sterile as incontestable “a = a.” The same happens in mathematical theorems as in propositions which affirm the identity of an object considered under two different aspects. He who should discover that such or such an historical personage had been the author of the letters of Junius or the man in the iron mask, would have done no more than discover that a is a? In all reasoning the understanding takes a step, and if it does not go astray by inconsiderately adopting a premise or deducing an illegitimate consequence, it acquires a new cognition; but if it did nothing else than repeat under diverse forms “a = a,” what unknown regions would it explore, [p. 440] what recondite truths would it conquer in the study of the exact sciences?

From the necessary intuitive connection between the consequence and the premises it seems to be inferred that it is not possible to see the premises without the consequence leaping to the eyes, spontaneously and without any effort of the mind. Given that the sum of the three angles of a triangle is equal to half the circumference, and that in every triangle the angles opposite to equal sides are equal, does it not obviously follow from this that each angle of the equilateral triangle is the sixth part of the circumference? And the spontaneity with which this proposition presents itself to the mind, by virtue of the juxtaposition of the first two, does it not prove that we see intuitively the equality of the two terms, as if we said ⅙ = ⅙? No, certainly. It is seen intuitively that “if in every triangle the angles opposite to equal sides are equal, in the equilateral triangle all the sides are equal, and therefore each angle is the third part of the sum of the three angles”; and it is also seen intuitively that “if the sum of the angles of every triangle is equal to half a circumference, each angle of the equilateral triangle is ⅙ of a circumference”; but we do not see intuitively that “each angle of the equilateral triangle is ⅙ of a circumference,” as it is seen intuitively that ⅙ is ⅙.

To throw some light on this subject let us consider it from a general point of view, embracing all possible relations. When we form a new judgment, due to observation or to reasoning, we do not form out of an idea an element which we previously perceived in it, but, on the contrary, we add to an idea a new element. But when this judgment has been converted into a cognition, that is, entrusted to memory, the primitive idea will have become an aggregate of the primitive idea and the new element. If, for example, new observations have shown us that all glass is idio-electric; if we conceive a physically necessary connection between the vitreous and the idio-electric, the idio-electric will become in the soul an element of the vitreous. If we have discovered that the force which makes sublunary bodies gravitate is the same force that [p. 441] makes the moon revolve around the earth, gravitation will be henceforth in our eyes a single force whose sphere of activity extends from the earth to the moon. In like manner, when it has been demonstrated that each angle of the equilateral triangle is a sixth of the circumference, there will be comprised henceforth in the idea of this triangle that of its measure, that of its equality to the space between two radii which intercept a sixth of a circumference. And so with the other relations. Shall we say that these cognitions then present themselves to us under the form, “an idio-electric thing is idio-electric,” “the force which makes bodies gravitate toward the earth is the force which makes bodies gravitate toward the earth,” “an inclination of sixty degrees is equal to an inclination of sixty degrees”? I believe that consciousness tells us that these formulas do not express what really passes in the soul. The primitive idea has acquired a new element; but we are not therefore authorized to say that between the primitive elements and the new one the soul perceives a connection such as that which it perceives in pronouncing the tautological and nugatory judgments, represented by the formula “a part of a is included in a,” “a is a,” “a = a.” If every cognition is a judgment entrusted to memory, to renew the cognition is to renew the judgment; and if in the judgment there was no intuitive perception of identity, why should there be in the cognition?

When we say that glass is idio-electric, we do not propose to affirm that an idio-electric thing is idio-electric; but that in glass, in the substance we call glass, before the phenomena of electricity were known, there has been discovered the quality of becoming electrified by friction; we affirm a fact, not a tautological proposition. In the same manner, when we say that each angle of the equilateral triangle is sixty degrees, we affirm, not that an angle of sixty degrees is equal to an angle of sixty degrees, but that from the idea of the equilateral triangle it follows, by a series of necessary intuitive connections, that each of its angles measures sixty degrees. This is what truly passes in the soul, and what we propose to express. Is this to say that a is a, or that a = a?

We perceive necessary connection only in the axioms and in [p. 442] the judgments which have for their object the actual existence of an affection of the soul. Intuitive evidence in mathematical theorems belongs, as we saw before, to the deductive process; and the evidence of the deductive process is the very evidence of the axioms, so far as it refers to the object, and the evidence of the actual affections of the soul, so far as it refers to the subject, that is, to the I that reasons. Wherein lies the evidence of the demonstration which proves to us that the sum of the angles of a polygon is equal to as many times two right angles as the polygon has sides, less two? In the necessary connection between each consequence and its premises, and in the evidence of the primordial elements of human reason, which is the evidence of actual affections.

IV

The mathematical sciences employ more ordinarily the deductive processes represented by the axioms: “if two things are separately equal to a third, they are equal to each other”; “equal quantities to which equal quantities are added, or from which they are taken away, are equal”; and others which concern the relation of equality.

But they sometimes avail themselves of other deductive processes, such as that represented by the axiom, “a thing cannot be and not be at the same time,” which does not differ substantially from that other, “if the existence of one thing is necessarily deduced from the existence of another and the first exists, the second also exists, and if the second does not exist, neither does the first.” They employ likewise that of identity, that of successive inclusion, proper to the regular syllogism, and several others. In reality, none of the demonstrative reasonings, that is, of those represented by a general proposition of intuitive evidence, lacks the force of concision which is proper to the mathematics; and if we do not see that in metaphysics use is made of some of them, it is because they are not applicable to the relation of more and less.

[p. 443]

There are, if I am not mistaken, in matter of quantities, deductive processes of incontestable evidence, and which, notwithstanding their superior simplicity, are little used, because the demonstration molded upon them is not believed to be so rigorous or so elegant as that obtained by the common means. As to the rigor of the demonstration, the opinion is false: the conviction obtained in one way is as irresistible as that which is reproduced in the other. And as to elegance, if this consists in the simplicity of the deduction, it does not seem to me doubtful that the deductive processes to which I allude deserve the preference. May we not infer with some foundation that the mathematicians, bent upon reducing all demonstrations to certain favorite types, have fallen into a mania similar to that of the Schoolmen? I shall explain myself by an example.

Let there be the straight line A B;

from the point A I draw a circle with

the radius A B, and from the point B

I describe another with the same ra‐

dius. Through the points of intersec‐

tion of the two circumferences I

draw the straight line C D. To conceive that all the points of this line are equally distant from the points A B, and that consequently the line C D is perpendicular to the line A B and divides it into two equal parts, it is only necessary to consider that, according to the construction, all the cases are equal with respect to A and to B, and therefore there is no reason whatever why any point of the line C D should be more distant from A than from B, or more from B than from A. If this were so, there would necessarily be a thing without sufficient reason for its being; which, in the relations of abstract ideas, perceived with clearness, is more repugnant to the understanding than in any other kind of matters. The perpendicularity, then, of C D, and the division of A B into two equal parts, are necessary consequences of the construction above indicated, and the reasoning is represented by the formula, “nothing is that has not sufficient reason.” A geometer will hardly grant that the demonstration obtained in this way is as rigorous and elegant as his own [p. 444] But may there not be something of prepossession in this? Is there any legitimate deductive process that ought to be proscribed from a science of reasoning? Ought the understanding to be forced to march perpetually in the same rut, and to renounce a part of the means with which nature has endowed it to investigate truth?

Analogy, which in matters of fact rarely offers conclusions to which entire confidence ought to be given, in the hypothetical sciences, on the contrary, irresistibly compels assent. Newton’s binomial theorem, (a + b)ⁿ = aⁿ + (n/1) aⁿ⁻¹ b + [n(n−1)/(1 · 2)] aⁿ⁻² b² + [n(n−1)(n−2)/(1 · 2 · 3)] aⁿ⁻³ b³ + etc., was a purely analogical deduction, in which from the formation of a certain number of powers the general law of the formation of all was drawn; a deduction, nevertheless, not less satisfactory to the understanding and not less intuitively necessary than that which was obtained afterward by adapting the reasoning to the usual types of mathematical demonstration. “The formula (says Dugald Stewart) expresses a relation between the exponents and the co-efficients of the different terms, which is found to hold in all cases, as far as the table of powers is carried by actual calculation”: there is no reason to believe that Newton attempted to prove the theorem in any other way; and nevertheless he was as firmly convinced of its truth in all possible cases as if he had had before his eyes the demonstrations which have since been given of it.

V

Although the mathematical sciences proceed upon suppositions and furnish us only hypothetical truths, we must not on that account regard them as useless for making known to us the reality of things: because 1st, the mathematical hypotheses correspond sometimes exactly to the reality of things; and 2d, it happens at other times that the hypothetical approaches the absolute so closely that the difference between the mathematical results and the real results is either imperceptible or may without inconvenience be neglected.

[p. 445]

If it is asked, for example, how much a certain number of fanegas of wheat would be worth, each fanega being worth so many reals, the result of the arithmetical operation would give with all exactness the real result, because the absolute data correspond exactly to the suppositions of the mathematical reasoning.

When it is desired to know the number of square varas which a given area comprises, if we can divide it into triangles and measure in them a certain number of angles and of sides, we shall obtain a result the more approximate the more careful and well directed the partial measurements have been; but however much care and precaution may be employed in a complicated operation of this kind, there will always be some difference between the absolute data and those which are taken for the bases of the calculation; and therefore it will not be possible to obtain completely exact results.

Nevertheless, so great has the care of man come to be in these operations, so well known and calculated are the causes of error, the fidelity of observations has been carried to such a point by means of ingenious machines which extend the reach of the senses and rectify their reports, and such precautions have been taken that errors, acting in contrary directions, may compensate one another, that it has been possible to raise the trigonometrical and geodetic measurements to a truly marvelous degree of exactness. In the greater part of the geometrical problems which concern the ordinary affairs of civil and rural industry, not even so much is needed in order that the hypothetical truths of mathematics may be incontestably useful in life.

The science of numbers and the science of extension had their first origin in the transactions and arts of society; arithmetic in sales, hereditary partitions, exchanges, loans, leases, wages; geometry in architecture and in the measurement of fields. When attention was directed to these objects, the necessity could not but be perceived of simplifying the questions and of reducing them to precise hypotheses, which is easy in these two sciences, by the nature of the qualities with which they deal.

On analysis and synthesis.—Difference of these procedures in the mathematical sciences and in physics.—Mathematical proposition.—Synthetic demonstration and analytic demonstration: characters of both.—Analysis and synthesis in natural philosophy.—Opinion of Newton.—Synthetic procedure in the philosophy of Condillac.—Two important consequences of the foregoing exposition.—Both procedures should be employed in the study of matter.

I

In every science, in every matter of fact, the fundamental or empirical reasoning, founded on the permanence of the laws of nature, is combined with demonstrative reasoning and analogical reasoning.

[p. 447]

The point of departure is always some fact. We know facts by observations, in which natural phenomena present themselves to us spontaneously; or by experiments, in which we combine or separate natural agencies at our pleasure in order to determine their constant consequences.

Moreover, even in the expression of facts, if we except the immediate and rigorous results of observations or experiments, and their immediate and rigorous consequences deduced by the principle of the invariability of the procedure of nature, all the rest is due either to demonstrative reasoning or to analogical reasoning.

Once a connection of the phenomena which we regard as cause or effect has been observed, we generalize it by the empirical principle, but confining it to the precise agents or agencies determined by observation; a first step in which we may go astray, qualifying as experimental truth an erroneous conception.

In contemplating the phenomena of gravitation, the first observations showed men that of sublunary bodies some, left to themselves, fell with greater or less velocity to the earth; and others, on the contrary, like vapors and smoke, if not held down by some external force, rose and dispersed in the atmosphere. The simplest reasoning of all, the most familiar to man, was that which deduced from these observations, as constant laws, the gravity of certain bodies, or their spontaneous descent to the earth, and the levity of others, that is, their tendency to rise in the atmosphere: purely empirical reasoning.

Smoke is light, lead is heavy, are expressions of two facts generalized by empirical reasoning, and exact expressions so far as with them we limit ourselves to affirming the ascent or descent of these substances in the atmospheric air.
