But when philosophers passed from this to the classification of bodies into heavy and light, understanding by heavy what has some weight, what naturally tends to descend to the earth, and does descend in fact if no external obstacle prevents it; and understanding by light what not only is absolutely [p. 448] devoid of this tendency, what has no weight whatever, but what has naturally a tendency to rise, and does rise in fact if no external obstacle prevents it, they went beyond the just limits of empirical reasoning; for nothing authorized them to believe that the descent of some bodies and the ascent of others in the atmospheric air was owing, in part at least, to some particular agency of the atmospheric air itself.

Sublunary bodies naturally heavy, and sublunary bodies naturally light, was the first formula of gravitation, and for many centuries passed for an unquestionable truth.

It was observed that two solid bodies of equal weight balanced each other in the scale; and that two liquids of different specific gravity, that is, of unequal weight under a given volume, balanced each other when their weights were equal; for example, by rising to heights inversely proportional to their specific gravity. On seeing, then, that water rose in pumps to a height of thirty-two feet and no more, it was natural to infer by analogy that the water was then in equilibrium with the atmospheric air, and that this air, reckoned until then among the light bodies, was in reality a heavy body. From the resemblance of effects was inferred the resemblance of causes.

If the air, it was then said, applying to this hypothesis the demonstrative reasoning which proceeds by the substitution of equal quantities; if the air balances a column of water thirty-two feet high, it will also balance a column of any other liquid which balances a column of water thirty-two feet high. Therefore a column of mercury of two feet and thirty-seven hundredths, which balances a column of water of thirty-two feet, will also balance a column of atmospheric air. Torricelli made the experiment, and the column of mercury rose in the vacuum twenty-eight inches, which are two feet and thirty-three hundredths; as close an approximation as could then reasonably be expected, considering the inevitable inexactness of the operations. Having assimilated one fact to another, we deduce from this assimilation, by demonstrative reasoning, another fact, which, when verified by observation or experiments, gives a degree [p. 449] of probability to the assimilation, especially if it is possible to appeal to the criterion of calculation, as happens in our example.

It was next said: if it is the weight of the air that sustains the mercury at a certain height, this height will be less according as the place at which the experiment is made is higher in the atmosphere: demonstrative reasoning conformed to the axiom “in order that the equality of two quantities may subsist, it is necessary that, if the one decreases, the other should decrease equally”; which is, in other terms, the axiom “if from equal quantities equal quantities are taken away, the remainders will be equal.” This new corollary of Torricelli and of Pascal was confirmed by repeated experiments. It was no longer doubted that the air was heavy; and the results of the attempts afterwards made to weigh the atmospheric fluid directly, by balancing in a delicate scale the weight of a vessel filled with air against the weight of an empty vessel, could be foreseen with entire confidence. The gravity of atmospheric air then took the character of an empirical truth.

Bodies whose specific gravity is less than that of water, when immersed in this liquid, rise. Was it not natural to infer from this that the fluids which rise in the atmosphere owe it to their lesser specific gravity compared with that of the atmospheric fluid? It is a plausible analogy that from the resemblance of effects we infer the resemblance of causes. “All sublunary bodies,” it was then said, “gravitate toward the earth”; an analogical generalization which could not be admitted with entire confidence and counted among the number of empirical truths until the particular facts which seemed to run counter to it, subjected to observation, to experiments and to calculation, were found to be in complete harmony with it.

Analogy thus conducts to the knowledge of the laws of nature. The results, conjectural at first, acquire more and more probability as they are verified by observation, experiments and calculation; until at length they inspire full confidence and take their place among empirical truths. It was recognized, then, as one of these, that in a vacuum all sublunary bodies abandoned to themselves

## PHILOS.    29

[p. 450]

whatever may be their specific gravity and their weight, fall with equal velocity. Therefore, all the parts into which these bodies are divisible descend with equal velocity in a vacuum.

But here three suppositions may be made: either the difference of specific gravity1 subsists indefinitely, however far the division may be carried, not only by human means but by the forces of nature; or bodies are so constituted that, the division being carried to a certain point, they all resolve themselves into elementary molecules, ultimately indivisible but of different weight in different bodies; or else they all resolve themselves into elementary molecules of an invariable weight. On the third supposition the weight of each body is the product of the velocity of gravitation by the number of its atoms or elementary molecules; and as the velocity of gravitation is a constant quantity, the quantity of matter is the number of its elementary molecules represented by the weight. On the first and second suppositions the weight of each body is the product of the velocity of gravitation by an unknown factor, which it has been agreed to call quantity of matter or of inertia, and which is likewise represented by the weight.

The first of these consequences is founded, in my view, on the principle of incompatibility; it is the conclusion of a demonstrative syllogism (that which the Schoolmen call conditional, in the modus tollens): “if sublunary bodies were resolvable into unequally heavy fractions, they would fall with different velocities in a vacuum; they fall with equal velocity in a vacuum; therefore they are all equally heavy.” Let us suppose, in effect, that sublunary bodies consisted of fractions of different gravities, so that, descending in a vacuum, the spaces traversed by them in a given time would be unequal, if they could move separately. It is not metaphysically impossible that, yielding to one another a part of their velocity, in order to move all together, the resulting velocity should be equal in all bodies. But if one bears in mind

1 Difference of weight under a given volume. [p. 451] the immense variety of elements and of structures of which bodies consist; if one bears in mind that all the compositions and decompositions which have been made in material substances have not produced a single one, elementary or complex, that appears to move with more or less velocity than the others, by the force of gravity, it will be necessary to regard it as immensely improbable that, on the supposition of different elements with different velocities of gravitation, the resulting velocity should be constantly one and the same. The equal velocity of gravitation of all the fractions and of all the molecules of matter over the whole surface of the earth ought therefore to have been received as one of the most incontestable empirical truths.

In whatever way the quantity of matter be considered, the density of bodies is their quantity of matter, their weight under a given volume; density and specific gravity are proportional to one another. So that between specific gravity and weight there is the same relation as between density and quantity of matter.

Another mathematical consequence of the equal velocity of gravitation of all bodies and of their smallest fractions at the surface of the earth is, that the descent of bodies in atmospheric air takes place precisely with various velocities, in proportion to the resistance which this fluid opposes to them. The resistance of the air cannot but increase with the volume of air which the moving body strives to displace, and consequently with the volume of the moving body. Therefore, one and the same quantity of matter, according as it occupies more or less volume, will lose more or less of its velocity in displacing the fluid in which it moves. If unequal quantities are taken from one and the same quantity, the remainders must be unequal.

We see that gravity, in each place on the earth, is a continuous and uniform force. Calculation has deduced from this fact several important consequences, which we shall content ourselves with indicating.

1st. Heavy bodies, in their descent, move with a uniformly accelerated velocity; and therefore the velocities acquired from the beginning of the motion are as the times.

[p. 452]

If the velocity of the heavy body at the end of the first second of its descent is as 1, at the end of the next second it will be as 2, at the end of the third as 3, etc.

2d. If at any instant of the fall the action of gravity is conceived to be suspended, the body will continue to descend with uniform motion, and the space which it has traversed from the beginning of its fall to that instant will be half the space which it will traverse during an equal time.

3d. If we divide the whole time of the descent of the heavy body into equal portions, the spaces traversed in these portions of time will form the series 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, etc. Observation, in accord with calculation, shows that the heavy body, in the first second, runs about 16 feet, in the second about 48, in the third about 80, in the fourth about 112, and so on in succession, running in each second nearly 32 feet more than in the preceding.

4th. The spaces traversed by the heavy body from the beginning of the motion are as the squares of the times or of the velocities acquired. If at the end of the first second the heavy body has traversed a space as 1, at the end of the second it will have traversed a space as 4, at the end of the third a space as 9, etc.

5th. The space traversed by the heavy body, in any portion of time, is equal to that which it would have traversed in the same time, moving uniformly with a velocity intermediate between the initial velocity and the final velocity.

6th. If a body is projected in the direction of gravity, the velocity of projection, which is constant, is added to that of gravity, which is uniformly accelerated; and if a body is projected in a direction contrary to that of gravity, the latter continuously and uniformly diminishes the former until it reduces it to zero. When this point is reached, the moving body descends, by the effect of gravity, through the space traversed, and at each point of its descent will have a velocity equal to that which it had at the same point in ascending.

7th. Bodies projected in a direction oblique or perpendicular to the direction of gravity describe parabolic lines.

[p. 453]

These consequences, however, offer results which differ somewhat from the real ones; because, setting out from a hypothesis, which is the motion of heavy bodies in a vacuum, they take no account of various circumstances which disturb and complicate it on the surface of the earth, among which the resistance of the air is the most powerful and constant. This resistance was calculated; an effort was made at least to neutralize it to a certain extent; and the approximation of the real results to the results of calculation was great enough to confirm the theory.

From the verticality of the line of gravity at all points of the terraqueous globe it follows that bodies, obeying this force, move as if it resided in the center of the globe; which may be explained either by supposing that it is exerted by a central point or mass of the earth, or by supposing that it results from the combined action of all the molecules that compose the globe. The possibility of the two suppositions is proved mathematically, and the reality of the second has been confirmed by observations and experiments which leave no room for doubt. That this force of attraction belongs to all the molecules of which our planet is composed is clearly shown by the slight inflections of the line of gravity and the variations in the intensity of this force, measured by the velocity which it produces, by reason of the irregularities of the figure of the earth.

II

“Gravity is a force which acts uniformly upon all the material particles in the terraqueous globe”: such is the general formula which analogy, extending the first empirical results, availing itself of demonstration and appealing to experience, raised at length to the rank of an empirical truth, of an indubitable natural law.

The intellectual procedure which generalizes, assimilates. Gravity, in itself, is similar in the stone that falls and in the vapors that rise, in the swift and vertical descent of lead and [p. 454] in the slow and fluctuating descent of the feather, in rectilinear motion and in parabolic motion.

The assimilation, verified by the means which we have set forth, is what justifies the analogical generalization and gives it the character of a law. If these means, instead of verifying it, gave results incompatible with it, it would be necessary to discover or correct it.

Analogy proceeds synthetically: it composes, it groups in a formula the facts which it knows and the facts which it conjectures, believing it perceives between the one and the other a bond of resemblance. Demonstrative reasoning develops the consequences of the formula; it brings together in a whole the elements contained in it, all the transformations of which it is capable in the various hypotheses to which it is possible to subject it; in a word, it analyzes. Observations and experiments, verifying the analytic results of calculation, confirm the analogy.

We have found the general law of terrestrial attraction; but how far do its effects extend? Are they purely sublunary? Or does the moon gravitate toward the earth, in the same manner as bodies placed on the surface of our globe? And what reason is there for supposing that the author of nature has granted this attractive power to the earth alone, and that all the great bodies which describe orbits around the sun, as the moon around the earth, do not gravitate toward that center, as the moon around the terraqueous globe? Here is a new assimilation, a new and important generalization, which demonstrative reasoning, developing its elements and analyzing them, must confirm or destroy.

Let us suppose that a sublunary body has received a strong impulse in a direction different from the vertical, in which gravity solicits it. Calculation demonstrates that this body will describe a curve whose concavity will face the surface of the earth, and that the greater the force of projection, the greater the space it must traverse before returning to the surface; that if it falls, it is by the combined effect of gravity and of the resistance of the air, which gradually diminish the impulse; that were it not for this resistance, a body hurled with sufficient force [p. 455] from the summit of a high mountain might make a complete revolution around the globe, and that in this case, returning to the point from which it had set out, it would begin its revolution anew and would perform it in the same manner as before. It would never fall, then, and would go on revolving perpetually as a satellite of the earth. Is not this the case of the moon? The analogy must have appeared the more probable, inasmuch as we do not see the influence of gravity fail on the loftiest summits, and no reason is perceived why it should not extend beyond the moon.

The same considerations may be applied to the other satellites. Will they not all weigh, will they not all gravitate around a primary planet, as the moon toward the earth? And is it not to be believed that the planets weigh, gravitate in the same manner toward the sun, as so many satellites of that great luminary? Analogy, which from the resemblance of effects infers that of causes, thus led to a glimpse of a general cause to which all the celestial cognitions are due.

Hitherto universal gravitation was no more than a plausible conjecture. It was necessary to study the celestial motions and to determine how far they conformed to the nature of this kind of forces so far as it was known from the phenomena of the earth. Fortunately, when the great Newton took up this problem, observations had established in an incontestable manner three facts, three empirical laws, the three laws of Kepler:

1st. “The areas described by the radii vectores of the planets in their circumsolar revolution are proportional to the times.” Newton deduced from this formula, by a rigorous calculation, that the force which solicits the planets is directed toward the center of the sun.

2d. “The planetary orbits are ellipses, and the sun occupies one of the foci.” Newton demonstrated that, this being so, the attractive force of the sun upon each planet decreases in inverse ratio to the square of the distance between the two.

3d. “The squares of the times of the revolutions of the planets are proportional to the cubes of their mean distance from the sun.” From this it was demonstratively deduced that the force which seems to attract them to the sun is one and the same for all, and [p. 456] only varies from one to another inversely as the square, as with respect to each planet.

The first law revealed in the sun an attraction similar to that of the earth; the other two gave a new element to the formula, an element which had not been possible to discern in sublunary gravitation, because the variations of distance from the center of the earth were not great enough, upon its surface, to produce sensible differences.

The comets themselves were found to be comprised within the empire of the solar attraction. The satellites, in their turn, were attracted to their primaries, as the primaries to the sun; and the moon confirmed it in a clearer manner, when a rigorous calculation showed that the force with which the earth acts upon it is exactly that which corresponds to the gravity of sublunary bodies, diminished inversely as the square of the distance; an ascertainment which, by introducing this element into terrestrial attraction, completed the resemblance. New observations and new calculations made it indubitable. The gravity of the earth and its rotatory motion necessarily produce the protuberance of the equator in our globe. Hence the gravity of the matter of which the other globes are composed, and their rotatory motion, must produce in them like effects: a deduction confirmed by observation as far as it has been able to extend.

Let us take one step more. The catalogue of the planets is increased. Orbs unknown to Newton inhabit our planetary system. Herschel announces the discovery of Uranus. Uranus draws after it a train of satellites, like Jupiter and Saturn. On the first day of our century Ceres is discovered. Successively Juno, Pallas and Vesta are found. Here, then, is Newton’s theory subjected to a multitude of unexpected proofs. Do these stars obey the laws of attraction promulgated by the English philosopher? They obey: and with punctual exactness as far as observations have been carried. The probabilities multiply, and that which results from their concurrence rises to a degree which can scarcely any longer be distinguished from complete physical certainty.

[p. 457]

But something is still wanting. The planets must not be attracted exclusively by the sun, nor the satellites by their primary planets: the sun must also be attracted by all of them, and all of them must attract one another reciprocally; and since the relations of all these forces vary at every moment, continual perturbations cannot fail to be produced, which disfigure the ellipticity of the orbits, change the situation of each ellipse in its plane, make this plane oscillate, and make the normal velocity of each planet and the time of its periodic revolution fluctuate within certain limits. Demonstrative reasoning announced it so; Newton recognized it; he himself was able to calculate some of these perturbations, and to show their conformity with the great principle; but the state of astronomy in his time did not permit him to carry out an analytical labor so delicate and complex. It was necessary that science should provide itself with new means and more perfect instruments. That glory was reserved for the successors of Newton, and above all for the illustrious Laplace. The calculation of the perturbations is not belied even by the comets in their vast and licentious orbits. Newton’s theory comes out victorious from all trials, and is so completely adjusted to the facts that it is now capable of determining them by itself alone; and if the phenomena led to the theory, it can in its turn announce the phenomena and describe them with more exactness than observation itself, which is incapable of measuring the last subdivisions of space and time. Such is the final triumph of Newtonian attraction, and the probability of analogical generalizations, submitted to the combined criterion of calculation and observation, is raised to a degree which admits of no increase.

Each of the great bodies that people space makes all the other bodies gravitate toward itself; it attracts them: a word by which it is not pretended to give an idea of the nature of this cause, but only to indicate its phenomena. But in what ratio are the different attractive powers of these various bodies to one another, as measured by the different velocities of gravitation which they would produce at equal distances? Observations and calculations show that the quantity of this attractive power does not [p. 458] bear any proportion to the volume of the attracting body. There is, then, a factor which, combined with the velocity of gravitation, measures the attractive agency of the attracting body. Whether this factor is the number of elementary molecules or atoms, supposing them all of equal weight in a terrestrial balance, we have no sufficiently solid grounds to affirm. This would doubtless be a simple procedure in the plan of nature, the atomistic theory being supposed. But neither is this deviation sufficiently proved, nor is the principle of simplicity one of those which by themselves alone inspire confidence.

III

I believe I have made known two procedures of frequent use in the physical sciences: analogical synthesis, which assimilates and generalizes, and mathematical analysis, which develops the formulas of analogy in order that new and varied observations may confirm or belie them. But there are matters to which calculation cannot be applied. Analogy may then serve, by virtue of the completeness and complexity of the resemblances it presents. The example we gave of the footprints stamped in the snow shows the degree of conviction which a great assemblage of exact resemblances is capable of producing in that analogy which proceeds from effects to causes.

The resemblance which exists between the organization of the brutes and our own, between the movements which they perform with their organs and those which we perform with ours, between the various stages of their existence and those to which ours is subject, is a complete resemblance, consisting of a number of partial resemblances that may almost be called infinite, each one of which is remarkable enough by itself. Hence it does not seem possible that any man should exist who, yielding to so powerful a combination of analogies, would not recognize in the animals, even in those whose structure approaches nearest to the human, an animation like our own, a sensitive substance, a soul in which phenomena are produced similar to those which [p. 459] consciousness reveals to us in ourselves, phenomena which involve numberless relations of causes and effects, of means and ends, in which a common type shines through with the greatest clearness. He who should delude himself, like Descartes, to the point of maintaining that animals are machines destitute of sensibility, would have to erase analogy from the catalogue of the means which serve man in the exploration of truth (for if it might be rejected in the present case, in which would it not have to be?); or rather, he would only succeed in discrediting by his own act the doctrine for whose admission it should be necessary to adopt a rule repugnant to common sense.

We know the existence of other human minds by the strongest of all analogical combinations. We perceive in other men an exterior organization most similar to our own, and from this we infer the existence of like resemblances in the parts and qualities which are not within reach of our senses. We recognize in them parts whose resemblance is the same as that of our sensitive organs; therefore they see, hear, smell, taste and feel as we do. We perceive movements most similar to those which we make to procure for ourselves the objects of our necessities, and that these objects may serve our convenience and pleasure; therefore in all other men there are necessities and desires like those we experience ourselves. We see them grow and die as we do; their language betrays thoughts like our own. The force of the total analogy is in the compound ratio of the infinite elementary analogies that concur; and there is no empirical reasoning which produces a more complete conviction.

IV

Analogy may also draw new force from the constant repetition of a certain plan of means and ends in the works of nature.1 The greater the number of connections of this

1 The analogy which proceeds from means to ends is an improper expression. It

ought to be said: “the analogy in which, from the resemblance of the [p. 460] kind which we see adjusting themselves to a uniform plan, the stronger is the conviction we form, by virtue of the simplicity and harmony of the laws that govern the universe, that the said things of the same kind will adjust themselves with equal uniformity to the same plan. One and the same end has been attained by certain means in an infinite number of cases; therefore the same end has been attained by the same means in other cases which have not been subject to my observation. Comparative anatomy offers us a multitude of examples of this. As the different structure of the various species of animals is in relation to their manner of life, by knowing the organs of an animal we can infer from them with sufficient assurance whether nature has destined it to live on land or in water; whether it can or cannot raise itself in the air; on what kind of food it is sustained, and whether it procures it by day or by night; whether it produces many young at a time or not, etc. Sometimes, from the presence of certain organs it may be inferred that others of a different kind exist; and it suffices, for example, to know the structure of the teeth in order to conjecture a great part of the habits and natural characters of the animal. Cuvier observes that a tusk destined to tear flesh is never found combined in any species with a hoof, which gives a good support to the weight of the body but is absolutely useless for seizing or grasping; whence it follows that solidungulate or bisulcate animals are all herbivorous, and that a foot with a hoof indicates flat molar teeth, a long alimentary canal and a voluminous stomach, or more than one stomach. The form of the teeth, the convolutions and dilatations of the alimentary canal, the force and abundance of the gastric juices are found exactly adapted to one another, and have fixed relations with the chemical composition, solidity and solubility of the food; so that on seeing a single one of these parts, an experienced observer can

phenomena, one of which we know to be destined for a certain end, we infer that the other is destined for a like end.” But we have wished to designate a certain kind of analogy by a brief phrase; and the inexactness of the expression cannot produce error. [p. 461] predict with sufficient certainty the conformation of the other parts of the same system of organs, and even conjecture with some probability the structure of the organs belonging to other functions.

But what is it that constitutes the force of these analogies? The constant repetition of one and the same plan of means and ends in numerous and diverse species of animals. A single contrary example would greatly diminish our confidence in them.

The force of the deduction seems to refer to the same end, in the beautiful example which Stewart has given us of the analogy that proceeds from a partial resemblance to a greater resemblance:

“The numberless references and dependencies between the material and the moral worlds, exhibited within the narrow sphere of our observation on this globe, encourage and even authorize us to conclude, that they both form parts of one and the same plan; a conclusion congenial to the best and noblest principles of our nature. Nothing, indeed, could be more inconsistent with that irresistible disposition which prompts every philosophical inquirer to argue from the known to the unknown, than to suppose that, while all the different bodies which compose the material universe are manifestly related to each other, as parts of a connected whole, the moral events which happen on our planet are quite insulated; and that the rational beings who inhabit it, and for whom we may reasonably presume it was brought into existence, have no relation whatever to other intelligent and moral natures. The presumption unquestionably is, that there is one great moral system, corresponding to the material system; and that the connections which we at present trace so distinctly among the sensible objects composing the one, are exhibited as so many intimations of some vast scheme, comprehending all the intelligent beings who compose the other. In this argument, as well as in numberless others, which analogy suggests in favor of our future prospects, the deductive procedure is of the same sort with that which first encouraged Newton to extend his physical speculations beyond the limits of the earth. The sole difference is, that he had an opportunity of verifying [p. 462] the results of his conjectures by an appeal to sensible facts; but this accidental circumstance (although it certainly affords peculiar satisfaction and conviction to the astronomer’s mind) does not affect the grounds on which the conjecture was originally formed, and only furnishes an experimental proof of the esteem which is due to the process of reasoning that produced it.”1

V

Of how little conjectures founded on analogy are worth, many proofs might be cited. The influence which the vulgar attribute to the moon upon atmospheric changes, and particularly upon rain, seems to be deduced from that which this orb undoubtedly exercises upon the tides; and yet it is belied by exact observations, continued through a great number of years. To the celestial phenomena in which something extraordinary was thought to be seen, such as eclipses and the appearances of comets, there was attributed, by an analogy of the same kind, though weaker and more distant, the production of physical and moral phenomena equally extraordinary: floods, pestilences and revolutions. The time which all the bodies of our planetary system, placed in a certain reciprocal situation, require in order to return to it and begin another similar series of movements and aspects, was calculated, well or ill; and a cycle of equal duration was supposed for the moral phenomena of the earth, which, restored to the point whence it set out, was to present another identical series of generations, destined to pass through the same phases until it finds itself again at the same point,

1 In this last phrase I have departed from the original expression, which is this:

“an experimental proof of the justness of the principles (the conjectures) on which it proceeded.” The first analogy which led to the generalization of gravity had doubtless its origin in the thought of likening the celestial movements to the sublunary; a thought afterwards confirmed by the exact resemblance between the one and the other, from which the identity of the resemblance of the causes was deduced. But in that first analogy (which is the one in question) I discover no exact principles, but a probable presumption.

[p. 463]

Alter erit tum Tiphys et altera quæ vehat Argo Delectos heroas; erunt etiam altera bella, Atque iterum ad Troyam magnus mittetur Achilles. [Then shall be another Tiphys, another Argo to bear chosen heroes; other wars too, and great Achilles sent again to Troy.]

In general, the principle which constitutes the force of analogies is the harmony, the simplicity, the unity which we attribute to the works of nature; a principle less sure in itself than that of empirical deductions; first, because nature may not be always uniform in her means; and second, because in the greater number of facts we cannot instruct ourselves sufficiently to deduce her plan; and just as it happens that discrepancies are reduced, when better understood, to a uniform law, so it happens also that apparent discrepancies, when better understood, resolve themselves into real discrepancies.

It is necessary, then, to appraise analogies at what they are worth, and not to receive them as experimental truths until after a long examination in which they have passed through numerous and varied observations without once being belied. Our confidence in them cannot be purified except by the verification of calculation, by the exactness and complexity of the resemblances, or by the constant repetition of a uniform plan in material productions.1

V

It will not be superfluous to observe that what is called observation in the physical sciences is often a vast series of perceptions and of reasonings. Given the situations, figures, distances and movements of the celestial bodies, we know no more

1 It was believed for some time that the presence of oxygen was necessary in combustion,

and that this gas was the only oxidizing principle, because no combustion had been noticed without oxygen, nor any acid of which oxygen was not an essential element. But subsequent knowledge showed that this judgment had been precipitate, and that in nature there exist various gaseous substances endowed in both respects with the same virtue as oxygen. Here is a case in which analogical generalization, though resting upon a not small number of phenomenal connections, was finally belied by experience. [p. 464] than individual facts and particular laws; but what reasonings, what calculations, what ingenious combinations of data have not been necessary to arrive at this knowledge? Let us fix upon a single point, which is apparently the most obvious: the situation of the bodies which we are able to see in the celestial spaces. The apparent situation is not the real situation. In order to deduce the reality from the appearance, it is required, first, to determine with precision the phenomenon as it presents itself to sight, and then to employ a calculation whose procedures have been deduced from numerous and varied observations which have fixed the data, and from previous calculations which by themselves alone form an extensive department of the mixed mathematics. Moreover, merely to determine each element of the apparent situation, the angular distance, for example, at which a star lies from the meridian, what previous knowledge has been necessary, and what ingenious and delicate instruments, which aid the senses and which have themselves been the work of preceding observations, reasonings and calculations! We have hardly been able to take a step outside ourselves, that is, outside the soul, except by the light of experience, that is, by means of reasonings founded upon our first observations. In this manner the affections of the soul were made signs of corporeal qualities and relations. And all the knowledge of the physical universe which we owe to the sciences has been acquired in the same manner. It forms an immense fabric raised upon the foundation of sensations.

Two forms are attributed to analogical reasoning. A fact is sometimes decomposed into several partial facts which reveal to us the details of the production of the first. The phases of the moon succeed one another with perpetual regularity, and at first we doubtless believed that each of them was born of the preceding, as it seems to us, for example, that in the soul recollection is born of perception, or in the organs of the animate body fatigue is brought about by exercise. But observations and reasonings showed us that these different aspects resulted from the different positions which the illuminated hemisphere of the [p. 465] moon took with respect to us. The idea of the moon more or less illuminated to our sight was converted into the idea of particular positions of this star, which presented to us a greater or smaller part of its dark hemisphere and of its lighted hemisphere. And these positions then appeared to us effects of the periodic revolution of this star around the earth; a revolution at first apparent, which we finally reduced to the real revolution in which the moon revolves around the earth, and together with the earth around the sun. “Sun’s light reflected by a greater or smaller part of the moon” was an idea replaced by this: “the sun’s light reflected constantly by one hemisphere of the moon, which at times shows itself to us entire and at times in part, this part increasing and diminishing according to the varying position which, with respect to the globe that gives it light and the globe on which we look at it, the moon takes in its movement around the one and the other.”

In this procedure of reasoning a fact has been decomposed: a link of the phenomenal chain has been subdivided into several elementary links. But at other times reasoning is a generalization which, recognizing the essential resemblance of several phenomena apparently different, classifies them under one name. Thus, in the elliptical motion of a star which moves around a center, describing arcs proportional to the times, there was conjectured at once the same phenomenon as the parabolic motion of sublunary bodies thrown in a direction perpendicular or oblique to the direction of terrestrial gravity; and analysis confirmed the conjecture.

Decomposition, nevertheless, is nothing more than the a posteriori proof of a previous conjectural generalization, or the road that leads to it a priori, by unfolding all the resemblances that intervene in the exhibition of phenomena. For in order to perceive the identity, or rather their essential resemblance, their uniform production by one and the same kind of causes, it is necessary to decompose them, to compare them with one another in all their details, and to ascertain in this way whether the apparent differences are not mere modifications produced by peculiar circumstances.

## PHILOS.    30

[p. 466]

Whether we begin with the synthesis that generalizes or with the analysis that decomposes, the combination of these two kinds of analogical reasoning is indispensable for obtaining sure results in the study of intellectual, moral and material nature.

## APPENDIX I DIFFERENCE BETWEEN EXPERIENCE AND ANALOGY, ACCORDING

## TO PREVOST AND STEWART

I

According to M. Prevost, of Geneva, “analogy originally signified the same thing as resemblance. But usage applies this word to distant resemblances; whence it happens that analogical conclusions are frequently hazardous, and it is necessary to deduce them with art. Whenever in our reasonings we make similar judgments about objects that have only a remote resemblance, we reason analogically. Close resemblance is that which serves as the foundation of the first generalization, which is called the species. Remote is that upon which the higher generalizations are founded, that is, the genus and its various degrees. There are cases between which the resemblance is so perfect that no sensible difference is found except that of place and time. When this second kind of resemblance is that which authorizes our reasonings, we shall say that we make use of analogy.”

Dugald Stewart adopts this same way of thinking. According to him, “between what we call experience and what we call analogy there is a difference, not of nature but of degree. The process is nearly, if not exactly, the same when we reason from species to species and when from individual to individual; but the common usage of language has established [p. 467] a distinction between the one and the other, referring our conclusions in the second case to experience, and in the first to analogy.”

I do not find sufficient precision in the doctrine of these two eminent philosophers, at least in so far as they give as the foundation of experience, that is, of entirely certain empirical deductions, specific resemblances, and as the foundation of analogical deductions, to which we do not lend equal faith, generic resemblances, or the resemblances involved in higher classifications.

In the first place, it seems to me (and I believe I have sufficiently demonstrated it) that in many of our analogical reasonings the deductive procedure is sometimes the inverse of, and sometimes different from, that which takes place in empirical reasonings from causes to effects, in the reasonings which we attribute to experience, taken in a strict sense.

In the second place, analogy proposes to find empirical truth; and, skillfully directed, it obtains it. Its results then become experimental, and enable us to reason with entire certainty from causes to effects. Analogy is a means; empirical truth, an end.

In the third place, we sometimes reason analogically by virtue of a mere specific resemblance.

A piece of Iceland spar produces for the first time in my sight the phenomenon of double refraction; I repeat the observation, the phenomenon continues. Every piece of Iceland spar, whatever its form and dimensions, produces the same phenomenon for me. It appears, then, that it is to the internal constitution of this substance that I must attribute it; and when varied experiments have confirmed this deduction and its probability has been converted into certainty, what at the beginning was no more than a mere analogy becomes a reasoning in which from my past experiments I deduce that Iceland spar has produced, and will always produce, the same phenomena.

Even when it is a question, then, of bodies comprised in a first generalization, which we call species, it seems that [p. 468] empirical reasoning always begins with an analogical reasoning. We need to determine with all precision the circumstances which influence the constant affection; and once they are determined, the analogical deduction acquires the security and firmness of an experimental deduction.

But other substances of different species produce, each in its own being, the same phenomenon. I note in them a quality in which they resemble one another. This quality is perhaps that which produces the phenomenon; a weak analogy. I see that many other bodies which agree in that quality and differ in all the others, produce it also. The connection between this common quality and the phenomenon in question acquires more and more probability. I note next certain constant rules to which the production of the phenomenon seems to be subject, and which make it vary; rules which establish a precise correspondence between the modifications of the quality and the modifications of the phenomenon. A rigorous calculation makes me see this correspondence down to the smallest details. Nothing more is lacking to analogy for wresting the secret. The connection between the quality and the phenomenon is for me a natural law. I know it now not only analogically but empirically. I announce with as much certainty that a substance endowed with that quality will produce the phenomenon, and will produce it in a certain particular way, as I announce that the magnet will attract iron and that fire will melt wax.

What we consider as experimental truths or indefectible natural laws have this character in our eyes only because an observation repeated infinite times has made them known to us: fire burns; every body that we cannot sustain in the air without some effort, falls; the impulse of any solid produces a concavity in any soft body. But the experimental character of these truths is not founded precisely upon specific resemblances, because the existence of the subsequent phenomenon is as certain when the antecedent phenomenon appears in substances of one and the same species, as when it appears in substances of the most diverse species.

What is certain in the doctrines of Prevost and Stewart is that the cognitions which we qualify as experimental are [p. 469] those in which the cause is, or seems to us to be, perfectly defined and circumscribed, so that as soon as it appears we identify it by a complete resemblance, and consequently deduce with entire certainty the effect; and if we have not arrived at the perfect determination of the cause, we cannot identify it, nor have we reason to suppose a perfect resemblance between the various cases; and our judgments are then mere analogies to which we do not assent with entire confidence.

II

“Upon what ground,” says Dugald Stewart, “do I conclude that the thrust of a sword through my breast, from side to side, would deprive me of life? According to the popular use of language, the obvious answer would be,—upon experience, and experience alone. But surely this account of the matter is extremely loose and incorrect; for where is the evidence that the internal structure of my body bears any resemblance to that of any of the other bodies which have been hitherto examined by anatomists? It is no answer to this question to tell me, that the experience of these anatomists has ascertained a uniformity of structure in every human subject which has as yet been dissected; and that, therefore, I am justified in concluding, that my body forms no exception to the general rule. My question does not relate to the soundness of this inference, but to the principle of my nature, which leads me thus not only to reason from the past to the future, but to reason from one thing to another, which, in its external marks, bears a certain degree of resemblance to it. Something more than experience, in the strict sense of the word, is needed to pass from the similar to the identical” (from a partial resemblance, I should say, to a complete resemblance); “and yet my inference in this instance is made with the most assured confidence in the infallibility of the result.”

I shall observe at the outset that by empirical reasoning we always deduce from the resemblance of the causes that of the effects; that human structure is an effect of human generation; and that once it is known that a body exists by virtue [p. 470] of a generation, it is deduced empirically from this knowledge that its structure is similar to that of the bodies which have made it a partaker of their being. This conclusion seems to me as rigorously comprised in experimental reasoning as that which I form when, on depositing a bulb of nard in the earth, I expect that the plant will yield stalks, leaves, flowers and fruits, of certain dimensions and forms. Reasoning founded on the permanence of the laws of nature proceeds not precisely from the identity, but from the complete resemblance of the causes. Such is the sense which it seems to me should be given to this principle, not only because it is the one commonly given to it, but because it is the one which represents in a complete manner the intellectual phenomenon of empirical reasoning.

Reciprocally, the external structure of a man or a quadruped having been observed in all its details, we infer by a sure analogy, which we already qualify as experience, that it is due to such a generation; whence, by means of the empirical principle, we deduce also that the internal structure conforms to the type of the species. The first deduction is very strong, because it is founded on a complexity of most numerous resemblances, and the repetition, which we see at every moment, of the same type in all the animals of the same species, confers in this case upon analogy a degree of force that yields not to that of the most indefectible empirical laws; in a word, it makes strictly experimental what by the deductive procedure is simply analogical. It must be recognized that analogy is susceptible of infinite degrees of force; that on reaching its maximum it has all the characters of true experience; and that even the first and least extensive generalizations, those which seem to us most strictly experimental, were at the beginning mere analogies which needed to be confirmed by repeating the observations.

III

Dugald Stewart distinguishes two kinds of general ideas: some which are so called because they are vague and incorrect; others [p. 471] which have been generalized methodically, in the way the logicians explain, that is, by carefully studying the individuals and perceiving their resemblances. Methodical generalization appears, according to this philosopher, to be that which gives foundation to empirical reasoning, as incorrect and vague generalization does to analogy. But in reality a good classification is as necessary for the experimental procedure as for the analogical. Experimental arguments are exposed to error when they turn upon imperfectly observed resemblances; and analogical arguments, on the contrary, rise to the most complete certainty when they rest upon numerous and well-analyzed resemblances. But what is the limit at which the one and the other mode of reasoning ceases to be fallible, that is, at which we can be sure that the observed resemblance comprises all the indispensable characters and conditions? It is not possible to designate it. In the progressive march of the sciences, theorems become ever more determinate and precise, by virtue of the new conditions and determinations which we discover in the fundamental resemblances.

There are no more methodical classifications, nor any resting on more numerous and careful observations, than those of natural history. Nothing is more common than analogical reasoning which supposes constant the combination of the same characters in all the individuals of a species, family or class, because in preceding observations we have seen them constantly united; and it is not rare afterwards to see this analogy belied by later observations. Thus we have seen suddenly disturbed by the ornithorhynchus of New Holland (ornithorinchus paradoxus) analogical conclusions that had come to be regarded as laws of animal nature.

[p. 472]

## APPENDIX II

## ERRONEOUS IDEAS OF REID AND CAMPBELL ON ANALOGY

Dr. Reid believes that analogy is of more use for answering objections than for serving as a foundation for judgments. Dr. Campbell, coinciding with this way of thinking, believes that analogy rarely refutes, but frequently repels refutation; like those arms which do not wound the enemy, but parry his blows. Dugald Stewart, without ignoring the happy use that may be made of analogy as a means of defense, believes that those two ingenious writers lowered the importance of this mode of reasoning as a means of proof and as a source of new knowledge. But not even Dugald Stewart himself seems to me to appreciate it sufficiently from this second point of view, when he says that, employed as a probative means, it produces no more than probable conjectures,     which        provoke          and    animate   to   new investigations.

The discoveries which are owed to analogy are innumerable; and the investigations to which it provokes must be considered as necessary steps of the analogical procedure.

I flatter myself that at bottom there is no real difference between the doctrine of Prevost and Stewart and my own way of thinking about analogy: my objections fall only upon phrases which do not seem to me to represent with sufficient clearness the experimental and analogical procedures.

## APPENDIX III

## ON HYPOTHESES

I

What is called hypothesis is nothing more than an analogy, weak in some cases, probable in others; until, by means of one or more of the characters which I have pointed out, it comes to have [p. 473] an irresistible force, and, ceasing then to be called hypothesis (a denomination to which a certain unfavorable idea has now been attached), comes to be placed among the scientific truths. That hypotheses are useful and even indispensable in the sciences is proved in an incontestable manner by their history. The theory of gravitation (as Stewart observes) had its origin in an analogical conjecture, which did not come to produce a sure assent until it could be proved by calculation that the force which makes heavy bodies descend upon the surface of the earth, and that which retains the moon in her orbit, are one and the same. The Copernican system furnishes another example of the same kind; for its sole recommendation, for a long time, was the superior simplicity and beauty with which it explained the phenomena of the heavens. In the mind of Copernicus this system (says Stewart) was a mere hypothesis; a reasoning founded on the order of nature, which always employs the simplest means to attain its ends.

“When Copernicus (says Maclaurin, quoted by Stewart) considered the form, disposition, and motions of the system, as they were then represented after Ptolemy, he found the whole void of order, symmetry, and proportion; like a piece made up of parts copied from different originals, which, not fitting each other, should rather represent a monster than a man. He therefore perused the writings of the ancient philosophers, to see whether any more rational account had ever been proposed of the motions of the Heavens. The first hint he had was from Cicero, who tells us, in his Academical Questions, that Nicetas, a Syracusian, had taught that the earth turns round on its axis, which made the whole heavens appear to a spectator on the earth to turn round it daily. Afterwards, from Plutarch he found that Philolaus, the Pythagorean, had taught that the earth moved annually round the sun. He immediately perceived, that, by allowing these two motions, all the perplexity, disorder, and confusion he had complained of in the celestial motions, vanished; and that, instead of these, a simple regular disposition of the orbits, and a harmony of the motions appeared, worthy of the great Author of the world.”

[p. 474]

“Of the truth of the Copernican hypothesis (continues Stewart) the discoveries of the last century have afforded many new proofs of a direct and even demonstrative nature; and yet it is to be believed that the analogical reasoning to which Maclaurin alludes appeared to Copernicus and Galileo, of itself, so conclusive as to supersede the necessity of any other kind of argument. The persecutions which Galileo encountered in defence of his supposed heresy sufficiently evince the faith which he reposed in his astronomical creed.”

“Few principles, great means in small number, infinite and varied phenomena; such,” says Bailly, “is the picture of the universe” . . . “Simplicity (says the same eloquent philosopher) is not an idea of the infancy of the world, but rather belongs to the maturity of men; it is the greatest of the truths which constant observation has wrested from the deceptive variety and multiplicity of effects.”

II

If hypotheses have been condemned with too great severity, in an age in which they have led to such portentous discoveries, and in which even the aberrations of hazardous conjectures and feeble analogies have been so fruitful, opening new fields of exploration to the understanding, it is not to be wondered at that final causes also have fallen into discredit, against which Bacon had already pronounced his famous anathema: “Causarum finalium inquisitio sterilis est, et tanquam virgo Deo consecrata nihil parit.” [The inquiry into final causes is barren, and, like a virgin consecrated to God, brings nothing forth.]

If when it is said that final causes are barren it is only meant that the end does not produce the means, a proposition is laid down which no one has doubted or can doubt. Who could ever have imagined that vision produced the structure of the eye? But if it is claimed that there are properly speaking no means nor ends but causes and effects, that eyes have not been made in order to see, but that we see because we have eyes, is not this to say that the concert, the proportion, the harmony which we admire in the universe have been the work of a blind necessity, and not of an ordering [p. 475] intelligence? and if there are means and ends, what reason can be given why these relations, evidently of high importance, should not be an object of investigation and study?

When it is a question of explaining a phenomenon, he would doubtless not proceed philosophically who should content himself with saying, even though he proved it, that the said phenomenon was ordained for the attainment of a certain end. The first object of philosophy is to scrutinize the efficient causes, or, speaking more properly, the determinate circumstances in which this or that effect is produced, the natural connections of phenomena, the laws that govern their appearance or disappearance. But a connection of means and ends appears to be for us a sure indication of a multitude of facts, and of connections of causes and effects, which in no other way would it be possible for us to attain. The existence of an organ in an unknown animal reveals to us a need by the satisfaction of which it must live, and consequently a part of the functions of the animal, of its nature, of its life; sensations and volitions on the one hand; movements, combinations and revolutions of material elements on the other; that is, vital actions in which causes and effects are developed. By what other road could Cuvier have ascended to the history (which can hardly be so called) of the species that peopled the earth before man appeared upon it, and of which only scattered remains are left? But leaving aside the fecundity of this kind of analogies with respect to the history of animals and the history of the globe, nothing obliges us to shut our eyes to the manifest indications of coordination and design which present themselves to us in the universe, and the knowledge of which is perhaps no less important for us than that of the machinery set in action by the Supreme Maker; for if the second enables us to modify the movements of matter and make it serve our well-being, comfort and pleasure, by the first we can ascend to a higher sphere, read in the great book of nature the attributes of the creating intelligence, and associate ourselves in a certain way with its plans. That man often deceives himself by supposing erroneous means or ends is not a valid argument [p. 476] against the study of this kind of relations, because he also often deceives himself by establishing imaginary connections of phenomena and false physical laws, and we do not say for that reason that the natural sciences are vain speculations unworthy of man.

## APPENDIX IV

## ON THE INDUCTION OF BACON

“For the knowledge of facts,” says Dugald Stewart, “observations and experiments are necessary . . . But observations and experiments are commonly no more than a preliminary step to a further procedure, which consists in first reducing particular facts to other facts more simple and comprehensive, and then applying these general facts, or laws of nature, to the synthetical explanation of particular phenomena. These two operations constitute the whole of philosophical investigation, and the great object of logic is to show in what manner we ought to conduct them.

“When we see that a phenomenon is preceded by a combination of different circumstances, it is impossible for human sagacity to perceive whether the phenomenon depends on all of them, or only on a part of them. To ascertain it, it is necessary to repeat the experiments and observations1 again and again, so that we may contemplate separately all the various circumstances one by one, until we discover with which of them the effect is conjoined. If the separation is not possible, in order to secure the same result it will be necessary to refer the effect to all the various circumstances which we have seen constantly united in the former trials.

“This comparison of cases, which resemble one another in some circumstances

1 Dugald Stewart speaks only of experiments; but in some cases it will not be im‐

possible to repeat the observations, in such a manner that we obtain the same separation of antecedents. [p. 477] and differ in others, is what is called induction. This, at least, appears to me to be the idea which, in general, Bacon of Verulam annexes to the word.

“Mathematics (says Dugald Stewart elsewhere) have also their induction; a species of proof on which the most scrupulous place extreme confidence, and which, although it does not manifest a necessary connection between the terms of the theorem, has nevertheless strength enough to convince us that it never fails. It was by induction (for example) that Newton discovered the algebraical formula by which we are enabled to determine any power whatever, raised from a binomial root, without performing the progressive multiplications. The formula expresses a relation between the exponents and the co-efficients of the different terms, which is found to hold in all cases, as far as the table of powers is carried by actual calculation; from which Newton inferred, that if this table were to be continued in infinitum, the same formula would correspond equally with every successive power.”

This induction is a simple analogy, and seems to me to bear only a feeble resemblance to the Baconian induction; for according to its celebrated author, “Inductio quae ad demonstrationem scientiarum erit utilis, naturam separare debet per rejectiones et exclusiones debitas.” [The induction which will be useful for the demonstration of the sciences must separate nature by due rejections and exclusions.]

That of Aristotle is also different. Our belief, says the Stagirite, always has for its foundation the syllogism or induction. Induction, he says afterwards, is an inference drawn from all the particulars comprised in it. If, for example, I should find by means of a particular demonstration that in the equilateral triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles, and should then discover the same equality in the isosceles, and lastly in the scalene, I could from this deduce with all certainty that the three angles of every triangle are equal to two right angles.

Aristotle is right in considering the syllogism and induction as two diverse modes of reasoning: for, let Dr. Wallis say what he will, Aristotelian induction is not reducible to any of the syllogistic formulas. A syllogism analogous to induction would not conclude, for example: “The [p. 478] man is a biped; the man is an animal; therefore the animal is a biped.” In induction, the middle and one of the extremes may be predicated indifferently of each other; the principle of identity is combined with that of resemblance, which is proper to the syllogism. If A is included in B, and A is the same as C, it follows necessarily that C is included in B.

If the enumeration is complete, like that of the triangles and that of the zone of the earth in the foregoing examples, the induction is conclusive; but the intellectual procedure is then so obvious and so rapid that it cannot be developed without seeming puerile and frivolous. When the enumeration is incomplete, the induction is either empirical or analogical: sealing-wax and cloth when rubbed have become electrified in a certain number of cases; therefore these two substances when rubbed become electrified in all cases: empirical induction. Several crystallized substances present to me the phenomenon of double refraction; therefore all crystallized substances present it: analogical induction.

Bacon’s deductive procedure is rather a method than a special deductive procedure. The following chapters will treat of method in the investigations of the sciences of fact.

## APPENDIX V

## ON ANALYSIS AND SYNTHESIS

In what I am about to say on these two reasoning methods I shall at the outset follow step by step the illustrious professor of Edinburgh, so often cited.

What mathematicians understand by analysis and synthesis is very different from what is signified by these words in the physical and moral sciences. If a hypothetical proposition is laid down, and by deducing from it a series of consequences we arrive at some known truth, from which, retracing the same steps, we can afterwards return to the point from which we set out, the first part of this procedure will be analytic, and the [p. 479] second synthetic. Thus in mathematics analysis proceeds from the unknown to the known, and synthesis the contrary. The first method is founded on this, that a proposition from which another that we know to be true is demonstratively deduced cannot but be true also; and the second, which is the more direct and natural, presents to us the truth of a proposition as a necessary consequence of other known truths.

Every mathematical proposition consists of two parts: the first contains certain suppositions; in the second a consequence of them is affirmed. For example: if, a point of the circumference of the circle being given, a perpendicular is drawn to a diameter, the perpendicular will be a mean proportional between the two segments of the diameter. According to the general procedure in the demonstrations of Euclid’s Elements, the data which the hypothetical part of the proposition to be demonstrated involves figure as premises of the reasoning; and from these premises a chain of consequences is deduced which from link to link leads us to the ground that is to be proved. This is a synthetic demonstration.

Let us suppose now that my reasoning proceeds in the inverse order: that, the truth of the theorem being supposed, I deduce from it, as a premise, the different consequences which it involves. If this series of deductions brings me to a consequence which I recognize as true, I affirm with all confidence that the fundamental premise is equally true; but if I end in a consequence which I know to be false, I deduce that the premise is no less so. Such is the analytic demonstration of the truth or falsity of a proposition.

It is clear that to convince another the most natural and agreeable method is the synthetic; but if we desire to assure ourselves of a doubtful proposition or to discover a new mode of demonstrating a theorem which we hold to be true, the most convenient investigation is the analytic. In effect, as it is probable that from the hypothetical part of the proposition many and various consequences are deduced, each of which involves many others, and as there are probably only one or very few [p. 480] roads that can lead to the proposed end, I have no other resource than to try successively those which first occur to me, until I find what I seek. This is properly to go groping, without order or method. The object sought may, in spite of my attempts, escape me; and if I succeed in attaining it, this fortunate result gives me no light for other similar investigations.

In the analytic method it is the reverse. There is a fixed point from which we set out, and it does not matter where the reasoning leads us, provided it end in a known truth. This method having been practiced a long time, there is acquired that security and tact which the Greeks call δύναμις ἀναλύσεως [power of analysis]; an acquisition of higher price than the most extensive knowledge of particular mathematical truths.

In synthesis the understanding proceeds like a spy who, landing at one corner of the frontier, had to direct himself by his own sagacity toward the capital of the State; in analysis, like an inhabitant of the capital, who desires, by any part of the frontier, to escape from the territory.

Let us now see what is meant by these words analysis and synthesis in natural philosophy. According to Newton, the analysis proper to this science consists in making experiments and observations, and drawing consequences from them, ascending from effects to causes, and from general causes to particular ones, until we end in the most extensive of all; while synthesis consists in assuming the causes which have been discovered and established as principles, and explaining by means of them the phenomena, proceeding from the more general to the less.

But the truth is that in physics, chemistry, the philosophy of the understanding, what is understood by analysis is the decomposition or resolution of a complex thing into its constituent elements, and this seems the more conformable to the etymology of the word ἀνάλυσις, which means the same as resolution or decomposition.

Synthesis, on the contrary, is a true composition, as its name indicates, and we have an example of it in the [p. 481] treatise on the sensations of Condillac, which some have inadvertently regarded as an analytic work. This philosopher supposes a statue; gives it successively the five external senses; examines the ideas, judgments and reasonings which arise from the separate exercise of each of them; and combining them all believes he forms the human understanding. There are in my opinion errors, and grave ones, in that work; and none greater perhaps than that of making all the operations and faculties of the soul consist in the single fact of sensation. But the procedure is rigorously synthetic.

From these observations of Dugald Stewart it seems to me that two consequences follow. The first is that in Newton’s analysis the reasoning is analogical; and the second that the study of nature and of the sciences excludes none of the methods; because, a cause being known, we may explore by means of synthesis the results of its application to all possible cases, even those which we have not had present in establishing it; or, comparing particular phenomena, we may rise progressively, by means of analogy, to general principles which embrace them all, and so much the more worthy of confidence as the resemblances which we discover among them are more numerous and perfect.

As to analysis and synthesis, which consist in a true resolution and composition, it seems to me also evident that neither of them ought to be excluded in the study of matter, nor in that of the social sciences. Would not, perchance, synthesis, which by combining various ingredients produces a substance of the same weight as all of them together, and of the same qualities as that body, be as satisfactory to the chemist who desires to know the constitutive principles of a body, as analysis, which decomposes it and shows separately its elements? Is it not certain that sensitive perception presents to consciousness a complex which cannot be well understood except by resolving it into its various elementary affections, and considering each of them separately; and that the idea of extension, for example, is better understood by combining the ideas which we owe to the sense of effort with the

## PHILOS.    31

[p. 482]

relative idea of succession? Undoubtedly there are objects which may be studied in the one way or the other; but the best of all methods will perhaps be that which combines these two; that which tests the result of decomposition by recomposing, or the result of synthesis by analyzing the compound.

In the sciences of fact the natural and even necessary course is to begin by studying particular phenomena in order to perceive their resemblances and connections and reduce them to general laws; a method at once analytic and analogical. But it happens many times that the result of this first generalization is not complete and exact; that some of the determining circumstances of the phenomenon have escaped the observer, or that the exact expression of each of them is not yet had. To complete the inquiry, we shall apply the principle already known to phenomena of the same species, but in part different from those which were first taken into consideration, and in this synthetic descent from causes to effects, from the general to the particular, we shall compare the demonstrative consequences of the principle with the new facts, in order to modify it so that it may represent them with precision and contain them all. Thus the march of the sciences is alternately analogical and demonstrative, analytic and synthetic. But not all the matters with which reasoning deals lend themselves to this double procedure, and in some cases the second might be nothing else than a repetition of the first in inverse order, with the same inexactnesses and errors.

[PDF 498]

On method, and especially on that which is proper to physical

investigations.

Of method.—Analysis and generalization.—Examples.—Case of the law of gravity.—Relation of cause and effect.—Sir John Herschel.—Rules in the study of the physical sciences.—Examples.

Method is properly the right procedure of the understanding in the investigation of truth.

I

In the investigation of physical nature, method embraces two special procedures, analysis and generalization.

If we analyze, for example, the phenomenon of sound, we shall find that it is composed of the partial phenomena which I am about to enumerate:

1.º A motion is excited in the sounding body.

2.º This motion is communicated to the air, or to some other medium interposed between the sounding body and the ear.

3.º The motion is propagated successively through the particles of the medium until it reaches the ear.

4.º In the ear it produces, by its particular mechanism, a certain affection of the auditory nerves.

5.º These nerves impressing us, there is produced in the soul a sensation of a certain kind, which varies according to various circumstances, such as the nature of the sounding body, its extent, its distance and situation, etc.

[p. 484]

But some of these partial phenomena may still be subdivided. The production of a particular sensation in consequence of a certain impression received by certain nerves is a phenomenon that admits of no further analysis. But the first of the phenomena enumerated is evidently divisible. What kind of motion is that which the sounding body undergoes, or in other terms, what series of motions takes place in its particles? I say the same with regard to the motion of the medium, the mechanism of the ear, or the nervous impression.

Let us now see an example of the procedure of generalization. There are a great number of transparent substances which, when exposed in a certain particular manner to a ray of light that has been given a certain preparation by being made to undergo various reflections or refractions (and which in consequence has acquired peculiar properties and is said to be polarized), exhibit very vivid and beautiful colors, disposed in streaks, bands and other regular forms, which seem to originate in the interior of their substances, and which, from the fact of their succeeding one another in a certain order, are called periodic colors. First generalization, deduced from observations: neither fluids nor opaque solid matter exhibit these periodic colors. Second generalization: not all transparent solids exhibit them, but only those in which another particular phenomenon, of which we have already spoken, takes place—that of double refraction. Both generalizations may be reduced to a single one, expressed thus: The phenomenon of periodic colors is developed in doubly refracting substances exposed to polarized light. And so we have the expression of a natural law, in which the phenomenon of periodic colors is associated with that of double refraction, either because the one is the cause of the other, or because both are effects of one and the same cause.

II

In physical investigations the first step is the exact observation of the facts, attending to all the circumstances that may influence them. In the fall of meteoric bodies [p. 485] there is seen a cloud that flashes with lightning, and a loud and prolonged noise is heard like that of thunder. This, and the blow and destruction that follow, caused this phenomenon to be confounded with that of the thunderbolt. But there is one circumstance that distinguishes them. In the former it has been noticed several times that the light and the din proceed from a very small isolated cloud in a clear sky; which never happens in atmospheric storms.

III

In all cases that admit of numeration and measurement, it is of the greatest importance to obtain precise data determining the space, weight, duration, or any other kind of quantity. It is a characteristic of the highest natural laws that they are susceptible of being expressed by means of quantitative formulas. Thus the law of universal gravitation does not express merely the vague fact of the mutual attraction of all material beings, but establishes an exact proportionality between the quantity of attractive force and the mass of the attracting body; nor does it tell us vaguely that its influence decreases with distance, but gives us the exact ratio of this decrease, the inverse of the square of the distance.

Since none of our senses makes us directly acquainted with quantity, at least in a precise manner, it is indispensable to avail ourselves of artificial means which furnish us the data necessary for calculating it. We cannot, by the mere effort we make in supporting two weights, ascertain the exact difference between them: with the aid of a balance we determine it with sufficient exactness. The sight cannot judge of two different degrees of illumination, even with both before it. Our judgments of quantities of duration, velocity, heat, etc., suffer from the same uncertainty. Hence the necessity of a multitude of instruments, without which the physical sciences would have progressed very slowly, and would have had to stop at their first steps or to abandon themselves to hypotheses and conjectures whose credibility it would have been impossible to appraise.

[p. 486]

IV

A relation of cause and effect, in order that we may recognize it as such, must have the following characters:

1.º The invariable connection of the two phenomena, that is, the invariable subsequence of the effect to the cause, unless another cause intervenes which counteracts the action of the first. But it must be borne in mind that in a great number of natural phenomena the effect is produced little by little, while the cause remains in being, or goes on growing gradually; so that the antecedence of the one of the two phenomena and the subsequence of the other become difficult to ascertain, although they really exist. At other times the effect follows the cause so instantaneously that no interval can be perceived, and it is difficult to decide which of the two phenomena ought to be regarded as the cause of the other.
