2.º That in things which admit of more and less, there be an increase or diminution of the effect when the cause increases or decreases; that there be proportionality between the two, when nothing hinders or limits the action of the cause; and that the effects produced by contrary causes be contrary.

Sir John Herschel, to whom I owe the matter of this chapter,1 deduces from these characters various rules for directing the understanding in the study of the physical sciences. The most important are the following:

1.ª We ought not to deny the existence of a cause in favor of which we have a body of strong and concordant analogies, although it may seem difficult to explain its action in the circumstances of the case.

2.ª Contrary or opposite facts are as instructive for the discovery of a cause as the facts which seem to prove its existence. For example, if moistened iron is placed in a closed vessel full of air, the weight of the

1 See his Preliminary Discourse on the Study of Natural Philosophy, a classic work,

which is as it were a catechism of logic for the study of the physical sciences. [p. 487] air is diminished; because a portion of air combines with the iron and rust is produced. And if the remaining air is examined, it is found to be no longer fit for combustion or for respiration. Therefore that which sustains flame and animal life exists in the portion of air which the iron separates and which covers it with rust. Therefore the air consists of two elements, the element which produces rust upon the iron, and serves for the respiration of animals and for combustion, and another, different element.

3.ª Causes are often revealed to us by the mere arrangement of the facts in the order of intensity in which some special quality shows itself. For example: sound consists in certain impulses of the air upon the organs of hearing. If a series of impulses of equal force is communicated to the ear at equal intervals of time, at first in slow succession, and then more and more rapidly, we hear at first a hoarse and confused sound, like that of a rattle, then a dull murmur, and then a humming, which by degrees takes on the character of a musical note, successively more and more acute, until it becomes so acute that the ear can no longer appreciate it. The vibrations of a slack string are separately audible, but as the tension of the string is increased, its vibrations become quicker, until we perceive no more than a broad line of shadow in which the string moves; and the sounds which before were heard separately are confounded by the shortness of the intervals, and seem to us to form a single uniform and continuous sound, which constitutes the tone of the string in its present state of tension. From this we infer that the greater or lesser gravity or acuteness of musical notes proceeds from the greater or lesser rapidity with which the impulses are communicated to the ear.

4.ª By removing the causes which counteract or modify the action of another cause, or by taking into consideration their power and their mode of operating, we shall be able to destroy the exceptions which seem to militate against the latter.

5.ª If by observations or experiments we can find two cases which agree in all their particulars but one, the influence of this particular in producing the phenomenon may by that means be made manifest. If, when the particular in question is wanting [p. 488] altogether, the phenomenon does not appear, and when it exists the phenomenon appears again, we may infer that the production of the phenomenon is due to it; and this influence will be the more certain if we find a manifest correspondence between the modifications of the two, and if, the one being inverted, the other is inverted. But if the total presence or absence of a particular alters only the degree or intensity of the phenomenon, we may infer that it is one of several causes or conditions which concur in producing it.

6.ª Complicated phenomena in which several causes concur may be simplified by subtracting the effect of all the known causes, thus leaving a residual phenomenon, the explanation of which we shall afterwards ascertain. For example, the return of Encke’s comet took place at periods which coincided more or less with the calculated epochs, taking into account the attractions of the sun and the planets as the sole causes; but when the effect of these causes was calculated with all rigor, it was found that it did not correspond exactly with the true motion of the planet; there remaining as a residue a slight anticipation of its reappearance, or in other terms a diminution of its periodic time, which cannot be explained by the laws of gravitation alone, and whose cause must therefore be ascertained. It now seems probable that this cause is the action of a certain exceedingly tenuous fluid diffused through space, whose existence is believed to be proved by other phenomena.

Another example: M. Arago observed that a magnetic needle suspended by a silken thread, and set in vibration, came more quickly to a state of rest when it was made to oscillate over a plate of copper. In both cases two causes concurred, the resistance of the air, which resists and little by little destroys all the motions executed in it, and the want of perfect mobility in the silken thread. But the effect of these causes being exactly known by observations made in the absence of the copper, there remained a residual phenomenon, produced by the presence of this metal. This led to the knowledge of a new and unexpected chain of relations between the magnetic needle and copper.

[p. 489]

By the means we have enumerated we arrive at one of these two results: either the phenomenon observed resolves itself into natural laws previously known; or we find a new law, a new connection of two phenomena, the one of which constantly brings the other in its train.

If we wish a specimen of this inductive procedure, let us suppose that it is desired to know the cause of dew. Above all, it is necessary that we should not confound dew with rain, or with the moisture produced by fog: dew is that moisture which appears as if spontaneously upon bodies exposed to the air, when no water falls in the form of rain or under any other visible form.

We have phenomena analogous to that of dew in the moisture with which a cold metal is covered when we breathe upon it; in that which appears on the outside of a glass of water recently drawn from a well, when the weather is warm; in that which appears on the inside of the panes of a window, when rain or hail suddenly cools the outer air; and in that which is seen running down the walls when a mild temperature succeeds a long frost: all these cases resemble one another in one thing: the object which is covered with dew is colder than the contiguous air.

Is this difference of temperature the cause of nocturnal dew? Is the object that is covered with dew colder than the surrounding air? There seems to be no reason for believing so. But the analogy between this case and the preceding ones is obvious: we ought not lightly to reject it (first rule). Let us submit the present case to an experiment. Let us place a thermometer in contact with the object, and put another at some distance, in such a way that the object has no action upon it: the result shows a higher temperature in the surrounding air than in the object. Whenever, then, a body contracts dew it is colder than the air that surrounds it. But is this greater coldness the cause of the dew, or rather its effect, as the vulgar imagine? To ascertain this, let us vary the circumstance (second rule).

On the surface of burnished metals no dew is produced [p. 490] at all, but on glass it is produced, and in great abundance; which proves that the nature of the body has much influence upon the phenomenon. If we expose to the air by night burnished surfaces of various substances, we obtain a scale of degrees in the production of the phenomenon (third rule). The bodies we expose to the air contract less dew in proportion as they conduct caloric better: a general law which is constantly observed in polished bodies.1

If, on the contrary, we expose rough surfaces to the air, the law sometimes fails; which proves that differences of surface also influence the phenomenon. Let us expose to the air one and the same substance, diversifying its surface, and another scale of degrees will appear: the surfaces which lose their heat soonest by radiation contract dew most copiously.2

By another series of experiments we discover a new scale, which depends upon the texture of bodies. Those which have a compact and solid texture, such as stones and metals, do not contract dew with the facility and abundance that are noticed in substances of loose and thin texture, such as cloth, wool, cotton; all of them substances suited to clothing, because they do not permit the passage of heat from the skin to the air; so that their outer surface may become very cold without the cold being propagated to the inner surface and to the skin.

1 A piece of wood burning at one of its ends may be held without inconvenience

by the other: in wood heat is not freely propagated; the same is true of glass. On the contrary, if a live coal is placed in a silver spoon, in a few moments the whole spoon grows hot, and we cannot touch it without burning ourselves; metals are conductors of heat.

2 All bodies continually radiate heat, some more, others less; a constant ex‐

change is thus effected between each body and those that surround it. Those which have more heat radiate more than those which have less; the former lose and the latter gain; and all thus tend to equalize their temperatures. Polished and shining surfaces absorb this radiant heat less than the others, and their emissive power follows the same law; a vessel of burnished metal loses its heat slowly, and, reflecting almost all that is transmitted to it by the radiation of the surrounding bodies, becomes warm with difficulty.

[p. 491]

It is observed also that dew is not deposited abundantly in situations which are not exposed to the open air; and that on cloudy nights it is not deposited at all; but if the clouds disperse, it soon begins to form. Bodies which are sheltered by others, or by a clouded sky, gain by radiation as much, or nearly as much, as they lose; but when exposed to a clear sky, a great part of the heat they emit escapes into space and is lost without compensation.

All these observations establish that if the surface of a body becomes colder than the air that surrounds it, dew is produced upon it; the more difficultly they grow warm (like glass and wool), the more easily they lose their heat by radiation, as happens through the roughness of the surface or through the absence of clouds, the more easily and copiously dew is produced. This phenomenon is therefore due to the loss of heat which bodies experience by radiation, and which makes their temperature lower than that of the surrounding air; for it is well known that cold bodies which are in contact with a mass of air that is much less cold condense the humid vapors contained in it, and cause them to appear under a liquid form. The surface is cooled in consequence of the general law of the radiation of heat, and the coldness of the surface condenses the atmospheric moisture in consequence of another general law to which vapors are subject. The phenomenon of dew is thus resolved into two known phenomenal connections.

[PDF 507]

On the causes of error.

General causes of error.—Predispositions and organic states.— Predispositions and moral states.—Intellectual habits.—Theoretical and practical men.—Exclusive devotion to one science.—Failings of memory.— Imagination.—Sign-ideas.—Dangers of error in the use of words.—Special causes of error, or sophisms.—Petitio principii.—Vicious circle.—Ignoratio elenchi.—Fallacia accidentis.—False deductions from analogies.—Two other kinds of illegitimate deductions: the sophism of authority and that of the contrary prejudice.

The causes of error are general or particular. The former constitute defects or vices inherent in the intellectual faculties or in the instruments they make use of; the latter are limited to the matter in hand.

§I

The general causes may be reduced to these seven heads: predispositions and organic states; predispositions and moral states; intellectual habits; slips of memory; precipitancy of the imagination; abuse of sign-ideas; imperfection of language, from which it comes that one and the same word is taken in various senses by different individuals, and not infrequently by one individual on different occasions.

I. To appreciate the influence of organization upon the acts of the understanding, it suffices to compare the two sexes from this point of view: man is less sensible to impressions [p. 493] of a slight kind; he fixes himself only upon objects that move him strongly; but in compensation his attention is capable of more prolonged efforts, his perceptions are more profound, his ideas more exact and more difficult to efface. In the intellectual system of woman there is more mobility, and in that of man more vigor and constancy.

From this essential difference proceed relative advantages and inconveniences: woman is not so well suited as man to studies that demand long and profound meditations, a larger stock of knowledge, and a more extended chain of reasonings; and man in his turn is not so well suited as woman to matters which require tact and sagacity rather than strength, minute and delicate observations, and an easy calculation that glides over the surface of objects.

We find differences no less characteristic in the ages, even setting aside what contributes to the correctness of intellectual operations, the fund of experience, which grows continually with age. The levity and precipitancy of the youthful understanding are proverbial; old age, on the contrary, is wavering and distrustful in the formation of its judgments, and all the more tenacious in adhering to those which it has once embraced. The memory of the young man is easy and ready, his fancies lively and rapid; the old man learns with difficulty, is forgetful, recalls distinctly only the ideas already acquired in the earlier periods of life, and if his understanding does not flag, at least his imagination grows every day less vigorous and less excitable.

And who is ignorant of the diverse shades which temperament gives to the functions of reason? Gay and ardent facility is the mark of the sanguine complexion; energy and constancy characterize the bilious temperament; depth, accompanied by timidity or reserve, the melancholic; the continuity of vigorous efforts, the phlegmatic. The immoderate development of the material wants dulls the intellectual faculties, as much as the predominance of nervous excitability sharpens and exalts them.

Thought is considerably modified, not only by [p. 494] constitutional and permanent differences, but by others which occur in one and the same individual, and which vary with the physical accidents of each moment, and with what we call humor. As there are persons whose general character is jovial or gloomy, so we have also days and hours in which we pass from one of these characters to the other, and which give various courses and tints to our ideas and judgments.

Nor are the effects of diseases less well known. Some go so far as to produce a complete disorder in the functions of the understanding. But leaving aside these extreme cases, and that of drunkenness caused by spirituous drink or opium, how different our judgments often are after a moderate diversion and during a laborious digestion!

It is easy to gather from what has been said the influence of organic predispositions and states upon the truth of judgments. The greater or lesser patience and thoroughness of our observations will make us more or less apt to perceive the qualities of objects, to conceive their relations, and to submit them to a rigorous analytic procedure. An unfaithful memory will introduce false data and omit the true. An ardent imagination will figure to itself what is not, and will distort the facts. We shall be excessively sensible to certain qualities of objects, and shall pass over the others. In sum, we shall often adopt inexact premises, from which we shall logically deduce erroneous consequences. On the other hand, if the mobility of intellectual acts facilitates and multiplies comparisons, the levity and precipitancy that often accompany them make us less circumspect in the deductive procedure: we shall adopt hazardous generalizations; we shall be inclined to exaggerate the value of analogies. And the same danger we shall run when organic influences dispose us to some particular kind of judgments: the melancholic will estimate the probabilities of unfortunate contingencies, as the sanguine the flattering and cheerful alternatives.

II. Moral predispositions and states act in the same manner. On the one hand, by calling attention with greater [p. 495] force to certain objects, to certain qualities and relations, and thus giving them an undue prominence; or on the other, they vitiate the deductive procedure, causing the understanding to adhere to sophisms, or to exaggerate the value of legitimate consequences. Thus those who are in possession of high public offices ordinarily represent things in a favorable light; while their less fortunate rivals paint them in other colors; and although much of this discrepancy must be attributed to the want of sincerity of both, no small part of it proceeds from other moral affections and from the different shades with which prosperous or adverse fortune presents the same objects to spectators.

But besides this general effect of the passions, there are certain moral predispositions which lead us astray or embarrass us in the exercise of reason, now inspiring us with an excessive confidence in our judgments, now frightening us with imaginary difficulties, which make us excessively reserved and circumspect, and disturb the natural and sure course of the understanding, now making us yield thoughtlessly to all impressions and to all glimmerings of reason or probability, and incapacitating us for the acquisition of solid and durable knowledge, the fruit of profound convictions.

III. Intellectual habits are often causes of error.

1.º There are men1 whose understanding habitually fixes upon specific and individual characters, upon the details of objects; others give a preferential attention to generalities, to observations; practical men, the former, whose authority is what they call experience, this word being taken in the limited signification of familiar and ordinary experience; speculative men, the latter, who investigate general laws, and see in every particular fact the application of a principle.

Each of these habits has its peculiar advantages and inconveniences. Scientific speculations diminish

1 Dugald Stewart, Philosophy of the Human Mind, ch. IV, 7, is our guide. [p. 496] in a certain manner the aptitude of the understanding for special applications in the exercise of the arts and in the conduct of public and private life. Accustomed to think in abstractions, to which the simple ideas of vigorous reasoning readily adapt themselves, speculative men are dazzled and confused by the complexity of concrete things, and commonly lack the sagacious tact of practical men, who are familiar with their various aspects and forms; a tact which consists, in my view, in a multitude of small analogies, which, although not expressed in precise formulas and rules, guide them with sufficient assurance in common affairs. General principles give us, in matters of fact, only approximate truths: each of them expresses an isolated phenomenal connection; and in nature phenomenal connections are continually mingling with and disturbing one another. General principles, therefore, are inapplicable to real facts and to practice unless accompanied by an exact appreciation of the disturbing influences and of the special circumstances. Hence it is that the mere theorist so frequently exposes himself, in practical applications, to the ridicule of the men whom, for the inferiority of their enlightenment, he despises.

In mechanics the rod and the weight are left out of account. The lever is considered as an inflexible mathematical line; cords as mathematical lines of perfect flexibility; the matter of this science thus enters into the domain of geometrical demonstrations; but its theorems represent natural phenomena inexactly. A machine adjusted to them would produce movements very different from those calculated. In the same way, politics reduces the various forms of government to certain general classes, to which we attribute certain characteristic tendencies; and although every government is more or less mixed, if not in its legal theory, at least in its manner of acting and in its real effects, we discourse upon the advantages and disadvantages of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy, as if there were political institutions corresponding exactly to our definitions. There is more. Supposing a form of government [p. 497] perfectly pure, its effects would be modified in great part by the concurrence of a countless number of causes: the antecedents of the people governed by it, the climate, religion, the industrial condition, intellectual culture, and various others; all of which, acting in concert, produce complex results exceedingly difficult to estimate. Hence the stormy and ephemeral duration of certain improvised institutions, whose articles are so many demonstrative deductions from abstract principles, but calculated only for a people in the abstract, or for a people lacking special determinations that run counter to them or modify them; a morally impossible supposition.

On the other hand, if mere practical men are endowed with a certain tact in their views and plans, it is only within the limited circle of their daily experience; beyond it they cannot take a step. They are incapable of applying their knowledge to new combinations of circumstances; incapable of filling important posts that demand extensive ideas; incapable even of enriching with original inventions the very arts they practice.

There are, then, two opposite habits equally fruitful in errors: that of the understanding which disregards special circumstances and busies itself with abstractions and generalizations, and that of those men who, giving exclusive attention to the aspects and forms within reach of daily experience, do not rise to general principles and extensive views.

2.º The exclusive pursuit of a science also commonly renders us less fit to reason soundly on objects not comprised in it. We cannot resist the pleasure of copying what Dr. Reid says on this subject.

“The mere mathematician is apt to apply measure and calculation to things which do not admit of it. Direct and inverse ratios have been applied by an ingenious author to measure human affections, and the moral worth of actions. An eminent mathematician attempted to ascertain by calculation the ratio in which the evidence of facts must decrease in the course of time, and fixed the period when the evidence of the facts on which Christianity is founded shall become

## PHILOS.    32

[p. 498]

evanescent, and when in consequence no faith shall be found on the earth. The ancient chemists were wont to explain all the mysteries of nature, and even of religion, by salt, sulphur, and mercury. Mr. Locke, I think, mentions an eminent musician, who believed that God created the world in six days, and rested the seventh, because there are but seven notes in music. I knew one of that profession, who thought that there could be only three parts in harmony, to wit, bass, tenor, and treble; because there are but three persons in the Trinity. Some have an undue admiration of antiquity, and contempt of whatever is modern; others go as far into the contrary extreme: the former are commonly persons who have passed their lives in the study of the ancient authors; the latter, persons who lack the knowledge necessary to judge of their merit. Some are afraid to venture a step out of the beaten track; others are fond of singularities, and of every thing that has the air of paradox. Most men have a predilection for the tenets of their sect or party, and still more for their own inventions.”

The mathematician, inured to demonstrative deductions, in a certain manner visible and mechanical, finds himself disoriented amid objects scarcely susceptible of precise definitions, amid resemblances and differences that are hidden and confounded by their imperceptible gradations, and in the use of vague, ambiguous words of variable signification. Hence those are mistaken who believe that geometry is a practical logic; as if the exercise of a single kind of reasoning, on matters that resemble no others in the clearness and distinctness of their objects, that surpass all others in the facility and uniformity of the deductive procedure, and in which a conflict of arguments and opinions is little less than impossible, could furnish a gymnastic suited to the intellectual faculties. One might as well say that the continued exercise of a single muscle or a single limb would suffice to form an athlete.

But from this point of view much worse is the philosophy [p. 499] of the Schools, reduced to employing the syllogism as its sole instrument, and lost in subtle abstractions that had not, like mathematics, any application whatever either to the natural sciences, the social sciences, or the arts. To the exclusive study of jurisprudence this drawback has also been imputed, of being a bias peculiar to the understanding, and of practicing it even in the proper exercise of jurisprudence itself. The study of languages has been regarded as a practical means of fitting the understanding for the perception of delicate and varied relations; but it is not equally suited to the development of extensive views; the analytical examination is far more exercised than the synthetic conceptions; and it might habituate us too much to labor over minutiae, and to hold the substance of thought in less esteem than its outward forms.

The best education of the understanding, that which most facilitates the investigation of truth in the sciences and in the affairs of life, is that which from an early age puts all the intellectual faculties in exercise.

The habits we have noted are bad only because they are exclusive; there are others essentially pernicious.

There is no more fruitful seed of errors than the custom of contenting ourselves with words and definitions that we do not understand. The first book put into a child’s hands is usually the grammar of the language, and in ours I know not one that is adapted to the capacities of the first age. The child learns to distinguish words from one another not by the definitions given him, unintelligible to him and even to adults, vague or false, but by means of those instinctive analogies that develop in him very early, and guide him in the first essays of speech. The analysis of the sentence is a thing that greatly exceeds his intelligence, and ought to be reserved for later.

Of another contrary vice the elementary books destined for the first age may be guilty. It is necessary that the child understand what he learns; but it may be injurious to him that the acquisition of his first knowledge be made altogether easy and smooth. He ought not to be formed into a passive receptacle of [p. 500] the ideas of others, to which he has nothing to add in the way of elaboration of any kind. He should be accustomed from an early age to struggle with difficulties. The art employed in making instruction excessively easy paralyzes and stifles those natural qualities which no art can give, and whose development is the first object of intellectual education.

Every error engenders errors; but there are some more and some less fruitful.

IV. Memory deceives us, either by introducing into the reasoning a false premise which we believe we have previously recognized as true, or by suppressing some one of the premises which we have recognized as true, and whose presence is important for the exactness of the reasoning.

This failing of memory may take place even in demonstrative reasoning; and as there is hardly a case in which it is not possible, Hume deduced from this that even demonstrated truths are never for the understanding more than merely probable. The consequence is rigorous; but at the same time it is undeniable that when the chain of reasonings that form the demonstration is not excessively long; when by means of diagrams or written signs we make the concatenation in a certain way visible; when we are sure of employing due attention at each step of the demonstrative procedure; when we repeat the operation many times, and other men repeat it for their part, and always with an invariable result; and when besides all this one demonstration can be verified by another and others, in the way we verify division by multiplying the divisor by the quotient to reproduce the dividend, the confidence of our assent leaves not the slightest room for doubt, and is incontestably superior to that which physical truths inspire in us, however assured we may be of them. Nor is it necessary that all these circumstances concur: attention and repetition will almost always suffice to give us complete assurance; and verification alone will produce the same effect.

V. Active consciousness, which contemplates spiritual affections and conceives relations among them, is the whole of human reason [p. 501] but even this intuitive procedure may sometimes deceive us; and that it is not so infallible as some suppose, we have an irrefragable proof in the systems and doctrines of the different schools with respect to psychological phenomena.

As soon as the imagination figures a thing to itself, it gives it a sort of existence in the soul; and if it is the soul itself that is the object of our study, who assures us that we do not confound with its spontaneous affections the works of the folle du logis [madwoman of the house]?1 I believe I see distinctly that space is a pure abstraction; for other understandings space is a real, infinite being, as eternal as God, as indemonstrable as God. The question turns wholly on the true appreciation of a concept, of a psychological fact. If I deceive myself, my imagination deceives me by making me see a pure abstraction where there is a reality; if the others deceive themselves, their imagination deceives them, making them see a reality where there is a pure abstraction. Who settles the question?

In the influence of organic predispositions, of moral predispositions, of intellectual habits, the imagination always has some share, combining, enlarging, separating, etc. It disfigures ideas, and in this way denaturalizes the signification of words. It fathers upon memory what is in reality only its own work. In a word, when it is not the sole culprit in the error, it is either the seducer or the accomplice.

VI. With regard to the exaggerated value of sign-ideas, it will suffice to reproduce what we said in paragraph 3.º of the second book.

Sign-ideas deceive us by making us attribute to the object signified what belongs only to its image. Thus man in general, as the savage figures him, cannot but differ greatly from man in general, as the civilized man figures him. Metaphorical sign-ideas deceive us by making us attribute to the object qualities which have only a vague and distant resemblance to its true qualities:

1 So Malebranche called the imagination. [p. 502] as when we fancy that ideas are imprinted on the memory in the way hard bodies are on a soft substance, and avail ourselves of this simple metaphor to explain the phenomena of memory; an explanation which, if we take it for anything other than a continued metaphor, will make us form most false ideas of our intellectual constitution. The reality that men have attributed to abstract qualities which, because substantives designate them, seem to us to have an independent existence, is an illusion of this kind. As to partial sign-ideas, I do not believe they involve any other contingency of error than that which consists in variation of signification, in the same way as happens with words and with all other kinds of signs.

VII. The dangers of error in the use of words consist:

1.º In our not having formed an exact and precise conception of their signification as generally understood; whence it will result that our judgments and those of others refer to different ideas represented by the same word; and that, combining in our understanding the one with the others, we shall form monstrous judgments and veritable absurdities.

2.º In many words having various significations, between which there is great resemblance; which makes us pass without perceiving it from one to another.

3.º In the complexity of the signification of many words, which makes us sometimes lose sight of some essential part of the idea they represent.

The abuse of words coincides in part with that of sign-ideas, for whenever we exaggerate the value of one of these, we alter the signification of the word that represents it.

§ II

The special causes of error called sophisms may be reduced to two orders: the one adulterate the foundations of judgment; the others vitiate the deductive procedure.

[p. 503]

## I. PETITIO PRINCIPII

To the first of these orders belongs the vice of reasoning which logicians call petitio principii.

There is begging the question when, to prove a proposition, we make use of an argument that supposes it.

We have mentioned the reasoning by which some pretend to prove that every new phenomenon necessarily has a cause. According to them, a phenomenon without a cause would have nothing for its cause, and nothing cannot be one. But those of the contrary opinion answer that he who denies the necessity of a cause denies by the very fact the necessity of referring a phenomenon to nothing as the cause that produces it. To oppose nothing to him as a cause is precisely to take for granted what is in dispute.

Samuel Clarke proves the necessity of causes in a similar manner. To say that a thing is produced and not to acknowledge a cause that produces it is like saying that a thing is produced and is not produced. The adversaries reply that he who says a thing has no cause says by the very fact that it is not produced; not acknowledging a cause, it is clear that he does not acknowledge production or producer; he recognizes in the effect a new fact, but not a produced fact. For those who believe in the necessity of causes, to begin to exist and to be produced, or to be produced, are one and the same thing. For those who deny it they are different things. It appears, then, that in the contradiction imputed to them there is a begging of the question.

It might perhaps be replied: that nothing can be the cause of anything is an evident proposition, an axiom; every proposition in which it is supposed that nothing can be a cause involves contradiction, because to be a cause is to act, and to act is to be. But is it not also evident that to have no positive cause is to have for cause nothing? What difference can be conceived between the one and the other? The conversion of having no cause into having nothing for cause is evident; and an evident conversion that transforms the proposition that is being refuted into a manifestly absurd proposition, because it involves so patent a contradiction, is not a begging of the question.

[p. 504]

The best way of turning the force of Clarke’s argument and of other analogous ones is to apply the same form of reasoning to a familiar case, of those in which the understanding cannot be dazzled by an apparent illusion. If, the truth of the premises being supposed, the consequence is drawn, we must condemn the deductive procedure as vicious.

Now, the conversion of having no cause into having nothing for cause is entirely similar to the conversion of a person’s having no enemies into nothing’s being the enemy of that person; an absurd consequence which attributes to nothing a positive quality, and from which it follows perforce either that the supposition of that person’s having no enemies involves an absurdity, or that the deductive procedure is uncertain. The first of these two alternatives is evidently false; therefore the second must be admitted.

In effect, if it were possible for anyone to make a reasoning like the foregoing, he would be answered: You proceed upon a false supposition, which is that this person must necessarily have enemies: there is no such necessity; and therefore the consequence you draw is illegitimate.

The conversion, then, of having no cause into having nothing for cause is not legitimate except on the supposition that every new existence must precisely have a cause. Consequently, the argument by which it is sought to prove that the denial of the principle of causality involves contradiction either supposes the necessity of the principle, and then suffers from the vice which logicians call petitio principii, or does not suppose it, and then the deduction is not legitimate.

The arguments by which it has also been sought to prove that the denial of the principle of sufficient reason involves contradiction suffer from the same defect; because, in substance, they reduce to saying that for an existence to have no sufficient reason is to have for sufficient reason the lack of all reason; is to suppose in nothing a determinative virtue so that a thing may be what it is and not something else; is to attribute to nothing a positive operation.

There are, then, irrecusable principles, principles which the human understanding [p. 505] feels itself compelled to accept by a law of its nature, and whose denial, nevertheless, involves no contradiction whatever: in a word, there are synthetic a priori principles. The pretended demonstrations involve a begging of the question.

## II. VICIOUS CIRCLE

The vice of reasoning called vicious circle bears some resemblance to the preceding one.

There is a vicious circle in reasoning when two propositions are proved reciprocally the one by the other.

Of this vice the estimate commonly made of the merit of the ancient writers in certain respects sometimes presents manifest examples. Here is one:

We judge that Homer’s expressions are the most proper possible, because they have been employed by Homer; and then we extol the exquisite propriety of the language of this great poet, because we say that he always employs the most proper expressions. The truth is that we cannot appreciate this quality of Homer’s language, because for that it would be necessary that we should know well the language that was spoken in his time and country, and we do not even know with certainty in what time and country he flourished. And in the same error, with slight difference, were ages later than Homer’s.

It sometimes happens that a great poet departs from propriety of language; and his very licenses, sponsored by an illustrious name, are afterwards received as proofs of the genuine signification of words. We then qualify as legitimate and proper what in its origin was truly an abuse. An expression is called proper because the great poet employs it, and one of the merits we attribute to the great poet is the constant propriety of the locutions he employs.

But this vicious circle of literary diction is not limited to language. In the appreciation of Homer’s beauties enters the preconceived judgment that everything that goes under his name is admirable and perfect. If a passage is truly beautiful [p. 506] we exaggerate its beauty; if, as sometimes happens, there is nothing in it to recommend it, we praise its simplicity, its naturalness, its candor. We judge a priori of the whole that everything in Homer is excellent; and then we pronounce a posteriori excellent everything that is found in his works.

Certain theories of the metrical laws of Greek tragedy seem to us to suffer from this vice. Certain metrical canons are proposed as founded on the universal usage of the writers; exceptions are found; and the texts are corrected to fit them to the doctrine. Proceeding on this evidently gratuitous principle, that what appears to happen rarely was never done, the universality of the canons is established by the corrections, and with the universality of the canons the corrections are justified.

## III. IGNORATIO ELENCHI

In the ignorance of the argument one proposition or doctrine is substituted for another, and what is made to tell for or against the first is turned in favor of or against the second.

In the refutation of what Dr. Reid called the ideal theory, meaning by that the common theory of ideas in his time, there is a manifest ignoratio elenchi.

The title of images may be given to ideas in two senses: in the first, which was that of the ancient philosophy, ideas were regarded as images of objects; in the second, ideas are only images of perceptions, and represented objects only as unknown causes that produce in the soul certain affections perceived by consciousness, between which and the corresponding material entities there is not and cannot be any resemblance whatever. This was, with some accidental modifications, the common doctrine when Dr. Reid wrote the arguments with which he refutes the gross hypotheses of the ancients, represented by the poetry of Lucretius, arguments which do not so much as touch the hem of the garment (if I may be allowed the expression) of the modern theory. “At the time of Dr. Reid’s publication,” says Dr. Brown, “the image in the mind was [p. 507] a mere metaphor, not a literal expression, as in the ancient school; it was as truly a mere relic of an obsolete theory of perception, as the rising and setting of the sun, of which use is still made in the language of astronomers, were relics of that obsolete astronomy, in which this great luminary was supposed to make his daily journey round the atom which he enlightened.”

Dr. Reid, in destroying what he calls the ideal theory, believes he has built upon solid foundations the belief in the material world, or in the substantiality of matter. But his arguments against ideas do not in the least weaken the logic of the spiritualists. He believes that, ideas once destroyed, the theory of Berkeley falls to the ground. But to uphold it against his attacks one has only to change a term: to substitute for the word ideas the words affections of the soul. The Berkeleians will not say, as before, that we perceive only ideas, not objects, and that between the one and the other there can be not the least resemblance. But they may very well say that Reid’s direct perception is an affection of the soul like any other; and that we truly perceive only our own affections, and not the supposed corporeal objects, between which and the affections of a mind there is not and cannot be the least resemblance.

The true merit of Reid does not consist, as he thought, in the refutation of a theory that no one remembered when he wrote. Direct perception, with which he thought to conjure away the consequences of the spiritualist philosophy, so frightful to him, is a false fact, a chimera; in spite of him, our notions of corporeal objects can only be symbolic representations, which bear to their causes only resemblances of relations, and tell us nothing, nor can tell us anything, about the nature and the absolute qualities of those causes. Reid’s great merit consists in having directed attention to the hidden principles of reasoning, and in having demonstrated their existence and their validity by irrefragable arguments.1

1 On this subject consult Lectures 27 and 28 of Brown, Philosophy of the Human

Mind.

[p. 508]

## § III

## I. FALLACIA ACCIDENTIS

We pass to the sophisms that consist in some vice of the deductive procedure.

The first is the one called by the Schoolmen fallacia accidentis. We fall into it when we take the accidental for the essential, or, in other terms, a casual connection of phenomena for a necessary connection. The sophism called non causa pro causa, which declares to be a cause what is not one, may be regarded as a species of the fallacy of accident; an error more frequent than that of mistaking fortuitous succession for causality: Post hoc: ergo propter hoc. Many vulgar mistakes, and not a few historical deductions, rest on this foundation alone. The depopulation of Spain, for example, is attributed to the colonization of the Americas, whereas it was due solely to the wretched administrative system established throughout the Spanish empire. With an equal or proportionally greater emigration the number of inhabitants of England or of Switzerland has not diminished.

II

The Schoolmen counted among the sophisms that de dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter, and vice versa: that is, the one that consists in taking the same word now in a general and absolute sense, now in a determinate sense; and that de sensu diviso ad sensum compositum et vice versa. The first evidently falls under the ambiguity of words, which is another of the species enumerated by the Aristotelians, but to which they did not give its full due extent.

III

In reality, the fallacies that depend on a vice of the deductive procedure are many and various; but it may be said that [p. 509] all consist in applying to the relations in question an axiom or type that does not belong to them. I shall recall only that the best means of bringing to light a vice of the deductive procedure in reasonings of this kind is to apply it to an analogous but simple and familiar example, where it may be palpably seen that, proceeding in the same manner in relations of the same kind, an erroneous conclusion is drawn from indubitable premises.

The celebrated syllogism with which Zeno pretended to demonstrate that there was no motion in the universe has never deceived anyone; and might rather serve as a mold by which to pronounce spurious the reasonings that resemble it. By a similar means it would always be easy to show the illegitimacy of a deduction in demonstrative arguments.

IV

In deductions from analogies there is always a danger of error, as we have explained elsewhere. It is necessary to appraise them at what they are worth, and not to exaggerate their probabilities.

We often err in them by letting ourselves be carried along, without examination, by a propensity of the understanding to picture things unknown by those we know familiarly. We judge of other men by what we ourselves are, or by what we have observed in the small circle within our reach. The egoist believes that generosity and sincere disinterestedness are hypocritical appearances, and the generous man is too much disposed to give credit to plausible eccentricities. In scientific imaginations there is a like tendency to explain the less known facts by the rational laws of which we have knowledge, going so far as to deny the existence of whatever cannot be conceived by them.

The attraction of an apparent simplicity or harmony is another of the causes that induce us to give too much credit to analogies. There is doubtless a beautiful simplicity in the works of nature, and everywhere we see tokens of a marvelous harmony in the varied phenomena of the universe. But [p. 510] guided by this principle we often deceive ourselves, because, in order to judge of what is truly simple and harmonious, we should need to know thoroughly the means it employs, the ends it proposes, and all the relations of the various materials it makes use of; conditions which we cannot, for the most part, fulfill.

The works of nature are not like those of man. A man may comprehend one of the latter thoroughly, and judge whether the artificer has availed himself of the simplest means, and whether all the steps of the work are perfectly adapted to one another. But it is a wisdom far superior to that of man which presides over the concatenation of natural phenomena: its plans, its first springs, the nature of the materials it employs, are revealed to us only partially and imperfectly, and often are lost to our view amid the complicated play of actions and reactions that present themselves to our sight and confound and overwhelm it.

V

I think it necessary to make particular mention of two very frequent kinds of illegitimate deductions: the sophism of authority, which makes us assent unreflectingly to the opinions of a man, or of an author of a favorite school (ipse dixit [he himself said it]), and that of the contrary prejudice, which makes us reject without examination the opinions of those whom, justly or unjustly, we regard with aversion or distrust.

“There are many things,” says Reid, “in which we are incompetent judges, and in such matters it is most reasonable to rely upon the judgment of those whom we believe to be competent and disinterested. Even in matters which we have access to know, authority always will have, and ought to have more or less weight, in proportion to the evidence on which our own judgment rests, and the opinion we have of the judgment and candour of those who differ from us, or agree with us. The modest man, conscious of his own fallibility in judging, is in danger of giving too much to authority; the arrogant, of giving [p. 511] too little. As there are persons in the world of so mean and abject a spirit that they rather choose to owe their subsistence to the charity of others than to labor to acquire it, so there are men also who may be called mere beggars and mendicants with regard to their opinions. Through laziness and indifference about truth, they leave to others the task of seeking truth or of combating error, and have enough at second hand to serve their occasions. They do not seek to know what is true on a given question, but what is said and thought on it, and their understanding, like their clothes, is cut according to the fashion.—This distemper of the understanding has taken so deep root in a great part of mankind, that it can hardly be said that they judge of anything but what immediately concerns their personal interest; nor is it peculiar to the ignorant; it infects all ranks. We may guess the opinions of the greater part of men when we know where they were born, what education they have received, and with whom they associate. These circumstances determine their opinions in religion, in politics, and in philosophy.”

The contrary prejudice is much less frequent. If we distrust the judgment and the sentiments of a writer, this will be a motive for weighing his reasons with greater care, or at least for remaining in doubt; but it can never be a motive for condemning an opinion as erroneous solely because it comes from some suspicious source.

The defects of the foregoing classification do not escape us. There are causes of error placed among the special ones which perhaps seem to belong to the general and permanent ones, such as the abuse of analogies, and prejudice in favor of authority. The truth is that there are certain individuals with habitual propensities of the understanding which in others are no more than possible determinations, arising from circumstances.

There are also causes of error which may appear to be repeated, and to be regarded as one and the same under different names, as in the [p. 512] vicious circle and in begging the question (petitio principii), in the abuse of sign-ideas and in the abuse of words. My object has been not only to make an enumeration of the various causes of error, but to present them under their different aspects. In this way it will be easier to recognize and avoid them.
